# The Data Scientist's Handbook

## _Statistics, Probability & Statistical Mechanics for Machine Learning_

**Author:** Professor of Data Science & Statistical Machine Learning **Edition:** First **Target Audience:** Intermediate-to-advanced practitioners seeking rigorous theoretical foundations

---

## Preface & Philosophy

This handbook is built on a single conviction: **you cannot master machine learning without mastering the mathematics that underlies it.** Every algorithm — from logistic regression to transformer attention — is a probabilistic model or an optimization over a statistical objective. The practitioner who understands _why_ an algorithm works, not just _how_ to call it, is the one who can debug it, extend it, and innovate beyond it.

This text is not a survey. It is a _mastery curriculum_. Each module follows a strict four-part structure:

|Phase|Purpose|
|---|---|
|**Conceptual Overview**|Build correct intuition before formalism|
|**Mathematical Formalization**|Precise definitions, theorems, and proofs|
|**Numerical Example**|Worked problems that solidify understanding|
|**Implementation**|Production-quality Python code|

The progression is deliberate: we begin with the axioms of probability — the bedrock upon which all of statistical machine learning is constructed — and ascend to the frontier of information-theoretic and statistical mechanics methods used in modern deep learning.

**A note on notation:** We use standard measure-theoretic notation where clarity demands it, but we do not assume a graduate-level measure theory background. All necessary concepts are introduced when needed.

# MODULE 1: Fundamental Probability & Bayes' Theorem

---

## 1.1 Conceptual Overview

### What Is Probability, Really?

Before writing a single equation, we must ask a foundational question: **what does it mean to assign a number to uncertainty?**

There are two competing schools of thought, and understanding both is essential for a machine learning practitioner:

**The Frequentist Interpretation** holds that probability is the _long-run relative frequency_ of an event across infinitely many repeated experiments. Under this view, the statement "the probability of heads is 0.5" means: if we flip the coin infinitely many times, exactly half will be heads. This interpretation is intuitive for physical processes but breaks down for one-time events — there is no meaningful frequentist probability for "the probability that it rained in London on January 1st, 1850."

**The Bayesian Interpretation** holds that probability is a _degree of rational belief_ — a measure of an agent's uncertainty given available information. This is far more general. It allows us to speak of the probability of any proposition, including model parameters, hypotheses, or past events. Bayesian probability is the native language of modern machine learning.

### Why Probability Is the Language of Machine Learning

Every machine learning model is, at its core, making predictions under uncertainty. Consider:

- A **classifier** outputs $P(y = 1 \mid \mathbf{x})$ — a probability, not a certainty.
- A **language model** assigns $P(\text{token}_{t+1} \mid \text{token}_{1:t})$ — a conditional probability distribution.
- **Regularization** (like L2 / Ridge) is secretly MAP estimation over a Gaussian prior — a probabilistic statement about parameter beliefs.
- **Dropout** is approximate Bayesian inference.
- **Generative models** (VAEs, diffusion models) explicitly learn data distributions $P(\mathbf{x})$.

Probability is not just a mathematical tool we use — it is the _conceptual framework_ within which learning from data is defined.

### Bayes' Theorem: The Central Engine of Statistical Learning

Bayes' Theorem is arguably the most important equation in all of machine learning. It answers the question: **given that I have observed some data, how should I rationally update my beliefs about the world?**

The intuition is:

$$\underbrace{P(\text{hypothesis} \mid \text{data})}_{\text{Posterior}} \propto \underbrace{P(\text{data} \mid \text{hypothesis})}_{\text{Likelihood}} \times \underbrace{P(\text{hypothesis})}_{\text{Prior}}$$

This is the _learning loop_ of all Bayesian inference — and, as we will see in Module 6, it is the foundation of MLE and MAP estimation.

---

## 1.2 Mathematical Formalization

### 1.2.1 The Kolmogorov Axioms

Probability is built on a triplet $(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P)$ called a **probability space**:

- $\Omega$ is the **sample space**: the set of all possible outcomes.
- $\mathcal{F}$ is a **$\sigma$-algebra** (sigma-algebra): a collection of subsets of $\Omega$ (called _events_) that is closed under complement and countable union.
- $P: \mathcal{F} \to [0,1]$ is a **probability measure** satisfying the three Kolmogorov Axioms.

> **Definition 1.1 (Kolmogorov Axioms, 1933):** A function $P: \mathcal{F} \to \mathbb{R}$ is a probability measure if and only if:
> 
> **Axiom 1 (Non-negativity):** $P(A) \geq 0$ for all $A \in \mathcal{F}$
> 
> **Axiom 2 (Normalization):** $P(\Omega) = 1$
> 
> **Axiom 3 (Countable Additivity):** For any countable collection of mutually exclusive events $A_1, A_2, \ldots$ with $A_i \cap A_j = \emptyset$ for $i \neq j$:
> 
> $$P!\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^{\infty} A_i\right) = \sum_{i=1}^{\infty} P(A_i)$$

These three axioms are sufficient to derive all of classical probability theory. The power of an axiomatic foundation is that every theorem we prove is guaranteed to be consistent.

**Key consequences derivable from the axioms:**

$$P(\emptyset) = 0 \tag{1.1}$$

$$P(A^c) = 1 - P(A) \tag{1.2}$$

$$P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B) \quad \text{(Inclusion-Exclusion)} \tag{1.3}$$

$$A \subseteq B \implies P(A) \leq P(B) \quad \text{(Monotonicity)} \tag{1.4}$$

---

### 1.2.2 Conditional Probability

The concept of **conditional probability** is where probability becomes _operational_ for machine learning. When we observe evidence, the sample space effectively collapses.

> **Definition 1.2 (Conditional Probability):** For events $A, B \in \mathcal{F}$ with $P(B) > 0$, the conditional probability of $A$ given $B$ is:
> 
> $$P(A \mid B) = \frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)} \tag{1.5}$$

**Intuition:** We restrict our universe to only those outcomes where $B$ has occurred, then ask: what fraction of _those_ outcomes also satisfy $A$?

This immediately gives us the **multiplication rule**:

$$P(A \cap B) = P(A \mid B) \cdot P(B) = P(B \mid A) \cdot P(A) \tag{1.6}$$

---

### 1.2.3 The Law of Total Probability

This law is essential for marginalizing over nuisance variables — a ubiquitous operation in ML.

> **Theorem 1.1 (Law of Total Probability):** If ${B_1, B_2, \ldots, B_n}$ is a **partition** of $\Omega$ (i.e., mutually exclusive and exhaustive: $\bigcup_i B_i = \Omega$ and $B_i \cap B_j = \emptyset$ for $i \neq j$), then for any event $A$:
> 
> $$P(A) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} P(A \mid B_i) \cdot P(B_i) \tag{1.7}$$

**Proof:** Since ${B_i}$ partitions $\Omega$, we have: $$A = A \cap \Omega = A \cap \left(\bigcup_i B_i\right) = \bigcup_i (A \cap B_i)$$

The events ${A \cap B_i}$ are mutually exclusive (since the $B_i$ are), so by Axiom 3: $$P(A) = \sum_i P(A \cap B_i) = \sum_i P(A \mid B_i) \cdot P(B_i) \qquad \blacksquare$$

---

### 1.2.4 Independence

> **Definition 1.3 (Independence):** Events $A$ and $B$ are **statistically independent** if and only if:
> 
> $$P(A \cap B) = P(A) \cdot P(B) \tag{1.8}$$

When $P(B) > 0$, this is equivalent to $P(A \mid B) = P(A)$ — knowing $B$ gives no information about $A$.

**Critical ML Warning:** Independence is a _strong_ assumption. Many ML models (e.g., Naive Bayes) make conditional independence assumptions that are empirically false but computationally tractable. Understanding this tension is central to model criticism.

---

### 1.2.5 Bayes' Theorem

> **Theorem 1.2 (Bayes' Theorem):** For events $A, B$ with $P(A) > 0$ and $P(B) > 0$:
> 
> $$\boxed{P(A \mid B) = \frac{P(B \mid A) \cdot P(A)}{P(B)}} \tag{1.9}$$

**Proof:** From the multiplication rule (1.6): $$P(A \cap B) = P(A \mid B) \cdot P(B) = P(B \mid A) \cdot P(A)$$

Dividing both sides by $P(B)$ gives the result. $\blacksquare$

**The general form** (using the Law of Total Probability to expand the denominator) is:

$$P(A_k \mid B) = \frac{P(B \mid A_k) \cdot P(A_k)}{\sum_{i} P(B \mid A_i) \cdot P(A_i)} \tag{1.10}$$

This denominator is called the **marginal likelihood** or **evidence**, and it acts as a normalization constant ensuring the posterior is a valid probability distribution.

### The ML Lexicon of Bayes' Theorem

In the context of statistical learning, let $\theta$ be model parameters and $\mathcal{D}$ be observed data:

$$\underbrace{P(\theta \mid \mathcal{D})}_{\text{Posterior}} = \frac{\underbrace{P(\mathcal{D} \mid \theta)}_{\text{Likelihood}} \cdot \underbrace{P(\theta)}_{\text{Prior}}}{\underbrace{P(\mathcal{D})}_{\text{Evidence}}} \tag{1.11}$$

|Term|Statistical Meaning|ML Role|
|---|---|---|
|**Prior** $P(\theta)$|Belief about parameters before seeing data|Regularization, inductive bias|
|**Likelihood** $P(\mathcal{D} \mid \theta)$|Probability of data given parameters|The model's fit to data|
|**Posterior** $P(\theta \mid \mathcal{D})$|Updated belief after observing data|What we ultimately want|
|**Evidence** $P(\mathcal{D})$|Probability of data under all hypotheses|Normalization; model selection|

---

## 1.3 Numerical Examples

### Example 1.1: Medical Diagnosis (Classic Bayes)

**Problem:** A disease affects 1% of the population. A diagnostic test has:

- **Sensitivity** (True Positive Rate): $P(\text{Test}^+ \mid \text{Disease}) = 0.99$
- **Specificity** (True Negative Rate): $P(\text{Test}^- \mid \text{No Disease}) = 0.95$

A randomly selected patient tests positive. What is the probability they actually have the disease?

**Solution:**

**Step 1:** Define events and state all given information. $$P(D) = 0.01, \quad P(D^c) = 0.99$$ $$P(T^+ \mid D) = 0.99, \quad P(T^+ \mid D^c) = 1 - 0.95 = 0.05$$

**Step 2:** Compute the marginal probability of testing positive via Total Probability. $$P(T^+) = P(T^+ \mid D) \cdot P(D) + P(T^+ \mid D^c) \cdot P(D^c)$$ $$P(T^+) = (0.99)(0.01) + (0.05)(0.99)$$ $$P(T^+) = 0.0099 + 0.0495 = 0.0594$$

**Step 3:** Apply Bayes' Theorem. $$P(D \mid T^+) = \frac{P(T^+ \mid D) \cdot P(D)}{P(T^+)} = \frac{(0.99)(0.01)}{0.0594} = \frac{0.0099}{0.0594} \approx \boxed{0.1667}$$

**Interpretation:** Despite a 99% sensitive test, a positive result only implies a ~16.7% probability of disease! This is the **base rate fallacy** — when the prior probability of an event is very low, even highly accurate tests yield many false positives. This result shocks most people and is a direct demonstration of why prior information is not optional — it is mathematically essential.

---

### Example 1.2: Naive Bayes Text Classification

**Problem:** We are building a spam classifier. From training data:

| | P(word | spam) | P(word | ham) | |---|---|---| | "buy" | 0.30 | 0.05 | | "free" | 0.25 | 0.02 |

$P(\text{spam}) = 0.40$. A new email contains both "buy" and "free". Classify it.

**Solution (assuming conditional word independence given class):**

**Step 1:** Compute unnormalized posteriors.

$$P(\text{spam} \mid \text{buy}, \text{free}) \propto P(\text{buy} \mid \text{spam}) \cdot P(\text{free} \mid \text{spam}) \cdot P(\text{spam})$$ $$= 0.30 \times 0.25 \times 0.40 = 0.030$$

$$P(\text{ham} \mid \text{buy}, \text{free}) \propto P(\text{buy} \mid \text{ham}) \cdot P(\text{free} \mid \text{ham}) \cdot P(\text{ham})$$ $$= 0.05 \times 0.02 \times 0.60 = 0.0006$$

**Step 2:** Normalize. $$P(\text{spam} \mid \text{buy}, \text{free}) = \frac{0.030}{0.030 + 0.0006} = \frac{0.030}{0.0306} \approx \boxed{0.980}$$

**Decision:** The email is classified as **spam** with 98.0% posterior probability. Notice that this entire classifier is nothing more than Bayes' Theorem applied with a conditional independence assumption.

---

## 1.4 Implementation

```python
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from fractions import Fraction

# =============================================================================
# MODULE 1: Fundamental Probability & Bayes' Theorem
# =============================================================================

# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# PART A: Verifying Kolmogorov Axioms via Simulation
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------

class ProbabilitySpaceSimulator:
    """
    Simulates a discrete probability space to empirically verify
    the Kolmogorov axioms and demonstrate convergence of empirical
    frequencies to true probabilities.
    """
    
    def __init__(self, n_outcomes: int, seed: int = 42):
        """
        Initialize a probability space with `n_outcomes` equally likely outcomes.
        The sample space Omega = {0, 1, ..., n_outcomes - 1}.
        """
        self.n = n_outcomes
        self.rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
        # True (uniform) probability of each outcome
        self.true_probs = np.ones(n_outcomes) / n_outcomes

    def simulate(self, n_trials: int) -> np.ndarray:
        """Draw n_trials samples from the probability space."""
        return self.rng.integers(0, self.n, size=n_trials)

    def empirical_prob(self, event: set, n_trials: int) -> float:
        """
        Estimate P(A) empirically as relative frequency.
        'event' is a subset of {0, 1, ..., n-1}.
        """
        samples = self.simulate(n_trials)
        return np.mean(np.isin(samples, list(event)))

    def verify_axioms(self, n_trials: int = 100_000):
        """
        Numerically verify all three Kolmogorov axioms.
        """
        omega = set(range(self.n))
        A = set(range(self.n // 2))          # First half of outcomes
        B = set(range(self.n // 4, self.n))  # Last 3/4 of outcomes
        A_inter_B = A & B
        A_union_B = A | B
        empty = set()

        print("=" * 55)
        print("  KOLMOGOROV AXIOMS: EMPIRICAL VERIFICATION")
        print(f"  Sample space size: {self.n}, Trials: {n_trials:,}")
        print("=" * 55)

        # Axiom 1: Non-negativity
        p_A = self.empirical_prob(A, n_trials)
        print(f"\nAxiom 1 (Non-negativity):   P(A) = {p_A:.4f} >= 0  ✓")

        # Axiom 2: Normalization
        p_omega = self.empirical_prob(omega, n_trials)
        print(f"Axiom 2 (Normalization):    P(Ω) = {p_omega:.4f} ≈ 1  ✓")

        # Axiom 3: Countable additivity (A and complement are mutually exclusive)
        A_comp = omega - A
        p_A_comp = self.empirical_prob(A_comp, n_trials)
        p_union = self.empirical_prob(A | A_comp, n_trials)
        print(f"Axiom 3 (Additivity):       P(A) + P(Aᶜ) = {p_A:.4f} + "
              f"{p_A_comp:.4f} = {p_A + p_A_comp:.4f} ≈ 1  ✓")

        # Inclusion-Exclusion as a consequence
        p_A_val = self.empirical_prob(A, n_trials)
        p_B_val = self.empirical_prob(B, n_trials)
        p_inter = self.empirical_prob(A_inter_B, n_trials)
        p_union_emp = self.empirical_prob(A_union_B, n_trials)
        p_union_formula = p_A_val + p_B_val - p_inter
        print(f"\nInclusion-Exclusion:        P(A∪B) (empirical)  = {p_union_emp:.4f}")
        print(f"                            P(A)+P(B)-P(A∩B)   = {p_union_formula:.4f}  ✓")
        print("=" * 55)


# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# PART B: Bayes' Theorem — Medical Diagnosis Example
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def bayes_medical_diagnosis(
    p_disease: float,
    sensitivity: float,
    specificity: float
) -> dict:
    """
    Compute P(Disease | Test+) using Bayes' Theorem.
    
    Parameters
    ----------
    p_disease   : float  — Prior probability of disease P(D)
    sensitivity : float  — P(Test+ | Disease)
    specificity : float  — P(Test- | No Disease)
    
    Returns
    -------
    dict with prior, likelihood, evidence, and posterior.
    """
    p_no_disease = 1.0 - p_disease
    p_pos_given_no_disease = 1.0 - specificity  # False positive rate
    
    # Law of Total Probability: compute P(Test+)
    evidence = (sensitivity * p_disease) + (p_pos_given_no_disease * p_no_disease)
    
    # Bayes' Theorem
    posterior = (sensitivity * p_disease) / evidence
    
    return {
        "prior":          p_disease,
        "likelihood":     sensitivity,
        "false_pos_rate": p_pos_given_no_disease,
        "evidence":       evidence,
        "posterior":      posterior,
    }


def plot_posterior_vs_prevalence(sensitivity: float, specificity: float):
    """
    Visualize how the posterior P(D|T+) changes as a function
    of disease prevalence P(D). This is a critical ML insight:
    the posterior is heavily determined by the prior.
    """
    prevalences = np.linspace(0.001, 0.5, 500)
    posteriors = [
        bayes_medical_diagnosis(p, sensitivity, specificity)["posterior"]
        for p in prevalences
    ]
    
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 5))
    ax.plot(prevalences * 100, posteriors, color="#1a6faf", lw=2.5, label="Posterior P(D|T+)")
    ax.axvline(x=1, color="#e84040", linestyle="--", lw=1.5, label="1% Prevalence (example)")
    ax.axhline(y=bayes_medical_diagnosis(0.01, sensitivity, specificity)["posterior"],
               color="#e84040", linestyle=":", lw=1.5)
    
    ax.fill_between(prevalences * 100, posteriors, alpha=0.12, color="#1a6faf")
    ax.set_xlabel("Disease Prevalence P(D) [%]", fontsize=13)
    ax.set_ylabel("Posterior P(D | Test+)", fontsize=13)
    ax.set_title(f"Bayes' Theorem: Posterior vs. Prior Prevalence\n"
                 f"(Sensitivity={sensitivity:.0%}, Specificity={specificity:.0%})", fontsize=13)
    ax.legend(fontsize=11)
    ax.grid(alpha=0.3)
    ax.set_xlim(0, 50)
    ax.set_ylim(0, 1)
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.savefig("bayes_posterior_prevalence.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight")
    plt.show()
    print("Figure saved: bayes_posterior_prevalence.png")


# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# PART C: Naive Bayes Classifier from Scratch
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------

class NaiveBayesClassifier:
    """
    A minimal, pedagogically transparent Naive Bayes classifier.
    Demonstrates Bayes' Theorem applied to multi-class classification.
    Uses log-probabilities for numerical stability.
    """
    
    def __init__(self):
        self.log_priors = {}        # log P(class)
        self.log_likelihoods = {}   # log P(feature | class)
        self.classes = []
    
    def fit(self, X: np.ndarray, y: np.ndarray, feature_names: list = None):
        """
        Estimate log-priors and log-likelihoods from training data.
        X: shape (n_samples, n_features) — binary feature matrix
        y: shape (n_samples,) — class labels
        """
        self.classes = np.unique(y)
        n_samples = len(y)
        
        for c in self.classes:
            X_c = X[y == c]
            n_c = len(X_c)
            
            # log P(class c): log prior
            self.log_priors[c] = np.log(n_c / n_samples)
            
            # log P(feature_j = 1 | class c): log likelihood with Laplace smoothing
            # Laplace smoothing prevents P=0 from destroying the posterior
            feature_probs = (X_c.sum(axis=0) + 1) / (n_c + 2)  # +1/+2 = Laplace
            self.log_likelihoods[c] = np.log(feature_probs)
        
        if feature_names:
            self.feature_names = feature_names
        
        return self
    
    def predict_log_posterior(self, x: np.ndarray) -> dict:
        """
        Compute log P(class | x) ∝ log P(x | class) + log P(class)
        for a single sample x.
        """
        log_posteriors = {}
        for c in self.classes:
            # Binary features: P(x|c) = prod_j P(f_j|c)^x_j * (1-P(f_j|c))^(1-x_j)
            log_like = np.sum(
                x * self.log_likelihoods[c] +
                (1 - x) * np.log(1 - np.exp(self.log_likelihoods[c]))
            )
            log_posteriors[c] = log_like + self.log_priors[c]
        return log_posteriors
    
    def predict(self, X: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
        """Return the MAP class prediction for each sample."""
        return np.array([
            max(self.predict_log_posterior(x), key=self.predict_log_posterior(x).get)
            for x in X
        ])


# =============================================================================
# MAIN: Run all demonstrations
# =============================================================================

if __name__ == "__main__":
    
    # --- A: Verify Kolmogorov Axioms ---
    sim = ProbabilitySpaceSimulator(n_outcomes=100, seed=42)
    sim.verify_axioms(n_trials=500_000)
    
    # --- B: Bayes' Theorem — Medical Diagnosis ---
    print("\n" + "=" * 55)
    print("  BAYES' THEOREM: MEDICAL DIAGNOSIS")
    print("=" * 55)
    result = bayes_medical_diagnosis(
        p_disease=0.01,
        sensitivity=0.99,
        specificity=0.95
    )
    print(f"\n  Prior P(Disease)           = {result['prior']:.4f}")
    print(f"  Likelihood P(T+|Disease)   = {result['likelihood']:.4f}")
    print(f"  False Positive Rate        = {result['false_pos_rate']:.4f}")
    print(f"  Evidence P(T+)             = {result['evidence']:.4f}")
    print(f"\n  ➤ Posterior P(Disease|T+)  = {result['posterior']:.4f}  ({result['posterior']*100:.1f}%)")
    print("=" * 55)
    
    # Plot: how posterior changes with prevalence
    plot_posterior_vs_prevalence(sensitivity=0.99, specificity=0.95)
    
    # --- C: Naive Bayes Spam Classifier ---
    print("\n" + "=" * 55)
    print("  NAIVE BAYES: SPAM CLASSIFICATION")
    print("=" * 55)
    
    # Training data: features = [contains "buy", contains "free"]
    # Labels: 1 = spam, 0 = ham
    X_train = np.array([
        [1, 1], [1, 0], [0, 1], [1, 1],  # spam
        [0, 0], [0, 0], [1, 0], [0, 0],  # ham
    ])
    y_train = np.array([1, 1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, 0])
    
    nb = NaiveBayesClassifier()
    nb.fit(X_train, y_train, feature_names=["buy", "free"])
    
    # Test: email containing "buy" and "free"
    x_test = np.array([1, 1])
    log_posts = nb.predict_log_posterior(x_test)
    
    # Convert log-posteriors to normalized probabilities
    log_vals = np.array(list(log_posts.values()))
    log_vals -= log_vals.max()           # numerical stability
    probs = np.exp(log_vals)
    probs /= probs.sum()
    
    for label, prob in zip(log_posts.keys(), probs):
        name = "spam" if label == 1 else "ham"
        print(f"\n  P({name:4s} | 'buy','free') = {prob:.4f}  ({prob*100:.1f}%)")
    
    pred = nb.predict(x_test.reshape(1, -1))[0]
    print(f"\n  ➤ Classification: {'SPAM' if pred == 1 else 'HAM'}")
    print("=" * 55)
```

|**Conditional Probability**|Every discriminative model: $P(y \mid \mathbf{x})$|

|**Bayes' Theorem**|MAP/MLE estimation; Bayesian neural networks; posterior inference|

## 1.6 Key Theorems Reference Card

$$P(A \mid B) = \frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)} \tag{Conditional Probability}$$

$$P(A) = \sum_i P(A \mid B_i) P(B_i) \tag{Total Probability}$$

$$P(A \mid B) = \frac{P(B \mid A) \cdot P(A)}{P(B)} \tag{Bayes' Theorem}$$

$$P(\theta \mid \mathcal{D}) \propto P(\mathcal{D} \mid \theta) \cdot P(\theta) \tag{Bayesian Learning}$$

Here is **Module 2** of the Mastery Handbook. This module builds the complete mathematical machinery of random variables — one of the most critical conceptual transitions in the entire curriculum.

---

# MODULE 2: Discrete & Continuous Random Variables

---

## 2.1 Conceptual Overview

### The Leap from Events to Numbers

In Module 1, we assigned probabilities to _events_ — subsets of a sample space. This is powerful, but it is cumbersome for practical use. When we flip a coin 100 times, we do not want to enumerate all $2^{100}$ possible outcomes; we want to work with the _number of heads_. When we measure a person's height, we want to work with a _real number on the real line_, not with abstract set-theoretic events.

This motivates one of the most elegant ideas in all of mathematics: the **random variable** — a function that maps the raw, messy sample space $\Omega$ into the clean, numerical real line $\mathbb{R}$.

A random variable does not "vary randomly" in some mystical sense. It is a perfectly deterministic function. The _randomness_ lives entirely in the underlying probability space $(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P)$. The random variable simply gives us a numerical lens through which to view that randomness.

### The Discrete/Continuous Divide

Once we have a random variable $X$, the first question we ask is: what kind of values can it take?

**Discrete random variables** take values in a finite or countably infinite set — counts, categories, integers. The number of patients arriving at an ER, the number of defects in a batch, the result of a die roll.

**Continuous random variables** take values in an uncountable set — typically an interval of $\mathbb{R}$. A person's exact height, the time until a machine fails, the pixel intensity of an image.

This distinction is not just taxonomic. It determines the entire mathematical machinery we use: PMFs vs. PDFs, sums vs. integrals, discrete vs. continuous optimization. Every neural network output layer makes this choice implicitly — a softmax output is a discrete PMF; a Gaussian policy in reinforcement learning is a continuous PDF.

### Why This Matters for Machine Learning

The type of random variable determines the loss function:

|Output Type|Random Variable|Distribution|Loss Function|
|---|---|---|---|
|Binary classification|Discrete (Bernoulli)|$\text{Bernoulli}(p)$|Binary cross-entropy|
|Multi-class|Discrete (Categorical)|$\text{Categorical}(\mathbf{p})$|Cross-entropy|
|Regression|Continuous (Gaussian)|$\mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)$|Mean squared error|
|Count prediction|Discrete (Poisson)|$\text{Poisson}(\lambda)$|Poisson deviance|
|Positive-valued|Continuous (Gamma)|$\text{Gamma}(\alpha, \beta)$|Gamma deviance|

Understanding random variables is understanding what your model is actually _assuming_ about the world.

---

## 2.2 Mathematical Formalization

### 2.2.1 Formal Definition of a Random Variable

> **Definition 2.1 (Random Variable):** Given a probability space $(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P)$, a **random variable** is a measurable function: $$X: \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$$ such that for every Borel set $B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, the pre-image $X^{-1}(B) = {\omega \in \Omega : X(\omega) \in B} \in \mathcal{F}$.

The measurability condition is what ensures that $P(X \in B)$ is well-defined — the event ${X \in B}$ must be in our $\sigma$-algebra $\mathcal{F}$ to have a probability.

---

### 2.2.2 The Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF)

The CDF is the universal descriptor of a random variable — it works for both discrete and continuous cases.

> **Definition 2.2 (Cumulative Distribution Function):** The CDF of a random variable $X$ is the function $F_X: \mathbb{R} \to [0,1]$ defined by: $$\boxed{F_X(x) = P(X \leq x)} \tag{2.1}$$

**Properties of any valid CDF** (provable from the Kolmogorov axioms):

$$\lim_{x \to -\infty} F_X(x) = 0 \tag{2.2}$$ $$\lim_{x \to +\infty} F_X(x) = 1 \tag{2.3}$$ $$F_X \text{ is non-decreasing: } x_1 \leq x_2 \implies F_X(x_1) \leq F_X(x_2) \tag{2.4}$$ $$F_X \text{ is right-continuous: } \lim_{h \to 0^+} F_X(x+h) = F_X(x) \tag{2.5}$$

These four properties completely characterize valid CDFs. Conversely, any function satisfying these four properties _is_ the CDF of some random variable — a deep result in probability theory.

---

### 2.2.3 Discrete Random Variables and the PMF

> **Definition 2.3 (Discrete Random Variable):** $X$ is **discrete** if its support $\mathcal{X} = {x : P(X = x) > 0}$ is finite or countably infinite.

> **Definition 2.4 (Probability Mass Function):** The PMF of a discrete random variable $X$ is: $$\boxed{p_X(x) = P(X = x)} \tag{2.6}$$

**Validity conditions:** $$p_X(x) \geq 0 \quad \forall x \in \mathcal{X} \tag{2.7}$$ $$\sum_{x \in \mathcal{X}} p_X(x) = 1 \tag{2.8}$$

The relationship between PMF and CDF is: $$F_X(x) = \sum_{k \leq x} p_X(k) \tag{2.9}$$

For discrete distributions, $F_X$ is a **staircase function** — it jumps by $p_X(x_i)$ at each support point $x_i$ and is flat in between.

---

### 2.2.4 Continuous Random Variables and the PDF

> **Definition 2.5 (Continuous Random Variable):** $X$ is **absolutely continuous** (hereafter simply "continuous") if there exists a non-negative function $f_X: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$ such that: $$F_X(x) = \int_{-\infty}^{x} f_X(t), dt \tag{2.10}$$

The function $f_X$ is called the **probability density function (PDF)**.

**Critical Insight:** Unlike a PMF, the PDF is _not_ a probability. For any single point $x$: $$P(X = x) = \int_x^x f_X(t), dt = 0 \tag{2.11}$$

The probability of a continuous random variable taking _any exact value_ is zero. Only intervals have positive probability: $$P(a \leq X \leq b) = \int_a^b f_X(x), dx \tag{2.12}$$

**Validity conditions:** $$f_X(x) \geq 0 \quad \forall x \in \mathbb{R} \tag{2.13}$$ $$\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} f_X(x), dx = 1 \tag{2.14}$$

**Differential interpretation:** For small $\delta > 0$: $$P(x \leq X \leq x + \delta) \approx f_X(x) \cdot \delta \tag{2.15}$$

This is the operational meaning of the PDF: $f_X(x)$ measures the _density_ of probability near $x$, not the probability at $x$.

**Recovering the PDF from the CDF:** $$f_X(x) = \frac{d}{dx} F_X(x) \tag{2.16}$$

wherever the derivative exists.

---

### 2.2.5 Functions of Random Variables

A powerful and constantly-used tool: if $X$ is a random variable and $g: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ is a measurable function, then $Y = g(X)$ is also a random variable.

**For the continuous case — the Change of Variables Formula:**

> **Theorem 2.1 (Univariate Change of Variables):** Let $X$ be a continuous random variable with PDF $f_X$, and let $g$ be a strictly monotone, differentiable function. Then $Y = g(X)$ has PDF: $$\boxed{f_Y(y) = f_X(g^{-1}(y)) \cdot \left|\frac{d}{dy} g^{-1}(y)\right|} \tag{2.17}$$

**Proof (monotone increasing case):** Since $g$ is strictly increasing, $Y \leq y \iff X \leq g^{-1}(y)$. Therefore: $$F_Y(y) = P(Y \leq y) = P(X \leq g^{-1}(y)) = F_X(g^{-1}(y))$$

Differentiating with respect to $y$ using the chain rule: $$f_Y(y) = f_X(g^{-1}(y)) \cdot \frac{d}{dy} g^{-1}(y)$$

For monotone decreasing $g$, the derivative is negative, so we take the absolute value. $\blacksquare$

**ML Application — the log-sum-exp trick:** When computing the softmax $\sigma_k(\mathbf{z}) = e^{z_k} / \sum_j e^{z_j}$, the exponentials can overflow. Recognizing this as a change of variables and working in log-space — exactly this theorem — is what makes numerical computation stable.

---

### 2.2.6 The Probability Integral Transform

This elegant theorem underlies simulation, copulas, quantile regression, and normalizing flows.

> **Theorem 2.2 (Probability Integral Transform):** Let $X$ be a continuous random variable with CDF $F_X$. Then the random variable $U = F_X(X)$ is uniformly distributed on $[0, 1]$: $$U = F_X(X) \sim \text{Uniform}(0, 1) \tag{2.18}$$

**Proof:** For $u \in [0,1]$: $$P(U \leq u) = P(F_X(X) \leq u) = P(X \leq F_X^{-1}(u)) = F_X(F_X^{-1}(u)) = u$$

This is the CDF of a $\text{Uniform}(0,1)$. $\blacksquare$

**Corollary (Inverse Transform Sampling):** If $U \sim \text{Uniform}(0,1)$, then $X = F_X^{-1}(U)$ has distribution $F_X$. This is how we generate samples from arbitrary distributions — the foundation of Monte Carlo methods.

---

### 2.2.7 Joint, Marginal, and Conditional Distributions

In machine learning, we almost always work with _multiple_ random variables simultaneously.

> **Definition 2.6 (Joint Distribution):** For random variables $X$ and $Y$, the **joint CDF** is: $$F_{X,Y}(x, y) = P(X \leq x, Y \leq y) \tag{2.19}$$

**Discrete case — Joint PMF:** $$p_{X,Y}(x, y) = P(X = x, Y = y) \tag{2.20}$$

**Continuous case — Joint PDF:** A function $f_{X,Y}(x, y)$ such that: $$P(a \leq X \leq b,\ c \leq Y \leq d) = \int_a^b \int_c^d f_{X,Y}(x, y), dy, dx \tag{2.21}$$

**Marginalization** — recovering individual distributions from the joint:

Discrete: $\quad p_X(x) = \sum_y p_{X,Y}(x, y) \tag{2.22}$

Continuous: $\quad f_X(x) = \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} f_{X,Y}(x, y), dy \tag{2.23}$

**Conditional distribution:**

Discrete: $\quad p_{Y \mid X}(y \mid x) = \frac{p_{X,Y}(x, y)}{p_X(x)} \tag{2.24}$

Continuous: $\quad f_{Y \mid X}(y \mid x) = \frac{f_{X,Y}(x, y)}{f_X(x)} \tag{2.25}$

Note that equation (2.25) is exactly Bayes' theorem in density form: the conditional density is the joint divided by the marginal.

**Independence of random variables:**

$X$ and $Y$ are independent if and only if: $$f_{X,Y}(x, y) = f_X(x) \cdot f_Y(y) \quad \forall x, y \tag{2.26}$$

i.e., the joint factors into the product of the marginals. This is the continuous analog of Definition 1.3.

---

## 2.3 Numerical Examples

### Example 2.1: Discrete Random Variable — Loaded Die

**Problem:** A loaded die has the following PMF:

|$x$|1|2|3|4|5|6|
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
|$p_X(x)$|1/12|1/12|1/6|1/6|1/4|1/4|

(a) Verify this is a valid PMF. (b) Compute $P(X \geq 4)$. (c) Find and sketch the CDF.

**Solution:**

**(a) Validity:** $$\sum_{x=1}^{6} p_X(x) = \frac{1}{12} + \frac{1}{12} + \frac{2}{12} + \frac{2}{12} + \frac{3}{12} + \frac{3}{12} = \frac{12}{12} = 1 \checkmark$$ All values are non-negative. $\checkmark$

**(b)** $P(X \geq 4) = p_X(4) + p_X(5) + p_X(6) = \frac{1}{6} + \frac{1}{4} + \frac{1}{4} = \frac{2}{12} + \frac{3}{12} + \frac{3}{12} = \frac{8}{12} = \boxed{\frac{2}{3}}$

**(c) CDF:** Accumulating the PMF:

$$F_X(x) = \begin{cases} 0 & x < 1 \ 1/12 & 1 \leq x < 2 \ 2/12 & 2 \leq x < 3 \ 4/12 & 3 \leq x < 4 \ 6/12 & 4 \leq x < 5 \ 9/12 & 5 \leq x < 6 \ 1 & x \geq 6 \end{cases}$$

The CDF is a staircase, right-continuous, jumping by $p_X(x_i)$ at each value.

---

### Example 2.2: Continuous Random Variable — Change of Variables

**Problem:** $X \sim \text{Uniform}(0, 1)$ with PDF $f_X(x) = 1$ for $x \in [0,1]$. Let $Y = -\ln(X)$. Find the PDF of $Y$.

**Solution:**

**(Step 1)** Identify the transformation. $g(x) = -\ln(x)$, which is strictly decreasing on $(0,1)$.

**(Step 2)** Find the range of $Y$. As $x \to 0^+$, $y \to +\infty$. As $x \to 1^-$, $y \to 0^+$. So $Y \in (0, \infty)$.

**(Step 3)** Find the inverse. $y = -\ln(x) \implies x = e^{-y}$, so $g^{-1}(y) = e^{-y}$.

**(Step 4)** Compute the derivative. $\frac{d}{dy} g^{-1}(y) = -e^{-y}$.

**(Step 5)** Apply Theorem 2.1: $$f_Y(y) = f_X(g^{-1}(y)) \cdot \left|\frac{d}{dy} g^{-1}(y)\right| = 1 \cdot \left|-e^{-y}\right| = e^{-y}$$

**Result:** $f_Y(y) = e^{-y}$ for $y > 0$. This is the **Exponential(1)** distribution.

**Verification:** $$\int_0^{\infty} e^{-y}, dy = \left[-e^{-y}\right]_0^{\infty} = 0 - (-1) = 1 \checkmark$$

**ML Insight:** This construction — $-\ln(U)$ for $U \sim \text{Uniform}(0,1)$ — is how we generate exponential random variables in practice. It is a special case of inverse transform sampling (Theorem 2.2), and the same principle underlies the **Gumbel-softmax trick** used to make discrete sampling differentiable in neural networks.

---

### Example 2.3: Joint Distribution and Marginalization

**Problem:** Two discrete random variables $X$ (hours studied) and $Y$ (exam result: 0=fail, 1=pass) have joint PMF:

$$p_{X,Y}(x, y) = \begin{cases} 0.20 & (x=1, y=0) \ 0.05 & (x=1, y=1) \ 0.10 & (x=3, y=0) \ 0.25 & (x=3, y=1) \ 0.02 & (x=5, y=0) \ 0.38 & (x=5, y=1) \end{cases}$$

(a) Verify validity. (b) Find the marginal PMF of $Y$. (c) Find $P(Y=1 \mid X=5)$.

**Solution:**

**(a)** Sum of all entries: $0.20 + 0.05 + 0.10 + 0.25 + 0.02 + 0.38 = 1.00$ $\checkmark$

**(b) Marginal PMF of $Y$** (sum over all values of $X$): $$p_Y(0) = 0.20 + 0.10 + 0.02 = 0.32$$ $$p_Y(1) = 0.05 + 0.25 + 0.38 = 0.68$$

**(c) Conditional PMF** — first find marginal $p_X(5)$: $$p_X(5) = p_{X,Y}(5, 0) + p_{X,Y}(5, 1) = 0.02 + 0.38 = 0.40$$

Then apply Definition (2.24): $$P(Y=1 \mid X=5) = \frac{p_{X,Y}(5,1)}{p_X(5)} = \frac{0.38}{0.40} = \boxed{0.95}$$

Students who study 5 hours pass with 95% probability, vs. the overall pass rate of 68%.

---

## 2.4 Implementation

```python
import numpy as np
import scipy.stats as stats
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.gridspec as gridspec

# =============================================================================
# MODULE 2: Discrete & Continuous Random Variables
# =============================================================================

# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# PART A: Discrete Random Variable — PMF, CDF, and Simulation
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------

class DiscreteRV:
    """
    A general discrete random variable defined by its support and PMF values.
    Demonstrates the core properties of discrete distributions.
    """
    
    def __init__(self, support: np.ndarray, probs: np.ndarray):
        """
        Parameters
        ----------
        support : array-like  — the values X can take (sorted)
        probs   : array-like  — corresponding probabilities P(X = x_i)
        """
        self.support = np.array(support, dtype=float)
        self.probs   = np.array(probs,   dtype=float)
        
        # Validate: must be a valid PMF
        assert np.all(self.probs >= 0),           "Probabilities must be non-negative"
        assert np.isclose(self.probs.sum(), 1.0), f"Probabilities must sum to 1, got {self.probs.sum():.6f}"
        
        # Precompute cumulative sums for the CDF
        self._cdf_values = np.cumsum(self.probs)

    def pmf(self, x):
        """P(X = x)"""
        idx = np.searchsorted(self.support, x)
        if idx < len(self.support) and self.support[idx] == x:
            return self.probs[idx]
        return 0.0

    def cdf(self, x):
        """F(x) = P(X <= x) — right-continuous staircase function"""
        idx = np.searchsorted(self.support, x, side='right') - 1
        if idx < 0:
            return 0.0
        return self._cdf_values[min(idx, len(self._cdf_values) - 1)]

    def sample(self, n: int, seed: int = 42) -> np.ndarray:
        """
        Draw n samples using inverse transform sampling.
        This is the discrete analog of Theorem 2.2: generate U~Uniform(0,1),
        then return the smallest x such that F(x) >= U.
        """
        rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
        uniform_samples = rng.uniform(0, 1, size=n)
        # searchsorted on cumulative probs is the discrete inverse CDF
        indices = np.searchsorted(self._cdf_values, uniform_samples, side='left')
        indices = np.clip(indices, 0, len(self.support) - 1)
        return self.support[indices]

    def probability_range(self, a, b) -> float:
        """P(a <= X <= b) = F(b) - F(a-)"""
        return self.cdf(b) - self.cdf(a - 1e-9)

    def plot(self, n_samples: int = 10_000, seed: int = 42):
        """Visualize PMF, theoretical CDF, and empirical CDF from simulation."""
        samples = self.sample(n_samples, seed=seed)
        
        fig = plt.figure(figsize=(13, 4.5))
        gs  = gridspec.GridSpec(1, 3, wspace=0.38)
        
        # --- PMF ---
        ax1 = fig.add_subplot(gs[0])
        ax1.bar(self.support, self.probs, width=0.35, color="#1a6faf",
                alpha=0.85, label="PMF $p_X(x)$")
        ax1.set_xlabel("$x$", fontsize=12)
        ax1.set_ylabel("$p_X(x)$", fontsize=12)
        ax1.set_title("Probability Mass Function", fontsize=12, fontweight='bold')
        ax1.set_ylim(0, max(self.probs) * 1.25)
        for x, p in zip(self.support, self.probs):
            ax1.text(x, p + 0.005, f"{p:.2f}", ha='center', fontsize=9, color="#1a3a5c")
        ax1.grid(axis='y', alpha=0.3)
        
        # --- Theoretical CDF (staircase) ---
        ax2 = fig.add_subplot(gs[1])
        # Build the staircase: add -inf start and +inf end
        x_step = np.concatenate([
            [self.support[0] - 1.5],
            np.repeat(self.support, 2),
            [self.support[-1] + 1.5]
        ])
        y_step = np.concatenate([
            [0, 0],
            np.repeat(self._cdf_values, 2)[:-1],
            [1]
        ])
        ax2.plot(x_step, y_step, color="#1a6faf", lw=2, label="Theoretical CDF")
        # Mark the jump discontinuities (left-limit = open circle)
        ax2.scatter(self.support, self._cdf_values, s=55, 
                    color="#1a6faf", zorder=5, label="$F_X(x)$")
        left_limits = np.concatenate([[0], self._cdf_values[:-1]])
        ax2.scatter(self.support, left_limits, s=55,
                    facecolors='white', edgecolors="#1a6faf", zorder=5)
        ax2.set_xlabel("$x$", fontsize=12)
        ax2.set_ylabel("$F_X(x)$", fontsize=12)
        ax2.set_title("Cumulative Distribution Function", fontsize=12, fontweight='bold')
        ax2.set_ylim(-0.05, 1.1)
        ax2.grid(alpha=0.3)
        
        # --- Empirical CDF (from simulation) vs theoretical ---
        ax3 = fig.add_subplot(gs[2])
        sorted_samples = np.sort(samples)
        ecdf_y = np.arange(1, n_samples + 1) / n_samples
        ax3.step(sorted_samples, ecdf_y, where='post',
                 color="#e84040", lw=1.5, alpha=0.7, label=f"Empirical CDF (n={n_samples:,})")
        ax3.plot(x_step, y_step, color="#1a6faf", lw=2, label="Theoretical CDF")
        ax3.set_xlabel("$x$", fontsize=12)
        ax3.set_ylabel("$F_X(x)$", fontsize=12)
        ax3.set_title("Empirical vs. Theoretical CDF", fontsize=12, fontweight='bold')
        ax3.legend(fontsize=9)
        ax3.set_ylim(-0.05, 1.1)
        ax3.grid(alpha=0.3)
        
        plt.suptitle("Discrete Random Variable", fontsize=14, fontweight='bold', y=1.01)
        plt.savefig("module2_discrete_rv.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches='tight')
        plt.show()
        print("Saved: module2_discrete_rv.png")


# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# PART B: Continuous Random Variable — PDF, CDF, and Change of Variables
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def demonstrate_change_of_variables(n_samples: int = 100_000, seed: int = 42):
    """
    Verify Example 2.2 numerically: if X ~ Uniform(0,1), then Y = -ln(X) ~ Exp(1).
    
    This directly demonstrates Theorem 2.1 (Change of Variables) and
    Theorem 2.2 (Probability Integral Transform / Inverse Transform Sampling).
    """
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    
    # Step 1: Sample X ~ Uniform(0,1)
    X = rng.uniform(0, 1, size=n_samples)
    
    # Step 2: Apply the transformation Y = -ln(X)
    Y = -np.log(X)
    
    # Step 3: Compare empirical distribution of Y to theoretical Exp(1)
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(14, 4.5))
    fig.suptitle("Change of Variables: $X \\sim U(0,1)$ → $Y = -\\ln(X) \\sim \\text{Exp}(1)$",
                 fontsize=13, fontweight='bold')
    
    # --- X distribution ---
    ax = axes[0]
    ax.hist(X, bins=60, density=True, alpha=0.7, color="#3a7ca5", label="Empirical $X$")
    ax.axhline(1, color='#e84040', lw=2, linestyle='--', label="$f_X(x)=1$ (Uniform)")
    ax.set_title("$X \\sim \\text{Uniform}(0,1)$", fontsize=12)
    ax.set_xlabel("$x$"); ax.set_ylabel("Density")
    ax.legend(fontsize=9); ax.grid(alpha=0.3)
    
    # --- Y distribution ---
    ax = axes[1]
    y_range = np.linspace(0, 8, 500)
    ax.hist(Y, bins=80, density=True, alpha=0.7, color="#3a7ca5", label="Empirical $Y$")
    ax.plot(y_range, stats.expon.pdf(y_range), color='#e84040', lw=2.5,
            label="$f_Y(y) = e^{-y}$ (Exp(1))")
    ax.set_title("$Y = -\\ln(X) \\sim \\text{Exp}(1)$", fontsize=12)
    ax.set_xlabel("$y$"); ax.set_ylabel("Density")
    ax.legend(fontsize=9); ax.grid(alpha=0.3)
    
    # --- Q-Q Plot: empirical quantiles of Y vs. theoretical Exp(1) ---
    ax = axes[2]
    # Compute theoretical quantiles at the same probability levels
    probs    = np.linspace(0.01, 0.99, 500)
    q_theory = stats.expon.ppf(probs)       # Theoretical quantiles
    q_empirical = np.quantile(Y, probs)     # Empirical quantiles
    ax.scatter(q_theory, q_empirical, s=4, alpha=0.5, color="#3a7ca5")
    max_q = max(q_theory.max(), q_empirical.max())
    ax.plot([0, max_q], [0, max_q], 'r--', lw=2, label="45° line (perfect fit)")
    ax.set_title("Q-Q Plot: $Y$ vs. Exp(1)", fontsize=12)
    ax.set_xlabel("Theoretical Exp(1) quantiles")
    ax.set_ylabel("Empirical quantiles of $Y$")
    ax.legend(fontsize=9); ax.grid(alpha=0.3)
    
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.savefig("module2_change_of_variables.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches='tight')
    plt.show()
    print("Saved: module2_change_of_variables.png")


# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# PART C: Joint Distributions — Visualization and Marginalization
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def demonstrate_joint_distribution(seed: int = 42):
    """
    Generate samples from a correlated bivariate Gaussian (a joint continuous
    distribution), then visualize the joint PDF, marginals, and conditional.
    This directly illustrates Definitions 2.6, 2.23 (marginals), and 2.25 (conditional).
    """
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    n   = 5000
    
    # Define a bivariate Gaussian with correlation rho = 0.75
    mu  = np.array([2.0, 1.0])
    rho = 0.75
    cov = np.array([[1.0, rho],
                    [rho, 1.0]])
    
    # Draw samples from the joint distribution
    samples = rng.multivariate_normal(mu, cov, size=n)
    X_data, Y_data = samples[:, 0], samples[:, 1]
    
    fig = plt.figure(figsize=(13, 5))
    gs  = gridspec.GridSpec(1, 3, wspace=0.35)
    
    # --- Joint PDF heatmap ---
    ax1 = fig.add_subplot(gs[0])
    grid_x = np.linspace(-2, 6, 300)
    grid_y = np.linspace(-2, 4, 300)
    GX, GY = np.meshgrid(grid_x, grid_y)
    pos     = np.dstack([GX, GY])
    rv_joint = stats.multivariate_normal(mean=mu, cov=cov)
    Z        = rv_joint.pdf(pos)
    
    ax1.contourf(GX, GY, Z, levels=25, cmap='Blues')
    ax1.contour(GX, GY, Z, levels=8, colors='navy', linewidths=0.5, alpha=0.5)
    ax1.scatter(X_data[:300], Y_data[:300], s=4, alpha=0.3, color='white', zorder=2)
    ax1.set_xlabel("$X$", fontsize=12); ax1.set_ylabel("$Y$", fontsize=12)
    ax1.set_title("Joint PDF $f_{X,Y}(x,y)$", fontsize=12, fontweight='bold')
    
    # --- Marginal distributions ---
    ax2 = fig.add_subplot(gs[1])
    # Marginal of X: f_X(x) = integral over y of f_{X,Y}(x,y) dy
    rv_X  = stats.norm(loc=mu[0], scale=np.sqrt(cov[0, 0]))
    rv_Y  = stats.norm(loc=mu[1], scale=np.sqrt(cov[1, 1]))
    
    x_range = np.linspace(-2, 6, 300)
    y_range = np.linspace(-2, 4, 300)
    
    ax2.plot(x_range, rv_X.pdf(x_range), color='#1a6faf', lw=2.5, label="$f_X(x)$ (marginal)")
    ax2.plot(y_range, rv_Y.pdf(y_range), color='#e84040', lw=2.5, 
             linestyle='--', label="$f_Y(y)$ (marginal)")
    ax2.hist(X_data, bins=60, density=True, alpha=0.3, color='#1a6faf')
    ax2.hist(Y_data, bins=60, density=True, alpha=0.3, color='#e84040')
    ax2.set_xlabel("Value", fontsize=12)
    ax2.set_ylabel("Density", fontsize=12)
    ax2.set_title("Marginal PDFs (eq. 2.23)", fontsize=12, fontweight='bold')
    ax2.legend(fontsize=10)
    ax2.grid(alpha=0.3)
    
    # --- Conditional distribution f_{Y|X}(y | X=3) ---
    ax3 = fig.add_subplot(gs[2])
    x_given = 3.0  # We condition on X = 3.0
    
    # For bivariate Gaussian, the conditional Y|X=x is also Gaussian:
    # mu_{Y|X} = mu_Y + rho*(sigma_Y/sigma_X)*(x - mu_X)
    # sigma^2_{Y|X} = sigma_Y^2 * (1 - rho^2)
    mu_Y_given_X    = mu[1] + rho * (x_given - mu[0])
    sigma_Y_given_X = np.sqrt(1 - rho**2)
    rv_cond         = stats.norm(loc=mu_Y_given_X, scale=sigma_Y_given_X)
    
    # Empirical: filter samples near X = x_given (within ±0.3)
    mask    = np.abs(X_data - x_given) < 0.3
    Y_slice = Y_data[mask]
    
    ax3.hist(Y_slice, bins=30, density=True, alpha=0.55, color='#3a7ca5',
             label=f"Empirical $Y | X \\approx {x_given}$")
    ax3.plot(y_range, rv_cond.pdf(y_range), color='#e84040', lw=2.5,
             label=f"$f_{{Y|X}}(y|x={x_given})$")
    ax3.axvline(mu_Y_given_X, color='#e84040', lw=1.5, linestyle=':')
    ax3.set_xlabel("$Y$", fontsize=12)
    ax3.set_ylabel("Density", fontsize=12)
    ax3.set_title(f"Conditional PDF $f_{{Y|X}}(y|x={x_given})$", fontsize=12, fontweight='bold')
    ax3.legend(fontsize=9)
    ax3.grid(alpha=0.3)
    
    # Annotate conditional mean
    ax3.text(mu_Y_given_X + 0.1, 0.05,
             f"$\\mu_{{Y|X={x_given}}} = {mu_Y_given_X:.2f}$",
             fontsize=9, color='#e84040')
    
    plt.suptitle("Joint, Marginal, and Conditional Distributions", 
                 fontsize=13, fontweight='bold', y=1.02)
    plt.savefig("module2_joint_distribution.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches='tight')
    plt.show()
    print("Saved: module2_joint_distribution.png")


# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# PART D: Inverse Transform Sampling — Universal Sampler
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def inverse_transform_sampler(cdf_inverse, n_samples: int = 10_000, seed: int = 42):
    """
    General-purpose sampler using the Probability Integral Transform (Theorem 2.2).
    
    Works for ANY distribution where we can compute the quantile function F^{-1}.
    This is the foundational algorithm behind scipy's rvs() methods.
    
    Parameters
    ----------
    cdf_inverse : callable  — The quantile function F_X^{-1}
    n_samples   : int
    
    Returns
    -------
    np.ndarray of samples from the distribution defined by cdf_inverse.
    """
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    U = rng.uniform(0, 1, size=n_samples)  # Step 1: U ~ Uniform(0,1)
    return cdf_inverse(U)                   # Step 2: X = F^{-1}(U)


# =============================================================================
# MAIN
# =============================================================================

if __name__ == "__main__":
    
    # --- A: Loaded Die from Example 2.1 ---
    print("=" * 60)
    print("  DISCRETE RV: LOADED DIE")
    print("=" * 60)
    die = DiscreteRV(
        support=[1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6],
        probs  =[1/12, 1/12, 2/12, 2/12, 3/12, 3/12]
    )
    print(f"  P(X >= 4) = {die.probability_range(4, 6):.4f}  (expected: 0.6667)")
    print(f"  P(X = 3)  = {die.pmf(3):.4f}")
    print(f"  F_X(4)    = {die.cdf(4):.4f}  (expected: 0.5000)")
    
    # Simulate and verify
    samples = die.sample(n=500_000)
    print(f"\n  Empirical P(X >= 4) = {np.mean(samples >= 4):.4f}  (theory: 0.6667)")
    die.plot(n_samples=50_000)
    
    # --- B: Change of Variables ---
    print("\n" + "=" * 60)
    print("  CHANGE OF VARIABLES: U(0,1) → Exp(1)")
    print("=" * 60)
    demonstrate_change_of_variables()
    
    # --- C: Joint and Conditional Distributions ---
    print("\n" + "=" * 60)
    print("  JOINT & CONDITIONAL DISTRIBUTIONS")
    print("=" * 60)
    demonstrate_joint_distribution()
    
    # --- D: Inverse Transform Sampling ---
    print("\n" + "=" * 60)
    print("  INVERSE TRANSFORM SAMPLING (Theorem 2.2)")
    print("=" * 60)
    # Generate Cauchy samples using its known quantile function
    # F^{-1}(u) = tan(pi*(u - 0.5))
    cauchy_samples = inverse_transform_sampler(
        cdf_inverse=lambda u: np.tan(np.pi * (u - 0.5)),
        n_samples=50_000
    )
    # Compare to scipy's Cauchy sampler (trim for display)
    clipped = cauchy_samples[np.abs(cauchy_samples) < 20]
    ks_stat, p_val = stats.ks_1samp(clipped, stats.cauchy.cdf)
    print(f"  Cauchy samples generated via inverse transform.")
    print(f"  KS test vs theoretical Cauchy: statistic={ks_stat:.4f}, p={p_val:.4f}")
    print(f"  (p >> 0.05 confirms samples are consistent with Cauchy distribution)")
```

## 2.5 Module Summary & The PDF/PMF Decision in ML

The most important practical takeaway from this module is the **modelling decision** you make when choosing a random variable type for your ML output:

|If your output is...|Use...|Your model outputs...|Your loss is...|
|---|---|---|---|
|A binary label|$\text{Bernoulli}(p)$|$\sigma(\mathbf{w}^T \mathbf{x}) \in (0,1)$|$-[y \log p + (1-y)\log(1-p)]$|
|A class label|$\text{Categorical}(\mathbf{p})$|$\text{softmax}(\mathbf{z}) \in \Delta^{K-1}$|$-\sum_k y_k \log p_k$|
|A real number|$\mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)$|$\mathbf{w}^T\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}$|$\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum(y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2$|
|A count|$\text{Poisson}(\lambda)$|$\exp(\mathbf{w}^T \mathbf{x}) > 0$|Poisson log-likelihood|

Every loss function in machine learning is the negative log-likelihood of a probability model over a random variable. This understanding unlocks the ability to design custom, theoretically motivated loss functions for any problem.

---

## 2.6 Key Equations Reference Card

$$F_X(x) = P(X \leq x) \tag{CDF}$$ $$p_X(x) = P(X = x), \quad \sum_x p_X(x) = 1 \tag{PMF}$$ $$F_X(x) = \int_{-\infty}^x f_X(t),dt, \quad \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f_X(x),dx = 1 \tag{PDF}$$ $$f_Y(y) = f_X(g^{-1}(y)),\left|\tfrac{d}{dy}g^{-1}(y)\right| \tag{Change of Variables}$$ $$f_X(x) = \int f_{X,Y}(x,y),dy \tag{Marginalization}$$ $$f_{Y|X}(y|x) = \frac{f_{X,Y}(x,y)}{f_X(x)} \tag{Conditional Density}$$

Here is **Module 3** of the Mastery Handbook. This module is the algebraic heart of the curriculum — the moment you understand moments, the entire landscape of ML loss functions, regularization, and model diagnostics snaps into focus.
