Here is **Module 5** of the Mastery Handbook — arguably the most profound module in the curriculum. The theorems here explain why machine learning _works at all_.

---

# MODULE 5: The Law of Large Numbers & the Central Limit Theorem

---

## 5.1 Conceptual Overview

### The Two Pillars of Statistical Inference

Every act of machine learning is an act of inference from a finite sample about an infinite population. When we train a model on 1 million images and expect it to work on images it has never seen, we are implicitly relying on two of the deepest theorems in mathematics. Without them, the entire enterprise of learning from data would be philosophically indefensible.

The **Law of Large Numbers (LLN)** guarantees _consistency_: given enough data, our empirical estimates converge to the true values. The sample mean converges to the population mean. Our empirical loss converges to the true expected loss. This is why training on more data generally helps — the LLN is at work.

The **Central Limit Theorem (CLT)** guarantees _quantifiable uncertainty_: even when we have only a finite sample, the distribution of our estimator has a predictable, Gaussian shape. This is why confidence intervals are possible, why hypothesis tests have known distributions, and why the noise in stochastic gradient descent behaves in a statistically tractable way.

Together, these two results form the mathematical justification for statistical machine learning:

- LLN: _More data → better estimates_ (point estimate consistency)
- CLT: _Finite data → quantifiable estimation error_ (distributional characterization)

### A Deeper Intuition

Think about what is being claimed. You have $n$ i.i.d. random variables $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n$ drawn from _any_ distribution whatsoever — it could be wildly skewed, multimodal, heavy-tailed. The LLN says their average $\bar{X}_n$ will converge to some fixed number $\mu$. The CLT says something even more astonishing: the _fluctuations_ of $\bar{X}_n$ around $\mu$, properly scaled by $\sqrt{n}$, are Gaussian — regardless of the original distribution. The Gaussian emerges not because data is Gaussian, but because _averaging is a smoothing operation_ that destroys the idiosyncrasies of any individual distribution.

This universality is what makes the Gaussian the central object of all of statistics.

---

## 5.2 Mathematical Formalization

### 5.2.1 Setup and Notation

Throughout this module, let $X_1, X_2, \ldots$ be an **i.i.d.** (independent and identically distributed) sequence of random variables with: $$\mathbb{E}[X_i] = \mu, \quad \text{Var}(X_i) = \sigma^2 < \infty$$

Define the **sample mean**: $$\bar{X}_n = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i \tag{5.1}$$

By linearity of expectation and independence: $$\mathbb{E}[\bar{X}_n] = \mu \tag{5.2}$$ $$\text{Var}(\bar{X}_n) = \frac{\sigma^2}{n} \tag{5.3}$$

Equation (5.3) is the mathematical statement that averaging reduces variance. Collecting twice as much data halves the variance of our estimate (quartering the standard deviation). This is the quantitative case for more data.

---

### 5.2.2 The Weak Law of Large Numbers

> **Theorem 5.1 (Weak Law of Large Numbers — WLLN):** For any $\varepsilon > 0$: $$\lim_{n \to \infty} P!\left(|\bar{X}_n - \mu| \geq \varepsilon\right) = 0 \tag{5.4}$$
> 
> Written compactly: $\bar{X}_n \xrightarrow{p} \mu$ (convergence _in probability_).

**Proof using Chebyshev's Inequality (Theorem 3.5):**

Apply Chebyshev to $\bar{X}_n$, which has mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2/n$:

$$P(|\bar{X}_n - \mu| \geq \varepsilon) \leq \frac{\text{Var}(\bar{X}_n)}{\varepsilon^2} = \frac{\sigma^2}{n\varepsilon^2}$$

As $n \to \infty$, the right-hand side $\to 0$ for any fixed $\varepsilon > 0$. $\blacksquare$

This proof is elegant precisely because it requires only finite variance — no knowledge of the distribution's shape. The Chebyshev inequality, derived purely from the definition of variance, is sufficient.

**What does convergence in probability mean?**

$\bar{X}_n \xrightarrow{p} \mu$ does _not_ mean $\bar{X}_n = \mu$ eventually. It means: for any tolerance $\varepsilon > 0$, no matter how small, the probability that $\bar{X}_n$ deviates from $\mu$ by more than $\varepsilon$ becomes negligible as $n$ grows. The estimate can still be wrong for any individual $n$ — it just becomes increasingly unlikely.

---

### 5.2.3 The Strong Law of Large Numbers

> **Theorem 5.2 (Strong Law of Large Numbers — SLLN):** With probability 1: $$P!\left(\lim_{n\to\infty} \bar{X}_n = \mu\right) = 1 \tag{5.5}$$
> 
> Written compactly: $\bar{X}_n \xrightarrow{a.s.} \mu$ (convergence _almost surely_).

Almost sure convergence is strictly stronger than convergence in probability. It says: with probability 1, the sequence $\bar{X}_1, \bar{X}_2, \ldots$ literally converges (in the analysis sense) to $\mu$. The set of sample paths that fail to converge has probability zero.

**Relationship between convergence modes:** $$\bar{X}_n \xrightarrow{a.s.} \mu \implies \bar{X}_n \xrightarrow{p} \mu \tag{5.6}$$

The converse does not hold in general. The full proof of the SLLN requires measure theory and is beyond our scope, but the WLLN proof above captures the essential mechanism.

**ML Interpretation:** The SLLN is the mathematical foundation of _empirical risk minimization_. The true risk (generalization error) is: $$R(f) = \mathbb{E}_{(x,y)}[\ell(f(x), y)]$$

The empirical risk on training data is: $$\hat{R}_n(f) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \ell(f(x_i), y_i)$$

The SLLN guarantees $\hat{R}_n(f) \xrightarrow{a.s.} R(f)$ for any fixed $f$ as $n \to \infty$. This is why minimizing training loss is a principled approach to minimizing true generalization error.

---

### 5.2.4 The Central Limit Theorem

The CLT is the crown jewel of classical probability theory. It requires a stronger assumption than the LLN — finite variance — but delivers a dramatically stronger conclusion about the _distributional_ behavior of $\bar{X}_n$.

Define the **standardized sample mean**: $$Z_n = \frac{\bar{X}_n - \mu}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}} = \frac{\sqrt{n}(\bar{X}_n - \mu)}{\sigma} \tag{5.7}$$

By construction, $\mathbb{E}[Z_n] = 0$ and $\text{Var}(Z_n) = 1$ for all $n$.

> **Theorem 5.3 (Central Limit Theorem):** Under the i.i.d. assumption with $\mathbb{E}[X_i]=\mu$ and $\text{Var}(X_i)=\sigma^2 < \infty$: $$Z_n = \frac{\sqrt{n}(\bar{X}_n - \mu)}{\sigma} \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}(0,1) \tag{5.8}$$
> 
> That is, for any $z \in \mathbb{R}$: $$\lim_{n\to\infty} P(Z_n \leq z) = \Phi(z) = \int_{-\infty}^z \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-t^2/2},dt \tag{5.9}$$

where $\Phi$ denotes the standard normal CDF.

---

### 5.2.5 Proof of the CLT via Moment Generating Functions

This is one of the most important proofs in the entire handbook. We prove the CLT using the MGF continuity theorem — the same machinery used in Module 3.

**Proof:**

Without loss of generality, assume $\mu = 0$ and $\sigma^2 = 1$ (standardize each $X_i$). Let $Y_i = X_i / \sigma$, so $\mathbb{E}[Y_i]=0$, $\mathbb{E}[Y_i^2]=1$.

Then $Z_n = \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\sum_{i=1}^n Y_i$.

**Step 1:** Find the MGF of $Z_n$.

Since the $Y_i$ are i.i.d. with MGF $M_Y(t)$, by property (3.21): $$M_{Z_n}(t) = M_{\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\sum Y_i}(t) = \left[M_Y!\left(\frac{t}{\sqrt{n}}\right)\right]^n \tag{5.10}$$

**Step 2:** Expand $M_Y(t/\sqrt{n})$ as a Taylor series around $t=0$.

By Theorem 3.1, the MGF has the expansion: $$M_Y(s) = 1 + \mathbb{E}[Y]\cdot s + \frac{\mathbb{E}[Y^2]}{2}\cdot s^2 + O(s^3) = 1 + 0 + \frac{1}{2}s^2 + O(s^3)$$

Substituting $s = t/\sqrt{n}$: $$M_Y!\left(\frac{t}{\sqrt{n}}\right) = 1 + \frac{t^2}{2n} + O!\left(\frac{1}{n^{3/2}}\right) \tag{5.11}$$

**Step 3:** Take the $n$-th power and pass to the limit.

$$M_{Z_n}(t) = \left[1 + \frac{t^2}{2n} + O!\left(\frac{1}{n^{3/2}}\right)\right]^n \tag{5.12}$$

Using the fundamental limit $\lim_{n\to\infty}\left(1 + \frac{a}{n}\right)^n = e^a$:

$$\lim_{n\to\infty} M_{Z_n}(t) = e^{t^2/2} \tag{5.13}$$

**Step 4:** Identify the limit.

But $e^{t^2/2}$ is precisely the MGF of $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$ (from equation 4.12 with $\mu=0$, $\sigma=1$). By the MGF Uniqueness Theorem (Module 3), convergence of MGFs implies convergence in distribution:

$$Z_n \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}(0,1) \qquad \blacksquare$$

**What makes this proof so illuminating:** The key step is (5.11). The first-order term vanishes (because $\mathbb{E}[Y]=0$), and the second-order term $t^2/(2n)$ is the _only_ term that survives the $n\to\infty$ limit after taking the $n$-th power. This is why only the first two moments matter — higher-order terms vanish. The Gaussian emerges as the distribution whose MGF is exactly the exponential of a quadratic — and a quadratic is precisely what remains when you keep only terms up to $t^2$ in the Taylor expansion.

---

### 5.2.6 The Berry-Esseen Theorem: How Fast Does the CLT Converge?

The CLT tells us the limit but not the rate. The Berry-Esseen theorem quantifies the finite-sample error.

> **Theorem 5.4 (Berry-Esseen):** Under the i.i.d. assumption, if $\rho = \mathbb{E}[|X_i - \mu|^3] < \infty$, then: $$\sup_{z \in \mathbb{R}} \left| P(Z_n \leq z) - \Phi(z) \right| \leq \frac{C\rho}{\sigma^3\sqrt{n}} \tag{5.14}$$
> 
> where $C \leq 0.4748$ (the best known constant).

**Interpretation:** The maximum error in the Gaussian approximation to the CDF decays at rate $1/\sqrt{n}$, proportional to the third absolute moment $\rho$ and inversely proportional to $\sigma^3$. This tells us:

- Heavy-tailed distributions (large $\rho$) need more data for the CLT to kick in.
- High-variance distributions (large $\sigma$) converge faster in normalized terms.
- For most practical distributions, the CLT approximation is excellent by $n \approx 30$.

---

### 5.2.7 The Delta Method: CLT for Functions of Estimators

A critical tool for ML practitioners: given that $\bar{X}_n$ is approximately Gaussian, what is the distribution of $g(\bar{X}_n)$ for a smooth function $g$?

> **Theorem 5.5 (Delta Method):** If $\sqrt{n}(\bar{X}_n - \mu) \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)$ and $g$ is differentiable at $\mu$ with $g'(\mu) \neq 0$, then: $$\sqrt{n}!\left(g(\bar{X}_n) - g(\mu)\right) \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}!\left(0,; \sigma^2 [g'(\mu)]^2\right) \tag{5.15}$$

**Proof:** First-order Taylor expansion: $g(\bar{X}_n) \approx g(\mu) + g'(\mu)(\bar{X}_n - \mu)$. Apply CLT to $(\bar{X}_n - \mu)$ and scale by $g'(\mu)$. $\blacksquare$

**Example:** If $X_i \sim \text{Bernoulli}(p)$, then $\bar{X}_n \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}(p, p(1-p)/n)$. By the delta method with $g(p) = \log(p/(1-p))$ (the log-odds): $$\sqrt{n}!\left(\log!\frac{\bar{X}_n}{1-\bar{X}_n} - \log!\frac{p}{1-p}\right) \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}!\left(0,; \frac{1}{p(1-p)}\right)$$

This is the asymptotic distribution of the log-odds ratio estimator — fundamental in logistic regression calibration.

---

### 5.2.8 The CLT for Stochastic Gradient Descent

This is the direct ML application. In mini-batch SGD, the gradient estimate at step $t$ is: $$\hat{\mathbf{g}}_t = \frac{1}{B}\sum_{i \in \mathcal{B}_t} \nabla_\theta \ell(\theta_t; x_i, y_i) \tag{5.16}$$

where $\mathcal{B}_t$ is a random mini-batch of size $B$. The true gradient is $\mathbf{g}_t = \mathbb{E}[\nabla_\theta \ell]$.

By the CLT: $$\hat{\mathbf{g}}_t - \mathbf{g}_t \approx \mathcal{N}!\left(\mathbf{0},; \frac{\Sigma}{B}\right) \tag{5.17}$$

where $\Sigma = \text{Cov}(\nabla_\theta \ell)$ is the gradient covariance matrix.

This has profound implications:

- **Larger batch size $B$**: gradient noise decreases as $1/B$ (variance) or $1/\sqrt{B}$ (std dev). Larger batches → cleaner gradients but more compute per step.
- **Gradient noise is approximately Gaussian** for sufficiently large $B$: this justifies the use of Gaussian assumptions in SGD analysis, noise-injected training, and Bayesian deep learning.
- **The noise covariance $\Sigma/B$** is the object Adam optimizer is implicitly estimating and compensating for via its second-moment running average.

---

### 5.2.9 The Multivariate CLT

For vector-valued random variables $\mathbf{X}_i \in \mathbb{R}^d$ with mean $\boldsymbol{\mu}$ and covariance matrix $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$:

> **Theorem 5.6 (Multivariate CLT):** $$\sqrt{n}(\bar{\mathbf{X}}_n - \boldsymbol{\mu}) \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}_d(\mathbf{0},, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}) \tag{5.18}$$

This follows from the univariate CLT applied to every linear combination $\mathbf{a}^\top \mathbf{X}_i$ (Cramér-Wold device). It underpins the asymptotic theory of the MLE estimator (Module 6).

---

## 5.3 Numerical Examples

### Example 5.1: Verifying the WLLN — Exponential Data

**Problem:** Let $X_i \sim \text{Exponential}(\lambda = 2)$, so $\mu = 1/\lambda = 0.5$. Track $\bar{X}_n$ for $n = 1, 10, 100, \ldots, 10000$.

**Chebyshev bound** for $\varepsilon = 0.1$: $$P(|\bar{X}_n - 0.5| \geq 0.1) \leq \frac{\sigma^2}{n\varepsilon^2} = \frac{1/\lambda^2}{n\varepsilon^2} = \frac{1/4}{n \cdot 0.01} = \frac{25}{n}$$

At $n = 100$: bound is $0.25$. At $n = 1000$: bound is $0.025$. At $n = 10000$: bound is $0.0025$. The bound decreases as $1/n$, confirming the WLLN.

---

### Example 5.2: CLT Approximation for a Skewed Distribution

**Problem:** $X_i \sim \text{Exponential}(1)$, so $\mu = 1$, $\sigma^2 = 1$, skewness $= 2$. The CLT says: $$\frac{\sqrt{n}(\bar{X}_n - 1)}{1} \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}(0,1)$$

The Berry-Esseen bound (5.14): $\rho = \mathbb{E}[|X-1|^3]$. For Exponential(1), $\rho = \mathbb{E}[|X-1|^3] = 2$ (computed numerically). So: $$\sup_z |P(Z_n \leq z) - \Phi(z)| \leq \frac{0.4748 \cdot 2}{1^3 \sqrt{n}} = \frac{0.9496}{\sqrt{n}}$$

At $n=30$: maximum CDF error $\leq 0.173$ — meaningful. At $n=100$: $\leq 0.095$. At $n=1000$: $\leq 0.030$ — very good approximation. This explains why the rule of thumb "$n \geq 30$" applies to symmetric distributions; for skewed distributions like Exponential, you may need $n \geq 100$.

---

### Example 5.3: The CLT and Mini-Batch Gradient Estimation

**Problem:** A loss function has gradient with true mean $g = 0.5$ and variance $\sigma^2_g = 4$ across data points. What batch size $B$ is needed to estimate the gradient within $\pm 0.1$ with 95% probability?

**Solution:** By the CLT, $\hat{g}_B \approx \mathcal{N}(g, \sigma^2_g/B)$. We need: $$P(|\hat{g}_B - g| \leq 0.1) \geq 0.95$$

From the 95% confidence requirement: $2 \cdot 1.96 \cdot \sigma_g/\sqrt{B} \leq 0.2$, so: $$\sqrt{B} \geq \frac{1.96 \cdot \sigma_g}{0.1} = \frac{1.96 \cdot 2}{0.1} = 39.2$$

$$B \geq 39.2^2 \approx \boxed{1537}$$

A batch size of approximately 1537 is needed. This quantitative result illustrates why large-batch training — for gradient accuracy — can require batch sizes in the thousands. In practice, smaller batches with beneficial noise are often preferred, but this calculation provides the theoretical baseline.

---

## 5.4 Implementation

```python
import numpy as np
import scipy.stats as stats
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.gridspec as gridspec
from matplotlib.animation import FuncAnimation

# =============================================================================
# MODULE 5: Law of Large Numbers & Central Limit Theorem
# =============================================================================

# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# PART A: Law of Large Numbers — Convergence Visualization
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def demonstrate_lln(distributions: list, n_max: int = 5000, n_paths: int = 8, seed: int = 42):
    """
    Visualize the WLLN for multiple distributions.
    Shows individual sample paths of X_bar_n and the Chebyshev bound.

    Parameters
    ----------
    distributions : list of (scipy_rv, true_mean, name) tuples
    n_max         : maximum sample size
    n_paths       : number of independent sample paths to show
    """
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, len(distributions), figsize=(6 * len(distributions), 5.5))
    if len(distributions) == 1:
        axes = [axes]

    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    ns  = np.arange(1, n_max + 1)

    for ax, (rv, true_mean, name) in zip(axes, distributions):
        sigma_sq = rv.var()

        # Draw n_paths independent sample paths
        for path_idx in range(n_paths):
            samples    = rv.rvs(size=n_max, random_state=rng)
            cumulative = np.cumsum(samples) / ns  # Running mean
            ax.plot(ns, cumulative, lw=0.8, alpha=0.55,
                    color='#1a6faf' if path_idx % 2 == 0 else '#3a9ad9')

        # True mean
        ax.axhline(true_mean, color='#e84040', lw=2, linestyle='--', label=f"True μ = {true_mean:.3f}")

        # Chebyshev ±ε envelope (ε = 0.1σ)
        eps = 0.15 * np.sqrt(sigma_sq)
        ax.fill_between(ns, true_mean - eps, true_mean + eps,
                        alpha=0.12, color='#e84040', label=f"±{eps:.3f} (ε={0.15:.2f}σ)")

        # Chebyshev probability bound: P(|X_bar - mu| >= eps) <= sigma^2 / (n * eps^2)
        chebyshev_bound = sigma_sq / (ns * eps**2)
        ax2 = ax.twinx()
        ax2.semilogy(ns, chebyshev_bound, color='#2ca02c', lw=1.5, linestyle=':',
                     label="Chebyshev bound P(|·|≥ε)")
        ax2.set_ylabel("Chebyshev bound (log scale)", color='#2ca02c', fontsize=9)
        ax2.tick_params(axis='y', labelcolor='#2ca02c')
        ax2.set_ylim(1e-4, 10)

        ax.set_title(f"LLN: {name}", fontsize=12, fontweight='bold')
        ax.set_xlabel("Sample size n", fontsize=11)
        ax.set_ylabel("Sample mean $\\bar{X}_n$", fontsize=11)
        ax.legend(fontsize=9, loc='upper right')
        ax.grid(alpha=0.3)

    plt.suptitle("Law of Large Numbers — Sample Mean Convergence", fontsize=14,
                 fontweight='bold', y=1.01)
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.savefig("module5_lln.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches='tight')
    plt.show()
    print("Saved: module5_lln.png")


# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# PART B: Central Limit Theorem — Empirical Verification
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def demonstrate_clt(
    rv,
    rv_name:  str,
    ns:       list = None,
    n_reps:   int  = 8000,
    seed:     int  = 42
):
    """
    Empirically verify the CLT for a given distribution.
    For each n in ns, draw n_reps independent sample means, standardize,
    and compare the empirical distribution to N(0,1).

    Also computes the Berry-Esseen bound at each n.
    """
    if ns is None:
        ns = [1, 5, 15, 30, 100, 500]

    mu     = rv.mean()
    sigma  = rv.std()
    rng    = np.random.default_rng(seed)

    # Third absolute central moment for Berry-Esseen
    samples_large = rv.rvs(size=200_000, random_state=rng)
    rho           = np.mean(np.abs(samples_large - mu)**3)
    BE_const      = 0.4748  # Best known Berry-Esseen constant

    fig = plt.figure(figsize=(16, 9))
    gs  = gridspec.GridSpec(2, 3, wspace=0.38, hspace=0.45)
    x_ref = np.linspace(-4, 4, 400)

    for idx, n in enumerate(ns):
        ax = fig.add_subplot(gs[idx // 3, idx % 3])

        # Simulate n_reps sample means of size n, then standardize
        all_samples   = rv.rvs(size=(n_reps, n), random_state=rng)
        sample_means  = all_samples.mean(axis=1)
        Z_n           = (sample_means - mu) / (sigma / np.sqrt(n))  # Eq. 5.7

        # Histogram of Z_n
        ax.hist(Z_n, bins=70, density=True, alpha=0.6, color='#1a6faf',
                label=f"$Z_{{n={n}}}$ ({n_reps:,} reps)")

        # Standard normal reference
        ax.plot(x_ref, stats.norm.pdf(x_ref), 'r-', lw=2.5,
                label="$\\mathcal{N}(0,1)$")

        # Berry-Esseen bound
        BE_bound = BE_const * rho / (sigma**3 * np.sqrt(n))

        # KS statistic (empirical vs theoretical N(0,1))
        ks_stat, _ = stats.kstest(Z_n, 'norm')

        ax.set_title(f"n = {n}   |   BE bound ≤ {BE_bound:.4f}   |   KS = {ks_stat:.4f}",
                     fontsize=10, fontweight='bold')
        ax.set_xlabel("$Z_n$", fontsize=11)
        ax.set_ylabel("Density", fontsize=11)
        ax.set_xlim(-4.5, 4.5); ax.set_ylim(0, 0.55)
        ax.legend(fontsize=8); ax.grid(alpha=0.3)

        # Annotate skewness of empirical distribution
        empirical_skew = stats.skew(Z_n)
        ax.text(0.98, 0.95, f"skew={empirical_skew:.3f}",
                transform=ax.transAxes, ha='right', va='top',
                fontsize=9, color='#1a6faf')

    plt.suptitle(f"Central Limit Theorem: {rv_name}  (μ={mu:.3f}, σ={sigma:.3f})",
                 fontsize=14, fontweight='bold', y=1.01)
    plt.savefig(f"module5_clt_{rv_name.replace(' ','_').lower()}.png",
                dpi=150, bbox_inches='tight')
    plt.show()
    print(f"Saved CLT verification for {rv_name}")

    # Print Berry-Esseen table
    print(f"\nBerry-Esseen Bounds  [ρ={rho:.4f}, σ={sigma:.4f}]")
    print(f"{'n':>8} {'BE bound':>12} {'KS stat':>12}")
    print("-" * 36)
    rng2 = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    for n in ns:
        all_s  = rv.rvs(size=(n_reps, n), random_state=rng2)
        Z_vals = (all_s.mean(axis=1) - mu) / (sigma / np.sqrt(n))
        ks, _  = stats.kstest(Z_vals, 'norm')
        be     = BE_const * rho / (sigma**3 * np.sqrt(n))
        print(f"{n:>8} {be:>12.6f} {ks:>12.6f}")


# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# PART C: CLT for Sums — MGF Convergence Visualization
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def mgf_convergence_to_gaussian(
    rv,
    rv_name: str,
    ns:      list = None,
    t_range: tuple = (-2, 2),
    seed:    int   = 42
):
    """
    Visualize Theorem 5.3 proof step by step:
    Shows M_{Z_n}(t) = [M_Y(t/sqrt(n))]^n converging to e^{t^2/2}.

    This is the direct numerical verification of the MGF proof of the CLT.
    """
    if ns is None:
        ns = [1, 2, 5, 10, 50]

    mu, sigma = rv.mean(), rv.std()
    rng       = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    t_vals    = np.linspace(t_range[0], t_range[1], 200)

    # Estimate M_Y(t) empirically from many samples of Y = (X - mu)/sigma
    n_est  = 500_000
    Y_samp = (rv.rvs(size=n_est, random_state=rng) - mu) / sigma

    fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 5.5))
    colors = plt.cm.viridis(np.linspace(0.1, 0.8, len(ns)))

    # Left: MGF of Z_n vs target e^{t^2/2}
    ax1.plot(t_vals, np.exp(t_vals**2 / 2), 'k-', lw=2.5, label="$e^{t^2/2}$ — $\\mathcal{N}(0,1)$ MGF")

    for n, col in zip(ns, colors):
        # Monte Carlo estimate of M_{Z_n}(t) = E[e^{tZ_n}]
        # Z_n = (1/sqrt(n)) * sum(Y_i) → we estimate using the standardized samples
        # Approximate via: [mean(e^{t*Y/sqrt(n)})]^n
        mgf_Zn = np.array([
            np.mean(np.exp(t / np.sqrt(n) * Y_samp))**n
            for t in t_vals
        ])
        ax1.plot(t_vals, mgf_Zn, lw=1.8, color=col, alpha=0.85,
                 label=f"$M_{{Z_{{n={n}}}}}(t)$")

    ax1.set_xlabel("$t$", fontsize=12)
    ax1.set_ylabel("MGF value", fontsize=12)
    ax1.set_title("MGF Convergence: $M_{Z_n}(t) \\to e^{t^2/2}$",
                  fontsize=12, fontweight='bold')
    ax1.legend(fontsize=9); ax1.grid(alpha=0.3); ax1.set_ylim(0, 8)

    # Right: Taylor approximation quality — show [1 + t²/(2n)]^n vs e^{t²/2}
    t_pos  = np.linspace(0, 2, 200)
    target = np.exp(t_pos**2 / 2)
    ax2.plot(t_pos, target, 'k-', lw=2.5, label="$e^{t^2/2}$ (limit)")

    for n, col in zip(ns, colors):
        # This is step 3 of the proof: (1 + t²/2n)^n
        approx = (1 + t_pos**2 / (2*n))**n
        ax2.plot(t_pos, approx, lw=1.8, color=col, alpha=0.85,
                 label=f"$(1 + t^2/2n)^n$,  n={n}")

    ax2.set_xlabel("$t$", fontsize=12)
    ax2.set_ylabel("Value", fontsize=12)
    ax2.set_title("CLT Proof Step 3: $(1 + t^2/2n)^n \\to e^{t^2/2}$",
                  fontsize=12, fontweight='bold')
    ax2.legend(fontsize=9); ax2.grid(alpha=0.3)

    plt.suptitle(f"MGF Convergence Proof of CLT  [{rv_name}]",
                 fontsize=13, fontweight='bold', y=1.01)
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.savefig("module5_mgf_convergence.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches='tight')
    plt.show()
    print("Saved: module5_mgf_convergence.png")


# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# PART D: SGD Gradient Noise — CLT in Action
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def sgd_gradient_noise_analysis(
    true_gradient: float = 0.5,
    gradient_std:  float = 2.0,
    batch_sizes:   list  = None,
    n_estimates:   int   = 10_000,
    seed:          int   = 42
):
    """
    Simulates mini-batch gradient estimates for a model where the per-sample
    gradient is Exponential (skewed, non-Gaussian) distributed.

    Demonstrates that the averaged mini-batch gradient is approximately Gaussian
    by CLT (Equation 5.17), regardless of per-sample gradient distribution.
    """
    if batch_sizes is None:
        batch_sizes = [1, 4, 16, 64, 256]

    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    # Per-sample gradients: shifted Exponential so mean = true_gradient
    lam     = 1 / gradient_std  # Exponential rate
    shift   = true_gradient - gradient_std  # shift so mean = true_gradient

    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, len(batch_sizes), figsize=(4 * len(batch_sizes), 4.5),
                              sharey=False)
    x_ref = np.linspace(-3, 3, 300)

    for ax, B in zip(axes, batch_sizes):
        # Simulate n_estimates mini-batch gradient estimates of batch size B
        per_sample = rng.exponential(scale=gradient_std, size=(n_estimates, B)) + shift
        batch_grads = per_sample.mean(axis=1)  # Mini-batch average

        # Standardize: Z = (g_hat - g) / (sigma_g / sqrt(B))
        Z = (batch_grads - true_gradient) / (gradient_std / np.sqrt(B))

        ax.hist(Z, bins=60, density=True, alpha=0.6, color='#1a6faf',
                label=f"B={B}")
        ax.plot(x_ref, stats.norm.pdf(x_ref), 'r-', lw=2, label="$\\mathcal{N}(0,1)$")

        ks, _ = stats.kstest(Z, 'norm')
        ax.set_title(f"Batch size B={B}\nKS={ks:.4f}", fontsize=10, fontweight='bold')
        ax.set_xlabel("Standardized $\\hat{g}_B$", fontsize=10)
        if B == batch_sizes[0]:
            ax.set_ylabel("Density", fontsize=10)
        ax.legend(fontsize=8); ax.grid(alpha=0.3)
        ax.set_xlim(-4, 4)

    plt.suptitle("CLT for Mini-Batch Gradients\n"
                 "(Per-sample gradients: Exponential — heavily skewed)",
                 fontsize=12, fontweight='bold', y=1.02)
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.savefig("module5_sgd_clt.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches='tight')
    plt.show()
    print("Saved: module5_sgd_clt.png")

# MAIN
# =============================================================================

if __name__ == "__main__":

    # --- A: LLN for three distributions ---
    print("="*60)

    print("="*60)
    distributions = [
```

Here is **Module 6** of the Mastery Handbook — the module where probability theory becomes machine learning. Every training algorithm you have ever used is secretly an instance of the theory developed here.

---

# MODULE 6: Estimation Theory — MLE & MAP

---

## 6.1 Conceptual Overview

### The Estimation Problem

In every supervised learning problem, we observe data $\mathcal{D} = {(x_1, y_1), \ldots, (x_n, y_n)}$ and wish to infer the parameters $\theta$ of a model that generated it. But _how_ should we infer $\theta$? What principle should guide us?

This question — the fundamental question of statistical inference — has two canonical answers:

The **frequentist answer** is Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE): choose $\theta$ that makes the observed data _most probable_ under the model. No prior beliefs, no subjective information — only the data speaks.

The **Bayesian answer** is Maximum A Posteriori Estimation (MAP): choose $\theta$ that maximizes the posterior distribution $P(\theta \mid \mathcal{D})$. This combines the likelihood with a prior belief about $\theta$.

These are not merely philosophical preferences — they lead to mathematically distinct estimators with different properties. And as we will prove, **every regularized objective in machine learning is MAP estimation in disguise**:

|ML Algorithm|Loss + Regularizer|Probabilistic Equivalent|
|---|---|---|
|Linear regression|MSE|MLE under Gaussian noise|
|Ridge regression|MSE + L2|MAP with Gaussian prior on $\theta$|
|Lasso regression|MSE + L1|MAP with Laplace prior on $\theta$|
|Logistic regression|Cross-entropy|MLE under Bernoulli likelihood|
|Logistic + L2 reg.|Cross-entropy + L2|MAP with Gaussian prior|
|Neural net (dropout)|—|Approximate Bayes|

Understanding this correspondence transforms regularization from a mysterious trick that "prevents overfitting" into a principled statement about your prior beliefs. The strength of regularization encodes your uncertainty about the parameters _before_ seeing the data.

### The Fisher Information and the Cramér-Rao Bound

Beyond finding estimates, we need to know how _good_ our estimates are. The **Fisher information** — the central object of estimation theory — quantifies how much information the data carries about the parameters. The **Cramér-Rao bound** then establishes the fundamental limit: no unbiased estimator can have variance smaller than the reciprocal of the Fisher information. This is the statistical analog of the Heisenberg uncertainty principle — there is an irreducible floor on estimation error imposed by the data-generating process itself.

---

## 6.2 Mathematical Formalization

### 6.2.1 The Likelihood Function

> **Definition 6.1 (Likelihood Function):** Given a parametric model $p(x \mid \theta)$ and i.i.d. observations $\mathcal{D} = {x_1, \ldots, x_n}$, the **likelihood function** is: $$\mathcal{L}(\theta; \mathcal{D}) = \prod_{i=1}^n p(x_i \mid \theta) \tag{6.1}$$

The likelihood $\mathcal{L}(\theta; \mathcal{D})$ is a function of $\theta$ for fixed data — it measures how compatible the parameter value $\theta$ is with the observed data. It is _not_ a probability distribution over $\theta$ (it does not integrate to 1 over $\theta$).

For computational convenience, we work with the **log-likelihood**: $$\ell(\theta; \mathcal{D}) = \log \mathcal{L}(\theta; \mathcal{D}) = \sum_{i=1}^n \log p(x_i \mid \theta) \tag{6.2}$$

The log transformation: (1) converts products to sums, enabling calculus; (2) is monotone, so maximizing $\ell$ is equivalent to maximizing $\mathcal{L}$; (3) prevents numerical underflow from multiplying many small probabilities.

---

### 6.2.2 Maximum Likelihood Estimation

> **Definition 6.2 (MLE):** The **maximum likelihood estimator** is: $$\hat{\theta}_{\text{MLE}} = \arg\max_{\theta} \ell(\theta; \mathcal{D}) = \arg\max_{\theta} \sum_{i=1}^n \log p(x_i \mid \theta) \tag{6.3}$$

**Derivation: MLE as minimizing KL divergence.** Define the empirical distribution $\hat{p}(x) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \delta(x - x_i)$. Then:

$$\frac{1}{n}\ell(\theta) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i \log p(x_i\mid\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{\hat{p}}[\log p(x\mid\theta)]$$

The KL divergence from $\hat{p}$ to $p(\cdot\mid\theta)$ is: $$D_{KL}(\hat{p} ,|, p(\cdot\mid\theta)) = \mathbb{E}_{\hat{p}}[\log\hat{p}(x)] - \mathbb{E}_{\hat{p}}[\log p(x\mid\theta)]$$

Since $\mathbb{E}_{\hat{p}}[\log\hat{p}]$ does not depend on $\theta$, minimizing $D_{KL}(\hat{p},|,p(\cdot\mid\theta))$ is equivalent to maximizing $\mathbb{E}_{\hat{p}}[\log p(x\mid\theta)]$, which is the MLE.

$$\boxed{\hat{\theta}_{\text{MLE}} = \arg\min_{\theta} D_{KL}(\hat{p} ,|, p(\cdot\mid\theta))} \tag{6.4}$$

The MLE is the parameter value that makes the model distribution _closest_ (in KL divergence) to the empirical distribution of the data. This is a profound geometric interpretation.

---

### 6.2.3 The Score Function and Fisher Information

> **Definition 6.3 (Score Function):** The **score** is the gradient of the log-likelihood with respect to $\theta$: $$s(\theta; x) = \nabla_\theta \log p(x \mid \theta) \tag{6.5}$$

**Key property of the score — zero mean under the true distribution:**

> **Theorem 6.1:** Under regularity conditions (interchange of differentiation and integration): $$\mathbb{E}_\theta[s(\theta; X)] = 0 \tag{6.6}$$

**Proof:** Differentiate the normalization identity $\int p(x\mid\theta),dx = 1$ with respect to $\theta$: $$\int \frac{\partial}{\partial\theta} p(x\mid\theta),dx = 0$$ $$\int \frac{\partial \log p(x\mid\theta)}{\partial\theta} \cdot p(x\mid\theta),dx = 0$$ $$\mathbb{E}_\theta!\left[\frac{\partial \log p(x\mid\theta)}{\partial\theta}\right] = 0 \qquad \blacksquare$$

> **Definition 6.4 (Fisher Information):** The **Fisher information** is the variance of the score: $$\mathcal{I}(\theta) = \text{Var}_\theta!\left[s(\theta; X)\right] = \mathbb{E}_\theta!\left[s(\theta; X)^2\right] \tag{6.7}$$

Since the score has zero mean (Theorem 6.1), $\mathcal{I}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}[s^2]$.

**Alternative form — the expected negative Hessian:**

> **Theorem 6.2 (Fisher Information — Hessian Form):** $$\mathcal{I}(\theta) = -\mathbb{E}_\theta!\left[\frac{\partial^2 \log p(x\mid\theta)}{\partial\theta^2}\right] \tag{6.8}$$

**Proof:** Differentiate the score identity $\mathbb{E}[\partial_\theta \log p] = 0$ again with respect to $\theta$: $$\mathbb{E}!\left[\frac{\partial^2 \log p}{\partial\theta^2}\right] + \mathbb{E}!\left[\left(\frac{\partial \log p}{\partial\theta}\right)^2\right] = 0$$

This gives $-\mathbb{E}[\partial^2_\theta \log p] = \mathbb{E}[(\partial_\theta \log p)^2] = \mathcal{I}(\theta)$. $\blacksquare$

The Hessian form is crucial: it says the Fisher information measures the _curvature_ of the log-likelihood at $\theta$. High curvature means the log-likelihood has a sharp peak at $\theta$ — small changes in $\theta$ dramatically change the likelihood — and therefore we can estimate $\theta$ precisely. Low curvature means a flat likelihood, and estimation is difficult. Fisher information = information in the literal sense.

---

### 6.2.4 The Cramér-Rao Lower Bound

This theorem establishes the fundamental limit of estimation — no matter how clever your estimator is, you cannot beat this bound.

> **Theorem 6.3 (Cramér-Rao Lower Bound):** For any **unbiased** estimator $\hat{\theta}(X_1,\ldots,X_n)$ of $\theta$ (i.e., $\mathbb{E}[\hat{\theta}] = \theta$): $$\text{Var}(\hat{\theta}) \geq \frac{1}{n,\mathcal{I}(\theta)} \tag{6.9}$$

**Proof using the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality:**

For a single observation. Consider the covariance between $\hat{\theta}(X)$ and the score $s(\theta; X)$: $$\text{Cov}(\hat{\theta}, s) = \mathbb{E}[\hat{\theta} \cdot s] - \mathbb{E}[\hat{\theta}],\mathbb{E}[s] = \mathbb{E}[\hat{\theta} \cdot s]$$

since $\mathbb{E}[s]=0$. Differentiating the unbiasedness condition $\mathbb{E}[\hat{\theta}] = \int \hat{\theta}(x) p(x\mid\theta),dx = \theta$ with respect to $\theta$: $$\int \hat{\theta}(x) \frac{\partial \log p}{\partial\theta} p(x\mid\theta),dx = 1$$ $$\mathbb{E}[\hat{\theta} \cdot s(\theta;X)] = 1$$

So $\text{Cov}(\hat{\theta}, s) = 1$. The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality gives: $$1 = \text{Cov}(\hat{\theta}, s)^2 \leq \text{Var}(\hat{\theta}) \cdot \text{Var}(s) = \text{Var}(\hat{\theta}) \cdot \mathcal{I}(\theta)$$

Therefore $\text{Var}(\hat{\theta}) \geq 1/\mathcal{I}(\theta)$. For $n$ i.i.d. observations, Fisher information adds: $\mathcal{I}_n(\theta) = n\mathcal{I}(\theta)$, giving $\text{Var}(\hat{\theta}) \geq 1/(n\mathcal{I}(\theta))$. $\blacksquare$

An estimator achieving this bound exactly is called **efficient**. The remarkable asymptotic result:

> **Theorem 6.4 (Asymptotic Efficiency of MLE):** Under regularity conditions, the MLE is asymptotically unbiased and achieves the Cramér-Rao bound: $$\sqrt{n}(\hat{\theta}_{\text{MLE}} - \theta) \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}!\left(0,; \frac{1}{\mathcal{I}(\theta)}\right) \tag{6.10}$$

This is the multivariate CLT (Theorem 5.6) applied to the score function, combined with a Taylor expansion of the score equation. The MLE is not just consistent — it is asymptotically the _best possible_ unbiased estimator.

---

### 6.2.5 MLE Examples — Deriving Estimators from First Principles

**Example A: MLE for Gaussian mean (known variance)**

$X_i \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)$, $\sigma^2$ known. Log-likelihood: $$\ell(\mu) = -\frac{n}{2}\log(2\pi\sigma^2) - \frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \mu)^2$$

Setting $\partial\ell/\partial\mu = 0$: $$\frac{1}{\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \mu) = 0 \implies \hat{\mu}_{\text{MLE}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n x_i = \bar{x} \tag{6.11}$$

The sample mean is the MLE for the Gaussian mean. Fisher information: $$\mathcal{I}(\mu) = -\mathbb{E}!\left[\frac{\partial^2 \log p}{\partial\mu^2}\right] = \frac{1}{\sigma^2}$$

CR bound: $\text{Var}(\hat{\mu}) \geq \sigma^2/n$. The sample mean achieves this exactly — it is efficient.

**Example B: MLE for Bernoulli parameter**

$X_i \sim \text{Bernoulli}(p)$. Log-likelihood: $$\ell(p) = \sum_i x_i \log p + (1-x_i)\log(1-p)$$

Setting $\partial\ell/\partial p = 0$: $$\frac{\sum x_i}{p} - \frac{n - \sum x_i}{1-p} = 0 \implies \hat{p}_{\text{MLE}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n x_i \tag{6.12}$$

The sample proportion is the MLE for the Bernoulli parameter.

**Example C: MLE for Poisson rate**

$X_i \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda)$. Log-likelihood: $$\ell(\lambda) = -n\lambda + \left(\sum_i x_i\right)\log\lambda - \sum_i \log(x_i!)$$

Setting $\partial\ell/\partial\lambda = 0$: $\hat{\lambda}_{\text{MLE}} = \bar{x}$ — again the sample mean.

---

### 6.2.6 MAP Estimation

> **Definition 6.5 (MAP Estimator):** The **Maximum A Posteriori** estimator is: $$\hat{\theta}_{\text{MAP}} = \arg\max_{\theta} P(\theta \mid \mathcal{D}) = \arg\max_{\theta}!\left[\log p(\mathcal{D}\mid\theta) + \log p(\theta)\right] \tag{6.13}$$

The MAP objective is the log-likelihood plus the log-prior. This is nothing other than a regularized log-likelihood, where the regularizer is $\log p(\theta)$.

**MAP = MLE + log-prior regularization:** $$\hat{\theta}_{\text{MAP}} = \arg\max_{\theta}\underbrace{\sum_{i=1}^n \log p(x_i\mid\theta)}_{\text{log-likelihood (data fit)}} + \underbrace{\log p(\theta)}_{\text{log-prior (regularizer)}} \tag{6.14}$$

---

### 6.2.7 The Prior-Regularizer Dictionary

This is the central translation table between Bayesian statistics and ML optimization.

**Ridge Regression = MAP with Gaussian Prior:**

Gaussian prior: $\theta \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \tau^2\mathbf{I})$. Then: $$\log p(\theta) = -\frac{|\theta|^2}{2\tau^2} + \text{const}$$

MAP objective (Gaussian likelihood + Gaussian prior): $$\hat{\theta}_{\text{MAP}} = \arg\min_\theta \underbrace{|\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{X}\theta|^2}_{\text{MSE (negative log-likelihood)}} + \underbrace{\frac{\sigma^2}{\tau^2}|\theta|^2}_{L_2 \text{ regularizer}} \tag{6.15}$$

The regularization coefficient $\lambda = \sigma^2/\tau^2$ encodes the ratio of noise variance to prior variance. A strong prior (small $\tau^2$) → large $\lambda$ → heavy regularization.

**Lasso = MAP with Laplace Prior:**

Laplace prior: $p(\theta_j) = \frac{\lambda}{2}\exp(-\lambda|\theta_j|)$. Then: $$\log p(\theta) = -\lambda|\theta|_1 + \text{const}$$

MAP objective: $$\hat{\theta}_{\text{MAP}} = \arg\min_\theta |\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{X}\theta|^2 + \frac{2\sigma^2}{\lambda}|\theta|_1 \tag{6.16}$$

Lasso's sparsity-inducing property comes directly from the sharp peak at zero of the Laplace prior — it assigns relatively high probability to sparse solutions.

**Summary — prior to regularizer correspondence:**

|Prior $p(\theta)$|Log-prior $\log p(\theta)$|Regularizer|ML Name|
|---|---|---|---|
|$\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \tau^2\mathbf{I})$|$-\frac{1}{2\tau^2}\|\theta\|^2$|$\lambda\|\theta\|_2^2$|Ridge / Weight decay|
|$\text{Laplace}(0, b)$|$-\frac{1}{b}\|\theta\|_1$|$\lambda\|\theta\|_1$|Lasso|
|Elastic Net|Mixture|$\lambda_1\|\theta\|_1 + \lambda_2\|\theta\|_2^2$|Elastic Net|
|$\text{Uniform}$|Constant|$0$ (no regularization)|Pure MLE|

---

### 6.2.8 Asymptotic Properties of MAP

As $n \to \infty$, the data overwhelms the prior: $\hat{\theta}_{\text{MAP}} \to \hat{\theta}_{\text{MLE}}$. This follows because the log-likelihood grows as $O(n)$ while the log-prior is $O(1)$. For large datasets, the prior becomes irrelevant — the regularization term is swamped by the data.

This is the Bayesian justification for why regularization matters most with small datasets and becomes less important as $n \to \infty$.

---

### 6.2.9 The EM Algorithm (Expectation-Maximization)

When data has **latent (hidden) variables** $Z$, direct MLE is often intractable. The EM algorithm is an iterative procedure that converges to the MLE by alternating between two steps.

**Setup:** Observed data $\mathbf{X}$, latent variables $\mathbf{Z}$, parameters $\theta$. We want: $$\hat{\theta} = \arg\max_\theta \log p(\mathbf{X}\mid\theta) = \arg\max_\theta \log \int p(\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Z}\mid\theta),d\mathbf{Z}$$

The log of an integral is intractable. EM introduces a lower bound via Jensen's inequality:

**ELBO derivation:**

For any distribution $q(\mathbf{Z})$: $$\log p(\mathbf{X}\mid\theta) = \log \int \frac{p(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Z}\mid\theta)}{q(\mathbf{Z})} q(\mathbf{Z}),d\mathbf{Z} \geq \int q(\mathbf{Z}) \log\frac{p(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Z}\mid\theta)}{q(\mathbf{Z})},d\mathbf{Z} = \mathcal{L}(q,\theta) \tag{6.17}$$

by Jensen's inequality ($\log$ is concave, so $\log\mathbb{E}[X] \geq \mathbb{E}[\log X]$).

> **Algorithm 6.1 (EM):**
> 
> **E-step:** Fix $\theta^{(t)}$. Compute: $$Q(\theta, \theta^{(t)}) = \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{Z}\mid\mathbf{X},\theta^{(t)}}!\left[\log p(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Z}\mid\theta)\right] \tag{6.18}$$
> 
> **M-step:** Maximize: $$\theta^{(t+1)} = \arg\max_\theta Q(\theta, \theta^{(t)}) \tag{6.19}$$

**Convergence guarantee:** $\ell(\theta^{(t+1)}) \geq \ell(\theta^{(t)})$ — the log-likelihood is guaranteed to be non-decreasing at every step.

**ML role:** EM is the foundation of Gaussian Mixture Models (GMMs), Hidden Markov Models (HMMs), and is the conceptual precursor to variational inference and the ELBO in VAEs.

---

## 6.3 Numerical Examples

### Example 6.1: Gaussian MLE — Full Derivation

**Problem:** $n=5$ observations: $\mathcal{D} = {2.1, 3.4, 2.8, 3.1, 2.6}$. Fit $\mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)$. Find $\hat{\mu}_{\text{MLE}}$ and $\hat{\sigma}^2_{\text{MLE}}$.

**Solution:**

Log-likelihood for Gaussian: $$\ell(\mu, \sigma^2) = -\frac{n}{2}\log(2\pi) - \frac{n}{2}\log\sigma^2 - \frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\mu)^2$$

**Step 1 — Score for $\mu$:** $$\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial\mu} = \frac{1}{\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\mu) = 0 \implies \hat{\mu} = \bar{x} = \frac{2.1+3.4+2.8+3.1+2.6}{5} = 2.8$$

**Step 2 — Score for $\sigma^2$:** $$\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial\sigma^2} = -\frac{n}{2\sigma^2} + \frac{1}{2\sigma^4}\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\hat{\mu})^2 = 0$$ $$\implies \hat{\sigma}^2 = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\hat{\mu})^2 = \frac{(-0.7)^2+(0.6)^2+(0)^2+(0.3)^2+(-0.2)^2}{5} = \frac{0.49+0.36+0+0.09+0.04}{5} = \frac{0.98}{5} = \boxed{0.196}$$

Note: the MLE for $\sigma^2$ divides by $n$, not $n-1$. It is **biased** — $\mathbb{E}[\hat{\sigma}^2_{\text{MLE}}] = \frac{n-1}{n}\sigma^2$. The unbiased sample variance $S^2 = \frac{1}{n-1}\sum(x_i-\bar{x})^2$ corrects for this bias. This is a key distinction: MLE optimizes likelihood but can be biased; unbiasedness is a separate desideratum.

---

### Example 6.2: MAP = Ridge Regression — Explicit Computation

**Problem:** Single predictor, 3 observations: $(x, y) \in {(1, 2.5), (2, 4.2), (3, 5.8)}$. Model: $y = \theta x + \varepsilon$, $\varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)$. Prior: $\theta \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \tau^2 = 4)$.

**MLE (no regularization):**

$$\hat{\theta}_{\text{MLE}} = \frac{\sum x_i y_i}{\sum x_i^2} = \frac{1(2.5)+2(4.2)+3(5.8)}{1^2+2^2+3^2} = \frac{2.5+8.4+17.4}{14} = \frac{28.3}{14} \approx 2.021$$

**MAP (with Gaussian prior):**

From equation (6.15) with $\sigma^2=1$, $\tau^2=4$, $\lambda = \sigma^2/\tau^2 = 0.25$: $$\hat{\theta}_{\text{MAP}} = \arg\min_\theta \sum_i(y_i - \theta x_i)^2 + 0.25\theta^2$$

Taking the derivative and setting to zero: $$-2\sum x_i(y_i - \theta x_i) + 0.5\theta = 0$$ $$\theta!\left(\sum x_i^2 + 0.25\right) = \sum x_i y_i$$ $$\hat{\theta}_{\text{MAP}} = \frac{28.3}{14 + 0.25} = \frac{28.3}{14.25} \approx \boxed{1.986}$$

The prior has pulled $\hat{\theta}$ slightly toward zero. With $\tau^2 = 4$ (moderately informative prior), the effect is small. With $\tau^2 = 0.1$ (very strong prior), the MAP would be close to 0.

---

### Example 6.3: Fisher Information for Bernoulli

**Problem:** Compute the Fisher information $\mathcal{I}(p)$ for $X \sim \text{Bernoulli}(p)$ and verify the CR bound is achieved by the sample proportion.

**Solution:**

$$\log p(x\mid p) = x\log p + (1-x)\log(1-p)$$

Score: $s(p; x) = \frac{x}{p} - \frac{1-x}{1-p} = \frac{x-p}{p(1-p)}$

Fisher information (variance of score): $$\mathcal{I}(p) = \mathbb{E}!\left[\left(\frac{X-p}{p(1-p)}\right)^2\right] = \frac{\text{Var}(X)}{p^2(1-p)^2} = \frac{p(1-p)}{p^2(1-p)^2} = \boxed{\frac{1}{p(1-p)}}$$

CR bound for $n$ observations: $\text{Var}(\hat{p}) \geq \frac{1}{n\mathcal{I}(p)} = \frac{p(1-p)}{n}$

Actual variance of sample proportion $\hat{p} = \bar{X}$: $\text{Var}(\hat{p}) = \frac{p(1-p)}{n}$.

The sample proportion **achieves the CR bound exactly** — it is an efficient estimator for $p$. $\blacksquare$

---

## 6.4 Implementation

```python
import numpy as np
import scipy.stats as stats
import scipy.optimize as opt
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.gridspec as gridspec
from typing import Callable, Optional

# =============================================================================
# MODULE 6: Estimation Theory — MLE & MAP
# =============================================================================

# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# PART A: Generic MLE via Numerical Optimization + Analytical Verification
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------

class MaximumLikelihoodEstimator:
    """
    General-purpose MLE via numerical optimization of the log-likelihood.
    Compares numerical results to analytical MLEs where available.
    Computes Fisher information and verifies the Cramér-Rao bound.
    """

    def __init__(self, log_likelihood_fn: Callable, param_names: list):
        """
        Parameters
        ----------
        log_likelihood_fn : callable(theta, data) -> float (scalar log-likelihood)
        param_names       : list of parameter name strings
        """
        self.ll_fn       = log_likelihood_fn
        self.param_names = param_names

    def fit(self, data: np.ndarray, theta_init: np.ndarray,
            bounds: Optional[list] = None) -> dict:
        """
        Find MLE by minimizing the negative log-likelihood.
        Uses scipy's L-BFGS-B for bounded optimization.
        """
        neg_ll = lambda theta: -self.ll_fn(theta, data)

        result = opt.minimize(
            neg_ll,
            x0     = theta_init,
            method = 'L-BFGS-B',
            bounds = bounds,
            options= {'ftol': 1e-12, 'gtol': 1e-10, 'maxiter': 1000}
        )

        theta_hat = result.x
        ll_max    = -result.fun

        # --- Fisher Information via numerical Hessian of log-likelihood ---
        # I(theta) = -E[d²log p / dtheta²] ≈ -H(ell)/n  at theta_hat
        hess      = self._numerical_hessian(theta_hat, data)
        fisher_info = -hess / len(data)   # Per-observation Fisher info

        # Standard errors from inverse of observed Fisher information
        n = len(data)
        try:
            se = np.sqrt(np.diag(np.linalg.inv(-hess)))
        except np.linalg.LinAlgError:
            se = np.full(len(theta_hat), np.nan)

        return {
            "theta_hat":    theta_hat,
            "log_lik":      ll_max,
            "se":           se,
            "fisher_info":  fisher_info,
            "cr_bound":     1.0 / (n * np.diag(fisher_info)),
            "converged":    result.success,
        }

    def _numerical_hessian(self, theta: np.ndarray, data: np.ndarray,
                           eps: float = 1e-5) -> np.ndarray:
        """Compute Hessian of total log-likelihood numerically."""
        d    = len(theta)
        hess = np.zeros((d, d))
        ll0  = self.ll_fn(theta, data)

        for i in range(d):
            for j in range(i, d):
                ei = np.zeros(d); ei[i] = eps
                ej = np.zeros(d); ej[j] = eps
                ll_ij = self.ll_fn(theta + ei + ej, data)
                ll_i  = self.ll_fn(theta + ei, data)
                ll_j  = self.ll_fn(theta + ej, data)
                h     = (ll_ij - ll_i - ll_j + ll0) / eps**2
                hess[i, j] = hess[j, i] = h

        return hess

    def profile_likelihood(self, data: np.ndarray, param_idx: int,
                           theta_hat: np.ndarray, n_points: int = 60) -> tuple:
        """
        Compute the profile log-likelihood for parameter param_idx,
        optimizing over all other parameters at each fixed value.
        Returns (param_values, profile_ll) for plotting.
        """
        se_approx = 0.3  # rough scale for grid
        lo = theta_hat[param_idx] - 3 * se_approx
        hi = theta_hat[param_idx] + 3 * se_approx
        grid   = np.linspace(lo, hi, n_points)
        pll    = np.zeros(n_points)
        n_free = len(theta_hat) - 1

        for k, val in enumerate(grid):
            if n_free == 0:
                pll[k] = self.ll_fn(np.array([val]), data)
            else:
                # Fix param_idx = val, optimize over others
                others_init = np.delete(theta_hat, param_idx)
                def neg_pll(others):
                    theta = np.insert(others, param_idx, val)
                    return -self.ll_fn(theta, data)
                res  = opt.minimize(neg_pll, others_init, method='Nelder-Mead',
                                    options={'xatol':1e-8,'fatol':1e-8,'maxiter':1000})
                pll[k] = -res.fun

        return grid, pll

    def print_summary(self, result: dict, analytical: Optional[dict] = None):
        """Print a structured MLE summary table."""
        n = len(self.param_names)
        print("\n" + "="*62)
        print("  MLE ESTIMATION SUMMARY")
        print("="*62)
        header = f"{'Parameter':<15} {'MLE':>10} {'Std Error':>12} {'CR Bound':>12}"
        if analytical:
            header += f"  {'Analytical':>12}"
        print(f"\n{header}")
        print("-"*62)
        for i, name in enumerate(self.param_names):
            row = (f"  {name:<13} {result['theta_hat'][i]:>10.5f} "
                   f"{result['se'][i]:>12.6f} "
                   f"{np.sqrt(result['cr_bound'][i]):>12.6f}")
            if analytical and name in analytical:
                row += f"  {analytical[name]:>12.5f}"
            print(row)
        print(f"\n  Log-likelihood at MLE: {result['log_lik']:.4f}")
        print(f"  Converged: {result['converged']}")
        print("="*62)


# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# PART B: MAP Estimation — Ridge vs Lasso vs MLE Comparison
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def map_vs_mle_comparison(
    n_features: int  = 10,
    n_samples:  int  = 30,
    true_sparse: bool = True,
    noise_std:   float = 1.0,
    seed:        int  = 42
):
    """
    Compares MLE (OLS), Ridge (MAP + Gaussian prior), and Lasso (MAP + Laplace prior)
    on a regression problem with sparse true coefficients.

    Demonstrates Eq. 6.15 and 6.16: regularization = prior log-probability.
    """
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)

    # True coefficients: sparse (many zeros)
    if true_sparse:
        theta_true = np.zeros(n_features)
        theta_true[:3] = [2.0, -1.5, 1.0]  # Only 3 active features
    else:
        theta_true = rng.normal(0, 1, n_features)

    # Generate data
    X = rng.normal(0, 1, (n_samples, n_features))
    y = X @ theta_true + rng.normal(0, noise_std, n_samples)

    # --- MLE (ordinary least squares) ---
    if n_samples >= n_features:
        theta_mle = np.linalg.lstsq(X, y, rcond=None)[0]
    else:
        theta_mle = np.full(n_features, np.nan)

    # --- Ridge (MAP: Gaussian prior, L2 regularization) ---
    # theta_MAP_ridge = argmin ||y - Xtheta||^2 + lambda ||theta||^2
    # Analytical: (X^T X + lambda I)^{-1} X^T y
    lambda_ridge = 1.0  # corresponds to prior variance tau^2 = noise^2 / lambda
    theta_ridge  = np.linalg.solve(
        X.T @ X + lambda_ridge * np.eye(n_features),
        X.T @ y
    )

    # --- Lasso (MAP: Laplace prior, L1 regularization) ---
    # Solved via coordinate descent (scipy/sklearn)
    from sklearn.linear_model import Lasso, Ridge
    lasso = Lasso(alpha=0.5, fit_intercept=False, max_iter=10000)
    lasso.fit(X, y)
    theta_lasso = lasso.coef_

    # Compute test MSE
    n_test    = 1000
    X_test    = rng.normal(0, 1, (n_test, n_features))
    y_test    = X_test @ theta_true + rng.normal(0, noise_std, n_test)

    def test_mse(theta):
        return np.mean((y_test - X_test @ theta)**2)

    print(f"\n{'Method':<15} {'Test MSE':>10} {'||theta||_1':>12} {'Nonzero':>10}")
    print("-"*50)
    estimators = [("MLE (OLS)", theta_mle), ("Ridge (MAP)", theta_ridge),
                  ("Lasso (MAP)", theta_lasso)]
    for name, theta in estimators:
        if np.any(np.isnan(theta)):
            print(f"  {name:<13} {'N/A (underdetermined)':>30}")
        else:
            mse   = test_mse(theta)
            l1    = np.sum(np.abs(theta))
            nz    = np.sum(np.abs(theta) > 0.01)
            print(f"  {name:<13} {mse:>10.4f} {l1:>12.4f} {nz:>10}")

    # --- Plot coefficient comparison ---
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(14, 4.5), sharey=True)
    feat_idx  = np.arange(n_features)

    for ax, (name, theta, color) in zip(axes, [
        ("True coefficients", theta_true, '#2ca02c'),
        ("Ridge MAP (L2 prior)", theta_ridge, '#1a6faf'),
        ("Lasso MAP (L1 prior)", theta_lasso, '#e84040'),
    ]):
        ax.bar(feat_idx, theta, color=color, alpha=0.75, edgecolor='white', lw=0.5)
        if not np.any(np.isnan(theta_mle)):
            ax.scatter(feat_idx, theta_mle, s=40, color='black', zorder=5,
                       marker='x', linewidths=1.5, label="MLE" if ax == axes[1] else "")
        ax.axhline(0, color='black', lw=0.8)
        ax.set_title(name, fontsize=12, fontweight='bold')
        ax.set_xlabel("Feature index", fontsize=11)
        ax.grid(axis='y', alpha=0.3)

    axes[0].set_ylabel("Coefficient value", fontsize=11)
    axes[1].legend(fontsize=9)
    plt.suptitle("MLE vs MAP Estimation: Effect of Prior (Regularizer)",
                 fontsize=13, fontweight='bold', y=1.01)
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.savefig("module6_map_vs_mle.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches='tight')
    plt.show()
    print("Saved: module6_map_vs_mle.png")


# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# PART C: Likelihood Surface + Cramér-Rao Bound Visualization
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def visualize_likelihood_and_cr_bound(seed: int = 42):
    """
    Visualizes the log-likelihood surface for a Gaussian model,
    shows MLE location, and demonstrates the CR bound via repeated estimation.
    """
    rng        = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    true_mu    = 2.0
    true_sigma = 1.5
    n          = 50
    n_reps     = 2000

    # --- Panel 1: Log-likelihood surface ---
    fig = plt.figure(figsize=(15, 5))
    gs  = gridspec.GridSpec(1, 3, wspace=0.38)

    ax1   = fig.add_subplot(gs[0])
    data  = rng.normal(true_mu, true_sigma, n)
    mu_grid    = np.linspace(0, 4, 200)
    sigma_grid = np.linspace(0.5, 3.5, 200)
    MU, SIG    = np.meshgrid(mu_grid, sigma_grid)

    # Compute log-likelihood on grid
    LL = np.zeros_like(MU)
    for i in range(200):
        for j in range(200):
            LL[i,j] = np.sum(stats.norm.logpdf(data, MU[i,j], SIG[i,j]))

    cf = ax1.contourf(MU, SIG, LL, levels=25, cmap='Blues')
    ax1.contour(MU, SIG, LL, levels=10, colors='navy', linewidths=0.5, alpha=0.4)
    plt.colorbar(cf, ax=ax1, label="Log-likelihood")

    # MLE
    mle_mu    = data.mean()
    mle_sigma = data.std(ddof=0)
    ax1.scatter([mle_mu], [mle_sigma], s=120, color='red', zorder=6,
                marker='*', label=f"MLE (μ={mle_mu:.2f}, σ={mle_sigma:.2f})")
    ax1.scatter([true_mu], [true_sigma], s=80, color='lime', zorder=6,
                marker='+', linewidths=2, label=f"True (μ={true_mu}, σ={true_sigma})")
    ax1.set_xlabel("μ", fontsize=12); ax1.set_ylabel("σ", fontsize=12)
    ax1.set_title("Log-likelihood surface\n$\\mathcal{N}(\\mu, \\sigma^2)$, n=50",
                  fontsize=11, fontweight='bold')
    ax1.legend(fontsize=9)

    # --- Panel 2: Sampling distribution of MLE vs CR bound ---
    ax2 = fig.add_subplot(gs[1])
    mu_hats = []
    for _ in range(n_reps):
        samp     = rng.normal(true_mu, true_sigma, n)
        mu_hats.append(samp.mean())

    mu_hats = np.array(mu_hats)
    cr_bound_std = true_sigma / np.sqrt(n)  # CR bound std = sigma/sqrt(n)
    empirical_std = mu_hats.std()

    ax2.hist(mu_hats, bins=60, density=True, alpha=0.6, color='#1a6faf',
             label=f"Empirical (std={empirical_std:.4f})")
    x_ref = np.linspace(true_mu - 4*cr_bound_std, true_mu + 4*cr_bound_std, 300)
    ax2.plot(x_ref, stats.norm.pdf(x_ref, true_mu, cr_bound_std),
             'r-', lw=2.5, label=f"CR bound N(μ, σ²/n)\nstd={cr_bound_std:.4f}")
    ax2.axvline(true_mu, color='green', lw=1.5, linestyle='--', label="True μ")
    ax2.set_xlabel("$\\hat{\\mu}_{MLE}$", fontsize=12)
    ax2.set_title(f"MLE sampling distribution\n(n={n}, {n_reps} reps)",
                  fontsize=11, fontweight='bold')
    ax2.legend(fontsize=9); ax2.grid(alpha=0.3)

    # --- Panel 3: CR bound vs n —— efficiency visualization ---
    ax3    = fig.add_subplot(gs[2])
    ns_arr = np.array([5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 200, 500])

    empirical_vars = []
    for n_val in ns_arr:
        mu_h = [rng.normal(true_mu, true_sigma, n_val).mean() for _ in range(n_reps)]
        empirical_vars.append(np.var(mu_h))

    cr_vars = true_sigma**2 / ns_arr

    ax3.loglog(ns_arr, empirical_vars, 'o-', color='#1a6faf', lw=2,
               ms=6, label="Empirical Var($\\hat{\\mu}$)")
    ax3.loglog(ns_arr, cr_vars, 'r--', lw=2, label="CR Bound = σ²/n")
    ax3.set_xlabel("Sample size n", fontsize=12)
    ax3.set_ylabel("Variance of $\\hat{\\mu}$", fontsize=12)
    ax3.set_title("Cramér-Rao Bound Achieved\nby Sample Mean",
                  fontsize=11, fontweight='bold')
    ax3.legend(fontsize=10); ax3.grid(alpha=0.3, which='both')

    plt.suptitle("Maximum Likelihood Estimation: Likelihood Surface & Cramér-Rao Bound",
                 fontsize=13, fontweight='bold', y=1.02)
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.savefig("module6_likelihood_cr.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches='tight')
    plt.show()
    print("Saved: module6_likelihood_cr.png")


# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# PART D: EM Algorithm for Gaussian Mixture Models
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def em_gmm(data: np.ndarray, K: int, n_iter: int = 100, seed: int = 42,
           tol: float = 1e-6) -> dict:
    """
    EM algorithm for a K-component Gaussian Mixture Model.
    Implements Equations 6.18 (E-step) and 6.19 (M-step).

    Parameters
    ----------
    data   : (n,) array of 1D observations
    K      : number of Gaussian components
    n_iter : maximum EM iterations
    seed   : random seed for initialization

    Returns dict with learned parameters and log-likelihood history.
    """
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    n   = len(data)

    # Random initialization
    mu     = rng.choice(data, K, replace=False)  # means
    sigma  = np.full(K, data.std())              # standard deviations
    pi     = np.ones(K) / K                      # mixing weights

    ll_history = []

    for iteration in range(n_iter):

        # === E-STEP: Compute responsibilities r_{ik} = P(Z_i=k | x_i, theta) ===
        # r_{ik} ∝ pi_k * N(x_i | mu_k, sigma_k^2)   [Eq. 6.18]
        log_resp = np.zeros((n, K))
        for k in range(K):
            log_resp[:, k] = np.log(pi[k] + 1e-300) + stats.norm.logpdf(data, mu[k], sigma[k])

        # Log-sum-exp for numerical stability
        log_sum = np.logaddexp.reduce(log_resp, axis=1)
        log_resp -= log_sum[:, np.newaxis]
        resp      = np.exp(log_resp)  # responsibilities: shape (n, K)

        # Log-likelihood at current parameters
        ll = log_sum.sum()
        ll_history.append(ll)

        if iteration > 0 and abs(ll - ll_history[-2]) < tol:
            print(f"  EM converged at iteration {iteration}")
            break

        # === M-STEP: Update parameters to maximize Q(theta, theta^t) ===
        # [Eq. 6.19]
        N_k   = resp.sum(axis=0)           # effective count for each component
        pi    = N_k / n                    # mixing weights
        mu    = (resp * data[:, None]).sum(axis=0) / N_k   # means
        sigma = np.sqrt(
            (resp * (data[:, None] - mu[None, :])**2).sum(axis=0) / N_k
        )  # standard deviations

    return {"pi": pi, "mu": mu, "sigma": sigma,
            "ll_history": ll_history, "responsibilities": resp}


def demonstrate_em_gmm(seed: int = 42):
    """Generate bimodal data and fit a 2-component GMM via EM."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    n   = 500

    # True GMM: 40% N(-2, 0.8²) + 60% N(3, 1.2²)
    n1   = int(0.4 * n)
    data = np.concatenate([
        rng.normal(-2.0, 0.8, n1),
        rng.normal( 3.0, 1.2, n - n1)
    ])
    rng.shuffle(data)

    result = em_gmm(data, K=2, seed=seed)

    print("\n" + "="*52)
    print("  EM ALGORITHM: GAUSSIAN MIXTURE MODEL")
    print("="*52)
    print(f"\n  {'Component':<12} {'π':>8} {'μ':>10} {'σ':>10}")
    print("  " + "-"*42)
    for k in range(2):
        print(f"  {k+1:<12} {result['pi'][k]:>8.4f} "
              f"{result['mu'][k]:>10.4f} {result['sigma'][k]:>10.4f}")

    # Plot
    fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4.5))

    x_plot = np.linspace(data.min() - 1, data.max() + 1, 500)
    ax1.hist(data, bins=50, density=True, alpha=0.5, color='gray', label="Data")
    mixture_pdf = np.zeros_like(x_plot)
    colors_k    = ['#1a6faf', '#e84040']
    for k in range(2):
        comp = result['pi'][k] * stats.norm.pdf(x_plot, result['mu'][k], result['sigma'][k])
        ax1.plot(x_plot, comp, lw=2, color=colors_k[k],
                 label=f"Comp {k+1}: π={result['pi'][k]:.2f}, μ={result['mu'][k]:.2f}")
        mixture_pdf += comp
    ax1.plot(x_plot, mixture_pdf, 'k-', lw=2.5, label="Mixture PDF")
    ax1.set_title("EM-fitted GMM", fontsize=12, fontweight='bold')
    ax1.legend(fontsize=9); ax1.grid(alpha=0.3)

    ax2.plot(result['ll_history'], color='#1a6faf', lw=2.5, marker='o', ms=3)
    ax2.set_xlabel("EM Iteration", fontsize=12)
    ax2.set_ylabel("Log-likelihood", fontsize=12)
    ax2.set_title("EM Log-likelihood (non-decreasing guaranteed)",
                  fontsize=12, fontweight='bold')
    ax2.grid(alpha=0.3)

    plt.suptitle("EM Algorithm: Gaussian Mixture Model", fontsize=13,
                 fontweight='bold', y=1.01)
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.savefig("module6_em_gmm.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches='tight')
    plt.show()
    print("Saved: module6_em_gmm.png")


# =============================================================================
# MAIN
# =============================================================================

if __name__ == "__main__":

    # --- A: MLE for Gaussian via numerical optimization ---
    print("="*62)
    print("  MLE: GAUSSIAN DISTRIBUTION")
    print("="*62)
    rng   = np.random.default_rng(42)
    data  = rng.normal(loc=2.0, scale=1.5, size=200)

    def gaussian_ll(theta, data):
        mu, log_sigma = theta
        sigma = np.exp(log_sigma)   # log-parameterize sigma > 0
        return np.sum(stats.norm.logpdf(data, mu, sigma))

    mle = MaximumLikelihoodEstimator(gaussian_ll, param_names=["mu", "log_sigma"])
    result = mle.fit(data, theta_init=np.array([0.0, 0.0]))
    mle.print_summary(result, analytical={"mu": data.mean(),
                                           "log_sigma": np.log(data.std(ddof=0))})

    # --- B: MAP vs MLE comparison ---
    print("\n\n" + "="*62)
    print("  MAP vs MLE: RIDGE vs LASSO vs OLS")
    print("="*62)
    map_vs_mle_comparison(n_features=10, n_samples=30, true_sparse=True)

    # --- C: Likelihood surface and CR bound ---
    print("\n\n" + "="*62)
    print("  LIKELIHOOD SURFACE & CRAMÉR-RAO BOUND")
    print("="*62)
    visualize_likelihood_and_cr_bound()
```

$$\hat\theta_\text{MLE} = \arg\max_\theta \sum_i \log p(x_i\mid\theta) \tag{MLE}$$ $$\hat\theta_\text{MLE} = \arg\min_\theta D_{KL}(\hat{p},|,p_\theta) \tag{KL interpretation}$$ $$\mathcal{I}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}[(\nabla_\theta\log p)^2] = -\mathbb{E}[\nabla^2_\theta\log p] \tag{Fisher info}$$ $$\text{Var}(\hat\theta) \geq \frac{1}{n,\mathcal{I}(\theta)} \tag{Cramér-Rao}$$ $$\hat\theta_\text{MAP} = \arg\max_\theta\left[\ell(\theta) + \log p(\theta)\right] \tag{MAP}$$ $$\text{Ridge} \equiv \text{MAP with }\theta\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\tau^2\mathbf{I}) \tag{L2 = Gaussian prior}$$ $$\text{Lasso} \equiv \text{MAP with }\theta_j\sim\text{Laplace}(0,b) \tag{L1 = Laplace prior}$$
