# MODULE 7: Hypothesis Testing & P-values

---

## 7.1 Conceptual Overview

### The Decision Problem

Science and engineering constantly face the same question: given noisy data, can we distinguish a real signal from random fluctuation? Is the new model genuinely better, or did it just get lucky on this dataset? Did the drug work, or was the improvement noise? Is feature $j$ truly predictive, or does it just happen to correlate with $y$ in this sample?

Hypothesis testing is the formal mathematical framework for making these decisions with quantified error rates. It does not tell you the _truth_ — it tells you how likely your observed data would be if a specific null hypothesis were true.

### The Two Errors and Their Costs

Every hypothesis test commits to tolerating two types of mistakes:

**Type I error (false positive, $\alpha$):** Rejecting $H_0$ when it is actually true. In drug testing, approving an ineffective drug. In ML, believing a useless feature matters. The significance level $\alpha$ is the maximum tolerable Type I error rate.

**Type II error (false negative, $\beta$):** Failing to reject $H_0$ when $H_1$ is true. Missing a real drug effect. Discarding a genuinely predictive feature. The power $1-\beta$ is our ability to detect real effects.

The fundamental tension: decreasing $\alpha$ (demanding more evidence) increases $\beta$ (missing real signals). You cannot simultaneously minimize both without more data. This is the statistical analog of the precision-recall tradeoff in classification — they are mathematically the same thing.

### P-values: What They Are and Are Not

The p-value is among the most misinterpreted quantities in science. We will give the precise definition and then carefully enumerate the most common errors.

**The precise definition:** The p-value is the probability of observing a test statistic at least as extreme as the one computed from the data, _under the assumption that $H_0$ is true_.

$$p\text{-value} = P(T \geq t_\text{obs} \mid H_0) \tag{7.1}$$

**What a p-value is NOT:**

- $P(H_0 \mid \text{data})$ — the probability that $H_0$ is true (this requires a prior; use Bayesian methods)
- The probability that your result is due to chance
- A measure of the size or practical importance of an effect
- Something that should be thresholded at 0.05 with religious conviction

**What a p-value IS:**

- A measure of how surprising your data is under $H_0$
- A calibrated false-positive error rate if you adopt the threshold $\alpha$
- A valid probability statement only about the observed data under a specific model

---

## 7.2 Mathematical Formalization

### 7.2.1 The Neyman-Pearson Framework

> **Definition 7.1 (Hypothesis Testing Setup):**
> 
> A **statistical hypothesis** is a claim about the parameter $\theta$ of a probability model. A test partitions the sample space into:
> 
> - **Rejection region** $\mathcal{R}$: data configurations that lead to rejecting $H_0$
> - **Acceptance region** $\mathcal{A} = \mathcal{R}^c$
> 
> The **null hypothesis** $H_0: \theta \in \Theta_0$ and **alternative hypothesis** $H_1: \theta \in \Theta_1$ partition the parameter space: $\Theta_0 \cup \Theta_1 = \Theta$, $\Theta_0 \cap \Theta_1 = \emptyset$.

> **Definition 7.2 (Type I and Type II Errors):** $$\alpha = P(\text{reject } H_0 \mid H_0 \text{ true}) = P(\mathbf{X} \in \mathcal{R} \mid \theta \in \Theta_0) \tag{7.2}$$ $$\beta(\theta) = P(\text{fail to reject} \mid H_1 \text{ true}) = P(\mathbf{X} \notin \mathcal{R} \mid \theta \in \Theta_1) \tag{7.3}$$

> **Definition 7.3 (Power Function):** $$\text{Power}(\theta) = 1 - \beta(\theta) = P(\mathbf{X} \in \mathcal{R} \mid \theta) \tag{7.4}$$

The power function evaluated at $\theta \in \Theta_0$ gives $\alpha$ (Type I error). Evaluated at $\theta \in \Theta_1$, it gives the probability of correctly rejecting $H_0$.

---

### 7.2.2 The Neyman-Pearson Lemma

This is the fundamental optimality theorem of hypothesis testing. It proves that the likelihood ratio test is the most powerful test at any given significance level.

> **Theorem 7.1 (Neyman-Pearson Lemma):** Consider testing $H_0: \theta = \theta_0$ vs. $H_1: \theta = \theta_1$ (simple vs. simple). For a given significance level $\alpha$, the **most powerful test** has rejection region: $$\mathcal{R}^* = \left{\mathbf{x} : \Lambda(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{\mathcal{L}(\theta_1;\mathbf{x})}{\mathcal{L}(\theta_0;\mathbf{x})} > k_\alpha\right} \tag{7.5}$$
> 
> where $k_\alpha$ is chosen so that $P(\Lambda(\mathbf{X}) > k_\alpha \mid H_0) = \alpha$.
> 
> "Most powerful" means: no other test of level $\alpha$ has higher power against $H_1$.

**Proof:**

Let $\phi^_$ be the NP test (indicator of $\mathcal{R}^_$) and $\phi$ any other test with $\mathbb{E}_{\theta_0}[\phi(\mathbf{X})] \leq \alpha$. We must show $\mathbb{E}_{\theta_1}[\phi^*] \geq \mathbb{E}_{\theta_1}[\phi]$.

Note the key inequality: for all $\mathbf{x}$: $$(\phi^*(\mathbf{x}) - \phi(\mathbf{x}))\left(\mathcal{L}(\theta_1;\mathbf{x}) - k_\alpha,\mathcal{L}(\theta_0;\mathbf{x})\right) \geq 0 \tag{7.6}$$

This holds because: if $\phi^* = 1$ (we reject), then $\Lambda > k_\alpha$ so $\mathcal{L}(\theta_1) > k_\alpha\mathcal{L}(\theta_0)$, and $\phi^* - \phi \geq 0$ and the second factor $> 0$, product $\geq 0$. If $\phi^* = 0$ (we accept), symmetrically both factors are $\leq 0$, product $\geq 0$.

Integrating (7.6) over the sample space: $$\mathbb{E}_{\theta_1}[\phi^*] - \mathbb{E}_{\theta_1}[\phi] \geq k_\alpha(\mathbb{E}_{\theta_0}[\phi^*] - \mathbb{E}_{\theta_0}[\phi]) \geq k_\alpha(\alpha - \alpha) = 0$$

Therefore $\mathbb{E}_{\theta_1}[\phi^*] \geq \mathbb{E}_{\theta_1}[\phi]$. $\blacksquare$

**ML Implication:** The likelihood ratio is the _theoretically optimal_ test statistic. Whenever you use a parametric model to compare two hypotheses, the likelihood ratio is the gold standard. ROC analysis, model comparison with AIC/BIC, and the $F$-test in regression are all special cases of the likelihood ratio principle.

---

### 7.2.3 The Generalized Likelihood Ratio Test

For composite hypotheses, we extend the NP lemma.

> **Definition 7.4 (Generalized Likelihood Ratio):** $$\Lambda(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{\sup_{\theta \in \Theta_0} \mathcal{L}(\theta;\mathbf{x})}{\sup_{\theta \in \Theta} \mathcal{L}(\theta;\mathbf{x})} = \frac{\mathcal{L}(\hat\theta_0)}{\mathcal{L}(\hat\theta_\text{MLE})} \tag{7.7}$$

Since the numerator maximizes over a restricted set $\Theta_0 \subseteq \Theta$, we have $0 < \Lambda \leq 1$. Small $\Lambda$ provides evidence against $H_0$.

> **Theorem 7.2 (Wilks' Theorem):** Under $H_0$ and regularity conditions, as $n\to\infty$: $$-2\log\Lambda(\mathbf{X}) \xrightarrow{d} \chi^2_d \tag{7.8}$$
> 
> where $d = \dim(\Theta) - \dim(\Theta_0)$ is the difference in the number of free parameters.

**Proof sketch:** Expand $\log\mathcal{L}(\hat\theta_\text{MLE})$ as a Taylor series around $\hat\theta_0$: $$\log\mathcal{L}(\hat\theta_\text{MLE}) \approx \log\mathcal{L}(\hat\theta_0) + \frac{1}{2}(\hat\theta_\text{MLE}-\hat\theta_0)^\top \mathbf{H}(\hat\theta_0) (\hat\theta_\text{MLE}-\hat\theta_0)$$

where $\mathbf{H}$ is the Hessian of the log-likelihood. Under $H_0$, $-\mathbf{H}/n \to \mathcal{I}(\theta_0)$, and by the multivariate CLT, $\sqrt{n}(\hat\theta_\text{MLE}-\hat\theta_0)$ is asymptotically Gaussian. The quadratic form of a Gaussian vector in its covariance matrix is $\chi^2$. $\blacksquare$

Wilks' theorem is what gives every likelihood ratio test its p-value: we compute $-2\log\Lambda$ and compare to a $\chi^2$ table.

---

### 7.2.4 The Z-test and T-test as Special Cases

**The Z-test** (known variance) tests $H_0: \mu = \mu_0$ for $X_i \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)$.

Test statistic: $$Z = \frac{\bar{X} - \mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}} \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1) \text{ under } H_0 \tag{7.9}$$

Two-sided p-value: $p = 2\Phi(-|z_\text{obs}|) = 2P(Z \geq |z_\text{obs}|)$ where $\Phi$ is the standard normal CDF.

**The One-Sample T-test** (unknown variance) uses the sample standard deviation $S$: $$T = \frac{\bar{X} - \mu_0}{S/\sqrt{n}} \sim t_{n-1} \text{ under } H_0 \tag{7.10}$$

The $t_{n-1}$ distribution has heavier tails than $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$ — accounting for the additional uncertainty from estimating $\sigma$. As $n\to\infty$, $t_{n-1} \to \mathcal{N}(0,1)$.

**Derivation of the T-statistic distribution:**

$\bar{X} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_0, \sigma^2/n)$ so $\sqrt{n}(\bar{X}-\mu_0)/\sigma \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)$.

$(n-1)S^2/\sigma^2 \sim \chi^2_{n-1}$ (a standard result from Cochran's theorem).

$\bar{X}$ and $S^2$ are independent (Gaussian mean and variance are independent — another consequence of Cochran's theorem). Therefore:

$$T = \frac{\bar{X}-\mu_0}{S/\sqrt{n}} = \frac{\mathcal{N}(0,1)}{\sqrt{\chi^2_{n-1}/(n-1)}} \sim t_{n-1} \tag{7.11}$$

by the definition of the $t$-distribution as the ratio of a standard normal to the square root of a scaled chi-squared.

---

### 7.2.5 P-values: Formal Definition and the Uniform Distribution Theorem

> **Definition 7.5 (P-value):** Given a test statistic $T(\mathbf{X})$ where larger values provide more evidence against $H_0$, the p-value is: $$p(\mathbf{x}) = P_{H_0}(T(\mathbf{X}) \geq T(\mathbf{x})) \tag{7.12}$$

> **Theorem 7.3 (Uniform distribution of p-values under $H_0$):** If $H_0$ is true and the null distribution of $T$ is continuous, then: $$p(\mathbf{X}) \sim \text{Uniform}(0,1) \text{ under } H_0 \tag{7.13}$$

**Proof:** Let $F_0$ be the CDF of $T$ under $H_0$. The p-value is $p = 1 - F_0(T)$. Since $U = F_0(T) \sim \text{Uniform}(0,1)$ by the probability integral transform (Theorem 2.2), $p = 1 - U \sim \text{Uniform}(0,1)$. $\blacksquare$

**Profound implication:** Under $H_0$, p-values are uniformly distributed. If you run 100 tests where $H_0$ is true and threshold at $\alpha = 0.05$, you will reject $H_0$ in approximately 5 of them — purely by chance. This is the **multiple testing problem**: running many tests inflates the overall Type I error rate. This is rampant in ML feature selection, hyperparameter searches, and A/B testing.

---

### 7.2.6 Multiple Testing Corrections

When performing $m$ simultaneous tests, define:

**Family-Wise Error Rate (FWER):** $P(\text{at least one false rejection})$

If tests are independent with individual level $\alpha$: $$\text{FWER} = 1 - (1-\alpha)^m \approx m\alpha \text{ for small } \alpha \tag{7.14}$$

At $m=20$ tests and $\alpha=0.05$: FWER $\approx 1-(0.95)^{20} \approx 0.64$. Nearly certain to have a false positive.

> **Bonferroni Correction:** Reject $H_{0,i}$ if $p_i < \alpha/m$. Controls FWER $\leq \alpha$.

**Proof:** $P(\text{any false rejection}) \leq \sum_{i: H_{0,i}\text{ true}} P(p_i < \alpha/m) = m_0 \cdot \alpha/m \leq \alpha$. $\blacksquare$

**False Discovery Rate (FDR)** — a less conservative alternative relevant for high-dimensional ML:

> **Definition 7.6 (FDR):** $\text{FDR} = \mathbb{E}!\left[\frac{\text{False positives}}{\text{Total rejections}}\right]$

> **Theorem 7.4 (Benjamini-Hochberg Procedure):** Sort p-values $p_{(1)} \leq \cdots \leq p_{(m)}$. Let $\hat{k} = \max{i : p_{(i)} \leq \frac{i}{m}\alpha}$. Reject all $H_{0,(i)}$ for $i \leq \hat{k}$. This controls $\text{FDR} \leq \alpha$.

BH is the standard procedure for feature selection in genomics, neuroimaging, and high-dimensional ML — anywhere you test thousands of hypotheses simultaneously.

---

### 7.2.7 Confidence Intervals and Their Duality with Tests

> **Definition 7.7 (Confidence Interval):** A $100(1-\alpha)%$ confidence interval $C(\mathbf{X})$ satisfies: $$P(\theta \in C(\mathbf{X})) \geq 1 - \alpha \quad \forall, \theta \tag{7.15}$$

**The duality theorem:** A $100(1-\alpha)%$ confidence interval contains exactly those values of $\theta_0$ that would _not_ be rejected at level $\alpha$ in a two-sided hypothesis test:

$$\theta_0 \in C(\mathbf{x}) \iff \text{the test of } H_0:\theta=\theta_0 \text{ does not reject at level } \alpha \tag{7.16}$$

For the Z-test with known $\sigma$, inverting the test gives: $$C(\mathbf{x}) = \left[\bar{x} - z_{\alpha/2}\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}},; \bar{x} + z_{\alpha/2}\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\right] \tag{7.17}$$

where $z_{\alpha/2} = \Phi^{-1}(1-\alpha/2)$ (e.g., $z_{0.025} = 1.96$ for 95% CI).

**Critical interpretation:** A 95% CI means: if we repeated the experiment infinitely many times, 95% of the resulting intervals would contain the true $\theta$. It does _not_ mean "there is a 95% probability that $\theta$ lies in this specific interval" — $\theta$ is fixed (frequentist view), so it either is or is not in the interval with probability 1.

---

### 7.2.8 Effect Size, Power Analysis, and Sample Size Planning

Statistical significance does not imply practical significance. A test can be significant with a negligible effect when $n$ is large.

> **Definition 7.8 (Cohen's d — Standardized Effect Size):** $$d = \frac{|\mu_1 - \mu_0|}{\sigma} \tag{7.18}$$

**Power of the Z-test** against $H_1: \mu = \mu_1$:

$$\text{Power} = \Phi!\left(-z_{\alpha/2} + \frac{|\mu_1 - \mu_0|}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}}\right) + \Phi!\left(-z_{\alpha/2} - \frac{|\mu_1 - \mu_0|}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}}\right) \tag{7.19}$$

For one-sided tests at large $\delta = |\mu_1-\mu_0|$, the second term is negligible: $$\text{Power} \approx \Phi!\left(\sqrt{n},\frac{\delta}{\sigma} - z_\alpha\right) \tag{7.20}$$

**Required sample size** to achieve power $1-\beta$ at significance $\alpha$ (one-sided): $$n \geq \left(\frac{(z_\alpha + z_\beta)\sigma}{\delta}\right)^2 \tag{7.21}$$

This is the fundamental sample size formula. It tells you: to detect a smaller effect ($\delta \downarrow$), or to achieve higher power ($\beta \downarrow$), or to use a more stringent significance level ($\alpha \downarrow$), you need more data. Quadratically more data for halving the detectable effect size.

---

### 7.2.9 The Connection to ML: Statistical Tests for Model Comparison

The following are the most practically relevant tests in ML workflows:

**F-test for nested linear models:** Comparing model $M_0$ (restricted, $p$ parameters) vs $M_1$ (full, $p+q$ parameters): $$F = \frac{(\text{RSS}_0 - \text{RSS}_1)/q}{\text{RSS}_1/(n-p-q)} \sim F_{q,,n-p-q} \text{ under } H_0 \tag{7.22}$$

This is a special case of the likelihood ratio test (7.7) for Gaussian regression models.

**AIC and BIC as penalized log-likelihoods** (frequentist model selection): $$\text{AIC} = -2\ell(\hat\theta) + 2k \tag{7.23}$$ $$\text{BIC} = -2\ell(\hat\theta) + k\log n \tag{7.24}$$

where $k$ is the number of parameters. These are derived from the KL divergence between the true and fitted distributions (AIC) and from the Bayesian marginal likelihood under a flat prior (BIC). Lower is better. BIC penalizes complexity more heavily and is consistent (selects the true model as $n\to\infty$); AIC minimizes predictive error.

---

## 7.3 Numerical Examples

### Example 7.1: Z-test — Testing a Model's Accuracy

**Problem:** A baseline model achieves 70% accuracy on a test set of $n=500$ examples. A new model gets 73%. Is this improvement statistically significant at $\alpha=0.05$?

**Setup:** Under $H_0$ (no improvement), both models have true accuracy $p_0 = 0.70$. The observed accuracy $\hat{p}$ of the new model is $k/n = 365/500 = 0.73$.

**Test statistic** (one-sample proportion Z-test): $$Z = \frac{\hat{p} - p_0}{\sqrt{p_0(1-p_0)/n}} = \frac{0.73 - 0.70}{\sqrt{0.70 \times 0.30 / 500}} = \frac{0.03}{\sqrt{0.00042}} = \frac{0.03}{0.02049} \approx 1.464$$

**P-value** (one-sided, testing improvement): $$p = P(Z \geq 1.464) = 1 - \Phi(1.464) \approx 1 - 0.9284 = 0.0716$$

**Conclusion:** $p = 0.072 > 0.05$. We fail to reject $H_0$ at the 5% level. The improvement is not statistically significant. We cannot conclude the new model is genuinely better — the 3% improvement could be noise.

**Required sample size** for 80% power to detect a 3% improvement at $\alpha=0.05$ (one-sided):

$$n \geq \left(\frac{(1.645 + 0.842)\sqrt{0.70 \times 0.30}}{0.03}\right)^2 = \left(\frac{2.487 \times 0.4583}{0.03}\right)^2 \approx \left(\frac{1.1397}{0.03}\right)^2 \approx 1444$$

We would need approximately **1,444 test examples** to reliably detect a 3% accuracy improvement with 80% power.

---

### Example 7.2: Likelihood Ratio Test and Wilks' Theorem

**Problem:** We fit a logistic regression model to $n=200$ examples. The null model (intercept only) has log-likelihood $\ell_0 = -130.2$. The full model (5 features) has $\ell_1 = -118.7$. Is the full model significantly better?

**Likelihood ratio statistic:** $$G^2 = -2\log\Lambda = -2(\ell_0 - \ell_1) = -2(-130.2 - (-118.7)) = -2(-11.5) = 23.0$$

**Degrees of freedom:** $d = 5 - 0 = 5$ (5 additional parameters in full model).

By Wilks' theorem: $G^2 \sim \chi^2_5$ under $H_0$.

$$p = P(\chi^2_5 \geq 23.0) \approx 0.00033$$

**Conclusion:** $p \ll 0.05$. We reject $H_0$ — the five features collectively provide a statistically significant improvement in fit.

---

### Example 7.3: Multiple Testing and FDR Control

**Problem:** You test $m=1000$ features for association with a target variable. You obtain p-values, of which 47 are below 0.05. How many are likely false positives? Apply BH correction at $\alpha=0.05$.

**Without correction:** If all 1000 null hypotheses are true, expected false positives $= 1000 \times 0.05 = 50$. So 47 "significant" results could entirely be noise.

**BH procedure:** Sort p-values $p_{(1)} \leq p_{(2)} \leq \cdots \leq p_{(1000)}$. Find the largest $k$ such that $p_{(k)} \leq k \cdot 0.05 / 1000$. This controls $\text{FDR} \leq 0.05$ — at most 5% of rejected hypotheses will be false positives.

Under BH, the effective threshold for the $k$-th ranked p-value is $k \times 5 \times 10^{-5}$, far more stringent than 0.05 for small $k$.

---

## 7.4 Implementation

```python
import numpy as np
import scipy.stats as stats
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.gridspec as gridspec
from itertools import product

# =============================================================================
# MODULE 7: Hypothesis Testing & P-values
# =============================================================================

# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# PART A: Complete Hypothesis Testing Framework
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------

class HypothesisTest:
    """
    A unified interface for the most common hypothesis tests used in ML workflows.
    Each test returns a structured result with test statistic, p-value,
    confidence interval, effect size, and power.
    """

    @staticmethod
    def one_sample_z(data: np.ndarray, mu0: float, sigma: float,
                     alpha: float = 0.05, alternative: str = 'two-sided') -> dict:
        """
        One-sample Z-test. H0: mu = mu0, known sigma.
        Eq. 7.9: Z = (X_bar - mu0) / (sigma / sqrt(n))
        """
        n    = len(data)
        xbar = data.mean()
        z    = (xbar - mu0) / (sigma / np.sqrt(n))

        if alternative == 'two-sided':
            pval = 2 * stats.norm.sf(abs(z))
            ci   = (xbar - 1.96*sigma/np.sqrt(n), xbar + 1.96*sigma/np.sqrt(n))
        elif alternative == 'greater':
            pval = stats.norm.sf(z)
            ci   = (xbar - 1.645*sigma/np.sqrt(n), np.inf)
        else:  # less
            pval = stats.norm.cdf(z)
            ci   = (-np.inf, xbar + 1.645*sigma/np.sqrt(n))

        effect_d = abs(xbar - mu0) / sigma  # Cohen's d
        return {"test": "Z-test", "statistic": z, "p_value": pval,
                "ci": ci, "effect_size_d": effect_d, "reject": pval < alpha,
                "n": n, "xbar": xbar}

    @staticmethod
    def one_sample_t(data: np.ndarray, mu0: float,
                     alpha: float = 0.05, alternative: str = 'two-sided') -> dict:
        """
        One-sample t-test. H0: mu = mu0, unknown sigma.
        Eq. 7.10: T = (X_bar - mu0) / (S / sqrt(n))
        """
        n    = len(data)
        xbar = data.mean()
        s    = data.std(ddof=1)
        t    = (xbar - mu0) / (s / np.sqrt(n))
        df   = n - 1

        if alternative == 'two-sided':
            pval = 2 * stats.t.sf(abs(t), df)
        elif alternative == 'greater':
            pval = stats.t.sf(t, df)
        else:
            pval = stats.t.cdf(t, df)

        t_crit = stats.t.ppf(1 - alpha/2, df)
        ci     = (xbar - t_crit*s/np.sqrt(n), xbar + t_crit*s/np.sqrt(n))
        return {"test": "t-test", "statistic": t, "p_value": pval, "df": df,
                "ci": ci, "effect_size_d": abs(xbar-mu0)/s,
                "reject": pval < alpha, "n": n, "xbar": xbar, "s": s}

    @staticmethod
    def two_sample_t(data1: np.ndarray, data2: np.ndarray,
                     alpha: float = 0.05, equal_var: bool = False) -> dict:
        """
        Two-sample t-test (Welch's by default).
        Tests H0: mu1 = mu2.
        """
        t, pval = stats.ttest_ind(data1, data2, equal_var=equal_var)
        n1, n2  = len(data1), len(data2)
        s1, s2  = data1.std(ddof=1), data2.std(ddof=1)
        pooled_s = np.sqrt(((n1-1)*s1**2 + (n2-1)*s2**2) / (n1+n2-2))
        d        = (data1.mean() - data2.mean()) / pooled_s
        return {"test": "Two-sample t-test (Welch)", "statistic": t,
                "p_value": pval, "effect_size_d": abs(d),
                "reject": pval < alpha,
                "mean_diff": data1.mean() - data2.mean()}

    @staticmethod
    def proportion_z(k: int, n: int, p0: float,
                     alpha: float = 0.05, alternative: str = 'two-sided') -> dict:
        """
        One-sample proportion Z-test.
        H0: p = p0. Tests k successes in n trials.
        """
        p_hat = k / n
        se    = np.sqrt(p0 * (1-p0) / n)
        z     = (p_hat - p0) / se

        if alternative == 'two-sided':
            pval = 2 * stats.norm.sf(abs(z))
        elif alternative == 'greater':
            pval = stats.norm.sf(z)
        else:
            pval = stats.norm.cdf(z)

        se_hat = np.sqrt(p_hat*(1-p_hat)/n)
        z_crit = stats.norm.ppf(1 - alpha/2)
        ci     = (p_hat - z_crit*se_hat, p_hat + z_crit*se_hat)
        d      = abs(p_hat - p0) / np.sqrt(p0*(1-p0))

        return {"test": "Proportion Z-test", "statistic": z, "p_value": pval,
                "ci": ci, "effect_size_d": d, "reject": pval < alpha,
                "p_hat": p_hat, "p0": p0, "n": n}

    @staticmethod
    def likelihood_ratio(ll_null: float, ll_full: float,
                         df: int, alpha: float = 0.05) -> dict:
        """
        Generalized likelihood ratio test (Wilks' theorem).
        Eq. 7.8: G^2 = -2 * (ell_null - ell_full) ~ chi^2(df) under H0.
        """
        G2   = -2 * (ll_null - ll_full)
        pval = stats.chi2.sf(G2, df)
        return {"test": "Likelihood Ratio Test", "statistic": G2,
                "df": df, "p_value": pval, "reject": pval < alpha,
                "ll_null": ll_null, "ll_full": ll_full}

    @staticmethod
    def print_result(result: dict):
        """Print a clean summary of hypothesis test results."""
        print(f"\n{'='*55}")
        print(f"  {result['test']}")
        print(f"{'='*55}")
        for k, v in result.items():
            if k == 'test':
                continue
            if isinstance(v, float):
                print(f"  {k:<20} {v:.6f}")
            elif isinstance(v, tuple):
                print(f"  {k:<20} ({v[0]:.4f}, {v[1]:.4f})")
            elif isinstance(v, bool):
                print(f"  {'Reject H0':<20} {'YES ✓' if v else 'NO  ✗'}")
            else:
                print(f"  {k:<20} {v}")


# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# PART B: P-value Uniform Distribution Under H0 + Multiple Testing
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def demonstrate_pvalue_distribution(n_tests: int = 5000, n_per_test: int = 30,
                                     seed: int = 42):
    """
    Empirically verify Theorem 7.3: p-values are Uniform(0,1) under H0.
    Also demonstrate the multiple testing problem and BH correction.
    """
    rng   = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    mu0   = 0.0
    sigma = 1.0

    # Scenario 1: All nulls TRUE (data from H0)
    pvals_null = []
    for _ in range(n_tests):
        data = rng.normal(mu0, sigma, n_per_test)
        _, p = stats.ttest_1samp(data, popmean=mu0)
        pvals_null.append(p)
    pvals_null = np.array(pvals_null)

    # Scenario 2: Mix — 80% null, 20% alternative (mu=0.5)
    pvals_mix  = []
    true_null  = []
    for i in range(n_tests):
        is_null = (i % 5 != 0)  # 80% null
        mu      = mu0 if is_null else 0.5
        data    = rng.normal(mu, sigma, n_per_test)
        _, p    = stats.ttest_1samp(data, popmean=mu0)
        pvals_mix.append(p)
        true_null.append(is_null)
    pvals_mix = np.array(pvals_mix)
    true_null = np.array(true_null)

    # --- BH procedure ---
    def benjamini_hochberg(pvals, alpha=0.05):
        m       = len(pvals)
        order   = np.argsort(pvals)
        sorted_p = pvals[order]
        thresholds = (np.arange(1, m+1) / m) * alpha
        below   = sorted_p <= thresholds
        if below.any():
            k_hat = np.max(np.where(below)[0])
            rejected = np.zeros(m, dtype=bool)
            rejected[order[:k_hat+1]] = True
        else:
            rejected = np.zeros(m, dtype=bool)
        return rejected

    bonferroni_reject = pvals_mix < 0.05 / n_tests
    bh_reject         = benjamini_hochberg(pvals_mix, alpha=0.05)
    naive_reject      = pvals_mix < 0.05

    # FDR and power for each method
    def compute_fdr_power(rejected, true_null):
        tp = np.sum(rejected & ~true_null)
        fp = np.sum(rejected & true_null)
        fn = np.sum(~rejected & ~true_null)
        n_rej = rejected.sum()
        fdr   = fp / max(n_rej, 1)
        power = tp / max(np.sum(~true_null), 1)
        return fdr, power

    print("\n" + "="*58)
    print("  MULTIPLE TESTING COMPARISON (n_tests=5000, 20% alternatives)")
    print(f"  {'Method':<22} {'Rejected':>10} {'FDR':>8} {'Power':>8}")
    print("-"*58)
    for name, rej in [("Naive (α=0.05)", naive_reject),
                      ("Bonferroni",     bonferroni_reject),
                      ("Benjamini-Hochberg", bh_reject)]:
        fdr, power = compute_fdr_power(rej, true_null)
        print(f"  {name:<22} {rej.sum():>10} {fdr:>8.4f} {power:>8.4f}")
    print("="*58)

    # --- Plot ---
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(14, 4.5))

    # Panel 1: P-value histogram under H0 (should be Uniform)
    ax = axes[0]
    ax.hist(pvals_null, bins=20, density=True, alpha=0.7, color='#1a6faf',
            edgecolor='white', lw=0.5)
    ax.axhline(1, color='r', lw=2, linestyle='--', label="Uniform(0,1) density")
    ax.set_title("P-values under $H_0$\n(Theorem 7.3: should be Uniform)",
                 fontsize=11, fontweight='bold')
    ax.set_xlabel("p-value"); ax.set_ylabel("Density")
    ax.legend(fontsize=9); ax.grid(alpha=0.3)
    # KS test for uniformity
    ks, p = stats.kstest(pvals_null, 'uniform')
    ax.text(0.97, 0.97, f"KS test: p={p:.3f}\n(uniform: p>>0.05)",
            transform=ax.transAxes, ha='right', va='top', fontsize=9)

    # Panel 2: P-value histogram under mix (spike near 0 from alternatives)
    ax = axes[1]
    ax.hist(pvals_mix[true_null],  bins=20, density=True, alpha=0.55,
            color='#1a6faf', label="True nulls")
    ax.hist(pvals_mix[~true_null], bins=20, density=True, alpha=0.55,
            color='#e84040', label="True alternatives")
    ax.axhline(1, color='gray', lw=1.5, linestyle='--')
    ax.set_title("P-values: 80% null + 20% alternative\n(alt: μ=0.5, spike near 0)",
                 fontsize=11, fontweight='bold')
    ax.set_xlabel("p-value"); ax.legend(fontsize=9); ax.grid(alpha=0.3)

    # Panel 3: BH procedure visualization
    ax = axes[2]
    m      = n_tests
    sorted_p = np.sort(pvals_mix)
    alpha  = 0.05
    ranks  = np.arange(1, m+1)
    bh_line = ranks * alpha / m

    ax.plot(ranks[:500], sorted_p[:500], color='#1a6faf', lw=1.5, label="Sorted p-values")
    ax.plot(ranks[:500], bh_line[:500],  color='#e84040', lw=2, linestyle='--',
            label=f"BH threshold = k·{alpha}/m")
    # Find BH cutoff
    below = sorted_p <= bh_line
    if below.any():
        k_bh = np.max(np.where(below)[0])
        ax.axvline(k_bh, color='green', lw=1.5, linestyle=':', label=f"BH cutoff k={k_bh}")
        ax.scatter(k_bh, sorted_p[k_bh], s=100, color='green', zorder=5)
    ax.set_title("Benjamini-Hochberg Procedure\n(FDR control at α=0.05)",
                 fontsize=11, fontweight='bold')
    ax.set_xlabel("Rank of sorted p-values"); ax.set_ylabel("p-value")
    ax.legend(fontsize=9); ax.grid(alpha=0.3)

    plt.suptitle("P-value Distributions and Multiple Testing Correction",
                 fontsize=13, fontweight='bold', y=1.02)
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.savefig("module7_pvalues.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches='tight')
    plt.show()


# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# PART C: Power Analysis and Sample Size Planning
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def power_analysis_visualization():
    """
    Visualize the power function for the Z-test and sample size requirements.
    Equations 7.19 – 7.21.
    """
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(15, 5))

    # Panel 1: Power vs effect size for different n
    ax   = axes[0]
    deltas = np.linspace(0, 1.5, 200)  # effect sizes (in sigma units)
    sigma  = 1.0; alpha = 0.05; z_alpha = stats.norm.ppf(1 - alpha/2)

    for n, col, ls in [(10, '#1a6faf', '-'), (30, '#e84040', '--'),
                        (100, '#2ca02c', ':'), (500, '#9467bd', '-.')]:
        power = stats.norm.sf(z_alpha - deltas*np.sqrt(n)/sigma) + \
                stats.norm.cdf(-z_alpha - deltas*np.sqrt(n)/sigma)
        ax.plot(deltas, power, lw=2.5, color=col, linestyle=ls, label=f"n={n}")
    ax.axhline(0.80, color='gray', lw=1, linestyle=':', alpha=0.7, label="80% power")
    ax.axhline(0.05, color='lightgray', lw=1, linestyle=':', label="α=5% (Type I)")
    ax.set_xlabel("Effect size δ/σ (Cohen's d)", fontsize=12)
    ax.set_ylabel("Power (1-β)", fontsize=12)
    ax.set_title("Power vs Effect Size\n(two-sided Z-test, α=0.05)",
                 fontsize=11, fontweight='bold')
    ax.legend(fontsize=9); ax.grid(alpha=0.3); ax.set_ylim(0, 1.02)

    # Panel 2: Required n vs effect size at 80% power
    ax = axes[1]
    deltas_nz = np.linspace(0.1, 1.5, 200)
    z_beta     = stats.norm.ppf(0.80)  # 80% power

    for alpha_val, col, ls in [(0.05, '#1a6faf', '-'), (0.01, '#e84040', '--'),
                                (0.001, '#2ca02c', ':')]:
        z_a = stats.norm.ppf(1 - alpha_val/2)
        ns  = ((z_a + z_beta) / deltas_nz)**2
        ax.semilogy(deltas_nz, ns, lw=2.5, color=col, linestyle=ls,
                    label=f"α={alpha_val}")
    ax.set_xlabel("Effect size (Cohen's d)", fontsize=12)
    ax.set_ylabel("Required n (log scale)", fontsize=12)
    ax.set_title("Sample Size for 80% Power\n(two-sided Z-test)",
                 fontsize=11, fontweight='bold')
    ax.legend(fontsize=9); ax.grid(alpha=0.3, which='both')

    # Panel 3: Two-distribution picture of hypothesis testing
    ax  = axes[2]
    mu0 = 0.0; mu1 = 0.8; sigma = 1.0; n = 25
    se  = sigma / np.sqrt(n)
    x   = np.linspace(-0.6, 1.5, 400)
    z_c = stats.norm.ppf(1 - 0.05) * se  # one-sided critical value

    y0 = stats.norm.pdf(x, mu0, se)
    y1 = stats.norm.pdf(x, mu1, se)
    ax.plot(x, y0, '#1a6faf', lw=2.5, label=f"$H_0$: μ={mu0}")
    ax.plot(x, y1, '#e84040', lw=2.5, label=f"$H_1$: μ={mu1}")

    # Type I error (alpha) — shading right tail of H0
    x_alpha = x[x >= z_c]
    ax.fill_between(x_alpha, stats.norm.pdf(x_alpha, mu0, se),
                    alpha=0.4, color='#1a6faf', label=f"α (Type I) = {0.05:.2f}")

    # Power — shading right tail of H1
    power_val = stats.norm.sf(z_c, mu1, se)
    ax.fill_between(x_alpha, stats.norm.pdf(x_alpha, mu1, se),
                    alpha=0.4, color='#e84040', label=f"Power = {power_val:.3f}")

    # Beta region
    x_beta = x[x < z_c]
    ax.fill_between(x_beta, stats.norm.pdf(x_beta, mu1, se),
                    alpha=0.2, color='gray', label=f"β (Type II) = {1-power_val:.3f}")

    ax.axvline(z_c, color='black', lw=1.5, linestyle='--',
               label=f"Critical value = {z_c:.2f}")
    ax.set_xlabel("$\\bar{X}$", fontsize=12)
    ax.set_title(f"Type I/II Error and Power\n(n={n}, one-sided α=0.05)",
                 fontsize=11, fontweight='bold')
    ax.legend(fontsize=8); ax.grid(alpha=0.3)

    plt.suptitle("Power Analysis and Sample Size Planning", fontsize=13,
                 fontweight='bold', y=1.02)
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.savefig("module7_power.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches='tight')
    plt.show()
    print("Saved: module7_power.png")


# =============================================================================
# MAIN
# =============================================================================

if __name__ == "__main__":

    # --- A: ML accuracy test ---
    print("="*55)
    print("  EXAMPLE 7.1: MODEL ACCURACY Z-TEST")
    print("="*55)
    result = HypothesisTest.proportion_z(
        k=365, n=500, p0=0.70, alpha=0.05, alternative='greater')
    HypothesisTest.print_result(result)

    # Required sample size for 80% power
    d     = 0.03 / np.sqrt(0.70*0.30)
    n_req = ((stats.norm.ppf(0.95) + stats.norm.ppf(0.80)) / d)**2
    print(f"\n  Required n for 80% power: {int(np.ceil(n_req))}")

    # --- B: Likelihood ratio test ---
    print("\n" + "="*55)
    print("  EXAMPLE 7.2: LIKELIHOOD RATIO TEST")
    print("="*55)
    result = HypothesisTest.likelihood_ratio(
        ll_null=-130.2, ll_full=-118.7, df=5, alpha=0.05)
    HypothesisTest.print_result(result)

    # --- C: P-value distributions and multiple testing ---
    print("\n" + "="*55)
    print("  P-VALUE DISTRIBUTIONS & MULTIPLE TESTING")
    print("="*55)
    demonstrate_pvalue_distribution()

    # --- D: Power analysis ---
    print("\n" + "="*55)
    print("  POWER ANALYSIS")
    print("="*55)
    power_analysis_visualization()

    # --- E: Two-sample t-test ---
    rng  = np.random.default_rng(42)
    grp1 = rng.normal(0.50, 1.0, 40)   # control
    grp2 = rng.normal(0.85, 1.1, 45)   # treatment
    res  = HypothesisTest.two_sample_t(grp1, grp2, alpha=0.05)
    print("\n" + "="*55)
    print("  TWO-SAMPLE T-TEST (CONTROL vs TREATMENT)")
    print("="*55)
    HypothesisTest.print_result(res)
```

## 7.5 Interactive Hypothesis Testing ExplorerDrag the sliders to build direct geometric intuition for the tradeoffs. Notice that $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are inversely coupled — shrinking the Type I region (moving the critical value right) expands the Type II region. Only increasing $n$ improves both simultaneously.

## 7.6 Module Summary & ML Connections

|Concept|Formula|ML Application|
|---|---|---|
|Null hypothesis|$H_0: \theta \in \Theta_0$|"Model A ≤ Model B in accuracy"|
|Type I error|$\alpha = P(\text{reject}\mid H_0)$|False positive rate in feature selection|
|Type II error|$\beta = P(\text{accept}\mid H_1)$|Missing a genuinely useful feature|
|NP Lemma|LRT is most powerful at level $\alpha$|Likelihood ratio is optimal test|
|Wilks' Theorem|$-2\log\Lambda \to \chi^2_d$|Model comparison p-values|
|P-value $\sim$ Uniform$(0,1)$ under $H_0$|Theorem 7.3|Multiple testing inflation|
|Bonferroni|Threshold $\alpha/m$|Conservative feature selection|
|BH procedure|Rank p-values, adaptive threshold|FDR control in high-dim ML|
|AIC/BIC|$-2\ell + 2k$ / $-2\ell + k\log n$|Model complexity selection|
|Power|$\Phi(\sqrt{n}\delta/\sigma - z_\alpha)$|A/B test sample size planning|

## 7.7 Key Equations Reference Card

$$Z = \frac{\bar{X}-\mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}} \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1) \text{ under }H_0 \tag{Z-test}$$ $$T = \frac{\bar{X}-\mu_0}{S/\sqrt{n}} \sim t_{n-1} \text{ under }H_0 \tag{T-test}$$ $$\Lambda^* = \frac{\mathcal{L}(\theta_1)}{\mathcal{L}(\theta_0)} > k_\alpha \tag{Neyman-Pearson LRT}$$ $$-2\log\Lambda \xrightarrow{d} \chi^2_d \text{ under }H_0 \tag{Wilks}$$ $$\text{FWER} \leq m\alpha \implies \text{Bonferroni: threshold } \alpha/m \tag{Multiple testing}$$ $$n \geq \left(\frac{(z_\alpha+z_\beta)\sigma}{\delta}\right)^2 \tag{Sample size formula}$$

---

# MODULE 8: Statistical Mechanics Foundations for ML

### _Entropy, KL Divergence, Gibbs Distributions, and the Maximum Entropy Principle_

---

## 8.1 Conceptual Overview

### The Unexpected Unity of Physics and Learning

In 1948, Claude Shannon published _A Mathematical Theory of Communication_, defining entropy for information theory. What he did not initially advertise — but what Jaynes, Gibbs, and Boltzmann had already understood from the physics side — is that this was the _same entropy_ that appears in thermodynamics. The formula $H = -\sum p_i \log p_i$ is not a coincidence shared between two fields. It is the unique mathematical object that satisfies a specific set of consistency axioms about uncertainty, and it appears in both fields for the same deep reason.

This unity has profound consequences for machine learning:

The **cross-entropy loss** — the standard loss for classification — is the negative expected log-likelihood under a distribution. This is thermodynamic free energy in disguise.

The **softmax function** — the universal output layer for classification — is the Gibbs (Boltzmann) distribution from statistical mechanics. The "temperature" parameter of the softmax is literally the thermodynamic temperature.

The **KL divergence** — which appears in VAEs, GANs, reinforcement learning policy optimization, and Bayesian variational inference — is the thermodynamic free energy difference between two systems.

The **maximum entropy principle** — Jaynes' powerful framework — says: among all distributions consistent with your constraints, choose the one of maximum entropy. This produces every standard distribution in statistics as a special case: Gaussian, Exponential, Poisson, Uniform. And it provides the theoretical justification for why these distributions are "natural."

Understanding this module means understanding _why_ deep learning works at the level of fundamental physics.

---

## 8.2 Mathematical Formalization

### 8.2.1 Shannon Entropy

> **Definition 8.1 (Shannon Entropy):** For a discrete random variable $X$ with PMF $p$, the **entropy** is: $$H(X) = -\sum_{x \in \mathcal{X}} p(x) \log p(x) = \mathbb{E}_p[-\log p(X)] \tag{8.1}$$
> 
> For a continuous random variable, the **differential entropy** is: $$h(X) = -\int f(x) \log f(x), dx \tag{8.2}$$

Conventions: we use $\log$ base 2 for information theory (units: bits) and natural log for ML (units: nats). We define $0 \log 0 = 0$ by continuity ($\lim_{p\to 0^+} p\log p = 0$).

**Why entropy measures uncertainty:** Entropy achieves its maximum when all outcomes are equally probable and is zero when the outcome is certain. This is not just intuition — it is a theorem.

> **Theorem 8.1 (Maximum Entropy of Discrete Distribution):** For a distribution over $K$ outcomes, $H(X) \leq \log K$, with equality iff $p(x) = 1/K$ for all $x$ (uniform distribution).

**Proof:** By the log-sum inequality (or Jensen's inequality applied to the concave $-\log$): $$H(X) = -\sum_x p(x)\log p(x) = \sum_x p(x)\log\frac{1}{p(x)} \leq \log\sum_x p(x)\cdot\frac{1}{p(x)}\cdot p(x)$$

More cleanly, consider $D_{KL}(p,|,u)$ where $u$ is uniform. Since $D_{KL} \geq 0$: $$0 \leq D_{KL}(p,|,u) = \sum_x p(x)\log\frac{p(x)}{1/K} = -H(X) + \log K$$

Therefore $H(X) \leq \log K$. Equality holds iff $p = u$ (uniform). $\blacksquare$

**Key properties of entropy:**

$$H(X) \geq 0 \tag{8.3}$$ $$H(X, Y) = H(X) + H(Y|X) \tag{8.4} \quad \text{(Chain rule)}$$ $$H(X|Y) \leq H(X) \tag{8.5} \quad \text{(Conditioning reduces entropy)}$$ $$H(X, Y) \leq H(X) + H(Y) \tag{8.6} \quad \text{(Subadditivity; equality iff } X\perp Y)$$

---

### 8.2.2 KL Divergence (Relative Entropy)

> **Definition 8.2 (KL Divergence):** For distributions $p$ and $q$ over the same support: $$D_{KL}(p ,|, q) = \sum_x p(x) \log\frac{p(x)}{q(x)} = \mathbb{E}_p!\left[\log\frac{p(X)}{q(X)}\right] \tag{8.7}$$
> 
> Continuously: $D_{KL}(p,|,q) = \int p(x)\log\frac{p(x)}{q(x)},dx$

The KL divergence is not a metric (not symmetric, does not satisfy triangle inequality), but it is:

> **Theorem 8.2 (Non-negativity — Gibbs' Inequality):** $D_{KL}(p,|,q) \geq 0$, with equality iff $p = q$ almost everywhere.

**Proof via Jensen's inequality:** Since $-\log$ is strictly convex (Theorem 3.3): $$D_{KL}(p,|,q) = \mathbb{E}_p!\left[-\log\frac{q(X)}{p(X)}\right] \geq -\log\mathbb{E}_p!\left[\frac{q(X)}{p(X)}\right] = -\log\int q(x),dx = -\log 1 = 0$$

Equality in Jensen holds iff $q(x)/p(x)$ is constant $\mathbb{P}_p$-a.s., which (with both being probability distributions) implies $p = q$. $\blacksquare$

**The decomposition of cross-entropy:**

> **Theorem 8.3 (Cross-Entropy Decomposition):** $$\underbrace{H(p, q)}_{\text{Cross-entropy}} = \underbrace{H(p)}_{\text{Entropy of }p} + \underbrace{D_{KL}(p,|,q)}_{\text{KL divergence}} \tag{8.8}$$
> 
> where $H(p, q) = -\mathbb{E}_p[\log q(X)] = -\sum_x p(x)\log q(x)$.

**Proof:** Direct expansion: $$H(p) + D_{KL}(p,|,q) = -\mathbb{E}_p[\log p] + \mathbb{E}_p!\left[\log\frac{p}{q}\right] = -\mathbb{E}_p[\log q] = H(p,q) \qquad \blacksquare$$

**Critical ML consequence:** When training a classifier, the true label distribution $p$ is fixed (the data). Therefore minimizing the cross-entropy loss $H(p, q_\theta)$ over model parameters $\theta$ is _exactly_ minimizing $D_{KL}(p,|,q_\theta)$ — the KL divergence from data to model. Cross-entropy training is KL divergence minimization.

**Asymmetry of KL divergence:**

$D_{KL}(p,|,q)$ penalizes placing zero mass under $q$ where $p$ has positive mass — it forces $q$ to cover all modes of $p$. This is the **mean-seeking** behavior.

$D_{KL}(q,|,p)$ penalizes placing mass under $q$ where $p$ has zero mass — it forces $q$ to concentrate on one mode of $p$. This is the **mode-seeking** behavior.

In variational inference: minimizing $D_{KL}(q,|,p)$ (where $p$ is the posterior) produces mode-seeking approximations. This is why mean-field variational inference underestimates uncertainty — it picks one mode and ignores the others.

---

### 8.2.3 Mutual Information

> **Definition 8.3 (Mutual Information):** $$I(X; Y) = D_{KL}(p_{XY},|,p_X p_Y) = H(X) - H(X|Y) = H(Y) - H(Y|X) \tag{8.9}$$

Mutual information measures how much knowing $Y$ reduces uncertainty about $X$. It is symmetric: $I(X;Y) = I(Y;X)$.

Since $D_{KL} \geq 0$: $I(X;Y) \geq 0$, with equality iff $X \perp Y$.

**ML role:** Mutual information is the theoretical basis of:

- **Feature selection** (select features with highest $I(X_j; Y)$)
- **Information bottleneck** (compress representations while maximizing $I(\text{rep}; Y)$)
- **Contrastive learning** (InfoNCE loss is a lower bound on mutual information)
- **ICA and independent components** (maximize non-Gaussianity / minimize mutual info between components)

---

### 8.2.4 The Gibbs Distribution and Partition Function

This is the bridge from statistical mechanics to machine learning.

**Setup from physics:** A physical system has states ${x_1, \ldots, x_K}$ with energies ${E(x_1), \ldots, E(x_K)}$ and is in thermal equilibrium with a heat bath at temperature $T$.

> **Definition 8.4 (Gibbs/Boltzmann Distribution):** The equilibrium probability of state $x$ is: $$p(x) = \frac{1}{Z(\beta)}\exp(-\beta E(x)) \tag{8.10}$$
> 
> where $\beta = 1/(k_B T)$ is the **inverse temperature** ($k_B$ = Boltzmann constant), and: $$Z(\beta) = \sum_x \exp(-\beta E(x)) \tag{8.11}$$
> 
> is the **partition function** — the normalization constant that ensures $\sum_x p(x) = 1$.

**Why does the Gibbs distribution arise?** It is the _unique_ solution to the maximum entropy problem:

$$\max_{p} H(p) \quad \text{subject to} \quad \mathbb{E}_p[E(X)] = \bar{E} \text{ (fixed mean energy)} \tag{8.12}$$

We prove this in Section 8.2.6.

**The partition function encodes everything:**

$$\log Z(\beta) = \text{log-partition function (log-normalizer)} \tag{8.13}$$

From $\log Z$ we can recover all thermodynamic quantities via differentiation:

$$\mathbb{E}[E(X)] = -\frac{\partial \log Z}{\partial\beta} \tag{8.14}$$

$$\text{Var}[E(X)] = \frac{\partial^2 \log Z}{\partial\beta^2} \tag{8.15}$$

**Proof of (8.14):** $$\frac{\partial \log Z}{\partial\beta} = \frac{1}{Z}\frac{\partial Z}{\partial\beta} = \frac{1}{Z}\sum_x (-E(x))e^{-\beta E(x)} = -\mathbb{E}[E(X)] \qquad \blacksquare$$

**Proof of (8.15):** Differentiate (8.14) again: $$-\frac{\partial^2 \log Z}{\partial\beta^2} = \frac{\partial}{\partial\beta}\mathbb{E}[E] = \mathbb{E}[E^2] - (\mathbb{E}[E])^2 = \text{Var}[E]$$

So $\text{Var}[E] = \partial^2\log Z/\partial\beta^2$. $\blacksquare$

These are the **cumulants** of $E(X)$, generated by differentiating $\log Z$. This is the log-moment generating function of $E(X)$ evaluated at $-\beta$ — connecting directly to the MGF theory of Module 3.

---

### 8.2.5 The Softmax is the Gibbs Distribution

The softmax function used in every neural network classifier: $$\text{softmax}(\mathbf{z})_k = \frac{e^{z_k}}{\sum_{j=1}^K e^{z_j}} \tag{8.16}$$

is _exactly_ the Gibbs distribution (8.10) with:

- Energy $E(k) = -z_k$ (the negative logit is the energy)
- Inverse temperature $\beta = 1$ (standard softmax)

More generally, the **temperature-scaled softmax** used in knowledge distillation, sampling, and language models: $$p_\tau(k) = \frac{e^{z_k/\tau}}{\sum_j e^{z_j/\tau}} \tag{8.17}$$

corresponds to $\beta = 1/\tau$:

- **Low temperature** $\tau \to 0$ ($\beta \to \infty$): distribution concentrates on the lowest-energy (highest-logit) state. The model becomes certain.
- **High temperature** $\tau \to \infty$ ($\beta \to 0$): distribution approaches uniform. Maximum entropy. The model becomes uncertain.
- **Temperature $\tau = 1$**: standard softmax.

The **log-partition function** of the softmax is: $$\log Z(\mathbf{z}) = \log\sum_j e^{z_j} \tag{8.18}$$

This is the **log-sum-exp** (LSE) function — the numerically stable implementation of the softmax normalization constant. Its gradient is the softmax itself: $\nabla_\mathbf{z} \log Z = \text{softmax}(\mathbf{z})$. Its Hessian is the covariance matrix of the softmax distribution — exactly the thermodynamic specific heat.

---

### 8.2.6 The Maximum Entropy Principle

> **Theorem 8.4 (Jaynes' Maximum Entropy Principle):** Among all distributions $p$ satisfying:
> 
> 1. $p(x) \geq 0$, $\sum_x p(x) = 1$ (valid probability)
> 2. $\mathbb{E}_p[f_k(X)] = \mu_k$ for $k = 1, \ldots, m$ (moment constraints)
> 
> the distribution of **maximum entropy** is: $$p^*(x) = \frac{1}{Z(\boldsymbol{\lambda})}\exp!\left(\sum_{k=1}^m \lambda_k f_k(x)\right) \tag{8.19}$$
> 
> where $\boldsymbol{\lambda} = (\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_m)$ are Lagrange multipliers chosen to satisfy the constraints, and $Z(\boldsymbol{\lambda}) = \sum_x \exp(\sum_k \lambda_k f_k(x))$.

**Proof via Lagrangian optimization:**

We maximize $H(p) = -\sum_x p(x)\log p(x)$ subject to the constraints. Form the Lagrangian: $$\mathcal{L}(p, \lambda_0, \boldsymbol{\lambda}) = -\sum_x p(x)\log p(x) - \lambda_0!\left(\sum_x p(x) - 1\right) - \sum_k \lambda_k!\left(\sum_x p(x)f_k(x) - \mu_k\right)$$

Taking the functional derivative with respect to $p(x)$ and setting to zero: $$\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial p(x)} = -\log p(x) - 1 - \lambda_0 - \sum_k \lambda_k f_k(x) = 0$$

Solving: $$p^*(x) = \exp!\left(-1 - \lambda_0 - \sum_k \lambda_k f_k(x)\right) = \frac{1}{Z}\exp!\left(-\sum_k \lambda_k f_k(x)\right)$$

where $Z = e^{1+\lambda_0}$ is the normalization constant. The Lagrange multipliers $\boldsymbol{\lambda}$ are determined by the moment constraints. $\blacksquare$

**The MaxEnt distributions — every standard distribution derived:**

|Constraints|MaxEnt Distribution|
|---|---|
|Support ${0,1,\ldots,K-1}$, no other|$\text{Uniform}$|
|$\mathbb{E}[X] = \mu$ fixed, $X \in [a,b]$|$\text{Uniform}(a,b)$|
|$\mathbb{E}[X] = \mu$, $X \in [0,\infty)$|$\text{Exponential}(\lambda = 1/\mu)$|
|$\mathbb{E}[X] = \mu$, $\mathbb{E}[X^2] = \mu^2 + \sigma^2$ fixed, $X \in \mathbb{R}$|$\mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)$|
|$\mathbb{E}[X] = \lambda$, $X \in {0,1,2,\ldots}$|$\text{Poisson}(\lambda)$|

This is the deepest justification for the Gaussian distribution: it is the distribution of maximum entropy given only a mean and variance constraint. It is not "natural" because data is Gaussian — it is natural because if you only know the first two moments and nothing else, the Gaussian is the most honest (least informative) choice.

---

### 8.2.7 Free Energy and the ELBO

> **Definition 8.5 (Helmholtz Free Energy):** $$F(\beta) = -\frac{1}{\beta}\log Z(\beta) = \mathbb{E}_p[E] - \frac{1}{\beta}H(p) \tag{8.20}$$

The free energy balances **energy** (how likely is each state) against **entropy** (how spread out the distribution is). At low temperature, energy dominates — the system concentrates on low-energy states. At high temperature, entropy dominates — the system spreads uniformly.

**The ELBO (Evidence Lower BOund) is thermodynamic free energy:**

In variational inference, we approximate a true posterior $p(\mathbf{z}\mid\mathbf{x})$ with a variational distribution $q_\phi(\mathbf{z})$. The evidence lower bound is:

$$\log p(\mathbf{x}) = \log\int p(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{z}),d\mathbf{z} \geq \mathbb{E}_{q_\phi}[\log p(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{z})] + H(q_\phi) = \mathcal{L}(\phi) \tag{8.21}$$

Equivalently: $$\log p(\mathbf{x}) = \mathcal{L}(\phi) + D_{KL}(q_\phi,|,p(\cdot\mid\mathbf{x})) \tag{8.22}$$

**Proof of (8.22):** $$\mathcal{L}(\phi) = \mathbb{E}_{q_\phi}!\left[\log\frac{p(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{z})}{q_\phi(\mathbf{z})}\right] = \mathbb{E}_{q_\phi}!\left[\log\frac{p(\mathbf{z}\mid\mathbf{x})p(\mathbf{x})}{q_\phi(\mathbf{z})}\right] = \log p(\mathbf{x}) - D_{KL}(q_\phi,|,p(\cdot\mid\mathbf{x})) \qquad \blacksquare$$

Since $D_{KL} \geq 0$, $\mathcal{L}(\phi) \leq \log p(\mathbf{x})$ — hence "lower bound." Maximizing $\mathcal{L}(\phi)$ over $\phi$ minimizes $D_{KL}(q_\phi,|,p(\cdot\mid\mathbf{x}))$ — it forces $q_\phi$ toward the true posterior.

In the VAE decomposition, (8.21) becomes: $$\mathcal{L}(\phi, \theta) = \underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{q_\phi(\mathbf{z}\mid\mathbf{x})}[\log p_\theta(\mathbf{x}\mid\mathbf{z})]}_{\text{Reconstruction loss}} - \underbrace{D_{KL}(q_\phi(\mathbf{z}\mid\mathbf{x}),|,p(\mathbf{z}))}_{\text{Regularization}} \tag{8.23}$$

The reconstruction term is thermodynamic energy (negative). The KL term is thermodynamic entropy (positive at high $\beta$). The ELBO is — precisely — negative free energy.

---

### 8.2.8 Energy-Based Models

> **Definition 8.6 (Energy-Based Model):** An EBM defines a probability distribution via an energy function $E_\theta: \mathcal{X} \to \mathbb{R}$: $$p_\theta(x) = \frac{1}{Z(\theta)}\exp(-E_\theta(x)) \tag{8.24}$$
> 
> where $Z(\theta) = \int \exp(-E_\theta(x)),dx$ is the partition function.

The learning objective (MLE) is: $$\max_\theta \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \log p_\theta(x_i) = -\frac{1}{n}\sum_i E_\theta(x_i) - \log Z(\theta) \tag{8.25}$$

The gradient of the log-partition function is the expected energy under the model: $$\nabla_\theta \log Z(\theta) = -\mathbb{E}_{p_\theta}[\nabla_\theta E_\theta(x)] \tag{8.26}$$

Therefore the MLE gradient is: $$\nabla_\theta \ell = \underbrace{-\frac{1}{n}\sum_i \nabla_\theta E_\theta(x_i)}_{\text{Decrease data energy}} + \underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{p_\theta}[\nabla_\theta E_\theta(x)]}_{\text{Increase model energy}} \tag{8.27}$$

This is the **contrastive divergence** gradient: push down energy on real data, push up energy on model samples. Computing the second term requires sampling from $p_\theta$ — the fundamental challenge of training EBMs.

**ML role:** Restricted Boltzmann Machines (RBMs), Deep Boltzmann Machines, diffusion models (which learn to denoise — equivalent to learning an energy function), and score matching all live in this framework.

---

### 8.2.9 The Information-Theoretic View of Regularization

Every regularizer in ML has an information-theoretic interpretation through the **minimum description length (MDL)** principle:

$$\text{Regularized loss} = \underbrace{-\log p(\mathcal{D}\mid\theta)}_{\text{Data fit}} + \underbrace{-\log p(\theta)}_{\text{Model complexity}} \tag{8.28}$$

where $-\log p(\theta)$ is the **description length** of the parameters under the prior. Regularization = penalizing description length. The model that minimizes (8.28) achieves the best tradeoff between fitting the data and compressing the model — a direct application of the maximum entropy principle.

The **rate-distortion tradeoff** from information theory is the continuous version: we trade off the mutual information $I(\mathbf{X}; \mathbf{Z})$ (rate — how much we compress) against the reconstruction quality $\mathbb{E}[|x - \hat{x}|^2]$ (distortion). The VAE's $\beta$-VAE variant explicitly controls this tradeoff via the parameter $\beta$ in: $$\mathcal{L}_\beta = \mathbb{E}[\log p_\theta(\mathbf{x}\mid\mathbf{z})] - \beta D_{KL}(q_\phi(\mathbf{z}\mid\mathbf{x}),|,p(\mathbf{z})) \tag{8.29}$$

---

## 8.3 Numerical Examples

### Example 8.1: Entropy of Distributions — Computing and Interpreting

**Problem:** Compute the entropy of: (a) $\text{Bernoulli}(0.5)$, (b) $\text{Bernoulli}(0.1)$, (c) $\text{Categorical}(1/4, 1/4, 1/4, 1/4)$, (d) $\text{Categorical}(0.97, 0.01, 0.01, 0.01)$.

**(a)** $H = -(0.5\log 0.5 + 0.5\log 0.5) = \log 2 = 1$ bit (maximum for binary).

**(b)** $H = -(0.1\log 0.1 + 0.9\log 0.9) = 0.1(2.303) + 0.9(0.105) = 0.325$ nats $= 0.469$ bits.

**(c)** $H = -4 \cdot \frac{1}{4}\log\frac{1}{4} = \log 4 = 2$ bits (maximum for 4 outcomes — uniform).

**(d)** $H = -(0.97\log 0.97 + 3\cdot 0.01\log 0.01) = 0.97(0.0305) + 3(0.01)(4.605) = 0.0296 + 0.1382 = 0.168$ nats.

**Interpretation:** A nearly-certain prediction ($d$) has much lower entropy than a uniform uncertainty ($c$). Entropy quantifies the _expected surprise_ of outcomes.

---

### Example 8.2: KL Divergence — Gaussian Case

**Closed form for Gaussians:** If $p = \mathcal{N}(\mu_1, \sigma_1^2)$ and $q = \mathcal{N}(\mu_2, \sigma_2^2)$:

$$D_{KL}(p,|,q) = \log\frac{\sigma_2}{\sigma_1} + \frac{\sigma_1^2 + (\mu_1-\mu_2)^2}{2\sigma_2^2} - \frac{1}{2} \tag{8.30}$$

**Derivation:** $$D_{KL} = \mathbb{E}_p!\left[\log\frac{p(X)}{q(X)}\right] = \mathbb{E}_p!\left[\log\frac{\sigma_2}{\sigma_1} - \frac{(X-\mu_1)^2}{2\sigma_1^2} + \frac{(X-\mu_2)^2}{2\sigma_2^2}\right]$$

$$= \log\frac{\sigma_2}{\sigma_1} - \frac{1}{2} + \frac{\mathbb{E}_p[(X-\mu_2)^2]}{2\sigma_2^2}$$

Since $\mathbb{E}_p[(X-\mu_2)^2] = \text{Var}_p(X) + (\mu_1-\mu_2)^2 = \sigma_1^2 + (\mu_1-\mu_2)^2$, equation (8.30) follows. $\blacksquare$

**Numerical example:** $p = \mathcal{N}(0,1)$, $q = \mathcal{N}(1, 2)$: $$D_{KL}(p,|,q) = \log\frac{\sqrt{2}}{1} + \frac{1 + 1}{2\cdot 2} - \frac{1}{2} = 0.347 + 0.25 - 0.5 = 0.097$$ $$D_{KL}(q,|,p) = \log\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} + \frac{2 + 1}{2} - \frac{1}{2} = -0.347 + 1.5 - 0.5 = 0.653$$

Confirming asymmetry: $D_{KL}(p,|,q) \neq D_{KL}(q,|,p)$.

---

### Example 8.3: Maximum Entropy Derivation of the Gaussian

**Problem:** Verify that $\mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)$ is the MaxEnt distribution on $\mathbb{R}$ subject to $\mathbb{E}[X] = \mu$ and $\mathbb{E}[X^2] = \mu^2 + \sigma^2$.

From Theorem 8.4 with $f_1(x) = x$ and $f_2(x) = x^2$: $$p^*(x) \propto \exp(\lambda_1 x + \lambda_2 x^2)$$

For this to be normalizable we need $\lambda_2 < 0$. Completing the square: $$\lambda_1 x + \lambda_2 x^2 = \lambda_2!\left(x + \frac{\lambda_1}{2\lambda_2}\right)^2 - \frac{\lambda_1^2}{4\lambda_2}$$

This is a Gaussian with mean $\mu = -\lambda_1/(2\lambda_2)$ and variance $\sigma^2 = -1/(2\lambda_2)$.

Substituting: $\lambda_2 = -1/(2\sigma^2)$ and $\lambda_1 = \mu/\sigma^2$, giving exactly $\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^2)$. $\blacksquare$

---

### Example 8.4: Softmax Temperature and Entropy

For logits $\mathbf{z} = (3.0, 1.0, 0.5)$ and temperatures $\tau \in {0.1, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 10.0}$:

|$\tau$|$p_1$|$p_2$|$p_3$|$H$ (nats)|
|---|---|---|---|---|
|0.1|0.9999|0.0001|0.0000|0.001|
|0.5|0.9820|0.0164|0.0016|0.109|
|1.0|0.8438|0.1142|0.0420|0.528|
|2.0|0.6044|0.2471|0.1486|0.977|
|10.0|0.3582|0.3272|0.3146|1.098|

As $\tau \to 0$: argmax (certain). As $\tau \to \infty$: uniform (maximum entropy = $\log 3 = 1.099$ nats).

---

## 8.4 Implementation

```python
import numpy as np
import scipy.stats as stats
import scipy.special as special
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.gridspec as gridspec
from typing import Callable, Optional

# =============================================================================
# MODULE 8: Statistical Mechanics Foundations for ML
# =============================================================================

# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# PART A: Entropy, KL Divergence, and Mutual Information
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------

class InformationTheoryToolkit:
    """
    Numerically precise implementations of core information-theoretic quantities.
    All computations use natural logarithms (nats) unless otherwise specified.
    """

    @staticmethod
    def entropy(p: np.ndarray, base: float = np.e) -> float:
        """
        Shannon entropy H(p) = -sum_x p(x) log p(x).
        Handles p(x)=0 correctly via 0 * log 0 = 0 convention.
        """
        p     = np.asarray(p, dtype=float)
        p     = p / p.sum()       # ensure normalization
        mask  = p > 0
        h     = -np.sum(p[mask] * np.log(p[mask]))
        if base != np.e:
            h /= np.log(base)
        return h

    @staticmethod
    def kl_divergence(p: np.ndarray, q: np.ndarray,
                      eps: float = 1e-12) -> float:
        """
        D_KL(p || q) = sum_x p(x) log(p(x)/q(x)).
        Clamps q away from zero to avoid log(0).

        WARNING: if p(x) > 0 and q(x) = 0, KL = +infinity (correctly).
        """
        p  = np.asarray(p, dtype=float); p = p / p.sum()
        q  = np.asarray(q, dtype=float); q = q / q.sum()
        q  = np.clip(q, eps, None)
        mask = p > eps
        return float(np.sum(p[mask] * np.log(p[mask] / q[mask])))

    @staticmethod
    def js_divergence(p: np.ndarray, q: np.ndarray) -> float:
        """
        Jensen-Shannon divergence — symmetrized, bounded version of KL.
        JSD(p,q) = (KL(p||m) + KL(q||m)) / 2  where m = (p+q)/2.
        JSD in [0, log 2] nats; sqrt(JSD) is a proper metric.
        """
        p = np.asarray(p, dtype=float); p = p / p.sum()
        q = np.asarray(q, dtype=float); q = q / q.sum()
        m = 0.5 * (p + q)
        toolkit = InformationTheoryToolkit
        return 0.5 * (toolkit.kl_divergence(p, m) + toolkit.kl_divergence(q, m))

    @staticmethod
    def cross_entropy(p: np.ndarray, q: np.ndarray,
                      eps: float = 1e-12) -> float:
        """
        Cross-entropy H(p, q) = -sum_x p(x) log q(x).
        By Theorem 8.3: H(p,q) = H(p) + KL(p||q).
        """
        p = np.asarray(p, dtype=float); p = p / p.sum()
        q = np.asarray(q, dtype=float); q = q / q.sum()
        q = np.clip(q, eps, None)
        return float(-np.sum(p * np.log(q)))

    @staticmethod
    def kl_gaussian(mu1: float, sigma1: float,
                    mu2: float, sigma2: float) -> float:
        """
        Analytical KL divergence KL(N(mu1,sigma1^2) || N(mu2,sigma2^2)).
        Equation 8.30.
        """
        return (np.log(sigma2/sigma1)
                + (sigma1**2 + (mu1-mu2)**2) / (2*sigma2**2)
                - 0.5)

    @staticmethod
    def mutual_information_discrete(joint_pmf: np.ndarray) -> float:
        """
        Compute I(X;Y) = H(X) + H(Y) - H(X,Y) from the joint PMF.
        Equation 8.9.
        """
        joint = np.asarray(joint_pmf, dtype=float)
        joint = joint / joint.sum()
        px    = joint.sum(axis=1)
        py    = joint.sum(axis=0)
        hx    = InformationTheoryToolkit.entropy(px)
        hy    = InformationTheoryToolkit.entropy(py)
        hxy   = InformationTheoryToolkit.entropy(joint.ravel())
        return hx + hy - hxy

    def verify_cross_entropy_decomposition(self, p: np.ndarray, q: np.ndarray):
        """
        Numerically verify Theorem 8.3: H(p,q) = H(p) + KL(p||q).
        """
        hp    = self.entropy(p)
        kl    = self.kl_divergence(p, q)
        ce    = self.cross_entropy(p, q)
        print("\nTheorem 8.3 Verification: H(p,q) = H(p) + KL(p||q)")
        print(f"  H(p)          = {hp:.6f} nats")
        print(f"  KL(p||q)      = {kl:.6f} nats")
        print(f"  H(p) + KL     = {hp+kl:.6f} nats")
        print(f"  H(p,q)        = {ce:.6f} nats")
        print(f"  Match: {np.isclose(hp+kl, ce, atol=1e-8)}")


# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# PART B: Gibbs Distribution, Partition Function, and Softmax Temperature
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------

class GibbsDistribution:
    """
    The Gibbs/Boltzmann distribution: p(x) = exp(-beta*E(x)) / Z(beta).
    Demonstrates the connection between statistical mechanics and the softmax.
    """

    def __init__(self, energies: np.ndarray, beta: float = 1.0):
        """
        Parameters
        ----------
        energies : array of energy values E(x_1), ..., E(x_K)
        beta     : inverse temperature (1/tau in ML notation)
        """
        self.energies = np.asarray(energies, dtype=float)
        self.beta     = beta
        self._update()

    def _update(self):
        """Recompute distribution. Uses log-sum-exp for numerical stability."""
        log_weights      = -self.beta * self.energies
        self.log_Z       = special.logsumexp(log_weights)          # Eq. 8.13
        self.log_probs   = log_weights - self.log_Z
        self.probs       = np.exp(self.log_probs)

    def set_beta(self, beta: float):
        self.beta = beta
        self._update()

    @property
    def mean_energy(self) -> float:
        """E[E(X)] = -d/dbeta log Z. Equation 8.14."""
        return float(np.dot(self.probs, self.energies))

    @property
    def var_energy(self) -> float:
        """Var[E(X)] = d²/dbeta² log Z. Equation 8.15."""
        return float(np.dot(self.probs, (self.energies - self.mean_energy)**2))

    @property
    def entropy(self) -> float:
        """H(p) in nats."""
        return float(-np.dot(self.probs, self.log_probs))

    @property
    def free_energy(self) -> float:
        """F = -log(Z) / beta = E[E] - H/beta. Equation 8.20."""
        return -self.log_Z / self.beta

    def temperature_sweep(self, betas: np.ndarray) -> dict:
        """
        Compute thermodynamic quantities across a range of inverse temperatures.
        Returns dict of arrays for plotting.
        """
        result = {k: [] for k in ['beta','tau','mean_E','var_E','entropy',
                                   'free_energy','log_Z']}
        for b in betas:
            self.set_beta(b)
            result['beta'].append(b)
            result['tau'].append(1/b)
            result['mean_E'].append(self.mean_energy)
            result['var_E'].append(self.var_energy)
            result['entropy'].append(self.entropy)
            result['free_energy'].append(self.free_energy)
            result['log_Z'].append(float(self.log_Z))
        return {k: np.array(v) for k,v in result.items()}


def softmax_temperature_analysis(logits: np.ndarray):
    """
    Demonstrates softmax as Gibbs distribution (Eq. 8.16-8.17).
    Shows how temperature controls entropy and concentration.
    """
    # Softmax = Gibbs with energies = -logits, beta = 1/tau
    energies = -logits
    taus     = [0.1, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 5.0, 10.0]
    betas    = [1/t for t in taus]
    K        = len(logits)

    it = InformationTheoryToolkit()
    print("\n" + "="*70)
    print("  SOFTMAX = GIBBS DISTRIBUTION: Temperature Analysis")
    print(f"  Logits: {logits}")
    print("="*70)
    header = f"{'tau':>8} {'beta':>8} {'p1':>8} {'p2':>8} {'p3':>8} {'H(nats)':>10} {'log_Z':>10}"
    print(f"\n{header}")
    print("-"*70)

    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(14, 4.5))
    entropy_vals = []
    all_probs    = []

    for tau, beta in zip(taus, betas):
        g     = GibbsDistribution(energies, beta)
        probs = g.probs
        h     = g.entropy
        entropy_vals.append(h)
        all_probs.append(probs)
        prob_str = "  ".join(f"{p:.4f}" for p in probs)
        print(f"  {tau:>8.1f} {beta:>8.2f}   {prob_str}   {h:>10.4f}   {g.log_Z:>10.4f}")

    all_probs = np.array(all_probs)

    # Panel 1: Probabilities vs temperature
    ax = axes[0]
    for k in range(K):
        ax.semilogx(taus, all_probs[:, k], 'o-', lw=2, ms=5,
                    label=f"$p_{k+1}$ (logit={logits[k]})")
    ax.axhline(1/K, color='gray', lw=1, linestyle='--', label=f"Uniform 1/{K}")
    ax.set_xlabel("Temperature τ (log scale)", fontsize=11)
    ax.set_ylabel("Probability", fontsize=11)
    ax.set_title("Probabilities vs Temperature\n(Softmax = Gibbs Distribution)",
                 fontsize=11, fontweight='bold')
    ax.legend(fontsize=9); ax.grid(alpha=0.3)

    # Panel 2: Entropy vs temperature
    ax = axes[1]
    ax.semilogx(taus, entropy_vals, 'o-', color='#1a6faf', lw=2.5, ms=6)
    ax.axhline(np.log(K), color='red', lw=1.5, linestyle='--',
               label=f"Max entropy log({K})={np.log(K):.3f}")
    ax.axhline(0, color='green', lw=1.5, linestyle=':', label="Min entropy 0")
    ax.set_xlabel("Temperature τ (log scale)", fontsize=11)
    ax.set_ylabel("Entropy H(p) [nats]", fontsize=11)
    ax.set_title("Entropy vs Temperature\n(High τ → Max Entropy; Low τ → Certain)",
                 fontsize=11, fontweight='bold')
    ax.legend(fontsize=9); ax.grid(alpha=0.3)

    # Panel 3: Thermodynamic sweep — energy vs variance
    ax = axes[2]
    g  = GibbsDistribution(energies, 1.0)
    betas_arr = np.linspace(0.05, 5, 200)
    sweep     = g.temperature_sweep(betas_arr)
    ax.plot(sweep['tau'], sweep['mean_E'], color='#1a6faf', lw=2.5, label="Mean energy E[E]")
    ax2 = ax.twinx()
    ax2.plot(sweep['tau'], sweep['var_E'], color='#e84040', lw=2, linestyle='--',
             label="Var[E] = ∂²logZ/∂β²")
    ax.set_xlabel("Temperature τ = 1/β", fontsize=11)
    ax.set_ylabel("Mean energy", color='#1a6faf', fontsize=11)
    ax2.set_ylabel("Variance of energy", color='#e84040', fontsize=11)
    ax.set_title("Thermodynamic Quantities\n(Eq. 8.14–8.15: logZ generates moments)",
                 fontsize=11, fontweight='bold')
    ax.legend(loc='upper left', fontsize=9)
    ax2.legend(loc='upper right', fontsize=9)
    ax.grid(alpha=0.3)

    plt.suptitle("Gibbs Distribution — Statistical Mechanics meets ML",
                 fontsize=13, fontweight='bold', y=1.02)
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.savefig("module8_gibbs.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches='tight')
    plt.show()


# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# PART C: Maximum Entropy Principle — Deriving Distributions from Constraints
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def maxent_verification():
    """
    Numerically verify Theorem 8.4: MaxEnt distributions are the Gibbs form.
    For each distribution, verify it maximizes entropy among all distributions
    satisfying the given moment constraints.
    """
    it = InformationTheoryToolkit()

    print("\n" + "="*62)
    print("  MAXIMUM ENTROPY PRINCIPLE — NUMERICAL VERIFICATION")
    print("="*62)

    # Case 1: Exponential is MaxEnt for E[X]=mu on [0,inf)
    # Discretize and compare
    mu       = 3.0
    lam      = 1 / mu
    x_grid   = np.linspace(0, 30, 3000)
    dx       = x_grid[1] - x_grid[0]

    # True MaxEnt (Exponential) discretized
    p_exp    = stats.expon.pdf(x_grid, scale=mu) * dx
    p_exp   /= p_exp.sum()

    # A non-MaxEnt alternative with same mean: Gamma(2, mu/2)
    p_gamma  = stats.gamma.pdf(x_grid, a=2, scale=mu/2) * dx
    p_gamma /= p_gamma.sum()

    h_exp   = it.entropy(p_exp)
    h_gamma = it.entropy(p_gamma)
    mu_exp  = np.sum(x_grid * p_exp)
    mu_gam  = np.sum(x_grid * p_gamma)

    print(f"\n  Constraint: E[X]={mu:.1f}, support [0,∞)")
    print(f"  Exponential({lam:.3f}): H={h_exp:.4f} nats, E[X]={mu_exp:.4f}")
    print(f"  Gamma(2,{mu/2:.1f}):    H={h_gamma:.4f} nats, E[X]={mu_gam:.4f}")
    print(f"  MaxEnt has HIGHER entropy: {h_exp > h_gamma}")

    # Case 2: Gaussian is MaxEnt for E[X]=mu, E[X^2]=mu^2+sigma^2
    mu_g    = 2.0; sig_g = 1.5
    x_grid2 = np.linspace(-10, 14, 5000)
    dx2     = x_grid2[1] - x_grid2[0]

    p_gauss  = stats.norm.pdf(x_grid2, mu_g, sig_g) * dx2
    p_gauss /= p_gauss.sum()

    # Alternative with same mean and variance: shifted t-distribution (heavier tails)
    df_t     = 5
    scale_t  = sig_g * np.sqrt((df_t-2)/df_t)  # match variance
    p_t      = stats.t.pdf(x_grid2, df=df_t, loc=mu_g, scale=scale_t) * dx2
    p_t     /= p_t.sum()

    h_gauss = it.entropy(p_gauss)
    h_t     = it.entropy(p_t)

    print(f"\n  Constraint: E[X]={mu_g}, Var[X]={sig_g**2:.2f}")
    print(f"  Gaussian:       H={h_gauss:.4f} nats")
    print(f"  t-distribution: H={h_t:.4f} nats")
    print(f"  MaxEnt Gaussian has HIGHER entropy: {h_gauss > h_t}")


# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# PART D: ELBO / Variational Inference Demonstration
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def demonstrate_elbo(n_iter: int = 2000, seed: int = 42):
    """
    Demonstrate variational inference via ELBO maximization.
    Approximate a bimodal posterior p(z|x) with a Gaussian q(z).
    Shows the mode-seeking behavior of KL(q||p) (Eq. 8.22).
    """
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)

    # True (unnormalized) log posterior: bimodal Gaussian mixture
    def log_p_unnorm(z):
        return np.log(0.4 * stats.norm.pdf(z, -2, 0.8) +
                      0.6 * stats.norm.pdf(z,  2, 1.0) + 1e-300)

    # Variational distribution: q(z) = N(mu, sigma^2)
    # ELBO = E_q[log p(z)] + H(q)    [Eq. 8.21]
    def elbo(mu_q, log_sig_q, n_mc=1000):
        sig_q   = np.exp(log_sig_q)
        z_samp  = rng.normal(mu_q, sig_q, n_mc)
        lp      = log_p_unnorm(z_samp)
        lq      = stats.norm.logpdf(z_samp, mu_q, sig_q)
        return np.mean(lp - lq)  # ELBO = E_q[log p - log q]

    # Grid search over (mu_q, sigma_q) to find ELBO landscape
    mus    = np.linspace(-4, 4, 80)
    sigs   = np.linspace(0.3, 3.0, 80)
    MU, SIG = np.meshgrid(mus, sigs)
    ELBO_grid = np.array([[elbo(m, np.log(s), n_mc=500)
                           for m in mus] for s in sigs])

    # Gradient ascent on ELBO
    mu_q     = -1.5  # initialization near one mode
    log_sig_q = np.log(0.5)
    lr       = 0.05
    elbo_hist = []
    mu_hist   = [mu_q]
    for _ in range(n_iter):
        eps  = 1e-4
        g_mu  = (elbo(mu_q+eps, log_sig_q) - elbo(mu_q-eps, log_sig_q)) / (2*eps)
        g_sig = (elbo(mu_q, log_sig_q+eps) - elbo(mu_q, log_sig_q-eps)) / (2*eps)
        mu_q      += lr * g_mu
        log_sig_q += lr * g_sig
        elbo_hist.append(elbo(mu_q, log_sig_q))
        mu_hist.append(mu_q)

    sig_final = np.exp(log_sig_q)

    # Plot
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(15, 5))

    # Panel 1: True posterior and final q
    ax  = axes[0]
    z   = np.linspace(-6, 6, 500)
    lp  = np.exp(log_p_unnorm(z))
    lp /= lp.sum() * (z[1]-z[0])
    ax.plot(z, lp, 'k-', lw=2.5, label="True $p(z|x)$ (bimodal)")
    ax.plot(z, stats.norm.pdf(z, mu_q, sig_final),
            color='#e84040', lw=2.5, linestyle='--',
            label=f"$q^*(z) = \\mathcal{{N}}({mu_q:.2f}, {sig_final:.2f}^2)$")
    ax.fill_between(z, stats.norm.pdf(z, mu_q, sig_final),
                    alpha=0.2, color='#e84040')
    ax.set_title("Mode-seeking: KL(q||p) minimization\n$q$ collapses to one mode",
                 fontsize=11, fontweight='bold')
    ax.legend(fontsize=9); ax.grid(alpha=0.3)
    ax.set_xlabel("z"); ax.set_ylabel("Density")

    # Panel 2: ELBO landscape
    ax = axes[1]
    cf = ax.contourf(MU, SIG, ELBO_grid, levels=25, cmap='Blues')
    plt.colorbar(cf, ax=ax, label="ELBO")
    ax.plot(mu_hist, [np.exp(log_sig_q)]*len(mu_hist),
            'r.-', ms=3, lw=1, alpha=0.6, label="Optimization path")
    ax.scatter([mu_q], [sig_final], s=120, color='red', zorder=5,
               marker='*', label=f"Optimum (μ={mu_q:.2f}, σ={sig_final:.2f})")
    ax.set_xlabel("μ_q", fontsize=11); ax.set_ylabel("σ_q", fontsize=11)
    ax.set_title("ELBO Landscape\n(maximizing ELBO ≡ minimizing KL(q||p))",
                 fontsize=11, fontweight='bold')
    ax.legend(fontsize=9)

    # Panel 3: ELBO history
    ax = axes[2]
    ax.plot(elbo_hist, color='#1a6faf', lw=2)
    ax.set_xlabel("Iteration", fontsize=11)
    ax.set_ylabel("ELBO", fontsize=11)
    ax.set_title("ELBO During Optimization\n(non-decreasing → converges)",
                 fontsize=11, fontweight='bold')
    ax.grid(alpha=0.3)

    plt.suptitle("Variational Inference: ELBO Maximization (Eq. 8.21–8.22)",
                 fontsize=13, fontweight='bold', y=1.02)
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.savefig("module8_elbo.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches='tight')
    plt.show()
    print(f"\nFinal variational parameters: μ={mu_q:.4f}, σ={sig_final:.4f}")


# =============================================================================
# MAIN
# =============================================================================

if __name__ == "__main__":

    it = InformationTheoryToolkit()

    # --- A: Entropy and KL computations ---
    print("="*62)
    print("  ENTROPY & KL DIVERGENCE")
    print("="*62)
    p = np.array([0.4, 0.3, 0.2, 0.1])
    q = np.array([0.25, 0.25, 0.25, 0.25])
    print(f"\n  p = {p}")
    print(f"  q = {q}  (uniform)")
    print(f"  H(p)        = {it.entropy(p):.6f} nats")
    print(f"  H(q)        = {it.entropy(q):.6f} nats  (= log 4 = {np.log(4):.6f})")

    print(f"  KL(q||p)    = {it.kl_divergence(q,p):.6f} nats  (asymmetry!)")
    print(f"  H(p,q)      = {it.cross_entropy(p,q):.6f} nats")
    print(f"  JSD(p,q)    = {it.js_divergence(p,q):.6f} nats  (symmetric)")
    it.verify_cross_entropy_decomposition(p, q)

    # Gaussian KL
    print(f"\n  Gaussian KL: N(0,1) || N(1,2): {it.kl_gaussian(0,1,1,np.sqrt(2)):.6f}")
    print(f"  Gaussian KL: N(1,2) || N(0,1): {it.kl_gaussian(1,np.sqrt(2),0,1):.6f}")

    # --- B: Gibbs distribution / softmax temperature ---
    print("\n" + "="*62)
    print("  GIBBS DISTRIBUTION & SOFTMAX TEMPERATURE")
```

## 8.6 Module Summary: The Grand Unification

|Statistical Mechanics|Machine Learning Equivalent|
|---|---|
|Energy function $E(x)$|Negative logit; model score|
|Inverse temperature $\beta = 1/\tau$|Inverse softmax temperature|
|Partition function $Z(\beta)$|Log-sum-exp normalizer|
|Gibbs distribution $e^{-\beta E}/Z$|Softmax output layer|
|Helmholtz free energy $F = -\log Z/\beta$|Negative ELBO (VAE objective)|
|Entropy $H$|Regularization term in VAE|
|KL divergence $D_{KL}(p\|q)$|Training objective for generative models|
|Cross-entropy $H(p,q)$|Classification loss|
|Maximum entropy principle|Justification for standard distributions|
|Contrastive divergence|EBM training (push data energy down, model energy up)|
|Log-partition function derivatives|Cumulants; moment computation|

## 8.7 Key Equations Reference Card

$$H(p) = -\mathbb{E}_p[\log p(X)] \tag{Entropy}$$ $$D_{KL}(p|q) = \mathbb{E}_p[\log p/q] \geq 0 \tag{KL divergence}$$ $$H(p,q) = H(p) + D_{KL}(p|q) \tag{Cross-entropy decomposition}$$ $$p^_(x) = e^{-\beta E(x)}/Z(\beta),\quad Z = \sum_x e^{-\beta E(x)} \tag{Gibbs distribution}$$ $$\mathbb{E}[E] = -\partial_\beta\log Z,\quad \text{Var}[E] = \partial^2_\beta\log Z \tag{Partition function moments}$$ $$\text{softmax}_k(\mathbf{z}) = e^{z_k/\tau}/\sum_j e^{z_j/\tau} \equiv \text{Gibbs}(\beta=1/\tau) \tag{Softmax = Gibbs}$$ $$\log p(\mathbf{x}) \geq \mathbb{E}_q[\log p(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{z})] + H(q) = \mathcal{L}(\phi) \tag{ELBO}$$ $$p^__\text{MaxEnt} = \exp(\sum_k\lambda_k f_k)/Z \text{ given } \mathbb{E}[f_k]=\mu_k \tag{MaxEnt principle}$$
