# MODULE 9: Multivariate Distributions & Covariance

### _The Geometry of Uncertainty in High Dimensions_

---

## 9.1 Conceptual Overview

### Why High-Dimensional Probability Is Different

Everything we built in Modules 1–8 was largely one-dimensional. Real ML operates in spaces of thousands, millions, or billions of dimensions. The transition to high dimensions is not merely a notational upgrade — it fundamentally changes the geometry of probability in ways that are deeply counterintuitive.

In high dimensions:

- Almost all the volume of a hypersphere is concentrated near its surface — not the center.
- Two randomly chosen vectors are almost surely nearly orthogonal.
- The nearest neighbor of any point is almost as far away as the farthest neighbor (the "curse of dimensionality").
- The Gaussian distribution concentrates its mass in a thin shell of radius $\sqrt{d}$ — the **typical set**.

Understanding these phenomena is not academic. They explain why neural networks need normalization layers, why covariance estimation is hard with few samples, why PCA works, and why certain kernel methods scale better than explicit feature maps.

### The Covariance Matrix as the Shape of Uncertainty

The covariance matrix $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ is the multivariate analog of variance. But while variance is a single number, the covariance matrix is a geometric object — a positive definite matrix that defines an ellipsoid in $\mathbb{R}^d$. Its eigenvectors are the principal axes of uncertainty; its eigenvalues are the variances along those axes.

This geometric view unlocks everything:

- **PCA** is finding the eigenvectors of $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ — the directions of maximum variance.
- **Mahalanobis distance** is Euclidean distance in the whitened coordinate system defined by $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$.
- **Gaussian Processes** are infinite-dimensional multivariate Gaussians, parameterized by a kernel that plays the role of $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$.
- **Factor Analysis** and **VAEs** learn low-rank approximations to $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$.
- **Batch Normalization** estimates and removes the diagonal of $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ at each layer.

The covariance matrix is not a statistical curiosity — it is the central object of multivariate statistics and the hidden architecture of every deep learning system.

---

## 9.2 Mathematical Formalization

### 9.2.1 The Multivariate Gaussian Distribution

> **Definition 9.1 (Multivariate Gaussian):** A random vector $\mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{R}^d$ has a **multivariate Gaussian distribution** $\mathbf{X} \sim \mathcal{N}_d(\boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma})$ if its PDF is: $$f(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{1}{(2\pi)^{d/2}|\boldsymbol{\Sigma}|^{1/2}} \exp!\left(-\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})^\top \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1} (\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})\right) \tag{9.1}$$
> 
> where $\boldsymbol{\mu} \in \mathbb{R}^d$ is the mean vector and $\boldsymbol{\Sigma} \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d}$ is a symmetric positive definite covariance matrix.

**The quadratic form** $(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})^\top\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})$ is the squared **Mahalanobis distance** from $\mathbf{x}$ to $\boldsymbol{\mu}$. Contours of constant density are ellipsoids defined by this quadratic form — not spheres, unless $\boldsymbol{\Sigma} = \sigma^2\mathbf{I}$.

**Moments:** $$\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{X}] = \boldsymbol{\mu} \tag{9.2}$$ $$\text{Cov}(\mathbf{X}) = \mathbb{E}[(\mathbf{X}-\boldsymbol{\mu})(\mathbf{X}-\boldsymbol{\mu})^\top] = \boldsymbol{\Sigma} \tag{9.3}$$

**MGF:** $$M_\mathbf{X}(\mathbf{t}) = \mathbb{E}[e^{\mathbf{t}^\top\mathbf{X}}] = \exp!\left(\boldsymbol{\mu}^\top\mathbf{t} + \frac{1}{2}\mathbf{t}^\top\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{t}\right) \tag{9.4}$$

---

### 9.2.2 The Covariance Matrix — Geometry and Decomposition

> **Definition 9.2 (Covariance Matrix):** For a random vector $\mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{R}^d$: $$\boldsymbol{\Sigma} = \text{Cov}(\mathbf{X}) = \mathbb{E}[(\mathbf{X}-\boldsymbol{\mu})(\mathbf{X}-\boldsymbol{\mu})^\top] \tag{9.5}$$

with entries $\Sigma_{ij} = \text{Cov}(X_i, X_j)$. The diagonal contains the marginal variances: $\Sigma_{ii} = \text{Var}(X_i)$.

**Key structural properties of any valid covariance matrix:**

A matrix $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ is a valid covariance matrix if and only if it is **symmetric positive semidefinite (SPSD)**: $\boldsymbol{\Sigma} = \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^\top$ and $\mathbf{v}^\top\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{v} \geq 0$ for all $\mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{R}^d$.

**Proof (necessity):** Symmetry is clear from the definition. For positive semidefiniteness, for any $\mathbf{v}$: $$\mathbf{v}^\top\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{v}^\top\mathbb{E}[(\mathbf{X}-\boldsymbol{\mu})(\mathbf{X}-\boldsymbol{\mu})^\top]\mathbf{v} = \mathbb{E}[(\mathbf{v}^\top(\mathbf{X}-\boldsymbol{\mu}))^2] \geq 0 \qquad \blacksquare$$

**The Spectral Decomposition** — the eigen-structure of $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$:

Since $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ is SPSD, it has the eigendecomposition: $$\boldsymbol{\Sigma} = \mathbf{U}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\mathbf{U}^\top = \sum_{j=1}^d \lambda_j \mathbf{u}_j\mathbf{u}_j^\top \tag{9.6}$$

where $\lambda_1 \geq \lambda_2 \geq \cdots \geq \lambda_d \geq 0$ are eigenvalues and $\mathbf{U} = [\mathbf{u}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{u}_d]$ is an orthonormal matrix of eigenvectors.

**Geometric interpretation:** The eigenvectors $\mathbf{u}_j$ are the **principal axes** of the uncertainty ellipsoid. The eigenvalues $\lambda_j$ are the **squared semi-axis lengths** — the variance in each principal direction. The density level sets ${(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})^\top\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu}) = c}$ are ellipsoids with axes $c\sqrt{\lambda_j}\mathbf{u}_j$.

**The Cholesky Decomposition:** $$\boldsymbol{\Sigma} = \mathbf{L}\mathbf{L}^\top \tag{9.7}$$

where $\mathbf{L}$ is lower triangular. This is the standard computational tool for sampling from $\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu},\boldsymbol{\Sigma})$: if $\mathbf{Z} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I})$, then $\mathbf{X} = \boldsymbol{\mu} + \mathbf{L}\mathbf{Z} \sim \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu},\boldsymbol{\Sigma})$.

---

### 9.2.3 Closure Properties of the Multivariate Gaussian

> **Theorem 9.1 (Linear Transformation):** If $\mathbf{X} \sim \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu},\boldsymbol{\Sigma})$ and $\mathbf{A} \in \mathbb{R}^{k\times d}$, $\mathbf{b} \in \mathbb{R}^k$: $$\mathbf{A}\mathbf{X} + \mathbf{b} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{A}\boldsymbol{\mu}+\mathbf{b},; \mathbf{A}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{A}^\top) \tag{9.8}$$

**Proof via MGF:** $M_{\mathbf{A}\mathbf{X}+\mathbf{b}}(\mathbf{t}) = e^{\mathbf{b}^\top\mathbf{t}} M_\mathbf{X}(\mathbf{A}^\top\mathbf{t}) = \exp(\mathbf{b}^\top\mathbf{t} + (\mathbf{A}\boldsymbol{\mu})^\top\mathbf{t} + \frac{1}{2}\mathbf{t}^\top(\mathbf{A}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{A}^\top)\mathbf{t})$, which is the MGF of $\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{A}\boldsymbol{\mu}+\mathbf{b}, \mathbf{A}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{A}^\top)$. $\blacksquare$

**ML consequence:** Every linear layer in a neural network — when input is approximately Gaussian — produces Gaussian output with covariance $\mathbf{W}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\text{in}}\mathbf{W}^\top$. This is the foundation of Gaussian process neural network analysis.

> **Theorem 9.2 (Conditional Distribution):** Partition $\mathbf{X} = (\mathbf{X}_1, \mathbf{X}_2)$ with $\boldsymbol{\mu} = (\boldsymbol{\mu}_1, \boldsymbol{\mu}_2)$ and: $$\boldsymbol{\Sigma} = \begin{pmatrix}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{11} & \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{12}\ \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{21} & \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{22}\end{pmatrix}$$
> 
> The conditional distribution is: $$\mathbf{X}_1 \mid \mathbf{X}_2 = \mathbf{x}_2 ;\sim; \mathcal{N}!\left(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{1|2},; \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{1|2}\right) \tag{9.9}$$
> 
> where: $$\boldsymbol{\mu}_{1|2} = \boldsymbol{\mu}_1 + \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{12}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{22}^{-1}(\mathbf{x}_2 - \boldsymbol{\mu}_2) \tag{9.10}$$ $$\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{1|2} = \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{11} - \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{12}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{22}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{21} \tag{9.11}$$

**Proof:** Completing the square in the joint Gaussian PDF. Partition $\mathbf{x} = (\mathbf{x}_1, \mathbf{x}_2)$ and write the joint log-density as a quadratic form. Isolate terms in $\mathbf{x}_1$:

$$\log f(\mathbf{x}_1, \mathbf{x}_2) = -\frac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix}\mathbf{x}_1-\boldsymbol{\mu}_1\\mathbf{x}_2-\boldsymbol{\mu}_2\end{pmatrix}^\top\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\begin{pmatrix}\mathbf{x}_1-\boldsymbol{\mu}_1\\mathbf{x}_2-\boldsymbol{\mu}_2\end{pmatrix} + \text{const}$$

Using the block matrix inversion formula, the $(\mathbf{x}_1, \mathbf{x}_1)$ block of $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}$ is $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{1|2}^{-1}$ (the Schur complement). The terms linear in $\mathbf{x}_1$ yield the conditional mean $\boldsymbol{\mu}_{1|2}$. This completes the square to give a Gaussian in $\mathbf{x}_1$. $\blacksquare$

**The key structural insight of (9.11):** The Schur complement $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{1|2} = \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{11} - \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{12}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{22}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{21}$ is the residual variance after _explaining_ $\mathbf{X}_1$ via $\mathbf{X}_2$. The term $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{12}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{22}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{21}$ is exactly the variance _removed_ by conditioning — the information $\mathbf{X}_2$ provides about $\mathbf{X}_1$.

**ML applications:**

- **Gaussian Process regression** uses (9.9–9.11) to compute posterior predictions given observations.
- **Kalman filtering** is sequential application of the conditional Gaussian formulas.
- **Linear regression** posterior under Gaussian prior is a direct application.

---

### 9.2.4 Principal Component Analysis — The Spectral Theory

PCA is not just a dimensionality reduction technique — it is the exact solution to a well-defined optimization problem involving the spectral decomposition of the covariance matrix.

> **Theorem 9.3 (PCA Optimality):** Given data with covariance $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$, the unit vector $\mathbf{v}_1 \in \mathbb{R}^d$ that maximizes the variance of the projection $\mathbf{v}_1^\top\mathbf{X}$ is the eigenvector of $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ corresponding to the largest eigenvalue $\lambda_1$: $$\mathbf{v}_1 = \arg\max_{|\mathbf{v}|=1} \mathbf{v}^\top\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{u}_1 \tag{9.12}$$
> 
> Recursively, the $k$-th principal component is the eigenvector $\mathbf{u}_k$ corresponding to $\lambda_k$, constrained to be orthogonal to $\mathbf{u}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{u}_{k-1}$.

**Proof (first component):** By Lagrange multipliers, maximize $\mathbf{v}^\top\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{v}$ subject to $|\mathbf{v}|^2 = 1$: $$\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{v},\lambda) = \mathbf{v}^\top\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{v} - \lambda(\mathbf{v}^\top\mathbf{v}-1)$$ $$\nabla_\mathbf{v}\mathcal{L} = 2\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{v} - 2\lambda\mathbf{v} = 0 \implies \boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{v} = \lambda\mathbf{v}$$

This is the eigenvalue equation. Substituting back: $\mathbf{v}^\top\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{v}^\top\lambda\mathbf{v} = \lambda$. So the variance is maximized by taking $\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{u}_1$ (eigenvector with largest $\lambda_1$). $\blacksquare$

**The explained variance ratio:** The fraction of total variance explained by the first $k$ components is: $$\text{EVR}(k) = \frac{\sum_{j=1}^k \lambda_j}{\sum_{j=1}^d \lambda_j} = \frac{\sum_{j=1}^k \lambda_j}{\text{tr}(\boldsymbol{\Sigma})} \tag{9.13}$$

**Whitening (Sphering):** The transformation $\mathbf{Z} = \boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{-1/2}\mathbf{U}^\top(\mathbf{X}-\boldsymbol{\mu})$ produces $\mathbf{Z} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I})$ — a spherical Gaussian. Whitening removes all linear correlations and equalizes variances. This is exactly what **Batch Normalization** approximates along each feature dimension.

---

### 9.2.5 The Wishart Distribution — Sampling Distributions of Covariance Matrices

When we estimate a covariance matrix from data, the sample covariance is random. Its distribution is the Wishart.

> **Definition 9.3 (Wishart Distribution):** If $\mathbf{X}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{X}_n \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}_d(\mathbf{0}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma})$, then: $$\mathbf{S} = \sum_{i=1}^n \mathbf{X}_i\mathbf{X}_i^\top \sim W_d(n, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}) \tag{9.14}$$

**Moments:** $$\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{S}] = n\boldsymbol{\Sigma} \tag{9.15}$$

So $\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}} = \mathbf{S}/n$ is an unbiased estimator of $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$.

**The Sample Covariance Matrix:** For centered data ${\mathbf{x}_i - \bar{\mathbf{x}}}$: $$\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_n = \frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n (\mathbf{x}_i-\bar{\mathbf{x}})(\mathbf{x}_i-\bar{\mathbf{x}})^\top \sim \frac{1}{n-1}W_d(n-1, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}) \tag{9.16}$$

**The curse of dimensionality for covariance estimation:** Estimating $\boldsymbol{\Sigma} \in \mathbb{R}^{d\times d}$ requires $O(d^2)$ parameters. We need $n \gg d$ for reliable estimation. When $n < d$ (more features than samples — common in genomics, NLP), $\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_n$ is singular and $\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_n^{-1}$ does not exist.

**Solutions:** Shrinkage estimators (e.g., Ledoit-Wolf), diagonal approximations, low-rank approximations (Factor Analysis), and regularized precision matrix estimation (Graphical Lasso).

---

### 9.2.6 Mahalanobis Distance and Anomaly Detection

> **Definition 9.4 (Mahalanobis Distance):** $$D_M(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\mu}) = \sqrt{(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})^\top\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})} \tag{9.17}$$

The Mahalanobis distance is Euclidean distance in the whitened space. It accounts for the scale and correlation structure of the data.

> **Theorem 9.4 (Mahalanobis and Chi-squared):** If $\mathbf{X} \sim \mathcal{N}_d(\boldsymbol{\mu},\boldsymbol{\Sigma})$: $$D_M(\mathbf{X},\boldsymbol{\mu})^2 = (\mathbf{X}-\boldsymbol{\mu})^\top\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}(\mathbf{X}-\boldsymbol{\mu}) \sim \chi^2_d \tag{9.18}$$

**Proof:** Let $\mathbf{Z} = \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1/2}(\mathbf{X}-\boldsymbol{\mu}) \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I})$ (by Theorem 9.1). Then $D_M^2 = \mathbf{Z}^\top\mathbf{Z} = \sum_{j=1}^d Z_j^2 \sim \chi^2_d$ by Definition 4.9. $\blacksquare$

**Anomaly detection:** A point $\mathbf{x}$ is declared anomalous if $D_M(\mathbf{x},\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}})^2 > \chi^2_{d,\alpha}$ (the $\alpha$-quantile of $\chi^2_d$). By Theorem 9.4, this gives a calibrated Type I error rate of $\alpha$ — only $\alpha$ fraction of normal points would be flagged. This is the principled statistical foundation for Mahalanobis-distance anomaly detection.

---

### 9.2.7 Gaussian Processes

A Gaussian Process (GP) is the infinite-dimensional generalization of the multivariate Gaussian — a distribution over _functions_ rather than vectors.

> **Definition 9.5 (Gaussian Process):** A **Gaussian Process** is a collection of random variables ${f(\mathbf{x})}_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{X}}$ such that any finite subcollection $(f(\mathbf{x}_1), \ldots, f(\mathbf{x}_n))$ has a multivariate Gaussian distribution: $$f \sim \mathcal{GP}(\mu(\cdot),, k(\cdot,\cdot)) \tag{9.19}$$
> 
> where $\mu: \mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R}$ is the **mean function** and $k: \mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R}$ is the **kernel (covariance) function**: $$\text{Cov}(f(\mathbf{x}), f(\mathbf{x}')) = k(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}') \tag{9.20}$$

The kernel $k$ plays the role of $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ in the finite-dimensional case — it encodes the prior beliefs about the smoothness and structure of $f$.

**GP Regression (Kriging):** Given observations $\mathbf{y} = f(\mathbf{X}) + \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}$ with $\boldsymbol{\varepsilon} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\sigma^2_n\mathbf{I})$, the posterior $f\mid\mathbf{y}$ is also a GP with:

$$\mu^_(\mathbf{x}^_) = \mathbf{k}^{_\top}(\mathbf{K} + \sigma^2_n\mathbf{I})^{-1}\mathbf{y} \tag{9.21}$$ $$\sigma^{_2}(\mathbf{x}^_) = k(\mathbf{x}^_,\mathbf{x}^_) - \mathbf{k}^{_\top}(\mathbf{K}+\sigma^2_n\mathbf{I})^{-1}\mathbf{k}^* \tag{9.22}$$

where $\mathbf{K}_{ij} = k(\mathbf{x}_i,\mathbf{x}_j)$ is the kernel matrix and $\mathbf{k}^__i = k(\mathbf{x}^_,\mathbf{x}_i)$.

Equations (9.21) and (9.22) are _exactly_ the conditional Gaussian formulas (9.10) and (9.11), applied to the infinite-dimensional setting. The GP posterior is the Bayesian optimal predictor under a Gaussian prior over functions.

**Common kernels:**

$$k_{\text{RBF}}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}') = \sigma^2\exp!\left(-\frac{|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}'|^2}{2\ell^2}\right) \tag{9.23}$$

$$k_{\text{Matérn}}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}') = \frac{2^{1-\nu}}{\Gamma(\nu)}\left(\frac{\sqrt{2\nu},|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}'|}{\ell}\right)^\nu K_\nu!\left(\frac{\sqrt{2\nu},|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}'|}{\ell}\right) \tag{9.24}$$

$$k_{\text{linear}}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}') = \mathbf{x}^\top\mathbf{x}' \tag{9.25}$$

The RBF kernel corresponds to an infinitely smooth function prior; the Matérn kernel allows controlled roughness via $\nu$; the linear kernel recovers Bayesian linear regression as a special case.

---

### 9.2.8 The Curse of Dimensionality

> **Theorem 9.5 (Concentration of Norm):** If $\mathbf{X} \sim \mathcal{N}_d(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I})$, then: $$\frac{|\mathbf{X}|}{\sqrt{d}} \xrightarrow{p} 1 \text{ as } d\to\infty \tag{9.26}$$

**Proof:** $|\mathbf{X}|^2 = \sum_{j=1}^d X_j^2 \sim \chi^2_d$. So $\mathbb{E}[|\mathbf{X}|^2]=d$ and $\text{Var}(|\mathbf{X}|^2)=2d$. By WLLN: $|\mathbf{X}|^2/d \xrightarrow{p} 1$. Since $|\mathbf{X}|/\sqrt{d} = \sqrt{|\mathbf{X}|^2/d}$ and $\sqrt{\cdot}$ is continuous, the result follows by the continuous mapping theorem. $\blacksquare$

This means that in high dimensions, all samples from $\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I})$ lie on a thin shell of radius approximately $\sqrt{d}$. There is essentially no mass near the origin — a profound departure from the one-dimensional intuition where the Gaussian concentrates near its mean. This is the **Gaussian typical set** and it explains:

- Why random weight initialization in deep networks must scale as $1/\sqrt{d}$ (Xavier/He initialization): to keep activations in the typical set.
- Why distance-based methods struggle in high dimensions: all points are nearly equidistant.
- Why the log-likelihood per dimension, not the raw likelihood, is the correct quantity to optimize.

---

### 9.2.9 Correlation, Partial Correlation, and Graphical Models

The **correlation matrix** is the normalized covariance: $$\mathbf{R}_{ij} = \frac{\Sigma_{ij}}{\sqrt{\Sigma_{ii}\Sigma_{jj}}} \in [-1,1] \tag{9.27}$$

The **precision matrix** (inverse covariance) $\boldsymbol{\Omega} = \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}$ encodes **partial correlations** — correlations between $X_i$ and $X_j$ after removing the linear effect of all other variables:

$$\rho_{ij\cdot\text{rest}} = -\frac{\Omega_{ij}}{\sqrt{\Omega_{ii}\Omega_{jj}}} \tag{9.28}$$

**If $\Omega_{ij} = 0$, then $X_i \perp X_j \mid \mathbf{X}_{\text{rest}}$** — conditional independence given all other variables. This is the foundation of **Gaussian Graphical Models**: the non-zero entries of $\boldsymbol{\Omega}$ define the edges of the independence graph. **Graphical Lasso** (L1-penalized MLE for $\boldsymbol{\Omega}$) learns sparse precision matrices — the probabilistic underpinning of causal discovery and feature interaction detection.

---

## 9.3 Numerical Examples

### Example 9.1: Conditional Gaussian — Linear Regression Recovered

**Problem:** $\mathbf{X} = (X, Y)^\top \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma})$ with: $$\boldsymbol{\Sigma} = \begin{pmatrix}4 & 3\ 3 & 9\end{pmatrix}$$

Find $Y \mid X = 2$.

**Solution:** Applying (9.10) and (9.11): $$\mu_{Y|X=2} = 0 + \frac{3}{4}(2 - 0) = 1.5$$ $$\sigma^2_{Y|X=2} = 9 - \frac{3 \cdot 3}{4} = 9 - 2.25 = 6.75$$

So $Y \mid X=2 \sim \mathcal{N}(1.5, 6.75)$.

The slope $\Sigma_{YX}/\Sigma_{XX} = 3/4 = 0.75$ is exactly the ordinary least squares regression coefficient of $Y$ on $X$ — OLS is the conditional mean of a bivariate Gaussian. Regression analysis is a special case of multivariate Gaussian conditioning.

---

### Example 9.2: Mahalanobis Anomaly Detection

**Problem:** Training data has $\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}} = (0, 0)^\top$ and $\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}} = \begin{pmatrix}4 & 2\ 2 & 3\end{pmatrix}$. Is the test point $\mathbf{x}^* = (3, 2)^\top$ anomalous at $\alpha = 0.05$?

**Step 1:** Compute $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}$. For a $2\times 2$ matrix: $$\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1} = \frac{1}{|\boldsymbol{\Sigma}|}\begin{pmatrix}3 & -2\ -2 & 4\end{pmatrix} = \frac{1}{8}\begin{pmatrix}3 & -2\ -2 & 4\end{pmatrix}$$

**Step 2:** Compute $D_M^2$: $$D_M^2 = (3,2)\cdot\frac{1}{8}\begin{pmatrix}3 & -2\ -2 & 4\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}3\ 2\end{pmatrix} = \frac{1}{8}(3,2)\begin{pmatrix}9-4\ -6+8\end{pmatrix} = \frac{1}{8}(3,2)\begin{pmatrix}5\ 2\end{pmatrix} = \frac{19}{8} = 2.375$$

**Step 3:** Compare to $\chi^2_{2,0.05} = 5.991$.

Since $2.375 < 5.991$, we fail to reject normality. The point is **not anomalous** at the 5% level.

Note: the Euclidean distance squared is $3^2 + 2^2 = 13$, which naively might seem large. The Mahalanobis distance correctly accounts for the variance scale and correlation.

---

### Example 9.3: PCA — Variance Explained

**Problem:** A $d=4$ dataset has $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ with eigenvalues $\lambda = (8, 3, 1, 0.2)$. How many components are needed to explain 90% of variance?

$$\text{Total variance} = 8 + 3 + 1 + 0.2 = 12.2$$

$$\text{EVR}(1) = 8/12.2 = 65.6% $$
$$$$
\text{EVR}(2) = (8+3)/12.2 = 90.2%
$$

**Two components** explain 90.2% of variance. The third eigenvalue of 1 means the third direction has the same variance as a standard normal — it contributes relatively little above noise.

---

## 9.4 Implementation

```python
import numpy as np
import scipy.stats as stats
import scipy.linalg as linalg
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.gridspec as gridspec
from matplotlib.patches import Ellipse
import matplotlib.transforms as transforms

# =============================================================================
# MODULE 9: Multivariate Distributions & Covariance
# =============================================================================

# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# PART A: Multivariate Gaussian — Sampling, Conditioning, Visualization
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------

class MultivariateGaussianToolkit:
    """
    Full implementation of multivariate Gaussian operations.
    Covers sampling, conditioning (Eqs. 9.9-9.11), Mahalanobis distance,
    and visualization of covariance ellipses.
    """

    def __init__(self, mu: np.ndarray, Sigma: np.ndarray):
        self.mu    = np.array(mu, dtype=float)
        self.Sigma = np.array(Sigma, dtype=float)
        self.d     = len(mu)

        # Eigendecomposition for geometric operations
        eigvals, eigvecs = np.linalg.eigh(self.Sigma)
        self.eigvals = eigvals[::-1]          # descending
        self.eigvecs = eigvecs[:, ::-1]       # corresponding eigenvectors
        self.L       = np.linalg.cholesky(self.Sigma)  # for sampling
        self.Sigma_inv = np.linalg.inv(self.Sigma)

    def sample(self, n: int, seed: int = 42) -> np.ndarray:
        """
        Sample via Cholesky: X = mu + L Z, Z ~ N(0,I).
        Theorem 9.1 with A = L.
        """
        rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
        Z   = rng.standard_normal((self.d, n))
        return (self.mu[:, None] + self.L @ Z).T  # (n, d)

    def logpdf(self, X: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
        """Log PDF: Eq. 9.1"""
        X   = np.atleast_2d(X)
        dev = X - self.mu
        # Solve L L^T x = dev^T instead of forming Sigma_inv
        maha_sq = np.sum(dev @ self.Sigma_inv * dev, axis=1)
        log_det = np.log(np.linalg.det(self.Sigma))
        return -0.5 * (self.d*np.log(2*np.pi) + log_det + maha_sq)

    def mahalanobis(self, X: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
        """
        Mahalanobis distance. Eq. 9.17.
        Under the true distribution, D_M^2 ~ chi2(d). Eq. 9.18.
        """
        X   = np.atleast_2d(X)
        dev = X - self.mu
        return np.sqrt(np.sum(dev @ self.Sigma_inv * dev, axis=1))

    def condition(self, observed_idx: list, observed_vals: np.ndarray):
        """
        Compute the conditional distribution X1 | X2 = x2.
        Equations 9.10 and 9.11.

        Parameters
        ----------
        observed_idx : indices of the observed variables (X2)
        observed_vals: their observed values

        Returns a new MultivariateGaussianToolkit for the conditional.
        """
        all_idx  = list(range(self.d))
        free_idx = [i for i in all_idx if i not in observed_idx]

        # Block partitioning
        mu1 = self.mu[free_idx]
        mu2 = self.mu[observed_idx]
        S11 = self.Sigma[np.ix_(free_idx, free_idx)]
        S12 = self.Sigma[np.ix_(free_idx, observed_idx)]
        S22 = self.Sigma[np.ix_(observed_idx, observed_idx)]

        S22_inv  = np.linalg.inv(S22)
        mu_cond  = mu1 + S12 @ S22_inv @ (observed_vals - mu2)   # Eq. 9.10
        Sig_cond = S11 - S12 @ S22_inv @ S12.T                   # Eq. 9.11

        # Ensure positive definiteness (numerical fix)
        Sig_cond = 0.5 * (Sig_cond + Sig_cond.T)
        return MultivariateGaussianToolkit(mu_cond, Sig_cond)

    def linear_transform(self, A: np.ndarray, b: np.ndarray = None):
        """
        Distribution of AX + b. Theorem 9.1: AX+b ~ N(A mu + b, A Sigma A^T).
        """
        if b is None:
            b = np.zeros(A.shape[0])
        return MultivariateGaussianToolkit(A @ self.mu + b, A @ self.Sigma @ A.T)

    def confidence_ellipse(self, ax, n_std: float = 2.0,
                           color: str = '#1a6faf', alpha: float = 0.2,
                           label: str = None):
        """
        Draw a covariance ellipse on a 2D axes (d=2 only).
        The ellipse encloses the n_std * sigma confidence region.
        """
        assert self.d == 2, "Ellipse visualization only for 2D"
        # Scale factor: chi2(2) quantile
        scale = np.sqrt(stats.chi2.ppf(stats.norm.cdf(n_std)**2 - 1 +
                                        stats.norm.cdf(n_std), df=2))

        eigvals, eigvecs = np.linalg.eigh(self.Sigma)
        angle  = np.degrees(np.arctan2(eigvecs[1,1], eigvecs[0,1]))
        w, h   = 2 * scale * np.sqrt(eigvals[1]), 2 * scale * np.sqrt(eigvals[0])

        ellipse = Ellipse(xy=self.mu, width=w, height=h,
                          angle=angle, facecolor=color, alpha=alpha,
                          edgecolor=color, linewidth=1.5, label=label)
        ax.add_patch(ellipse)


# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# PART B: PCA from Scratch
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------

class PCA:
    """
    Principal Component Analysis via the spectral decomposition of Sigma.
    Theorem 9.3: eigenvectors of Sigma maximize projected variance.
    """

    def __init__(self, n_components: int = None, whiten: bool = False):
        self.n_components = n_components
        self.whiten       = whiten

    def fit(self, X: np.ndarray):
        """
        Compute PCA from data matrix X of shape (n, d).
        Uses eigendecomposition of the sample covariance matrix.
        """
        n, d = X.shape
        self.n_components = self.n_components or d

        self.mean_  = X.mean(axis=0)
        X_centered  = X - self.mean_

        # Sample covariance (Eq. 9.16)
        self.cov_   = X_centered.T @ X_centered / (n - 1)

        # Eigendecomposition (Eq. 9.6)
        eigvals, eigvecs = np.linalg.eigh(self.cov_)
        # Sort descending
        idx              = np.argsort(eigvals)[::-1]
        self.eigvals_    = eigvals[idx]                    # lambda_1 >= ... >= lambda_d
        self.eigvecs_    = eigvecs[:, idx]                 # columns = principal directions

        # Select top n_components
        self.components_ = self.eigvecs_[:, :self.n_components].T   # (k, d)
        self.explained_variance_       = self.eigvals_[:self.n_components]
        self.explained_variance_ratio_ = self.eigvals_ / self.eigvals_.sum()
        self.cumulative_evr_           = np.cumsum(self.explained_variance_ratio_)

        return self

    def transform(self, X: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
        """Project X onto principal components."""
        Z = (X - self.mean_) @ self.components_.T     # (n, k)
        if self.whiten:
            Z /= np.sqrt(self.explained_variance_)    # whitening
        return Z

    def inverse_transform(self, Z: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
        """Reconstruct from principal component scores."""
        if self.whiten:
            Z = Z * np.sqrt(self.explained_variance_)
        return Z @ self.components_ + self.mean_

    def reconstruction_error(self, X: np.ndarray) -> float:
        """MSE of reconstruction using k components."""
        Z    = self.transform(X)
        Xrec = self.inverse_transform(Z)
        return float(np.mean((X - Xrec)**2))

    def print_summary(self):
        print(f"\n{'='*52}")
        print(f"  PCA SUMMARY  (top {self.n_components} of {len(self.eigvals_)} components)")
        print(f"{'='*52}")
        print(f"  {'Component':<12} {'Eigenvalue':>12} {'EVR':>10} {'Cumul EVR':>12}")
        print(f"  {'-'*48}")
        for k in range(min(self.n_components, 10)):
            print(f"  {'PC'+str(k+1):<12} {self.eigvals_[k]:>12.4f} "
                  f"{self.explained_variance_ratio_[k]:>10.4f} "
                  f"{self.cumulative_evr_[k]:>12.4f}")
        print(f"{'='*52}")


# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# PART C: Gaussian Process Regression
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------

class GaussianProcessRegressor:
    """
    GP Regression with RBF kernel.
    Implements the conditional Gaussian formulas (Eqs. 9.21-9.22).
    """

    def __init__(self, length_scale: float = 1.0, amplitude: float = 1.0,
                 noise_var: float = 0.01):
        self.l     = length_scale   # controls smoothness (ℓ in Eq. 9.23)
        self.amp   = amplitude      # output scale
        self.noise = noise_var      # sigma_n^2

    def rbf_kernel(self, X1: np.ndarray, X2: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
        """
        RBF (squared exponential) kernel. Eq. 9.23.
        k(x, x') = amp^2 * exp(-||x-x'||^2 / (2 * l^2))
        """
        X1 = np.atleast_2d(X1)
        X2 = np.atleast_2d(X2)
        sq_dist = np.sum(X1**2, axis=1, keepdims=True) + \
                  np.sum(X2**2, axis=1) - 2 * X1 @ X2.T
        return self.amp**2 * np.exp(-sq_dist / (2 * self.l**2))

    def fit(self, X_train: np.ndarray, y_train: np.ndarray):
        """
        Compute K + sigma_n^2 I and its Cholesky for prediction.
        """
        self.X_train = np.atleast_2d(X_train).T if X_train.ndim == 1 else X_train
        self.y_train = y_train
        K      = self.rbf_kernel(self.X_train, self.X_train)
        self.K_noisy = K + self.noise * np.eye(len(y_train))   # K + sigma_n^2 I
        self.L_chol  = np.linalg.cholesky(self.K_noisy)        # for stable inversion
        # alpha = (K + sigma_n^2 I)^{-1} y  (solve via Cholesky)
        self.alpha   = linalg.cho_solve(
            (self.L_chol, True), y_train)
        return self

    def predict(self, X_test: np.ndarray):
        """
        GP posterior mean and variance. Eqs. 9.21-9.22.
        """
        X_test  = np.atleast_2d(X_test).T if X_test.ndim == 1 else X_test
        k_star  = self.rbf_kernel(X_test, self.X_train)       # k* vector

        # Posterior mean: k*^T (K + sigma_n^2 I)^{-1} y
        mu_star = k_star @ self.alpha                         # Eq. 9.21

        # Posterior variance: k** - k*^T (K + sigma_n^2 I)^{-1} k*
        v       = linalg.solve_triangular(self.L_chol, k_star.T, lower=True)
        k_starstar = self.rbf_kernel(X_test, X_test)
        var_star    = np.diag(k_starstar) - np.sum(v**2, axis=0) # Eq. 9.22

        return mu_star, np.maximum(var_star, 0)    # clip numerical negatives


# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# PART D: Full Visualization Suite
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def full_visualization(seed: int = 42):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)

    fig = plt.figure(figsize=(18, 12))
    gs  = gridspec.GridSpec(3, 4, wspace=0.38, hspace=0.48)

    # ---- Panel 1: Covariance ellipses ----
    ax = fig.add_subplot(gs[0, 0])
    for Sig, color, label in [
        (np.array([[3,0],[0,1]]),    '#1a6faf', 'σ²=[3,1], ρ=0'),
        (np.array([[3,1.5],[1.5,1]]),'#e84040', 'σ²=[3,1], ρ=0.87'),
        (np.array([[1,0],[0,3]]),    '#2ca02c', 'σ²=[1,3], ρ=0'),
    ]:
        mvg  = MultivariateGaussianToolkit(np.zeros(2), Sig)
        samp = mvg.sample(200, seed=rng.integers(9999))
        ax.scatter(samp[:,0], samp[:,1], s=5, alpha=0.35, color=color)
        mvg.confidence_ellipse(ax, n_std=2, color=color, alpha=0.15, label=label)
    ax.set_title("Covariance Ellipses\n(2-σ confidence regions)", fontsize=10, fontweight='bold')
    ax.legend(fontsize=7); ax.grid(alpha=0.3); ax.set_aspect('equal')

    # ---- Panel 2: Conditional Gaussian ----
    ax = fig.add_subplot(gs[0, 1])
    Sigma = np.array([[4., 3.],[3., 9.]])
    mvg   = MultivariateGaussianToolkit(np.zeros(2), Sigma)
    samp  = mvg.sample(500, seed=42)
    ax.scatter(samp[:,0], samp[:,1], s=6, alpha=0.4, color='#888', zorder=1)

    x_vals = [-2, 0, 2]
    colors_c = ['#1a6faf','#e84040','#2ca02c']
    x_plot   = np.linspace(-8, 8, 200)
    for x_obs, col in zip(x_vals, colors_c):
        cond = mvg.condition([0], np.array([x_obs]))
        y_pdf = stats.norm.pdf(x_plot, cond.mu[0], np.sqrt(cond.Sigma[0,0]))
        ax.plot(x_plot*0.5 + x_obs, y_pdf*3, color=col, lw=2, alpha=0.85,
                label=f"$X_2|X_1={x_obs}$")
        ax.axvline(x_obs, color=col, lw=0.8, linestyle='--', alpha=0.5)
    ax.set_title("Conditional Gaussians\n(Eqs. 9.10–9.11)", fontsize=10, fontweight='bold')
    ax.legend(fontsize=7); ax.grid(alpha=0.3)
    ax.set_xlabel("$X_1$"); ax.set_ylabel("$X_2$")

    # ---- Panel 3: PCA ----
    ax = fig.add_subplot(gs[0, 2])
    mean_t = np.array([2., 1.])
    cov_t  = np.array([[4., 2.5],[2.5., 2.]])
    X_data = rng.multivariate_normal(mean_t, cov_t, 300)
    pca    = PCA(n_components=2).fit(X_data)

    ax.scatter(X_data[:,0], X_data[:,1], s=6, alpha=0.4, color='gray')
    for k in range(2):
        vec = pca.eigvecs_[:, k]
        scl = np.sqrt(pca.eigvals_[k]) * 2
        ax.annotate("", xy=mean_t + scl*vec, xytext=mean_t,
                    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle='->', color=['#1a6faf','#e84040'][k],
                                    lw=2.5))
        ax.text(*(mean_t + scl*vec*1.15), f"PC{k+1}\nλ={pca.eigvals_[k]:.2f}",
                fontsize=8, color=['#1a6faf','#e84040'][k], ha='center')
    ax.set_title("PCA Principal Components\n(Theorem 9.3: max-variance directions)",
                 fontsize=10, fontweight='bold')
    ax.grid(alpha=0.3); ax.set_aspect('equal')

    # ---- Panel 4: Explained Variance Ratio ----
    ax = fig.add_subplot(gs[0, 3])
    d_high    = 20
    eigvals_h = np.exp(-0.3 * np.arange(d_high))  # synthetic decay
    eigvals_h /= eigvals_h.sum()
    cumevr    = np.cumsum(eigvals_h)
    ax.bar(range(1,d_high+1), eigvals_h*100, color='#1a6faf', alpha=0.7, label="EVR")
    ax2 = ax.twinx()
    ax2.plot(range(1,d_high+1), cumevr*100, 'r-o', ms=3, lw=2, label="Cumul EVR")
    ax2.axhline(90, color='green', lw=1, linestyle='--', label="90% threshold")
    ax.set_xlabel("Principal component"); ax.set_ylabel("EVR %")
    ax2.set_ylabel("Cumul EVR %")
    ax.set_title("Explained Variance Ratio\n(Eq. 9.13)", fontsize=10, fontweight='bold')
    ax.legend(loc='center right', fontsize=8)
    ax2.legend(loc='upper left', fontsize=8)

    # ---- Panel 5: Mahalanobis distance distribution ----
    ax = fig.add_subplot(gs[1, :2])
    mvg2  = MultivariateGaussianToolkit(np.array([0.,0.]), np.array([[2.,1.],[1.,3.]]))
    samp2 = mvg2.sample(2000, seed=42)
    d_m   = mvg2.mahalanobis(samp2)
    dm_sq = d_m**2

    ax.hist(dm_sq, bins=50, density=True, alpha=0.6, color='#1a6faf',
            label="Empirical $D_M^2$")
    x_chi = np.linspace(0, 15, 300)
    ax.plot(x_chi, stats.chi2.pdf(x_chi, df=2), 'r-', lw=2.5,
            label="$\\chi^2(d=2)$ (Theorem 9.4)")
    thresh = stats.chi2.ppf(0.95, df=2)
    ax.axvline(thresh, color='green', lw=2, linestyle='--',
               label=f"95% threshold = {thresh:.2f}")
    ax.fill_between(x_chi[x_chi>thresh],
                    stats.chi2.pdf(x_chi[x_chi>thresh], df=2),
                    alpha=0.3, color='green', label="5% anomaly region")
    ax.set_xlabel("$D_M^2$"); ax.set_ylabel("Density")
    ax.set_title("Mahalanobis Distance ~ $\\chi^2(d)$ — Anomaly Detection Threshold",
                 fontsize=11, fontweight='bold')
    ax.legend(fontsize=9); ax.grid(alpha=0.3)

    # ---- Panel 6: Gaussian Process ----
    ax = fig.add_subplot(gs[1, 2:])
    np.random.seed(42)

    y_tr  = np.sin(X_tr) + 0.3*np.random.randn(len(X_tr))
    X_ts  = np.linspace(-6, 6, 200)

    gp = GaussianProcessRegressor(length_scale=1.5, amplitude=1.2, noise_var=0.05)
    gp.fit(X_tr, y_tr)
    mu, var = gp.predict(X_ts)
    std  = np.sqrt(var)

    ax.scatter(X_tr, y_tr, s=60, color='black', zorder=5, label="Observations")
    ax.plot(X_ts, mu, '#1a6faf', lw=2.5, label="GP posterior mean")
    ax.fill_between(X_ts, mu-2*std, mu+2*std, alpha=0.2, color='#1a6faf',
                    label="±2σ uncertainty")
    ax.plot(X_ts, np.sin(X_ts), 'r--', lw=1.5, alpha=0.7, label="True $\\sin(x)$")
    ax.set_title("Gaussian Process Regression\n(Infinite-dim Multivariate Gaussian, Eqs. 9.21–9.22)",
                 fontsize=11, fontweight='bold')
    ax.legend(fontsize=9); ax.grid(alpha=0.3)

    # ---- Panel 7: Curse of Dimensionality ----
    ax = fig.add_subplot(gs[2, :2])
    dims    = [1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 200, 500]
    n_samp  = 2000
    norms_mean = []; norms_std = []
    for d in dims:
        Z = rng.standard_normal((n_samp, d))
        norms = np.linalg.norm(Z, axis=1)
        norms_mean.append(norms.mean())
        norms_std.append(norms.std())
    norms_mean = np.array(norms_mean)
    norms_std  = np.array(norms_std)

    ax.errorbar(dims, norms_mean/np.sqrt(dims), yerr=norms_std/np.sqrt(dims),
                fmt='o-', color='#1a6faf', lw=2, ms=6, capsize=4,
                label="Empirical $\\|\\mathbf{X}\\|/\\sqrt{d}$")
    ax.axhline(1, color='r', lw=2, linestyle='--',
               label="Theorem 9.5: limit = 1")
    ax.set_xscale('log')
    ax.set_xlabel("Dimension d (log scale)")
    ax.set_ylabel("$\\|\\mathbf{X}\\|/\\sqrt{d}$")
    ax.set_title("Concentration of Norm (Curse of Dimensionality)\nTheorem 9.5: $\\|X\\|/\\sqrt{d} \\to 1$",
                 fontsize=11, fontweight='bold')
    ax.legend(fontsize=9); ax.grid(alpha=0.3, which='both')

    # ---- Panel 8: Precision matrix / graphical model ----
    ax = fig.add_subplot(gs[2, 2:])
    Omega = np.array([[2, -0.8, 0, 0.5],
                      [-0.8, 2, -0.6, 0],
                      [0, -0.6, 2, 0.3],

    Sigma_from_Om = np.linalg.inv(Omega)

    # Plot precision matrix as heatmap

    plt.colorbar(im, ax=ax, shrink=0.85, label="Precision $\\Omega_{ij}$")
    ax.set_xticks(range(4)); ax.set_yticks(range(4))
    ax.set_xticklabels(feat_names); ax.set_yticklabels(feat_names)
    for i in range(4):
        for j in range(4):
            ax.text(j, i, f"{Omega[i,j]:.1f}", ha='center', va='center',
                    fontsize=10, fontweight='bold',
                    color='white' if abs(Omega[i,j]) > 0.5 else 'black')
    ax.set_title("Precision Matrix $\\boldsymbol{\\Omega}=\\boldsymbol{\\Sigma}^{-1}$\n"
                 "Zero entries = conditional independence (Eq. 9.28)",
                 fontsize=10, fontweight='bold')

    plt.suptitle("Module 9: Multivariate Distributions & Covariance — Complete Gallery",
                 fontsize=14, fontweight='bold', y=1.01)
    plt.savefig("module9_full_gallery.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches='tight')
    plt.show()
    print("Saved: module9_full_gallery.png")
```

# MODULE 10: Cost Functions & Convex Optimization

### _From Loss Landscapes to Gradient Descent_

---

## 10.1 Conceptual Overview

### The Central Problem of Machine Learning

Every machine learning algorithm, at its core, solves an optimization problem. We have a model parameterized by $\theta$, a dataset $\mathcal{D}$, and a measure of how badly the model is performing — the **loss function** $\mathcal{L}(\theta)$. The goal is to find the $\theta^*$ that minimizes this loss.

This sounds simple. It is not. The loss landscape of a deep neural network is a surface in a space of millions or billions of dimensions, riddled with saddle points, flat plateaus, sharp ravines, and numerous local minima. Understanding the geometry of this landscape — and the algorithms that navigate it — is the difference between a practitioner who tunes hyperparameters by intuition and one who does so by understanding.

### Why Convexity Is the Dividing Line

The theory of optimization splits cleanly at one boundary: **convexity**. For convex loss functions (linear regression, logistic regression, SVMs), every local minimum is a global minimum, gradient descent is guaranteed to converge, and the theory is complete and beautiful. For non-convex loss functions (deep neural networks), none of these guarantees hold — yet in practice, modern optimizers find remarkably good solutions. Understanding why requires the theory of this module and the next.

### Loss Functions Are Probabilistic Assumptions

As we established in Module 6, every loss function is a negative log-likelihood under some distributional assumption. The choice of loss function is not aesthetic — it is a statement about your model of the world:

- **MSE** → assumes Gaussian noise
- **Cross-entropy** → assumes Bernoulli/Categorical output
- **MAE** → assumes Laplace noise
- **Huber loss** → assumes a mixture of Gaussian and Laplace noise
- **Hinge loss** → the SVM loss, with no clean probabilistic interpretation but strong geometric motivation

---

## 10.2 Mathematical Formalization

### 10.2.1 The Empirical Risk Minimization Framework

> **Definition 10.1 (Empirical Risk):** Given a loss function $\ell: \mathcal{Y} \times \mathcal{Y} \to \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$ and dataset $\mathcal{D} = {(\mathbf{x}_i, y_i)}_{i=1}^n$, the **empirical risk** of a model $f_\theta$ is: $$\hat{\mathcal{R}}(\theta) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \ell(f_\theta(\mathbf{x}_i), y_i) \tag{10.1}$$

> **Definition 10.2 (Regularized Empirical Risk):** Adding a regularization term $\Omega(\theta)$: $$\mathcal{L}(\theta) = \underbrace{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \ell(f_\theta(\mathbf{x}_i), y_i)}_{\text{data fidelity}} + \underbrace{\lambda,\Omega(\theta)}_{\text{regularization}} \tag{10.2}$$

The regularization term penalizes model complexity, encoding a prior belief (Module 6). The hyperparameter $\lambda \geq 0$ controls the tradeoff — as established in Module 3's bias-variance decomposition.

---

### 10.2.2 Key Loss Functions — Derivations and Properties

**A. Mean Squared Error (MSE)**

$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{MSE}}(\theta) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2 \tag{10.3}$$

As proved in Module 3 (Example 3.1): MSE $\equiv$ negative log-likelihood under $y_i \sim \mathcal{N}(\hat{y}_i, \sigma^2)$.

**Gradient:** $\nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}_{\text{MSE}} = -\frac{2}{n}\sum_i (y_i - \hat{y}_i)\nabla_\theta \hat{y}_i$

**B. Mean Absolute Error (MAE)**

$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{MAE}}(\theta) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n |y_i - \hat{y}_i| \tag{10.4}$$

MAE is the negative log-likelihood under $y_i \sim \text{Laplace}(\hat{y}_i, b)$. It is **more robust to outliers** than MSE (quadratic vs linear penalty) but **non-differentiable at zero** — requiring subgradient methods.

**C. Huber Loss (Smooth MAE)**

$$\mathcal{L}_{\delta}(r) = \begin{cases} \frac{1}{2}r^2 & |r| \leq \delta \ \delta(|r| - \frac{\delta}{2}) & |r| > \delta \end{cases}, \quad r = y - \hat{y} \tag{10.5}$$

The Huber loss is quadratic near zero (like MSE, differentiable) and linear in the tails (like MAE, robust). The hyperparameter $\delta$ controls the transition. It is the optimal loss when residuals are a mixture of Gaussian and Laplace.

**D. Binary Cross-Entropy**

$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{BCE}}(\theta) = -\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \left[y_i\log\hat{p}_i + (1-y_i)\log(1-\hat{p}_i)\right] \tag{10.6}$$

where $\hat{p}_i = \sigma(f_\theta(\mathbf{x}_i)) \in (0,1)$. This is the negative log-likelihood under $y_i \sim \text{Bernoulli}(\hat{p}_i)$ and the KL divergence between the empirical label distribution and the model (Module 8, Theorem 8.3).

**E. Categorical Cross-Entropy**

$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{CE}}(\theta) = -\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{k=1}^K y_{ik}\log\hat{p}_{ik} \tag{10.7}$$

where $\hat{\mathbf{p}}_i = \text{softmax}(f_\theta(\mathbf{x}_i))$. This is the negative log-likelihood under $y_i \sim \text{Categorical}(\hat{\mathbf{p}}_i)$. For one-hot $y_{ik}$, this reduces to $-\log\hat{p}_{i,\text{true class}}$ — the negative log-probability of the correct class.

**F. Hinge Loss (SVM)**

$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{hinge}}(\theta) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \max(0,, 1 - y_i f_\theta(\mathbf{x}_i)) \tag{10.8}$$

where $y_i \in {-1, +1}$. The hinge loss penalizes predictions that are either wrong _or_ correct but not confident enough (within margin 1). Points with $y_i f_\theta(\mathbf{x}_i) > 1$ (correct and outside margin) incur zero loss.

**G. KL Divergence Loss**

$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{KL}}(\theta) = D_{KL}(p,|,q_\theta) = \sum_x p(x)\log\frac{p(x)}{q_\theta(x)} \tag{10.9}$$

Used in VAEs, knowledge distillation, and reinforcement learning (PPO). Non-negative by Theorem 8.2.

---

### 10.2.3 Convexity — The Geometry of Guarantees

> **Definition 10.3 (Convex Set):** A set $\mathcal{C} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ is **convex** if for all $\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \in \mathcal{C}$ and $t \in [0,1]$: $$t\mathbf{x} + (1-t)\mathbf{y} \in \mathcal{C} \tag{10.10}$$

> **Definition 10.4 (Convex Function):** A function $f: \mathcal{C} \to \mathbb{R}$ is **convex** if for all $\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \in \mathcal{C}$ and $t \in [0,1]$: $$f(t\mathbf{x} + (1-t)\mathbf{y}) \leq t,f(\mathbf{x}) + (1-t),f(\mathbf{y}) \tag{10.11}$$

The function lies **below the chord** connecting any two points on its graph. If the inequality is strict for $\mathbf{x} \neq \mathbf{y}$ and $t \in (0,1)$, $f$ is **strictly convex**.

**First-order characterization:**

> **Theorem 10.1:** A differentiable $f$ is convex iff: $$f(\mathbf{y}) \geq f(\mathbf{x}) + \nabla f(\mathbf{x})^\top(\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{x}) \quad \forall, \mathbf{x},\mathbf{y} \tag{10.12}$$

The function lies **above every tangent hyperplane**. The tangent is a global underestimator.

**Second-order characterization:**

> **Theorem 10.2:** A twice-differentiable $f$ is convex iff: $$\nabla^2 f(\mathbf{x}) \succeq \mathbf{0} \quad \forall, \mathbf{x} \tag{10.13}$$

The Hessian is positive semidefinite everywhere — the function curves upward in every direction.

> **Theorem 10.3 (Global Optimality of Local Minima):** If $f$ is convex and $\mathbf{x}^_$ is a local minimum, then $\mathbf{x}^_$ is a **global minimum**.

**Proof:** Suppose $\mathbf{x}^_$ is a local minimum but not global. Then there exists $\mathbf{y}$ with $f(\mathbf{y}) < f(\mathbf{x}^_)$. For small $t > 0$, consider $\mathbf{z}_t = \mathbf{x}^* + t(\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{x}^_)$. By convexity: $$f(\mathbf{z}_t) \leq (1-t)f(\mathbf{x}^_) + t,f(\mathbf{y}) < f(\mathbf{x}^*)$$

But $\mathbf{z}_t \to \mathbf{x}^_$ as $t \to 0$, contradicting $\mathbf{x}^_$ being a local minimum. $\blacksquare$

**Strong convexity:**

> **Definition 10.5 (Strong Convexity):** $f$ is **$\mu$-strongly convex** ($\mu > 0$) if: $$f(\mathbf{y}) \geq f(\mathbf{x}) + \nabla f(\mathbf{x})^\top(\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{x}) + \frac{\mu}{2}|\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{x}|^2 \tag{10.14}$$

Strong convexity guarantees a **unique** global minimum and **linear convergence** of gradient descent. The quadratic lower bound means the function curves away from the tangent at rate $\mu$.

---

### 10.2.4 Gradient Descent — The Universal Optimizer

> **Algorithm 10.1 (Gradient Descent):** Initialize $\theta^{(0)}$. For $t = 0, 1, 2, \ldots$: $$\theta^{(t+1)} = \theta^{(t)} - \eta,\nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}(\theta^{(t)}) \tag{10.15}$$

where $\eta > 0$ is the **learning rate** (step size).

**Geometric intuition:** The negative gradient $-\nabla\mathcal{L}$ points in the direction of steepest descent. Taking a step of size $\eta$ in this direction decreases the loss — as long as $\eta$ is not too large.

**Convergence analysis for smooth convex functions:**

> **Theorem 10.4 (GD Convergence — Convex, $L$-smooth):** If $\mathcal{L}$ is convex and $L$-smooth ($|\nabla^2\mathcal{L}| \leq L$), with learning rate $\eta \leq 1/L$, then after $T$ steps: $$\mathcal{L}(\theta^{(T)}) - \mathcal{L}(\theta^_) \leq \frac{|\theta^{(0)} - \theta^_|^2}{2\eta T} \tag{10.16}$$

This is $O(1/T)$ convergence — called **sublinear**.

**Proof sketch:** By $L$-smoothness, the quadratic upper bound gives: $$\mathcal{L}(\theta^{(t+1)}) \leq \mathcal{L}(\theta^{(t)}) - \eta|\nabla\mathcal{L}(\theta^{(t)})|^2 + \frac{L\eta^2}{2}|\nabla\mathcal{L}(\theta^{(t)})|^2$$

Setting $\eta = 1/L$: $\mathcal{L}(\theta^{(t+1)}) \leq \mathcal{L}(\theta^{(t)}) - \frac{1}{2L}|\nabla\mathcal{L}|^2$. Summing over $T$ steps and using the first-order convexity condition yields (10.16). $\blacksquare$

> **Theorem 10.5 (GD Convergence — Strongly Convex):** If $\mathcal{L}$ is $\mu$-strongly convex and $L$-smooth, with $\eta = 1/L$: $$|\theta^{(T)} - \theta^_|^2 \leq \left(1 - \frac{\mu}{L}\right)^T |\theta^{(0)} - \theta^_|^2 \tag{10.17}$$

This is **linear convergence** — exponential decay of the error at rate $(1 - \mu/L)$.

The ratio $\kappa = L/\mu$ is the **condition number**. Ill-conditioned problems ($\kappa \gg 1$) converge slowly — this is why preconditioning and adaptive optimizers (Adam, Module 11) are critical.

---

### 10.2.5 Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD)

Full gradient descent requires computing $\nabla\mathcal{L}(\theta) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i \nabla\ell_i(\theta)$ — a sum over all $n$ data points. For large $n$, this is computationally prohibitive.

> **Algorithm 10.2 (SGD):** At each step $t$, sample a single index $i_t \sim \text{Uniform}{1,\ldots,n}$ and update: $$\theta^{(t+1)} = \theta^{(t)} - \eta_t,\nabla\ell_{i_t}(\theta^{(t)}) \tag{10.18}$$

The stochastic gradient $\nabla\ell_{i_t}$ is an **unbiased estimator** of the true gradient: $$\mathbb{E}_{i_t}[\nabla\ell_{i_t}(\theta)] = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i\nabla\ell_i(\theta) = \nabla\mathcal{L}(\theta) \tag{10.19}$$

But it has variance: $\text{Var}(\nabla\ell_{i_t}) = \mathbb{E}[|\nabla\ell_{i_t} - \nabla\mathcal{L}|^2] = \sigma^2_{\text{grad}}$

**SGD convergence** requires **diminishing learning rates** $\eta_t \to 0$ satisfying the Robbins-Monro conditions: $$\sum_{t=1}^\infty \eta_t = \infty, \quad \sum_{t=1}^\infty \eta_t^2 < \infty \tag{10.20}$$

e.g., $\eta_t = \eta_0/\sqrt{t}$ or $\eta_t = \eta_0/t$.

**SGD noise as regularization:** The gradient noise in SGD has a regularizing effect — it prevents the optimizer from settling into sharp minima (high curvature) and biases it toward **flat minima** which generalize better. This is the theoretical basis for why SGD often outperforms full-batch gradient descent on test data.

---

### 10.2.6 Mini-Batch Gradient Descent

> **Algorithm 10.3 (Mini-batch GD):** Sample a batch $\mathcal{B}_t \subset {1,\ldots,n}$ of size $B$ and update: $$\theta^{(t+1)} = \theta^{(t)} - \eta,\frac{1}{B}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{B}_t}\nabla\ell_i(\theta^{(t)}) \tag{10.21}$$

By the CLT (Module 5, Eq. 5.17): the mini-batch gradient estimate has variance $\sigma^2_{\text{grad}}/B$. The tradeoff:

|Batch size $B$|Gradient variance|Steps per epoch|Memory|Best for|
|---|---|---|---|---|
|1 (SGD)|$\sigma^2$|$n$|Minimal|Online learning|
|$B$ (mini-batch)|$\sigma^2/B$|$n/B$|Moderate|Deep learning|
|$n$ (full-batch)|0|1|Maximum|Small datasets, convex|

**The linear scaling rule:** Empirically, if you increase batch size by factor $k$, increasing $\eta$ by factor $k$ approximately maintains the same convergence trajectory (because the effective gradient step magnitude is preserved). This is used in large-scale distributed training.

---

### 10.2.7 The Gradient Descent Landscape — Saddle Points and Non-Convexity

For deep networks, $\mathcal{L}(\theta)$ is highly non-convex. Critical points ($\nabla\mathcal{L} = 0$) include:

- **Global minima:** $\nabla^2\mathcal{L} \succ 0$, lowest loss
- **Local minima:** $\nabla^2\mathcal{L} \succ 0$, not globally minimal
- **Saddle points:** $\nabla^2\mathcal{L}$ has both positive and negative eigenvalues
- **Plateaus:** $\nabla\mathcal{L} \approx 0$ but $\mathcal{L}$ not at minimum

**Saddle points dominate in high dimensions.** At a random critical point in $d$ dimensions, the probability that the Hessian is positive definite (local minimum) is exponentially small in $d$ — nearly all critical points are saddle points. SGD noise helps escape saddle points because gradient noise has components along negative curvature directions.

> **Theorem 10.6 (Strict Saddle Property):** For many neural network architectures (linear networks, matrix factorization), all local minima are global minima, and all saddle points have at least one direction of negative curvature. Gradient descent with noise converges to global minima.

This is the theoretical justification for why deep learning works despite non-convexity.

---

### 10.2.8 Learning Rate — The Most Critical Hyperparameter

The learning rate $\eta$ determines:

**Too large ($\eta > 2/L$):** Gradient descent **diverges** — it overshoots the minimum and loss increases.

**Too small:** Gradient descent converges but **extremely slowly** — each step makes negligible progress.

**Just right ($\eta \approx 1/L$):** Fastest convergence — each step fully descends the local quadratic approximation.

**Learning rate schedules:**

$$\eta_t = \eta_0 \cdot \gamma^t \quad \text{(exponential decay)} \tag{10.22}$$ $$\eta_t = \eta_0 / \sqrt{t} \quad \text{(polynomial decay, satisfies Robbins-Monro)} \tag{10.23}$$ $$\eta_t = \eta_{\min} + \frac{1}{2}(\eta_{\max}-\eta_{\min})\left(1 + \cos\frac{\pi t}{T}\right) \quad \text{(cosine annealing)} \tag{10.24}$$

**Warmup:** Starting with small $\eta$ and increasing prevents instability from large early gradients — critical for Transformer training where the loss landscape is particularly sharp at initialization.

---

### 10.2.9 Stochastic Gradient Descent — The Langevin Dynamics View

With constant learning rate $\eta$ and isotropic noise, SGD satisfies: $$\theta^{(t+1)} = \theta^{(t)} - \eta\nabla\mathcal{L}(\theta^{(t)}) + \sqrt{\eta},\boldsymbol{\xi}_t, \quad \boldsymbol{\xi}_t \approx \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \sigma^2\mathbf{I}) \tag{10.25}$$

This is **Stochastic Gradient Langevin Dynamics (SGLD)** — a discretization of the Langevin SDE: $$d\theta = -\nabla\mathcal{L}(\theta),dt + \sqrt{2\eta},d\mathbf{W}_t$$

The stationary distribution of this SDE is $p^*(\theta) \propto \exp(-\mathcal{L}(\theta)/\eta)$ — a **Gibbs distribution** (Module 8) with temperature $\eta$. SGD is implicitly performing Bayesian posterior sampling at temperature $\eta$. This deep connection between optimization and sampling is the theoretical foundation of **Bayesian deep learning**.

---

## 10.3 Numerical Examples

### Example 10.1: Gradient Descent on a Convex Quadratic

**Problem:** Minimize $f(\theta) = \frac{1}{2}\theta^\top\mathbf{A}\theta - \mathbf{b}^\top\theta$ where $\mathbf{A} = \begin{pmatrix}4&1\1&2\end{pmatrix}$, $\mathbf{b} = \begin{pmatrix}3\1\end{pmatrix}$.

**Analytical solution:** $\theta^* = \mathbf{A}^{-1}\mathbf{b}$. $|\mathbf{A}| = 8-1=7$, $\mathbf{A}^{-1} = \frac{1}{7}\begin{pmatrix}2&-1\-1&4\end{pmatrix}$. $$\theta^* = \frac{1}{7}\begin{pmatrix}6-1\-3+4\end{pmatrix} = \frac{1}{7}\begin{pmatrix}5\1\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}5/7\1/7\end{pmatrix}$$

**Condition number:** Eigenvalues of $\mathbf{A}$: $\lambda = 3 \pm \sqrt{2}$, so $L = 3+\sqrt{2} \approx 4.41$, $\mu = 3-\sqrt{2} \approx 1.59$, $\kappa = L/\mu \approx 2.77$.

**Optimal learning rate:** $\eta^* = 2/(L+\mu) = 2/6 = 1/3$

**GD update:** $\theta^{(t+1)} = \theta^{(t)} - \eta(\mathbf{A}\theta^{(t)} - \mathbf{b})$

Starting from $\theta^{(0)} = (0,0)^\top$:

Step 1: $\theta^{(1)} = (0,0) - \frac{1}{3}(0,0-3,-1)^\top = (1, 1/3)^\top$ Step 2: $\theta^{(2)} = (1,1/3) - \frac{1}{3}(4+1/3-3, 1+2/3-1)^\top = (1,1/3) - \frac{1}{3}(4/3, 2/3)^\top \approx (0.556, 0.111)^\top$

Converging toward $(5/7, 1/7) \approx (0.714, 0.143)$.

By Theorem 10.5, convergence rate per step: $(1-\mu/L)^T = (1-1/2.77)^T \approx 0.639^T$. After 10 steps: error $\approx 0.639^{10} \approx 0.006$ — less than 1% of initial error.

---

### Example 10.2: Loss Function Comparison for Outlier Robustness

Given residuals $r = {0.1, 0.3, -0.2, 5.0}$ (one outlier at 5.0):

|Loss|Values|Total|
|---|---|---|
|MSE|$0.01 + 0.09 + 0.04 + 25.0$|**25.14**|
|MAE|$0.1 + 0.3 + 0.2 + 5.0$|**5.60**|
|Huber ($\delta=1$)|$0.005 + 0.045 + 0.02 + (1)(5-0.5)$|**4.57**|

The outlier dominates MSE (625× amplification), moderately affects Huber, and is treated linearly by MAE. This quantitative comparison motivates loss function choice in robust regression.

---

## 10.4 Implementation

```python
import numpy as np
import scipy.linalg as la
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.gridspec as gridspec
from typing import Callable, Optional, Tuple
from dataclasses import dataclass, field

# =============================================================================
# MODULE 10: Cost Functions & Convex Optimization
# =============================================================================

# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# PART A: Loss Function Library
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------

class LossFunctions:
    """
    Complete library of loss functions with value, gradient, and
    probabilistic interpretation.
    """

    @staticmethod
    def mse(y_true: np.ndarray, y_pred: np.ndarray) -> Tuple[float, np.ndarray]:
        """
        Mean Squared Error. Eq. 10.3.
        Probabilistic basis: Gaussian noise model (Module 3, Example 3.1).
        Returns (loss, gradient w.r.t. y_pred).
        """
        r    = y_pred - y_true
        loss = np.mean(r**2)
        grad = 2 * r / len(y_true)
        return loss, grad

    @staticmethod
    def mae(y_true: np.ndarray, y_pred: np.ndarray) -> Tuple[float, np.ndarray]:
        """
        Mean Absolute Error. Eq. 10.4.
        Probabilistic basis: Laplace noise model.
        Uses subgradient at 0.
        """
        r    = y_pred - y_true
        loss = np.mean(np.abs(r))
        grad = np.sign(r) / len(y_true)
        return loss, grad

    @staticmethod
    def huber(y_true: np.ndarray, y_pred: np.ndarray,
              delta: float = 1.0) -> Tuple[float, np.ndarray]:
        """
        Huber loss. Eq. 10.5.
        Combines MSE robustness (|r|<=delta) with MAE robustness (|r|>delta).
        """
        r    = y_pred - y_true
        mask = np.abs(r) <= delta
        loss_quad = 0.5 * r**2
        loss_lin  = delta * (np.abs(r) - 0.5*delta)
        loss = np.mean(np.where(mask, loss_quad, loss_lin))
        grad = np.where(mask, r, delta * np.sign(r)) / len(y_true)
        return loss, grad

    @staticmethod
    def binary_cross_entropy(y_true: np.ndarray,
                              y_pred: np.ndarray,
                              eps: float = 1e-12) -> Tuple[float, np.ndarray]:
        """
        Binary cross-entropy. Eq. 10.6.
        Probabilistic basis: Bernoulli likelihood.
        y_pred must be in (0,1) — apply sigmoid before calling.
        """
        p    = np.clip(y_pred, eps, 1 - eps)
        loss = -np.mean(y_true*np.log(p) + (1-y_true)*np.log(1-p))
        grad = (p - y_true) / (p*(1-p)) / len(y_true)
        return loss, grad

    @staticmethod
    def categorical_cross_entropy(y_true: np.ndarray,
                                   y_pred: np.ndarray,
                                   eps: float = 1e-12) -> Tuple[float, np.ndarray]:
        """
        Categorical cross-entropy. Eq. 10.7.
        y_true: one-hot (n, K). y_pred: softmax output (n, K).
        """
        p    = np.clip(y_pred, eps, 1.0)
        loss = -np.mean(np.sum(y_true * np.log(p), axis=1))
        grad = -(y_true / p) / len(y_true)
        return loss, grad

    @staticmethod
    def hinge(y_true: np.ndarray, y_pred: np.ndarray) -> Tuple[float, np.ndarray]:
        """
        Hinge loss for binary SVM. Eq. 10.8.
        y_true in {-1, +1}.
        """
        margin = y_true * y_pred
        loss   = np.mean(np.maximum(0, 1 - margin))
        grad   = np.where(margin < 1, -y_true, 0) / len(y_true)
        return loss, grad

    @classmethod
    def compare_losses(cls, y_true: np.ndarray, y_pred_range: np.ndarray,
                       y_fixed: float = 0.0):
        """
        Plot all loss functions as a function of prediction for fixed y_true.
        Visualizes the loss landscape shape.
        """
        fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 5))

        # Regression losses
        ax = axes[0]
        preds   = y_pred_range
        y_fixed_arr = np.full_like(preds, y_fixed)

        losses = {}
        for name, fn, kw in [
            ("MSE",        cls.mse,   {}),
            ("MAE",        cls.mae,   {}),
            ("Huber(δ=1)", cls.huber, {"delta": 1.0}),
            ("Huber(δ=2)", cls.huber, {"delta": 2.0}),
        ]:
            vals = [fn(np.array([y_fixed]), np.array([p]), **kw)[0] for p in preds]
            losses[name] = vals
            ax.plot(preds, vals, lw=2.5, label=name)

        ax.axvline(y_fixed, color='gray', lw=1, linestyle='--', label=f"y_true={y_fixed}")
        ax.set_title("Regression Loss Functions\n(Loss vs Prediction for fixed $y=0$)",
                     fontsize=12, fontweight='bold')
        ax.set_xlabel("Predicted value $\\hat{y}$")
        ax.set_ylabel("Loss")
        ax.legend(fontsize=10); ax.grid(alpha=0.3); ax.set_xlim(-5, 5); ax.set_ylim(0, 10)

        # Classification losses
        ax  = axes[1]
        margins = np.linspace(-3, 3, 300)
        for name, loss_fn, col, ls in [
            ("Hinge",             lambda m: np.maximum(0, 1-m), '#1a6faf', '-'),
            ("Log (sigmoid BCE)", lambda m: np.log1p(np.exp(-m)), '#e84040', '--'),
            ("Exp (AdaBoost)",    lambda m: np.exp(-m), '#2ca02c', ':'),
            ("0-1 (ideal)",       lambda m: (m < 0).astype(float), '#888', '-.'),
        ]:
            ax.plot(margins, loss_fn(margins), lw=2.5, color=col, linestyle=ls, label=name)
        ax.axvline(0, color='gray', lw=1, linestyle=':', alpha=0.7)
        ax.axvline(1, color='gray', lw=1, linestyle=':', alpha=0.7, label="Margin=1")
        ax.set_title("Classification Loss Functions\n(Loss vs margin $y\\hat{f}(x)$)",
                     fontsize=12, fontweight='bold')
        ax.set_xlabel("Margin $y \\cdot f(x)$"); ax.set_ylabel("Loss")
        ax.legend(fontsize=9); ax.grid(alpha=0.3); ax.set_xlim(-3, 3); ax.set_ylim(0, 5)

        plt.suptitle("Loss Function Comparison", fontsize=14, fontweight='bold', y=1.02)
        plt.tight_layout()
        plt.savefig("module10_loss_functions.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches='tight')
        plt.show()


# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# PART B: Gradient Descent Optimizer with Full Diagnostics
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------

@dataclass
class OptimizerResult:
    theta_history:  np.ndarray
    loss_history:   np.ndarray
    grad_norm_history: np.ndarray
    n_iterations:   int
    converged:      bool
    final_theta:    np.ndarray
    final_loss:     float


class GradientDescentOptimizer:
    """
    Gradient Descent with multiple variants and convergence diagnostics.
    Implements: Full-batch GD, SGD, and Mini-batch GD.
    Verifies convergence theorems (Theorems 10.4 and 10.5).
    """

    def __init__(self, loss_fn: Callable, grad_fn: Callable):
        """
        Parameters
        ----------
        loss_fn : callable(theta) -> float
        grad_fn : callable(theta) -> array (gradient)
        """
        self.loss_fn = loss_fn
        self.grad_fn = grad_fn

    def full_batch_gd(self,
                      theta_init: np.ndarray,
                      eta: float = 0.01,
                      n_iter: int = 1000,
                      tol: float = 1e-8) -> OptimizerResult:
        """
        Full-batch gradient descent. Algorithm 10.1 (Eq. 10.15).
        theta_{t+1} = theta_t - eta * grad L(theta_t)
        """
        theta   = theta_init.copy().astype(float)
        t_hist  = [theta.copy()]
        l_hist  = [self.loss_fn(theta)]
        gn_hist = []

        for t in range(n_iter):
            grad    = self.grad_fn(theta)
            gn      = np.linalg.norm(grad)
            gn_hist.append(gn)

            if gn < tol:
                return OptimizerResult(
                    np.array(t_hist), np.array(l_hist), np.array(gn_hist),
                    t, True, theta, l_hist[-1])

            theta  -= eta * grad
            t_hist.append(theta.copy())
            l_hist.append(self.loss_fn(theta))

        gn_hist.append(np.linalg.norm(self.grad_fn(theta)))
        return OptimizerResult(
            np.array(t_hist), np.array(l_hist), np.array(gn_hist),
            n_iter, False, theta, l_hist[-1])

    def sgd(self,
            theta_init: np.ndarray,
            per_sample_grad_fn: Callable,
            n_samples: int,
            eta_fn: Callable = None,
            n_epochs: int = 10,
            seed: int = 42) -> OptimizerResult:
        """
        Stochastic Gradient Descent. Algorithm 10.2 (Eq. 10.18).
        per_sample_grad_fn: callable(theta, i) -> gradient for sample i.
        eta_fn: callable(t) -> learning rate at step t (None = constant 0.01).
        """
        rng    = np.random.default_rng(seed)
        theta  = theta_init.copy().astype(float)
        if eta_fn is None:
            eta_fn = lambda t: 0.01

        t_hist, l_hist, gn_hist = [theta.copy()], [self.loss_fn(theta)], []
        step   = 0

        for epoch in range(n_epochs):
            indices = rng.permutation(n_samples)
            for i in indices:
                grad    = per_sample_grad_fn(theta, i)
                eta     = eta_fn(step)
                theta  -= eta * grad
                step   += 1

            l_hist.append(self.loss_fn(theta))
            t_hist.append(theta.copy())
            gn      = np.linalg.norm(self.grad_fn(theta))
            gn_hist.append(gn)

        return OptimizerResult(
            np.array(t_hist), np.array(l_hist), np.array(gn_hist),
            n_epochs, False, theta, l_hist[-1])

    def minibatch_gd(self,
                     theta_init: np.ndarray,
                     X: np.ndarray,
                     y: np.ndarray,
                     batch_loss_grad_fn: Callable,
                     batch_size: int = 32,
                     eta: float = 0.01,
                     n_epochs: int = 20,
                     seed: int = 42) -> OptimizerResult:
        """
        Mini-batch Gradient Descent. Algorithm 10.3 (Eq. 10.21).
        """
        rng    = np.random.default_rng(seed)
        theta  = theta_init.copy().astype(float)
        n      = len(X)

        t_hist, l_hist, gn_hist = [theta.copy()], [self.loss_fn(theta)], []

        for epoch in range(n_epochs):
            perm = rng.permutation(n)
            for start in range(0, n, batch_size):
                idx   = perm[start:start+batch_size]
                Xb, yb = X[idx], y[idx]
                _, grad = batch_loss_grad_fn(theta, Xb, yb)
                theta  -= eta * grad

            l_hist.append(self.loss_fn(theta))
            t_hist.append(theta.copy())
            gn_hist.append(np.linalg.norm(self.grad_fn(theta)))

        return OptimizerResult(
            np.array(t_hist), np.array(l_hist), np.array(gn_hist),
            n_epochs, False, theta, l_hist[-1])


# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# PART C: Convergence Verification and Visualization
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def demonstrate_gd_convergence(seed: int = 42):
    """
    Verifies Theorems 10.4 and 10.5 on a quadratic loss function.
    Compares full-batch GD, SGD, and mini-batch GD.
    Shows effect of learning rate and condition number.
    """
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)

    # Setup: Quadratic f(theta) = 0.5 theta^T A theta - b^T theta
    # Minimum at theta* = A^{-1} b
    A = np.array([[4., 1.], [1., 2.]])
    b = np.array([3., 1.])
    theta_star = np.linalg.solve(A, b)

    # Problem parameters
    eigvals = np.linalg.eigvalsh(A)
    L, mu   = eigvals.max(), eigvals.min()
    kappa   = L / mu
    eta_opt = 2 / (L + mu)     # optimal learning rate for strongly convex

    print(f"\n{'='*60}")
    print(f"  QUADRATIC OPTIMIZATION — CONVERGENCE ANALYSIS")
    print(f"{'='*60}")
    print(f"  L (smoothness constant): {L:.4f}")
    print(f"  μ (strong convexity):    {mu:.4f}")
    print(f"  κ = L/μ (condition #):   {kappa:.4f}")
    print(f"  Optimal η:               {eta_opt:.4f}")
    print(f"  θ* (analytical):         {theta_star}")

    # Loss and gradient functions
    loss_fn = lambda t: 0.5 * t @ A @ t - b @ t
    grad_fn = lambda t: A @ t - b

    optimizer = GradientDescentOptimizer(loss_fn, grad_fn)

    # ---- Full-batch GD with different learning rates ----
    fig = plt.figure(figsize=(16, 10))
    gs  = gridspec.GridSpec(2, 3, wspace=0.38, hspace=0.45)

    # Panel 1: Loss landscape with GD trajectory
    ax = fig.add_subplot(gs[0, 0])
    t1 = np.linspace(-0.5, 2.5, 300)
    t2 = np.linspace(-0.5, 1.5, 300)
    T1, T2 = np.meshgrid(t1, t2)
    Z  = np.array([[loss_fn(np.array([x,y])) for x in t1] for y in t2])
    ax.contourf(T1, T2, Z, levels=20, cmap='Blues', alpha=0.7)
    ax.contour(T1, T2, Z, levels=15, colors='navy', linewidths=0.5, alpha=0.4)

    theta_init = np.array([0., 0.])
    for eta, col, ls, lbl in [(0.1, '#e84040', '-', f'η=0.1 (small)'),
                               (eta_opt, '#2ca02c', '--', f'η={eta_opt:.3f} (optimal)'),
                               (0.45, '#9467bd', ':', 'η=0.45 (large)')]:
        res = optimizer.full_batch_gd(theta_init, eta=eta, n_iter=30)
        ax.plot(res.theta_history[:,0], res.theta_history[:,1],
                'o-', ms=4, lw=2, color=col, linestyle=ls, alpha=0.85, label=lbl)
    ax.scatter(*theta_star, s=120, color='red', zorder=6, marker='*', label=f'θ* = {theta_star.round(3)}')
    ax.set_title("GD Trajectories\n(Loss Landscape)", fontsize=11, fontweight='bold')
    ax.set_xlabel("θ₁"); ax.set_ylabel("θ₂")
    ax.legend(fontsize=8); ax.set_xlim(-0.5, 2.5); ax.set_ylim(-0.5, 1.5)

    # Panel 2: Convergence rate — Theorem 10.4 (O(1/T)) vs Theorem 10.5 (linear)
    ax = fig.add_subplot(gs[0, 1])
    n_iter = 100
    for eta, col, lbl in [(eta_opt, '#1a6faf', f'η={eta_opt:.3f} (optimal)'),
                           (0.1, '#e84040', 'η=0.10'),
                           (0.05, '#2ca02c', 'η=0.05')]:
        res = optimizer.full_batch_gd(theta_init, eta=eta, n_iter=n_iter)
        excess = res.loss_history - loss_fn(theta_star)
        ax.semilogy(np.maximum(excess, 1e-16), lw=2, color=col, label=lbl)

    # Theoretical convergence rate (Theorem 10.5)
    iters     = np.arange(n_iter + 1)
    rate_theor = (1 - mu/L)**iters * np.linalg.norm(theta_init - theta_star)**2 * L/2
    ax.semilogy(rate_theor, 'k--', lw=1.5, alpha=0.7, label=f'Theory: $(1-μ/L)^T$ (Thm 10.5)')
    ax.set_xlabel("Iteration T")
    ax.set_ylabel("Excess loss $\\mathcal{L}(θ^T) - \\mathcal{L}(θ^*)$ (log)")
    ax.set_title("Convergence Rate\n(Theorems 10.4 & 10.5)", fontsize=11, fontweight='bold')
    ax.legend(fontsize=8); ax.grid(alpha=0.3, which='both')

    # Panel 3: Effect of condition number
    ax = fig.add_subplot(gs[0, 2])
    for kap, col in [(2, '#1a6faf'), (10, '#e84040'), (50, '#2ca02c'), (200, '#9467bd')]:
        # Construct A with given condition number
        A_k    = np.diag([kap * 1., 1.0])
        b_k    = np.array([1., 1.])
        L_k, mu_k = kap * 1.0, 1.0
        eta_k  = 2 / (L_k + mu_k)
        lf_k   = lambda t, A=A_k, b=b_k: 0.5*t@A@t - b@t
        gf_k   = lambda t, A=A_k, b=b_k: A@t - b
        opt_k  = GradientDescentOptimizer(lf_k, gf_k)
        theta_star_k = np.linalg.solve(A_k, b_k)
        res_k  = opt_k.full_batch_gd(np.zeros(2), eta=eta_k, n_iter=200)
        excess_k = res_k.loss_history - lf_k(theta_star_k)
        ax.semilogy(np.maximum(excess_k, 1e-16), lw=2, color=col,
                    label=f'κ={kap}, η={eta_k:.3f}')
    ax.set_xlabel("Iteration"); ax.set_ylabel("Excess loss (log scale)")
    ax.set_title("Effect of Condition Number κ\non Convergence Speed",
                 fontsize=11, fontweight='bold')
    ax.legend(fontsize=8); ax.grid(alpha=0.3, which='both')

    # Panels 4-6: GD vs SGD vs Mini-batch on linear regression
    n, d = 500, 2
    X_data = rng.normal(0, 1, (n, d))
    theta_true = np.array([1.5, -0.8])
    y_data = X_data @ theta_true + rng.normal(0, 0.3, n)

    # Loss and gradient functions for linear regression
    def lr_loss(theta): return np.mean((X_data @ theta - y_data)**2)
    def lr_grad(theta): return 2 * X_data.T @ (X_data @ theta - y_data) / n
    def lr_grad_sample(theta, i): return 2 * X_data[i] * (X_data[i] @ theta - y_data[i])
    def lr_batch_loss_grad(theta, Xb, yb):
        r    = Xb @ theta - yb
        loss = np.mean(r**2)
        grad = 2 * Xb.T @ r / len(yb)
        return loss, grad

    theta_star_lr = np.linalg.lstsq(X_data, y_data, rcond=None)[0]
    opt_lr = GradientDescentOptimizer(lr_loss, lr_grad)

    ax = fig.add_subplot(gs[1, :])
    res_gd  = opt_lr.full_batch_gd(np.zeros(d), eta=0.1, n_iter=50)
    res_sgd = opt_lr.sgd(np.zeros(d), lr_grad_sample, n,
                         eta_fn=lambda t: 0.1/np.sqrt(t+1), n_epochs=50, seed=42)
    res_mb4  = opt_lr.minibatch_gd(np.zeros(d), X_data, y_data,
                                    lr_batch_loss_grad, batch_size=4, eta=0.05, n_epochs=50)
    res_mb64 = opt_lr.minibatch_gd(np.zeros(d), X_data, y_data,
                                    lr_batch_loss_grad, batch_size=64, eta=0.05, n_epochs=50)

    opt_loss = lr_loss(theta_star_lr)
    for res, col, lbl in [(res_gd, '#1a6faf', 'Full GD (B=500)'),
                           (res_sgd, '#e84040', 'SGD (B=1, η∝1/√t)'),
                           (res_mb4, '#2ca02c', 'Mini-batch (B=4)'),
                           (res_mb64, '#9467bd', 'Mini-batch (B=64)')]:
        excess = np.maximum(res.loss_history - opt_loss, 1e-10)
        ax.semilogy(excess, lw=2, color=col, label=lbl)

    ax.set_xlabel("Epoch (pass over data)")
    ax.set_ylabel("Excess loss (log scale)")
    ax.set_title("GD vs SGD vs Mini-batch GD — Linear Regression\n"
                 "(SGD noisy but cheap per step; Full-GD smooth but expensive)",
                 fontsize=12, fontweight='bold')
    ax.legend(fontsize=10); ax.grid(alpha=0.3, which='both')

    plt.suptitle("Gradient Descent: Convergence Theory & Empirical Verification",
                 fontsize=14, fontweight='bold', y=1.01)
    plt.savefig("module10_gradient_descent.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches='tight')
    plt.show()
    print("Saved: module10_gradient_descent.png")


# =============================================================================
# MAIN
# =============================================================================

if __name__ == "__main__":

    # --- A: Loss function comparison ---
    print("=" * 60)
    print("  LOSS FUNCTION COMPARISON")
    print("=" * 60)
    lf = LossFunctions()
    y_true = np.array([0., 0., 0., 0.])
    y_pred = np.array([0.1, 0.3, -0.2, 5.0])  # outlier at index 3

    print(f"\n  Residuals: {y_pred}")
    print(f"  (True = 0 for all, outlier at index 3 = 5.0)\n")
    for name, fn, kw in [("MSE",        lf.mse,   {}),
                          ("MAE",        lf.mae,   {}),
                          ("Huber(δ=1)", lf.huber, {"delta": 1.0})]:
        loss, _ = fn(y_true, y_pred, **kw)
        print(f"  {name:<15} Loss = {loss:.4f}")
```

## 10.7 Key Equations Reference Card

$$\mathcal{L}(\theta) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i\ell(f_\theta(\mathbf{x}_i),y_i) + \lambda\Omega(\theta) \tag{Regularized risk}$$ $$f \text{ convex} \iff f(\mathbf{y})\geq f(\mathbf{x})+\nabla f(\mathbf{x})^\top(\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{x}) \tag{First-order condition}$$ $$f \text{ convex} \iff \nabla^2 f(\mathbf{x})\succeq\mathbf{0} \tag{Second-order condition}$$ $$\theta^{(t+1)} = \theta^{(t)} - \eta\nabla\mathcal{L}(\theta^{(t)}) \tag{Gradient descent}$$ $$\mathcal{L}(\theta^{(T)})-\mathcal{L}^_\leq\frac{|\theta^{(0)}-\theta^_|^2}{2\eta T} \tag{Sublinear convergence}$$ $$|\theta^{(T)}-\theta^_|^2\leq(1-\mu/L)^T|\theta^{(0)}-\theta^_|^2 \tag{Linear convergence}$$ $$\text{Var}(\hat{g}_B)=\sigma^2_{\text{grad}}/B \tag{Mini-batch variance (CLT)}$$
