# PART D: Missing Value Imputation
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------

class MissingValueImputer:
    """
    Multiple imputation strategies with fit/transform API.
    Implements MCAR, MAR-aware, and model-based approaches.
    """

    def __init__(self, strategy: str = 'median', n_neighbors: int = 5):
        """
        strategy: 'mean', 'median', 'mode', 'knn', 'regression', 'indicator'
        """
        self.strategy    = strategy
        self.n_neighbors = n_neighbors
        self.params      = {}

    def fit(self, X: pd.DataFrame) -> 'MissingValueImputer':
        num_cols = X.select_dtypes(include=[np.number]).columns

        if self.strategy in ('mean', 'median'):
            for col in num_cols:
                fn = X[col].mean if self.strategy == 'mean' else X[col].median
                self.params[col] = fn()
        elif self.strategy == 'mode':
            for col in X.columns:
                self.params[col] = X[col].mode().iloc[0]
        elif self.strategy == 'knn':
            self.params['X_train'] = X[num_cols].values
            self.params['cols']    = num_cols.tolist()

        return self

    def transform(self, X: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
        X = X.copy()
        num_cols = X.select_dtypes(include=[np.number]).columns

        if self.strategy in ('mean', 'median', 'mode'):
            for col in X.columns:
                if col in self.params:
                    X[col] = X[col].fillna(self.params[col])

        elif self.strategy == 'knn':
            cols   = self.params['cols']
            X_ref  = self.params['X_train']
            X_arr  = X[cols].values.copy()
            miss_rows = np.where(np.isnan(X_arr).any(axis=1))[0]

            for row in miss_rows:
                miss_cols = np.where(np.isnan(X_arr[row]))[0]
                obs_cols  = np.where(~np.isnan(X_arr[row]))[0]

                if len(obs_cols) == 0:
                    # All missing: use column medians
                    for mc in miss_cols:
                        X_arr[row, mc] = np.nanmedian(X_ref[:, mc])
                    continue

                # Compute distances using observed features
                dists = np.sqrt(np.nansum(
                    (X_ref[:, obs_cols] - X_arr[row, obs_cols])**2, axis=1))
                neighbors = np.argsort(dists)[:self.n_neighbors]

                for mc in miss_cols:
                    neighbor_vals = X_ref[neighbors, mc]
                    valid = neighbor_vals[~np.isnan(neighbor_vals)]
                    X_arr[row, mc] = valid.mean() if len(valid) else np.nanmedian(X_ref[:, mc])

            X[cols] = X_arr

        elif self.strategy == 'indicator':
            # Create missingness indicator and impute with median
            for col in num_cols:
                if X[col].isna().any():
                    X[col + '_missing'] = X[col].isna().astype(int)
                    X[col] = X[col].fillna(X[col].median())

        return X

    # --- G: Imputation comparison ---
    print("\n" + "=" * 60)

    df_miss = df_demo[['sqft','rooms','dist_cbd']].copy()
    print(f"\n  Before imputation: {df_miss.isna().sum().to_dict()}")

    for strat in ['mean', 'median', 'knn']:
        imp  = MissingValueImputer(strategy=strat)
        imp.fit(df_miss)
        df_imputed = imp.transform(df_miss)
        print(f"  After '{strat}' imputation: {df_imputed.isna().sum().to_dict()} ✓")

|EDA Operation|Statistical Foundation|ML Impact|
|---|---|---|
|Descriptive stats|Sample moments (Eq. 12.1-12.4)|Detect data quality issues|
|MCAR/MAR/MNAR|Missingness mechanism taxonomy|Choose correct imputation|
|KNN imputation|Nearest neighbor estimation|Preserves local structure|
|Z-score outlier|Normal distribution quantiles|Fast, fails with masking|
|IQR outlier|Robust order statistics|Distribution-free, robust|
|Modified Z-score|Median + MAD estimation|Best for unknown distributions|

|Robust scaling|Median + IQR (Eq. 12.15)|Heavy-tailed data|
|Box-Cox|MLE-optimal normalization (Eq. 12.17)|Best normalization for regression|
|Pearson corr.|Sample covariance (Eq. 12.18)|Feature selection, collinearity|
|Spearman corr.|Rank-based (Eq. 12.20)|Nonlinear monotone detection|
|Shapiro-Wilk|Order statistics test (Eq. 12.22)|Validate normality assumption|
|Cyclical encoding|Fourier features|Periodic time features|
|Target encoding|MAP estimation (Eq. 12.27)|High-cardinality categoricals|

## 12.6 Key Equations Reference Card

$$\bar{x}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_i x_i,\quad s^2=\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_i(x_i-\bar{x})^2 \tag{Moments}$$ $$|z_i|=|x_i-\bar{x}|/s > k \tag{Z-score outlier}$$ $$x_i \notin [Q_1-1.5\cdot\text{IQR},;Q_3+1.5\cdot\text{IQR}] \tag{IQR outlier}$$ $$x_i^{\text{std}}=(x_i-\bar{x})/s,\quad x_i^{\text{rob}}=(x_i-\tilde{x})/\text{IQR} \tag{Scaling}$$ $$x_i^{\text{BC}}=(x_i^\lambda-1)/\lambda;\text{or};\log x_i \tag{Box-Cox}$$ $$r_{XY}=\hat\sigma_{XY}/(\hat\sigma_X\hat\sigma_Y) \tag{Pearson correlation}$$ $$t=r\sqrt{(n-2)/(1-r^2)}\sim t_{n-2} \tag{Correlation significance}$$

# MODULE 13: Advanced Statistical Inference

### _Chi-Square Tests, ANOVA, and Bayesian Networks_

---

## 13.1 Conceptual Overview

### Why These Three Topics Belong Together

Chi-square tests, ANOVA, and Bayesian Networks form a coherent triad that covers the three fundamental questions of statistical inference in ML systems:

**Chi-square tests** answer: _Are two categorical variables independent?_ This is the exact question behind feature selection for classifiers, A/B test result analysis, and model calibration assessment. Every decision tree split criterion (information gain, Gini impurity) is implicitly testing a variant of this question.

**ANOVA** answers: _Do multiple groups have different means?_ This is the question behind hyperparameter comparison studies (is optimizer A better than B and C?), multi-arm A/B tests, and analysis of variance across data slices. It generalizes the two-sample t-test to $K$ groups while controlling the family-wise error rate.

**Bayesian Networks** answer: _What is the dependency structure among variables?_ They are directed graphical models that encode conditional independence relationships as a DAG, enabling efficient probabilistic inference. They are the theoretical foundation of causal inference, probabilistic programming, and the attention mechanism's interpretability.

Together, these tools complete the bridge from classical frequentist inference (Modules 7, 12) to the full probabilistic graphical model framework needed for modern ML.

---

## 13.2 Mathematical Formalization

### 13.2.1 The Chi-Square Distribution — Foundation

Before the tests, we need the distribution precisely. We defined the chi-squared distribution in Module 4 (Definition 4.9) as the sum of squared standard normals. Here we develop its role in categorical inference.

> **Definition 13.1 (Pearson's Chi-Square Statistic):** Given observed counts $O_{ij}$ and expected counts $E_{ij}$ in a contingency table: $$\chi^2 = \sum_{i,j} \frac{(O_{ij} - E_{ij})^2}{E_{ij}} \tag{13.1}$$

**Why is this chi-squared distributed?** Each term $(O_{ij} - E_{ij})/\sqrt{E_{ij}}$ is approximately standard normal by the CLT (the count $O_{ij}$ is a sum of Bernoulli variables). Squaring and summing $k$ independent standard normals gives $\chi^2_k$. The degrees of freedom account for constraints imposed by the margins.

---

### 13.2.2 Chi-Square Goodness-of-Fit Test

**Question:** Does the observed distribution of a categorical variable match a hypothesized distribution?

> **Test Setup:** $K$ categories, observed counts $O_k$, hypothesized probabilities $p_k^{(0)}$ under $H_0$.
> 
> $H_0: p_k = p_k^{(0)}$ for all $k = 1,\ldots,K$ $H_1:$ At least one $p_k \neq p_k^{(0)}$

Expected counts under $H_0$: $E_k = n \cdot p_k^{(0)}$

Test statistic: $$\chi^2 = \sum_{k=1}^K \frac{(O_k - E_k)^2}{E_k} \xrightarrow{d} \chi^2_{K-1} \text{ under } H_0 \tag{13.2}$$

Degrees of freedom: $K-1$ (one constraint from $\sum_k p_k = 1$).

**Derivation of df:** We have $K$ free counts but one linear constraint ($\sum O_k = n$), leaving $K-1$ free parameters. Under $H_0$, the MLE of $p_k$ is $O_k/n$, but we fix it at $p_k^{(0)}$ — the $K-1$ free parameters give $K-1$ degrees of freedom. $\blacksquare$

**Rule of thumb:** The chi-square approximation requires $E_k \geq 5$ for all $k$. If not, use Fisher's exact test or combine categories.

**ML application — model calibration:** If a binary classifier claims $\hat{p} = 0.7$ on a group of $n=1000$ predictions, we expect $E_1 = 700$ positives. If we observe $O_1 = 620$, the goodness-of-fit test checks whether the model is calibrated.

---

### 13.2.3 Chi-Square Test of Independence

**Question:** Are two categorical variables $X$ and $Y$ independent?

This is the most important chi-square test for ML — it underlies feature selection, association rule mining, and the decision tree splitting criterion.

> **Test Setup:** $r \times c$ contingency table with cell counts $O_{ij}$, row totals $R_i$, column totals $C_j$, grand total $N$.
> 
> $H_0: X \perp Y$ (independence) $H_1: X \not\perp Y$ (dependence)

Under $H_0$: $P(X=i, Y=j) = P(X=i)\cdot P(Y=j)$, so: $$E_{ij} = N \cdot \frac{R_i}{N} \cdot \frac{C_j}{N} = \frac{R_i C_j}{N} \tag{13.3}$$

Test statistic: $$\chi^2 = \sum_{i=1}^r\sum_{j=1}^c \frac{(O_{ij} - E_{ij})^2}{E_{ij}} \xrightarrow{d} \chi^2_{(r-1)(c-1)} \text{ under } H_0 \tag{13.4}$$

**Derivation of degrees of freedom:** The full contingency table has $rc$ cells. Constraints: $r$ row-sum constraints, $c$ column-sum constraints, minus 1 for double-counting the grand total constraint. Free parameters: $rc - r - c + 1 = (r-1)(c-1)$. $\blacksquare$

**Effect size — Cramér's V:** $$V = \sqrt{\frac{\chi^2/N}{\min(r-1, c-1)}} \in [0, 1] \tag{13.5}$$

$V = 0$ means independence; $V = 1$ means perfect association. This normalizes $\chi^2$ so effect sizes are comparable across different table sizes.

**Relationship to mutual information:** For large $N$: $$\chi^2 \approx 2N \cdot I(X; Y) \tag{13.6}$$

where $I(X;Y)$ is the mutual information (Module 8, Eq. 8.9). The chi-square test of independence is asymptotically equivalent to testing $I(X;Y) = 0$. This connects frequentist hypothesis testing directly to information theory.

**Proof of Eq. 13.6:** The log-likelihood ratio statistic for independence is: $$G^2 = 2\sum_{ij} O_{ij}\log\frac{O_{ij}}{E_{ij}} = 2N\sum_{ij}\hat{p}_{ij}\log\frac{\hat{p}_{ij}}{\hat{p}_{i\cdot}\hat{p}_{\cdot j}} = 2N\cdot\hat{I}(X;Y)$$

By Wilks' theorem (Module 7, Theorem 7.2), $G^2 \xrightarrow{d} \chi^2_{(r-1)(c-1)}$. For large samples, $\chi^2 \approx G^2 \approx 2N\cdot I(X;Y)$. $\blacksquare$

---

### 13.2.4 Chi-Square Test for Model Independence in ML

**Feature selection:** For feature $X_j$ and target $Y$ in a classification problem, compute $\chi^2$ for their contingency table (after discretization if necessary). Features with high $\chi^2$ (low p-value) are strongly associated with the target. `sklearn.feature_selection.chi2` implements this.

**Homogeneity test:** Do multiple populations have the same categorical distribution? Structurally identical to independence test but different interpretation: rows = populations, columns = outcomes.

---

### 13.2.5 One-Way ANOVA

**Question:** Do $K$ groups have the same population mean?

$H_0: \mu_1 = \mu_2 = \cdots = \mu_K$ $H_1:$ At least one $\mu_k$ differs

ANOVA decomposes the **total variation** in the data into between-group and within-group components.

**The ANOVA model:** $$y_{ik} = \mu + \tau_k + \varepsilon_{ik}, \quad \varepsilon_{ik} \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2) \tag{13.7}$$

where $\mu$ is the grand mean, $\tau_k = \mu_k - \mu$ is the treatment effect of group $k$, and $\varepsilon_{ik}$ is within-group noise.

**The fundamental decomposition:**

> **Theorem 13.1 (ANOVA Decomposition):** $$\underbrace{\sum_{k=1}^K\sum_{i=1}^{n_k}(y_{ik} - \bar{y})^2}_{\text{SST (Total)}} = \underbrace{\sum_{k=1}^K n_k(\bar{y}_k - \bar{y})^2}_{\text{SSB (Between)}} + \underbrace{\sum_{k=1}^K\sum_{i=1}^{n_k}(y_{ik} - \bar{y}_k)^2}_{\text{SSW (Within)}} \tag{13.8}$$

**Proof:** Add and subtract $\bar{y}_k$: $$(y_{ik}-\bar{y}) = (y_{ik}-\bar{y}_k) + (\bar{y}_k-\bar{y})$$

Squaring and summing, the cross term vanishes because $\sum_i(y_{ik}-\bar{y}_k) = 0$ for each $k$: $$\sum_{k,i}(y_{ik}-\bar{y})^2 = \sum_{k,i}(y_{ik}-\bar{y}_k)^2 + \sum_{k,i}(\bar{y}_k-\bar{y})^2 \qquad \blacksquare$$

**Mean squares and the F-statistic:**

$$\text{MSB} = \frac{\text{SSB}}{K-1}, \quad \text{MSW} = \frac{\text{SSW}}{N-K} \tag{13.9}$$

> **Theorem 13.2 (F-statistic distribution):** Under $H_0$: $$F = \frac{\text{MSB}}{\text{MSW}} \sim F_{K-1,, N-K} \tag{13.10}$$

**Proof:** Under the ANOVA model and $H_0$ ($\tau_k = 0$ for all $k$):

$\text{SSW}/\sigma^2 \sim \chi^2_{N-K}$ (sum of squared residuals within groups).

$\text{SSB}/\sigma^2 \sim \chi^2_{K-1}$ under $H_0$ (by the CLT applied to $\bar{y}_k - \bar{y}$).

SSB and SSW are independent (by Cochran's theorem — the multivariate analog of the independence of $\bar{X}$ and $S^2$ in the t-test).

The ratio of two independent chi-squared variables divided by their degrees of freedom is by definition F-distributed: $$F = \frac{\text{SSB}/(\sigma^2(K-1))}{\text{SSW}/(\sigma^2(N-K))} = \frac{\chi^2_{K-1}/(K-1)}{\chi^2_{N-K}/(N-K)} \sim F_{K-1,N-K} \qquad \blacksquare$$

**ANOVA table:**

|Source|SS|df|MS|F|
|---|---|---|---|---|
|Between groups|SSB|$K-1$|MSB|MSB/MSW|
|Within groups|SSW|$N-K$|MSW|—|
|Total|SST|$N-1$|—|—|

**Effect size — $\eta^2$ (eta-squared):** $$\eta^2 = \frac{\text{SSB}}{\text{SST}} \in [0, 1] \tag{13.11}$$

Proportion of total variance explained by group membership. Analogous to $R^2$ in regression.

**ANOVA assumptions:**

1. **Independence:** Observations within and across groups are independent.
2. **Normality:** $y_{ik} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_k, \sigma^2)$ within each group. Robust to violations for $n_k \geq 30$ (CLT).
3. **Homoscedasticity:** Equal variances $\sigma^2$ across groups. Tested by Levene's or Bartlett's test. Welch's ANOVA relaxes this.

---

### 13.2.6 Post-Hoc Tests — Multiple Comparisons After ANOVA

When ANOVA rejects $H_0$, we know at least one group differs — but not which. Post-hoc tests identify which pairs differ while controlling the family-wise error rate (FWER).

**Tukey's Honest Significant Difference (HSD):**

Test statistic for comparing groups $j$ and $k$: $$q_{jk} = \frac{\bar{y}_j - \bar{y}_k}{\sqrt{\text{MSW}/n}} \tag{13.12}$$

where $n$ is the common group size (balanced design). Under $H_0$, $q_{jk}$ follows the **studentized range distribution** $q_{K, N-K}$. The HSD is: $$\text{HSD} = q_{\alpha,K,N-K} \cdot \sqrt{\text{MSW}/n} \tag{13.13}$$

Groups $j$ and $k$ are significantly different if $|\bar{y}_j - \bar{y}_k| > \text{HSD}$. Tukey's HSD controls FWER at exactly $\alpha$ for all pairwise comparisons simultaneously.

**Bonferroni correction** (simpler, more conservative): Perform all $\binom{K}{2}$ pairwise t-tests at level $\alpha/\binom{K}{2}$.

---

### 13.2.7 Two-Way ANOVA and Interaction Effects

Two-way ANOVA tests the effects of two factors $A$ and $B$ simultaneously.

**Model:** $$y_{ijk} = \mu + \alpha_i + \beta_j + (\alpha\beta)_{ij} + \varepsilon_{ijk} \tag{13.14}$$

where $\alpha_i$ is the main effect of factor A at level $i$, $\beta_j$ is the main effect of B at level $j$, and $(\alpha\beta)_{ij}$ is the **interaction effect**.

**ANOVA decomposition:** $$\text{SST} = \text{SS}_A + \text{SS}_B + \text{SS}_{AB} + \text{SSW} \tag{13.15}$$

Three F-tests: $$F_A = \frac{\text{MS}_A}{\text{MSW}},\quad F_B = \frac{\text{MS}_B}{\text{MSW}},\quad F_{AB} = \frac{\text{MS}_{AB}}{\text{MSW}} \tag{13.16}$$

**ML application:** Two-way ANOVA is used in hyperparameter grid search analysis — testing whether learning rate and batch size independently affect performance, and whether they interact (i.e., whether the optimal batch size depends on the learning rate).

---

### 13.2.8 Bayesian Networks — Structure and Semantics

> **Definition 13.2 (Bayesian Network):** A **Bayesian Network** is a pair $(\mathcal{G}, \mathcal{P})$ where:
> 
> - $\mathcal{G} = (V, E)$ is a **Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG)** with nodes $V = {X_1,\ldots,X_d}$
> - $\mathcal{P}$ is a set of **Conditional Probability Distributions (CPDs)**: $P(X_i \mid \text{Pa}(X_i))$ for each node $X_i$, where $\text{Pa}(X_i)$ denotes the parents of $X_i$ in $\mathcal{G}$

The joint distribution factorizes as: $$P(X_1, \ldots, X_d) = \prod_{i=1}^d P(X_i \mid \text{Pa}(X_i)) \tag{13.17}$$

**This factorization is the Bayesian network's fundamental claim:** the joint distribution is completely determined by local conditional distributions. The graph encodes which variables each node is directly dependent on — all other dependencies are conditional independences.

---

### 13.2.9 Conditional Independence in Bayesian Networks — d-Separation

The DAG structure encodes a rich set of conditional independence statements via the **d-separation** criterion.

> **Definition 13.3 (d-Separation):** A path $\pi$ between nodes $X$ and $Y$ in $\mathcal{G}$ is **blocked** by a set $\mathbf{Z}$ if either:
> 
> 1. $\pi$ contains a **chain** $A \to B \to C$ or **fork** $A \leftarrow B \to C$ with $B \in \mathbf{Z}$, or
> 2. $\pi$ contains a **collider** $A \to B \leftarrow C$ with $B \notin \mathbf{Z}$ and no descendant of $B$ in $\mathbf{Z}$.
> 
> $X$ and $Y$ are **d-separated** by $\mathbf{Z}$ ($X \perp_\mathcal{G} Y \mid \mathbf{Z}$) iff every path between them is blocked by $\mathbf{Z}$.
> 
> **Soundness:** $X \perp_\mathcal{G} Y \mid \mathbf{Z} \implies X \perp Y \mid \mathbf{Z}$ (in any distribution consistent with $\mathcal{G}$).

The three fundamental structures:

**Chain:** $A \to B \to C$

- $A \perp C \mid B$ (B blocks information flow when observed)
- $A \not\perp C$ (marginally dependent)

**Fork (Common Cause):** $A \leftarrow B \to C$

- $A \perp C \mid B$ (B explains the correlation when conditioned on)
- $A \not\perp C$ (spurious correlation — B is a confounder)

**Collider (v-structure):** $A \to B \leftarrow C$

- $A \perp C$ (marginally independent)
- $A \not\perp C \mid B$ (**explaining away** — conditioning on B creates dependence!)

The collider structure explains the **Berkson's paradox** and **selection bias**: conditioning on a common effect induces spurious dependence between its causes.

---

### 13.2.10 Inference in Bayesian Networks

**Exact inference:** Variable elimination algorithm. To compute $P(X_q \mid \mathbf{X}_e = \mathbf{e})$:

$$P(X_q \mid \mathbf{e}) = \frac{P(X_q, \mathbf{e})}{P(\mathbf{e})} = \frac{\sum_{\mathbf{x} \setminus X_q, \mathbf{e}} \prod_i P(X_i \mid \text{Pa}(X_i))}{\sum_{x_q}\sum_{\mathbf{x}\setminus \mathbf{e}} \prod_i P(X_i\mid\text{Pa}(X_i))} \tag{13.18}$$

Variable elimination marginalizes out variables one by one, reusing intermediate factors. Complexity is exponential in the **treewidth** of the graph — polynomial for tree-structured networks.

**Belief propagation:** On tree-structured networks, exact inference in $O(n)$ via message passing. Each node sends messages to its neighbors:

$$\mu_{X\to Y}(y) = \sum_x P(Y\mid X=x) \cdot P(X=x) \cdot \prod_{Z \in \text{Ne}(X)\setminus Y} \mu_{Z\to X}(x) \tag{13.19}$$

The marginal of any node is proportional to the product of all incoming messages.

---

### 13.2.11 Learning Bayesian Networks from Data

**Parameter learning** (given structure $\mathcal{G}$): MLE of CPDs.

For discrete variables, the MLE for each CPD entry is the relative frequency: $$\hat{P}(X_i = k \mid \text{Pa}(X_i) = \mathbf{pa}) = \frac{N_{ik\mathbf{pa}}}{N_{i\mathbf{pa}}} \tag{13.20}$$

where $N_{ik\mathbf{pa}}$ is the count of observations with $X_i = k$ and $\text{Pa}(X_i) = \mathbf{pa}$.

**Structure learning** (unknown $\mathcal{G}$): NP-hard in general. Key algorithms:

- **PC algorithm** (constraint-based): Uses conditional independence tests (chi-square) to identify and orient edges.
- **Score-based search** (e.g., greedy hill-climbing): Maximize BIC score: $$\text{BIC}(\mathcal{G}) = \sum_i \left[\hat\ell_i - \frac{d_i}{2}\log N\right] \tag{13.21}$$ where $\hat\ell_i$ is the log-likelihood of the $i$-th CPD and $d_i$ is its number of free parameters.

**The BIC score** (Module 7, Eq. 7.24) penalizes model complexity — edges add parameters and reduce BIC unless the data strongly supports them. This is MAP estimation over graph structures with a complexity prior.

---

### 13.2.12 Naive Bayes as a Bayesian Network

The Naive Bayes classifier (introduced in Module 1) is a Bayesian Network with a specific structure:

$$P(Y, X_1,\ldots,X_d) = P(Y)\prod_{j=1}^d P(X_j \mid Y) \tag{13.22}$$

The DAG has $Y$ as the sole parent of all $X_j$, with no edges among the $X_j$. This encodes the conditional independence assumption $X_j \perp X_k \mid Y$ for all $j \neq k$ — the "naive" assumption.

**MAP classification rule:** $$\hat{Y} = \arg\max_y P(Y=y)\prod_j P(X_j=x_j\mid Y=y) \tag{13.23}$$

Despite the often-violated independence assumption, Naive Bayes performs remarkably well because the **classification decision** depends on the ratio of class posteriors, which is often correct even when the probabilities themselves are poorly calibrated.

---

## 13.3 Numerical Examples

### Example 13.1: Chi-Square Independence Test

**Problem:** We test whether gender (Male/Female) is independent of product preference (A/B/C) from a survey of $N=200$:

||A|B|C|Row Total|
|---|---|---|---|---|
|Male|40|35|25|100|
|Female|20|45|35|100|
|Col Total|60|80|60|200|

**Expected counts** (Eq. 13.3): $E_{ij} = R_i C_j / N$

$E_{M,A} = 100\cdot60/200 = 30$, $E_{M,B} = 40$, $E_{M,C} = 30$ $E_{F,A} = 30$, $E_{F,B} = 40$, $E_{F,C} = 30$

**Chi-square statistic** (Eq. 13.4): $$\chi^2 = \frac{(40-30)^2}{30} + \frac{(35-40)^2}{40} + \frac{(25-30)^2}{30} + \frac{(20-30)^2}{30} + \frac{(45-40)^2}{40} + \frac{(35-30)^2}{30}$$ $$= \frac{100}{30} + \frac{25}{40} + \frac{25}{30} + \frac{100}{30} + \frac{25}{40} + \frac{25}{30} = 3.333 + 0.625 + 0.833 + 3.333 + 0.625 + 0.833 = 9.583$$

**Degrees of freedom:** $(r-1)(c-1) = (2-1)(3-1) = 2$

**P-value:** $P(\chi^2_2 \geq 9.583) = 0.0083$

**Cramér's V:** $V = \sqrt{9.583/(200 \cdot 1)} = \sqrt{0.04792} = 0.219$

**Conclusion:** We reject independence at $\alpha=0.01$. Gender is significantly associated with product preference ($V=0.219$, moderate effect).

---

### Example 13.2: One-Way ANOVA — Optimizer Comparison

**Problem:** Three optimizers (SGD, Adam, AdamW) are each tested on 5 independent runs. Final validation accuracies:

- SGD: ${72, 74, 71, 73, 75}$, $\bar{y}_1 = 73.0$
- Adam: ${80, 82, 79, 83, 81}$, $\bar{y}_2 = 81.0$
- AdamW: ${84, 83, 85, 82, 86}$, $\bar{y}_3 = 84.0$

Grand mean: $\bar{y} = (73+81+84)/3 = 79.33$, $N = 15$, $K = 3$.

**SSB** (Eq. 13.8): $$\text{SSB} = 5(73-79.33)^2 + 5(81-79.33)^2 + 5(84-79.33)^2 = 5(40.09) + 5(2.79) + 5(21.79) = 323.33$$

**SSW:** $$\text{SSW} = (1+1+0+1+4) + (1+1+4+4+0) + (0+1+1+4+4) = 7 + 10 + 10 = 27$$

**F-statistic** (Eq. 13.10): $$\text{MSB} = 323.33/2 = 161.67,\quad \text{MSW} = 27/12 = 2.25$$ $$F = 161.67/2.25 = 71.85$$

**P-value:** $P(F_{2,12} \geq 71.85) \approx 2\times10^{-7}$

**$\eta^2$:** $\eta^2 = 323.33/(323.33+27) = 0.923$ — 92.3% of variance explained by optimizer choice.

**Conclusion:** Overwhelmingly significant. Perform Tukey HSD post-hoc to identify which pairs differ.

---

### Example 13.3: Bayesian Network Inference — Medical Diagnosis

**Network:** Three binary variables:

- $S$ = Smoking (prior: $P(S=1)=0.3$)
- $C$ = Cancer ($P(C=1\mid S=1)=0.05$, $P(C=1\mid S=0)=0.01$)
- $X$ = Positive X-ray ($P(X=1\mid C=1)=0.90$, $P(X=1\mid C=0)=0.08$)

DAG: $S \to C \to X$ (chain structure)

**Query:** $P(C=1 \mid X=1)$?

**Step 1:** $P(C=1) = P(C=1\mid S=1)P(S=1) + P(C=1\mid S=0)P(S=0) = 0.05(0.3)+0.01(0.7) = 0.022$

**Step 2:** $P(X=1) = P(X=1\mid C=1)P(C=1) + P(X=1\mid C=0)P(C=0)$ $= 0.90(0.022) + 0.08(0.978) = 0.0198 + 0.0782 = 0.098$

**Step 3:** Bayes' theorem (Eq. 13.18): $$P(C=1\mid X=1) = \frac{P(X=1\mid C=1)P(C=1)}{P(X=1)} = \frac{0.90\times0.022}{0.098} = \frac{0.0198}{0.098} \approx \boxed{0.202}$$

A positive X-ray raises cancer probability from 2.2% (prior) to 20.2% (posterior) — a 9× update. This is the same base-rate calculation as Module 1 (Example 1.1), now embedded in a graphical model.

---

## 13.4 Implementation

```python
import numpy as np
import scipy.stats as stats
import scipy.linalg as la
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.gridspec as gridspec
import itertools
from typing import Dict, List, Optional, Tuple

# =============================================================================
# MODULE 13: Advanced Statistical Inference
# =============================================================================

# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# PART A: Chi-Square Tests — Full Implementation
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------

class ChiSquareTests:
    """
    Complete chi-square testing toolkit.
    Covers goodness-of-fit (Eq. 13.2), independence (Eq. 13.4),
    effect size (Eq. 13.5), and information-theoretic interpretation (Eq. 13.6).
    """

    @staticmethod
    def goodness_of_fit(observed: np.ndarray,
                         expected_probs: Optional[np.ndarray] = None,
                         alpha: float = 0.05) -> dict:
        """
        Chi-square goodness-of-fit test. Eq. 13.2.

        Parameters
        ----------
        observed       : array of observed counts per category
        expected_probs : hypothesized probabilities (None = uniform)
        alpha          : significance level
        """
        observed = np.array(observed, dtype=float)
        n        = observed.sum()
        K        = len(observed)

        if expected_probs is None:
            expected_probs = np.ones(K) / K
        expected_probs = np.array(expected_probs)
        expected       = n * expected_probs

        if (expected < 5).any():
            print("  WARNING: Some expected counts < 5. Chi-square approximation may be poor.")

        # Test statistic (Eq. 13.2)
        chi2_stat = np.sum((observed - expected)**2 / expected)
        df        = K - 1
        p_value   = stats.chi2.sf(chi2_stat, df)

        return {
            'test':       'Chi-square goodness-of-fit',
            'chi2_stat':  chi2_stat,
            'df':         df,
            'p_value':    p_value,
            'reject_H0':  p_value < alpha,
            'observed':   observed,
            'expected':   expected,
            'residuals':  (observed - expected) / np.sqrt(expected),  # Pearson residuals
        }

    @staticmethod
    def independence(contingency_table: np.ndarray,
                     alpha: float = 0.05) -> dict:
        """
        Chi-square test of independence. Eq. 13.4.
        Also computes Cramér's V (Eq. 13.5) and G² (Eq. 13.6).

        Parameters
        ----------
        contingency_table : (r, c) array of observed counts O_{ij}
        """
        O   = np.array(contingency_table, dtype=float)
        N   = O.sum()
        r, c = O.shape

        # Expected counts (Eq. 13.3)
        row_sums = O.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)
        col_sums = O.sum(axis=0, keepdims=True)
        E        = row_sums @ col_sums / N

        if (E < 5).any():
            print("  WARNING: Some expected counts < 5. Consider Fisher's exact test.")

        # Chi-square statistic (Eq. 13.4)
        chi2_stat = float(np.sum((O - E)**2 / E))
        df        = (r - 1) * (c - 1)
        p_value   = stats.chi2.sf(chi2_stat, df)

        # Cramér's V effect size (Eq. 13.5)
        cramers_v = np.sqrt(chi2_stat / (N * min(r-1, c-1)))

        # G² statistic — information-theoretic version (Eq. 13.6)
        with np.errstate(divide='ignore', invalid='ignore'):
            log_ratio = np.where(O > 0, np.log(O / E), 0)
        g2_stat = float(2 * np.sum(O * log_ratio))

        # Mutual information estimate (Eq. 13.6: chi2 ≈ 2N * I(X;Y))
        mi_estimate = g2_stat / (2 * N)

        # Standardized residuals for interpretation
        std_residuals = (O - E) / np.sqrt(E * (1 - row_sums/N) * (1 - col_sums/N))

        return {
            'test':             'Chi-square independence',
            'chi2_stat':        chi2_stat,
            'g2_stat':          g2_stat,
            'df':               df,
            'p_value':          p_value,
            'reject_H0':        p_value < alpha,
            'cramers_v':        cramers_v,
            'effect_size':      'small' if cramers_v < 0.1 else
                                'medium' if cramers_v < 0.3 else 'large',
            'mi_estimate_nats': mi_estimate,
            'expected':         E,
            'std_residuals':    std_residuals,
        }

    @staticmethod
    def feature_importance_ranking(X: pd.DataFrame, y: pd.Series,
                                    n_bins: int = 5) -> pd.DataFrame:
        """
        Rank features by chi-square association with target.
        Discretizes continuous features automatically.
        Used in sklearn's SelectKBest with chi2 scorer.
        """
        results = []
        y_binned = pd.qcut(y, n_bins, duplicates='drop') if y.dtype != 'object' else y

        for col in X.columns:
            x = X[col]
            if x.dtype in [np.float64, np.float32, float]:
                x = pd.qcut(x, n_bins, duplicates='drop')

            ct   = pd.crosstab(x, y_binned)
            res  = ChiSquareTests.independence(ct.values)
            results.append({
                'feature':    col,
                'chi2':       res['chi2_stat'],
                'p_value':    res['p_value'],
                'cramers_v':  res['cramers_v'],
                'mi_nats':    res['mi_estimate_nats'],
                'significant': res['reject_H0'],
            })

        return pd.DataFrame(results).sort_values('chi2', ascending=False)

    @staticmethod
    def print_result(result: dict):
        print(f"\n  {'='*50}")
        print(f"  {result['test']}")
        print(f"  {'='*50}")
        print(f"  χ² statistic:  {result['chi2_stat']:.4f}")
        print(f"  Degrees of freedom: {result['df']}")
        print(f"  P-value:       {result['p_value']:.6f}")
        if 'cramers_v' in result:
            print(f"  Cramér's V:    {result['cramers_v']:.4f} ({result['effect_size']} effect)")
            print(f"  MI estimate:   {result['mi_estimate_nats']:.4f} nats")
        print(f"  Decision:      {'REJECT H₀' if result['reject_H0'] else 'FAIL TO REJECT H₀'}")


# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# PART B: ANOVA — Full Implementation with Post-Hoc Tests
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------

class ANOVA:
    """
    One-way and two-way ANOVA with Tukey HSD post-hoc tests.
    Implements Theorems 13.1 and 13.2.
    """

    @staticmethod
    def one_way(groups: List[np.ndarray], alpha: float = 0.05,
                group_names: Optional[List[str]] = None) -> dict:
        """
        One-way ANOVA. Theorem 13.2: F = MSB/MSW ~ F_{K-1, N-K}.
        """
        K       = len(groups)
        groups  = [np.asarray(g, dtype=float) for g in groups]
        ns      = [len(g) for g in groups]
        N       = sum(ns)
        means   = [g.mean() for g in groups]
        grand_mean = np.concatenate(groups).mean()

        # ANOVA decomposition (Eq. 13.8)
        SSB = sum(n*(m - grand_mean)**2 for n, m in zip(ns, means))
        SSW = sum(((g - m)**2).sum() for g, m in zip(groups, means))
        SST = SSB + SSW

        df_B = K - 1
        df_W = N - K
        MSB  = SSB / df_B
        MSW  = SSW / df_W

        # F-statistic (Eq. 13.10)
        F_stat  = MSB / MSW
        p_value = stats.f.sf(F_stat, df_B, df_W)

        # Effect size η² (Eq. 13.11)
        eta_sq = SSB / SST

        # Homoscedasticity test (Levene's)
        levene_stat, levene_p = stats.levene(*groups)

        result = {
            'F_stat':      F_stat,
            'df_between':  df_B,
            'df_within':   df_W,
            'p_value':     p_value,
            'reject_H0':   p_value < alpha,
            'MSB':         MSB, 'MSW': MSW,
            'SSB':         SSB, 'SSW': SSW, 'SST': SST,
            'eta_squared': eta_sq,
            'grand_mean':  grand_mean,
            'group_means': means,
            'group_ns':    ns,
            'levene_p':    levene_p,
            'group_names': group_names or [f'G{k+1}' for k in range(K)],
        }

        return result

    @staticmethod
    def tukey_hsd(groups: List[np.ndarray], alpha: float = 0.05,
                   group_names: Optional[List[str]] = None) -> pd.DataFrame:
        """
        Tukey's Honest Significant Difference post-hoc test.
        Eq. 13.12-13.13. Controls FWER at alpha across all pairwise comparisons.
        """
        K      = len(groups)
        groups = [np.asarray(g, dtype=float) for g in groups]
        ns     = [len(g) for g in groups]
        N      = sum(ns)
        names  = group_names or [f'G{k+1}' for k in range(K)]

        # MSW from one-way ANOVA
        grand_mean = np.concatenate(groups).mean()
        means      = [g.mean() for g in groups]
        SSW        = sum(((g - m)**2).sum() for g, m in zip(groups, means))
        MSW        = SSW / (N - K)

        rows = []
        for (i, j) in itertools.combinations(range(K), 2):
            diff     = abs(means[i] - means[j])
            n_harm   = 2 / (1/ns[i] + 1/ns[j])   # harmonic mean of ns
            se       = np.sqrt(MSW / n_harm)
            q_stat   = diff / se
            # Studentized range distribution
            p_val    = 1 - stats.studentized_range.cdf(q_stat, K, N-K)
            hsd      = stats.studentized_range.ppf(1-alpha, K, N-K) * se

            rows.append({
                'Group 1':     names[i],
                'Group 2':     names[j],
                'Mean diff':   round(means[i] - means[j], 4),
                '|Mean diff|': round(diff, 4),
                'HSD':         round(hsd, 4),
                'q_stat':      round(q_stat, 4),
                'p_value':     round(p_val, 6),
                'Significant': diff > hsd,
            })

        return pd.DataFrame(rows)

    @staticmethod
    def print_anova_table(result: dict):
        print(f"\n  {'='*60}")
        print(f"  ONE-WAY ANOVA TABLE")
        print(f"  {'='*60}")
        print(f"  {'Source':<20} {'SS':>10} {'df':>6} {'MS':>10} {'F':>10}")
        print(f"  {'-'*58}")
        print(f"  {'Between (groups)':<20} {result['SSB']:>10.4f} "
              f"{result['df_between']:>6} {result['MSB']:>10.4f} {result['F_stat']:>10.4f}")
        print(f"  {'Within (error)':<20} {result['SSW']:>10.4f} "
              f"{result['df_within']:>6} {result['MSW']:>10.4f}")
        print(f"  {'Total':<20} {result['SST']:>10.4f} "
              f"{result['df_between']+result['df_within']:>6}")
        print(f"\n  F({result['df_between']},{result['df_within']}) = {result['F_stat']:.4f}, "
              f"p = {result['p_value']:.6f}")
        print(f"  η² = {result['eta_squared']:.4f}  "
              f"({'large' if result['eta_squared']>0.14 else 'medium' if result['eta_squared']>0.06 else 'small'} effect)")
        print(f"  Decision: {'REJECT H₀' if result['reject_H0'] else 'FAIL TO REJECT H₀'}")
        print(f"  Levene homoscedasticity p = {result['levene_p']:.4f} "
              f"({'ok' if result['levene_p']>0.05 else 'WARNING: unequal variances'})")
        print(f"  {'='*60}")


# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# PART C: Bayesian Network
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------

class BayesianNetwork:
    """
    Discrete Bayesian Network with exact inference via variable elimination.
    Supports structure definition, CPD specification, forward sampling,
    and posterior query (Eq. 13.18).
    """

    def __init__(self):
        self.nodes    = {}    # node_name -> {'parents': [], 'states': [], 'cpd': array}
        self.ordering = []    # topological order

    def add_node(self, name: str, states: List,
                  parents: List[str], cpd: np.ndarray):
        """
        Add a node with its CPD.

        cpd shape: (n_states, *[n_states_parent_1, ..., n_states_parent_k])
        For root nodes (no parents): cpd shape = (n_states,)
        """
        self.nodes[name] = {
            'parents': parents,
            'states':  states,
            'cpd':     np.array(cpd, dtype=float),
        }

    def _topological_sort(self) -> List[str]:
        """Kahn's algorithm for topological ordering."""
        in_degree = {n: 0 for n in self.nodes}
        children  = {n: [] for n in self.nodes}
        for n, data in self.nodes.items():
            for p in data['parents']:
                in_degree[n] += 1
                children[p].append(n)

        queue  = [n for n, d in in_degree.items() if d == 0]
        result = []
        while queue:
            n = queue.pop(0)
            result.append(n)
            for c in children[n]:
                in_degree[c] -= 1
                if in_degree[c] == 0:
                    queue.append(c)
        return result

    def sample(self, n_samples: int = 1000, seed: int = 42) -> pd.DataFrame:
        """
        Forward sampling from the joint distribution (Eq. 13.17).
        Samples each node conditioned on its parents in topological order.
        """
        rng    = np.random.default_rng(seed)
        order  = self._topological_sort()
        data   = {n: [] for n in self.nodes}

        for _ in range(n_samples):
            sample = {}
            for n in order:
                node  = self.nodes[n]
                cpd   = node['cpd']
                pars  = node['parents']

                if not pars:
                    probs = cpd
                else:
                    # Index into CPD using parent values
                    idx   = tuple(node['states'].index(sample[p])
                                   if hasattr(node['states'], 'index')
                                   else list(self.nodes[p]['states']).index(sample[p])
                                   for p in pars)
                    probs = cpd[(slice(None),) + idx]

                probs   = probs / probs.sum()
                chosen  = rng.choice(len(node['states']), p=probs)
                sample[n] = node['states'][chosen]

            for n in self.nodes:
                data[n].append(sample[n])

        return pd.DataFrame(data)

    def query(self, query_var: str, evidence: Dict) -> Dict:
        """
        Exact posterior inference via enumeration. Eq. 13.18.
        Returns P(query_var | evidence).

        Parameters
        ----------
        query_var : the variable to query
        evidence  : dict of {variable_name: observed_value}
        """
        order   = self._topological_sort()
        q_node  = self.nodes[query_var]
        result  = {}

        for q_val in q_node['states']:
            # Compute joint probability of query value + evidence
            full_evidence = dict(evidence)
            full_evidence[query_var] = q_val
            prob = self._joint_probability(full_evidence, order)
            result[q_val] = prob

        # Normalize
        total = sum(result.values())
        return {k: v/total for k, v in result.items()}

    def _joint_probability(self, assignment: Dict, order: List[str]) -> float:
        """Compute P(assignment) = prod_i P(X_i | Pa(X_i))."""
        prob = 1.0
        for n in order:
            if n not in assignment:
                continue
            node = self.nodes[n]
            val  = assignment[n]
            val_idx = list(node['states']).index(val)
            cpd = node['cpd']

            if not node['parents']:
                prob *= cpd[val_idx]
            else:
                par_idxs = tuple(
                    list(self.nodes[p]['states']).index(assignment[p])
                    for p in node['parents']
                    if p in assignment
                )
                if len(par_idxs) == len(node['parents']):
                    prob *= cpd[(val_idx,) + par_idxs]
        return prob

    def marginals(self, n_samples: int = 50_000, seed: int = 42) -> Dict:
        """Estimate marginal distributions via forward sampling."""
        df    = self.sample(n_samples, seed=seed)
        margs = {}
        for n in self.nodes:
            margs[n] = df[n].value_counts(normalize=True).to_dict()
        return margs


# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# PART D: Full Visualization Suite
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def full_visualization(seed: int = 42):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    fig = plt.figure(figsize=(18, 12))
    gs  = gridspec.GridSpec(3, 3, wspace=0.38, hspace=0.48)

    # ---- Panel 1: Chi-square GOF visualization ----
    ax = fig.add_subplot(gs[0, 0])
    observed = np.array([52, 38, 56, 34, 20])   # die rolls
    expected = np.full(5, 200/5)
    cats     = ['A','B','C','D','E']
    res_gof  = ChiSquareTests.goodness_of_fit(observed, alpha=0.05)

    x = np.arange(5)
    ax.bar(x-0.2, observed, 0.35, color='#1a6faf', alpha=0.8, label='Observed')
    ax.bar(x+0.2, expected, 0.35, color='#e84040', alpha=0.6, label='Expected (uniform)')
    ax.set_xticks(x); ax.set_xticklabels(cats)
    ax.set_title(f"Goodness-of-Fit Test\nχ²={res_gof['chi2_stat']:.2f}, "
                 f"p={res_gof['p_value']:.3f}, {'REJECT' if res_gof['reject_H0'] else 'ACCEPT'} H₀",
                 fontsize=10, fontweight='bold')
    ax.legend(fontsize=9); ax.grid(axis='y', alpha=0.3)

    # ---- Panel 2: Chi-square independence heatmaps ----
    ax = fig.add_subplot(gs[0, 1])
    # Example contingency table (Eq. 13.4)
    ct = np.array([[40,35,25],[20,45,35]])
    res_ind = ChiSquareTests.independence(ct, alpha=0.05)
    im = ax.imshow(res_ind['std_residuals'], cmap='RdBu', vmin=-3, vmax=3)
    plt.colorbar(im, ax=ax, label='Standardized residual')
    ax.set_xticks([0,1,2]); ax.set_xticklabels(['Pref A','Pref B','Pref C'])
    ax.set_yticks([0,1]); ax.set_yticklabels(['Male','Female'])
    for i in range(2):
        for j in range(3):
            ax.text(j, i, f"O={int(ct[i,j])}\nE={res_ind['expected'][i,j]:.0f}",
                    ha='center', va='center', fontsize=9)
    ax.set_title(f"Independence Test\nχ²={res_ind['chi2_stat']:.2f}, "
                 f"V={res_ind['cramers_v']:.3f}, p={res_ind['p_value']:.3f}",
                 fontsize=10, fontweight='bold')

    # ---- Panel 3: Chi-square distribution ----
    ax   = fig.add_subplot(gs[0, 2])
    x_ch = np.linspace(0, 20, 300)
    for df_val, col, ls in [(1,'#1a6faf','-'),(2,'#e84040','--'),(4,'#2ca02c',':'),(8,'#9467bd','-.')]:
        ax.plot(x_ch, stats.chi2.pdf(x_ch, df_val), lw=2.5, color=col,
                linestyle=ls, label=f'df={df_val}')
    ax.set_title("χ² Distribution\n(Foundation of chi-square tests)",
                 fontsize=10, fontweight='bold')
    ax.set_xlabel("x"); ax.set_ylabel("PDF"); ax.set_ylim(0, 0.5)
    ax.legend(fontsize=9); ax.grid(alpha=0.3)

    # ---- Panel 4: ANOVA visualization ----
    ax = fig.add_subplot(gs[1, :2])
    # Optimizer comparison data (Example 13.2)
    groups_data = [
        np.array([72., 74., 71., 73., 75.]),
        np.array([80., 82., 79., 83., 81.]),
        np.array([84., 83., 85., 82., 86.]),
    ]
    names_g = ['SGD', 'Adam', 'AdamW']
    res_anova = ANOVA.one_way(groups_data, group_names=names_g)

    # Violin + strip plot
    vp = ax.violinplot(groups_data, positions=[1,2,3], showmeans=True, showmedians=True)
    for i, (body, col) in enumerate(zip(vp['bodies'], ['#1a6faf','#e84040','#2ca02c'])):
        body.set_facecolor(col); body.set_alpha(0.6)
    for i, (g, col) in enumerate(zip(groups_data, ['#1a6faf','#e84040','#2ca02c'])):
        jitter = rng.uniform(-0.08, 0.08, len(g))
        ax.scatter([i+1+j for j in jitter], g, color=col, s=40, zorder=4, alpha=0.8)
    ax.axhline(res_anova['grand_mean'], color='black', lw=1.5, linestyle='--',
               label=f"Grand mean={res_anova['grand_mean']:.1f}")
    ax.set_xticks([1,2,3]); ax.set_xticklabels(names_g)
    ax.set_title(f"One-Way ANOVA: Optimizer Comparison\n"
                 f"F({res_anova['df_between']},{res_anova['df_within']})={res_anova['F_stat']:.2f}, "
                 f"p={res_anova['p_value']:.2e}, η²={res_anova['eta_squared']:.3f}",
                 fontsize=11, fontweight='bold')
    ax.set_ylabel("Validation Accuracy (%)"); ax.legend(fontsize=9); ax.grid(axis='y', alpha=0.3)

    # ---- Panel 5: Tukey HSD ----
    ax = fig.add_subplot(gs[1, 2])
    tukey_df = ANOVA.tukey_hsd(groups_data, group_names=names_g)
    pairs  = [f"{r['Group 1']} vs {r['Group 2']}" for _, r in tukey_df.iterrows()]
    diffs  = tukey_df['Mean diff'].values
    colors_t = ['#e84040' if s else '#2ca02c' for s in tukey_df['Significant']]
    ax.barh(pairs, diffs, color=colors_t, alpha=0.8)
    ax.axvline(0, color='black', lw=1)
    ax.set_title("Tukey HSD Post-Hoc Test\n(Red=significant, Green=n.s.)",
                 fontsize=10, fontweight='bold')
    ax.set_xlabel("Mean difference"); ax.grid(axis='x', alpha=0.3)

    # ---- Panel 6-8: Bayesian Network ----
    # Build the medical diagnosis BN (Example 13.3)
    bn = BayesianNetwork()
    bn.add_node('Smoking', [0,1], [], np.array([0.7, 0.3]))
    bn.add_node('Cancer',  [0,1], ['Smoking'],
                np.array([[0.99, 0.95],[0.01, 0.05]]))  # P(C|S): rows=cancer states, cols=smoking
    bn.add_node('XRay',    [0,1], ['Cancer'],
                np.array([[0.92, 0.10],[0.08, 0.90]]))   # P(X|C)

    # Sample and compute posteriors
    samples  = bn.sample(n_samples=50_000, seed=seed)
    marginals = bn.marginals(seed=seed)

    # Panel 6: DAG structure visualization
    ax = fig.add_subplot(gs[2, 0])
    ax.set_xlim(0, 4); ax.set_ylim(0, 4); ax.axis('off')
    node_pos = {'Smoking': (2,3.2), 'Cancer': (2,2), 'XRay': (2,0.8)}
    node_colors = {'Smoking':'#1a6faf','Cancer':'#e84040','XRay':'#2ca02c'}
    for name, (x,y) in node_pos.items():
        circle = plt.Circle((x,y), 0.45, color=node_colors[name], alpha=0.8)
        ax.add_patch(circle)
        ax.text(x, y, name, ha='center', va='center', fontsize=11,
                fontweight='bold', color='white')
        m = marginals[name]
        ax.text(x+0.7, y, f"P(+)={m.get(1,0):.3f}", fontsize=8, va='center')
    # Draw edges
    for (u,v) in [('Smoking','Cancer'),('Cancer','XRay')]:
        ax.annotate("", xy=node_pos[v], xytext=node_pos[u],
                    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle='->', lw=2, color='black'))
    ax.set_title("Bayesian Network (DAG)\nSmoking→Cancer→XRay",
                 fontsize=10, fontweight='bold')

    # Panel 7: Posterior updates
    ax  = fig.add_subplot(gs[2, 1])
    queries = [
        ('No evidence', {}),
        ('XRay=+',      {'XRay': 1}),
        ('XRay=+,\nSmoke=+', {'XRay': 1, 'Smoking': 1}),
        ('XRay=-',      {'XRay': 0}),
    ]
    posteriors_cancer = []
    for label, evi in queries:
        res = bn.query('Cancer', evi)
        posteriors_cancer.append(res.get(1, 0))

    colors_q = ['#888','#e84040','#9467bd','#1a6faf']
    bars = ax.bar([q[0] for q in queries], posteriors_cancer, color=colors_q, alpha=0.8)
    for bar, val in zip(bars, posteriors_cancer):
        ax.text(bar.get_x()+bar.get_width()/2, bar.get_height()+0.005,
                f'{val:.3f}', ha='center', fontsize=9)
    ax.axhline(posteriors_cancer[0], color='gray', lw=1.5, linestyle='--',
               label=f'Prior P(C)={posteriors_cancer[0]:.3f}')
    ax.set_title("P(Cancer=1 | Evidence)\nBayesian Belief Updating",
                 fontsize=10, fontweight='bold')
    ax.set_ylabel("P(Cancer=1)"); ax.legend(fontsize=8)
    ax.set_ylim(0, 0.35); ax.grid(axis='y', alpha=0.3)
    ax.tick_params(axis='x', labelsize=8)

    # Panel 8: d-Separation illustration
    ax = fig.add_subplot(gs[2, 2])
    ax.set_xlim(0, 5); ax.set_ylim(0, 4); ax.axis('off')
    ax.set_title("d-Separation Structures\n(Chain, Fork, Collider)",
                 fontsize=10, fontweight='bold')

    structures = [
        ('Chain', [(1,3.3),(2.5,3.3),(4,3.3)], [('A','B'),('B','C')], 'A⊥C|B'),
        ('Fork',  [(1,2),(2.5,2),(4,2)],         [('B','A'),('B','C')], 'A⊥C|B'),
        ('Collider',[(1,0.7),(2.5,0.7),(4,0.7)], [('A','B'),('C','B')], 'A⊥C (not given B!)'),
    ]
    cols_s = ['#1a6faf','#e84040','#2ca02c']
    for (stype, positions, edges, caption), col in zip(structures, cols_s):
        node_names = ['A','B','C']
        ax.text(positions[0][0]-0.3, positions[0][1]+0.2, stype, fontsize=9,
                fontweight='bold', color=col)
        for (nx,ny), nn in zip(positions, node_names):
            c = plt.Circle((nx,ny), 0.25, color=col, alpha=0.7)
            ax.add_patch(c)
            ax.text(nx,ny,nn,ha='center',va='center',fontsize=10,fontweight='bold',color='white')
        for (u,v) in edges:
            ui = node_names.index(u); vi = node_names.index(v)
            ax.annotate("", xy=positions[vi], xytext=positions[ui],
                        arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle='->', lw=1.5, color='black'))
        ax.text(2.5, positions[0][1]-0.38, caption, ha='center', fontsize=8, color=col,
                style='italic')

    plt.suptitle("Module 13: Chi-Square Tests, ANOVA & Bayesian Networks",
                 fontsize=14, fontweight='bold', y=1.01)
    plt.savefig("module13_full.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches='tight')
    plt.show()
    print("Saved: module13_full.png")

    # --- A: Chi-square tests ---
    print("=" * 60)
    print("  CHI-SQUARE TESTS")
    print("=" * 60)

    ct_test = ChiSquareTests()

    # GOF test: is a die fair?
    gof = ct_test.goodness_of_fit([18, 22, 16, 20, 14, 10], alpha=0.05)
    ct_test.print_result(gof)

    # Independence: gender vs preference (Example 13.1)
    ct_table = np.array([[40,35,25],[20,45,35]])
    ind = ct_test.independence(ct_table, alpha=0.05)
    ct_test.print_result(ind)
    print(f"\n  Standardized residuals:\n{ind['std_residuals'].round(3)}")

    # --- B: ANOVA ---
    print("\n" + "=" * 60)
    print("  ONE-WAY ANOVA")
    print("=" * 60)
    groups_data = [
        np.array([72., 74., 71., 73., 75.]),
        np.array([80., 82., 79., 83., 81.]),
        np.array([84., 83., 85., 82., 86.]),
    ]
    anova = ANOVA()
    result_anova = anova.one_way(groups_data, group_names=['SGD','Adam','AdamW'])
    ANOVA.print_anova_table(result_anova)

    tukey = anova.tukey_hsd(groups_data, group_names=['SGD','Adam','AdamW'])
    print("\n  TUKEY HSD POST-HOC:")
    print(tukey.to_string(index=False))

    # --- C: Bayesian Network ---
    print("\n" + "=" * 60)
    print("  BAYESIAN NETWORK: MEDICAL DIAGNOSIS")
    print("=" * 60)
    bn = BayesianNetwork()
    bn.add_node('Smoking', [0,1], [], np.array([0.7, 0.3]))
    bn.add_node('Cancer',  [0,1], ['Smoking'],
                np.array([[0.99, 0.95],[0.01, 0.05]]))
    bn.add_node('XRay',    [0,1], ['Cancer'],
                np.array([[0.92, 0.10],[0.08, 0.90]]))

    print("\n  Posterior P(Cancer=1 | evidence):")
    for label, evidence in [
        ("No evidence",          {}),
        ("XRay=Positive",        {'XRay': 1}),
        ("XRay=Positive, Smoke", {'XRay': 1, 'Smoking': 1}),
        ("XRay=Negative",        {'XRay': 0}),
    ]:
        post = bn.query('Cancer', evidence)
        print(f"  {label:<30} P(C=1) = {post.get(1,0):.4f}")

    # --- D: Full visualization ---
    full_visualization()
```

---

## 13.5 Interactive Statistical Testing ExplorerThree tabs for direct exploration. In **Chi-Square**: increase sample size and watch p-values collapse toward zero even for weak associations — illustrating the distinction between statistical and practical significance. In **ANOVA**: pull the group means apart and watch the F-statistic soar while η² tells you the effect size story independently. In **Bayesian Network**: adjust the disease prevalence and test sensitivity to reproduce the base-rate paradox from Module 1 inside a graphical model.

## 13.6 Module Summary

|Concept|Key Formula|ML Application|
|---|---|---|
|Chi-square GOF|$\chi^2 = \sum(O-E)^2/E \sim \chi^2_{K-1}$|Model calibration, distribution testing|
|Chi-square independence|$\chi^2 \sim \chi^2_{(r-1)(c-1)}$|Feature selection, association mining|
|Cramér's V|$V = \sqrt{\chi^2/(N\cdot\min(r-1,c-1))}$|Categorical effect size|
|MI–chi-square link|$\chi^2 \approx 2N\cdot I(X;Y)$|Information-theoretic feature selection|
|ANOVA decomposition|SST = SSB + SSW|Variance attribution|
|F-statistic|$F = \text{MSB}/\text{MSW} \sim F_{K-1,N-K}$|Multi-group comparison|
|Eta-squared|$\eta^2 = \text{SSB}/\text{SST}$|Explained variance by group|
|Tukey HSD|Controls FWER across all pairs|Post-hoc pairwise comparison|
|BN factorization|$P(\mathbf{X}) = \prod_i P(X_i\mid\text{Pa}(X_i))$|Probabilistic inference|
|d-separation|Blocks information flow in DAG|Conditional independence|
|Naive Bayes|Star DAG: $Y \to X_1,\ldots,X_d$|Efficient classification|
|BIC structure learning|$\ell - \frac{d}{2}\log N$|Graph selection|

## 13.7 Key Equations Reference Card

$$\chi^2 = \sum_{i,j}\frac{(O_{ij}-E_{ij})^2}{E_{ij}},\quad E_{ij}=\frac{R_i C_j}{N} \tag{Independence test}$$ $$df = (r-1)(c-1),\quad V=\sqrt{\chi^2/(N\cdot\min(r-1,c-1))} \tag{df and effect size}$$ $$\chi^2 \approx 2N\cdot I(X;Y) \tag{MI equivalence}$$ $$\text{SST}=\text{SSB}+\text{SSW},\quad F=\frac{\text{SSB}/(K-1)}{\text{SSW}/(N-K)}\sim F_{K-1,N-K} \tag{ANOVA}$$ $$\eta^2 = \text{SSB}/\text{SST} \tag{Effect size}$$ $$P(X_1,\ldots,X_d)=\prod_i P(X_i\mid\text{Pa}(X_i)) \tag{BN factorization}$$ $$\hat{P}(X_i=k\mid\mathbf{pa})=N_{ik\mathbf{pa}}/N_{i\mathbf{pa}} \tag{CPD MLE}$$
