```python
def full_visualization(seed: int = 42):
    """Comprehensive visualization of all clustering and anomaly detection algorithms."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    fig = plt.figure(figsize=(18, 14))
    gs  = gridspec.GridSpec(3, 4, wspace=0.38, hspace=0.48)

    # ---- Generate diverse datasets ----
    # Dataset 1: Blobs (K-Means friendly)
    from sklearn.datasets import make_blobs, make_moons, make_circles
    X_blobs, y_blobs = make_blobs(n_samples=200, centers=3,
                                   cluster_std=0.8, random_state=42)
    # Dataset 2: Moons (DBSCAN friendly)
    X_moons, y_moons = make_moons(n_samples=200, noise=0.08, random_state=42)
    # Dataset 3: Circles (DBSCAN)
    X_circ, y_circ   = make_circles(n_samples=200, noise=0.05, factor=0.5, random_state=42)
    # Anomaly dataset: Gaussian + outliers
    X_norm = rng.normal(0, 1, (200, 2))
    X_anom = rng.uniform(-6, 6, (20, 2))
    X_all  = np.vstack([X_norm, X_anom])
    y_all  = np.array([1]*200 + [-1]*20)

    # ---- Panel 1: K-Means on blobs ----
    ax = fig.add_subplot(gs[0, 0])
    km = KMeans(K=3, n_init=10, seed=42).fit(X_blobs)
    colors_km = ['#1a6faf','#e84040','#2ca02c']
    for k, col in enumerate(colors_km):
        mask = km.labels_ == k
        ax.scatter(X_blobs[mask,0], X_blobs[mask,1], s=15, alpha=0.7, color=col)
        ax.scatter(*km.centroids_[k], s=200, marker='*', color=col,
                   edgecolors='black', lw=1.5, zorder=5)
    sil = km.silhouette_score(X_blobs)
    ax.set_title(f"K-Means (K=3)\nWCSS={km.inertia_:.1f}, Sil={sil:.3f}",
                 fontsize=10, fontweight='bold')
    ax.grid(alpha=0.3)

    # ---- Panel 2: K-Means on moons (failure case) ----
    ax = fig.add_subplot(gs[0, 1])
    km2 = KMeans(K=2, n_init=10, seed=42).fit(X_moons)
    for k, col in enumerate(['#1a6faf','#e84040']):
        mask = km2.labels_ == k
        ax.scatter(X_moons[mask,0], X_moons[mask,1], s=15, alpha=0.7, color=col)
    ax.set_title("K-Means on Moons\n(Fails: assumes convex clusters)",
                 fontsize=10, fontweight='bold')
    ax.grid(alpha=0.3)

    # ---- Panel 3: DBSCAN on moons (success) ----
    ax = fig.add_subplot(gs[0, 2])
    db = DBSCAN(eps=0.3, min_pts=5).fit(X_moons)
    colors_db = {0:'#1a6faf', 1:'#e84040', -1:'black'}
    for label, col in colors_db.items():
        mask = db.labels_ == label
        if mask.sum() > 0:
            ax.scatter(X_moons[mask,0], X_moons[mask,1], s=15, alpha=0.8,
                       color=col, marker='o' if label >= 0 else 'x')
    ax.set_title(f"DBSCAN on Moons\n(ε=0.3, MinPts=5): {db.n_clusters_} clusters, "
                 f"{db.n_noise_} noise",
                 fontsize=10, fontweight='bold')
    ax.grid(alpha=0.3)

    # ---- Panel 4: DBSCAN on circles ----
    ax = fig.add_subplot(gs[0, 3])
    db2 = DBSCAN(eps=0.15, min_pts=5).fit(X_circ)
    for label in np.unique(db2.labels_):
        mask = db2.labels_ == label
        col  = '#1a6faf' if label == 0 else '#e84040' if label == 1 else 'black'
        ax.scatter(X_circ[mask,0], X_circ[mask,1], s=15, alpha=0.8, color=col)
    ax.set_title(f"DBSCAN on Circles\n({db2.n_clusters_} clusters, arbitrary shape)",
                 fontsize=10, fontweight='bold')
    ax.grid(alpha=0.3)

    # ---- Panel 5: K selection (elbow + silhouette) ----
    ax = fig.add_subplot(gs[1, :2])
    k_range = list(range(2, 9))
    opt_k   = KMeans.optimal_k(X_blobs, k_range, seed=42)
    ax.plot(k_range, opt_k['wcss'], 'o-', color='#1a6faf', lw=2.5, ms=6,
            label='WCSS (elbow)')
    ax.set_xlabel("Number of clusters K", fontsize=11)
    ax.set_ylabel("WCSS", color='#1a6faf', fontsize=11)
    ax2 = ax.twinx()
    ax2.plot(k_range, opt_k['silhouette'], 's--', color='#e84040', lw=2.5, ms=6,
             label='Silhouette (Eq. 18.7)')
    ax2.set_ylabel("Silhouette score", color='#e84040', fontsize=11)
    ax.set_title("Optimal K Selection: Elbow + Silhouette\n(Both agree: K=3 optimal)",
                 fontsize=11, fontweight='bold')
    ax.legend(loc='upper right', fontsize=9)
    ax2.legend(loc='center right', fontsize=9)
    ax.grid(alpha=0.3)

    # ---- Panel 6: Hierarchical clustering dendrogram ----
    ax = fig.add_subplot(gs[1, 2:])
    # Use small subset for dendrogram clarity
    X_small = X_blobs[:30]
    Z = sch.linkage(X_small, method='ward')
    sch.dendrogram(Z, ax=ax, color_threshold=8,
                   above_threshold_color='gray', leaf_rotation=90, leaf_font_size=7)
    ax.axhline(8, color='#e84040', lw=2, linestyle='--', label='Cut → 3 clusters')
    ax.set_title("Hierarchical Clustering Dendrogram\n(Ward linkage, Eq. 18.11)",
                 fontsize=10, fontweight='bold')
    ax.set_ylabel("Merge distance"); ax.legend(fontsize=9)

    # ---- Panels 7-8: Isolation Forest ----
    ax = fig.add_subplot(gs[2, :2])
    ifo = IsolationForest(n_trees=100, sample_size=64,
                           contamination=0.09, seed=42)
    ifo.fit(X_all)
    scores = ifo.score_samples(X_all)
    preds  = ifo.predict(X_all)

    # Scatter with anomaly scores as color
    sc_plot = ax.scatter(X_all[:,0], X_all[:,1], c=scores,
                          cmap='RdYlGn_r', s=20, vmin=0.3, vmax=0.8)
    plt.colorbar(sc_plot, ax=ax, label='Anomaly score (1=most anomalous)')

    # Mark detected anomalies
    anom_mask = preds == -1
    ax.scatter(X_all[anom_mask,0], X_all[anom_mask,1], s=80, facecolors='none',
               edgecolors='red', lw=2, label=f'Detected anomalies ({anom_mask.sum()})')

    # True anomalies
    true_anom = y_all == -1
    ax.scatter(X_all[true_anom,0], X_all[true_anom,1], s=15,
               color='red', alpha=0.4, label=f'True anomalies ({true_anom.sum()})')
    ax.set_title("Isolation Forest Anomaly Detection\n(Eq. 18.14: score=2^{-path/c(n)})",
                 fontsize=11, fontweight='bold')
    ax.legend(fontsize=8); ax.grid(alpha=0.3)

    # ---- Panel 9: Score distribution ----
    ax = fig.add_subplot(gs[2, 2:])
    ax.hist(scores[y_all==1],  bins=30, alpha=0.7, color='#1a6faf',
            density=True, label='Normal (y=1)')
    ax.hist(scores[y_all==-1], bins=10, alpha=0.7, color='#e84040',
            density=True, label='Anomaly (y=-1)')
    ax.axvline(ifo.threshold_, color='black', lw=2, linestyle='--',
               label=f'Threshold={ifo.threshold_:.3f}')
    ax.set_xlabel("Anomaly score"); ax.set_ylabel("Density")
    ax.set_title("Anomaly Score Distribution\n(Normal vs Anomaly — clear separation)",
                 fontsize=11, fontweight='bold')
    ax.legend(fontsize=9); ax.grid(alpha=0.3)

    plt.suptitle("Module 18: Clustering & Anomaly Detection",
                 fontsize=14, fontweight='bold', y=1.01)
    plt.savefig("module18_full.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches='tight')
    plt.show()
    print("Saved: module18_full.png")

    print(f"\n  True anomalies:    15")
    print(f"  Detected:          {(preds==-1).sum()}")
    print(f"  TP={tp}, FP={fp}, FN={fn}, TN={tn}")
    print(f"  Precision:         {tp/(tp+fp+1e-8):.4f}")
    print(f"  Recall:            {tp/(tp+fn+1e-8):.4f}")
    print(f"  Mean score normal: {scores[:300].mean():.4f}")
    print(f"  Mean score anom:   {scores[300:].mean():.4f}")

    # --- Full visualization ---
```

|Algorithm|Cluster Shape|Requires K|Handles Noise|Complexity|Best For|
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
|K-Means|Convex, spherical|Yes|No (pulls toward center)|$O(nKdT)$|Large datasets, spherical clusters|
|GMM|Elliptical|Yes|Soft (low weight)|$O(nKd^2T)$|Overlapping, elliptical clusters|
|DBSCAN|Arbitrary|No|Yes (label -1)|$O(n\log n)$|Arbitrary shape, known density|
|Hierarchical|Arbitrary|No (post-hoc)|Limited|$O(n^2\log n)$|Unknown K, hierarchical structure|
|Isolation Forest|N/A (anomaly)|N/A|N/A|$O(nT\psi)$|High-dimensional anomalies|
|One-Class SVM|N/A (anomaly)|N/A|N/A|$O(n^2d)$|Nonlinear support estimation|

## 18.7 Key Equations Reference Card

$$\mathcal{L} = \sum_{k=1}^K\sum_{\mathbf{x}_i\in C_k}|\mathbf{x}_i-\boldsymbol\mu_k|^2 \tag{K-Means WCSS}$$ $$z_i = \arg\min_k|\mathbf{x}_i-\boldsymbol\mu_k|^2,\quad \boldsymbol\mu_k = \frac{1}{|C_k|}\sum_{i\in C_k}\mathbf{x}_i \tag{Lloyd's steps}$$ $$s_i = \frac{b_i-a_i}{\max(a_i,b_i)} \tag{Silhouette}$$ $$d_{\text{Ward}} = \frac{|C_i||C_j|}{|C_i|+|C_j|}|\boldsymbol\mu_i-\boldsymbol\mu_j|^2 \tag{Ward linkage}$$ $$s(\mathbf{x},n) = 2^{-\mathbb{E}[\ell(\mathbf{x})]/c(n)} \tag{Isolation Forest score}$$ $$c(n) = 2H(n-1) - 2(n-1)/n \tag{Expected path length}$$ $$\text{NMI} = 2I(\text{clusters};\text{labels})/(H_\text{clusters}+H_\text{labels}) \tag{Cluster validation}$$

# MODULE 19: Dimensionality Reduction — t-SNE & UMAP

### _From the Crowding Problem to Riemannian Geometry_

---

## 19.1 Conceptual Overview

### The Visualization Problem

Modern datasets live in thousands of dimensions. A single gene expression profile is 20,000-dimensional; a word embedding is 768-dimensional; an image patch is 50,000-dimensional. Human visual systems process two or three dimensions. The challenge of dimensionality reduction for visualization is to find a 2D or 3D representation that faithfully preserves the structure of the high-dimensional data.

PCA (Module 9) solves this problem for **linear** structure — it finds the 2D projection that preserves the maximum variance. But the most interesting structure in real data is almost never linear. Cell types in single-cell RNA sequencing form branching trajectories. Word embeddings cluster by semantic category with nonlinear boundaries. MNIST digits form curved manifolds in pixel space.

**t-SNE** and **UMAP** are nonlinear dimensionality reduction methods that preserve **local structure** — the neighborhood relationships between nearby points — rather than global variance. They produce visualizations where similar points cluster together regardless of whether that similarity is captured by a linear projection.

### The Fundamental Tradeoff

Both algorithms face the same fundamental tension:

**Preserving local structure** (nearby points remain nearby) conflicts with **preserving global structure** (the relative positions of distant clusters). You cannot perfectly do both in fewer dimensions — this is a mathematical consequence of the Whitney embedding theorem and the curse of dimensionality.

t-SNE prioritizes local structure almost exclusively. It produces beautiful, well-separated local clusters but distorts global distances — the relative positions of clusters carry no meaning. UMAP makes a better tradeoff, preserving both local and global structure more faithfully, and runs significantly faster.

---

## 19.2 Mathematical Formalization

### 19.2.1 The Crowding Problem — Why Linear Methods Fail

**Setup:** The data lies on a manifold $\mathcal{M}$ of intrinsic dimension $m$ embedded in ambient space $\mathbb{R}^D$. We want to represent it in $\mathbb{R}^d$ with $d \ll D$, ideally $d = 2$ or $3$.

**The crowding problem** (van der Maaten & Hinton, 2008): In the high-dimensional space, a point has many more neighbors than in the low-dimensional space. Specifically, the volume of a ball of radius $r$ scales as $r^D$ in $\mathbb{R}^D$ but only $r^d$ in $\mathbb{R}^d$. When $D \gg d$, there is dramatically more room in high dimensions — points that should be moderately far apart in high dimensions cannot all be simultaneously far apart in the 2D map without crowding into the center.

**Quantitative statement:** If a point has $K$ nearest neighbors in $\mathbb{R}^D$ that are roughly equidistant at distance $r$, then in $\mathbb{R}^2$ those same $K$ points cannot all be at distance $r$ — many must be closer. The 2D representation cannot accommodate the high-dimensional neighborhood structure without compression.

This is why PCA's Gaussian low-dimensional distribution (which places probability mass throughout the entire embedding space) fails — it pushes moderate-distance points too close together, collapsing the local structure.

---

### 19.2.2 t-SNE: Student-t Distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding

t-SNE (van der Maaten & Hinton, 2008) solves the crowding problem by using a **heavy-tailed distribution** in the low-dimensional space that allows moderate-distance points to be spread much farther apart.

**Step 1: Construct high-dimensional similarity matrix**

For each pair of points $i, j$, define the conditional similarity (probability that $i$ would pick $j$ as its neighbor):

$$p_{j|i} = \frac{\exp(-|\mathbf{x}_i - \mathbf{x}_j|^2 / 2\sigma_i^2)}{\sum_{k\neq i}\exp(-|\mathbf{x}_i - \mathbf{x}_k|^2 / 2\sigma_i^2)} \tag{19.1}$$

The bandwidth $\sigma_i$ is chosen so that the **perplexity** matches a user-specified value:

$$\text{Perp}(P_i) = 2^{H(P_i)} \tag{19.2}$$

where $H(P_i) = -\sum_j p_{j|i}\log_2 p_{j|i}$ is the Shannon entropy of the conditional distribution. Perplexity is approximately the effective number of neighbors considered for each point — typically set to 5–50.

The perplexity condition is solved by binary search on $\sigma_i$ for each point: find $\sigma_i$ such that $2^{H(P_i)} = \text{Perp}$.

Symmetrize: $$p_{ij} = \frac{p_{j|i} + p_{i|j}}{2n} \tag{19.3}$$

This ensures $p_{ij} = p_{ji}$ (the similarity is symmetric) and $\sum_{i,j}p_{ij} = 1$.

**Step 2: Define low-dimensional similarity**

For the 2D embedding points ${\mathbf{y}_i}$, use the **Student-t distribution with 1 degree of freedom** (Cauchy distribution):

$$q_{ij} = \frac{(1 + |\mathbf{y}_i - \mathbf{y}_j|^2)^{-1}}{\sum_{k\neq l}(1 + |\mathbf{y}_k - \mathbf{y}_l|^2)^{-1}} \tag{19.4}$$

**Why the Student-t distribution?** For $\nu=1$, the Student-t has heavy tails — it puts more probability mass at moderate to large distances compared to a Gaussian. This means that to match a moderate-to-high $p_{ij}$ in high dimensions, the corresponding $q_{ij}$ in low dimensions can have $\mathbf{y}_i$ and $\mathbf{y}_j$ much farther apart. The heavy tail allows the 2D map to spread out moderate-distance points without crowding.

**Quantitative:** For a Gaussian in high dimensions, $p_{ij} \propto e^{-d^2/2\sigma^2}$. For the Student-t in low dimensions, $q_{ij} \propto (1+d'^2)^{-1}$. Setting $p_{ij} = q_{ij}$ and solving: $d' = \sqrt{e^{d^2/2\sigma^2} - 1} \gg d$ for large $d$. The Student-t allows moderate distances in high dimensions to become large distances in low dimensions.

**Step 3: Minimize KL divergence**

> **Objective:** Minimize the KL divergence between high-dimensional similarities $P$ and low-dimensional similarities $Q$: $$\mathcal{L}_{\text{t-SNE}} = D_{KL}(P|Q) = \sum_{i,j} p_{ij}\log\frac{p_{ij}}{q_{ij}} \tag{19.5}$$

This is exactly the KL divergence from Module 8 (Eq. 8.7). Minimizing it forces the low-dimensional $Q$ distribution to match the high-dimensional $P$ distribution.

**The gradient** (key for implementation):

$$\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\mathbf{y}_i} = 4\sum_j (p_{ij} - q_{ij})(1 + |\mathbf{y}_i - \mathbf{y}_j|^2)^{-1}(\mathbf{y}_i - \mathbf{y}_j) \tag{19.6}$$

**Interpretation of the gradient:**

The gradient has two competing forces:

- When $p_{ij} > q_{ij}$ (points too far apart in embedding): attractive force pulling $\mathbf{y}_i$ toward $\mathbf{y}_j$
- When $p_{ij} < q_{ij}$ (points too close in embedding): repulsive force pushing $\mathbf{y}_i$ away from $\mathbf{y}_j$

The factor $(1 + |\mathbf{y}_i - \mathbf{y}_j|^2)^{-1}$ from the Student-t kernel makes repulsive forces decay slowly with distance — ensuring well-separated clusters are pushed far apart.

**Mode-seeking behavior:** Since t-SNE minimizes $D_{KL}(P|Q)$ (not $D_{KL}(Q|P)$), it is mode-seeking (Module 8) — it strongly penalizes placing zero mass under $Q$ where $P$ has positive mass (nearby points must remain nearby). It is less concerned about placing $Q$ mass where $P$ has zero mass (distant points may cluster together). This asymmetry is why t-SNE prioritizes local over global structure.

**Optimization tricks:**

- **Early exaggeration:** Multiply all $p_{ij}$ by a factor $\alpha \approx 12$ for the first ~250 iterations. This makes the attractive forces much stronger, encouraging tight cluster formation early.
- **Momentum:** Use gradient descent with momentum (Module 11, Eq. 11.1) for stable optimization.
- **Barnes-Hut approximation:** Approximate the sum in $q_{ij}$ using a quad-tree/oct-tree, reducing complexity from $O(n^2)$ to $O(n\log n)$.

**Complexity:** $O(n^2)$ exact, $O(n\log n)$ with Barnes-Hut.

---

### 19.2.3 t-SNE Hyperparameters and Interpretation Pitfalls

**Perplexity** (5–50, default 30): Controls the effective neighborhood size. Low perplexity emphasizes very local structure; high perplexity sees more global structure. Always try multiple values.

**Learning rate** (10–1000, default 200): Too small → poor optimization; too large → embedding explodes.

**Initialization:** Random or PCA (faster convergence). PCA initialization preserves more global structure.

**Critical interpretation warnings** (Wattenberg et al., 2016):

1. **Cluster sizes are meaningless.** t-SNE normalizes the perplexity per point — dense and sparse clusters appear similarly sized.
2. **Distances between clusters are meaningless.** The repulsive forces push all clusters apart equally — the space between clusters carries no information about inter-cluster similarity.
3. **Topology can be wrong.** Clusters that appear separate may be connected; non-cluster structure (gradients, curves) may appear as clusters.
4. **Always run multiple times.** t-SNE is stochastic — different runs may give qualitatively different embeddings.

---

### 19.2.4 UMAP: Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection

UMAP (McInnes et al., 2018) builds on a rigorous mathematical foundation — Riemannian geometry and algebraic topology — to produce embeddings that better preserve global structure while being significantly faster than t-SNE.

**Theoretical foundation:** UMAP assumes the data is uniformly distributed on a Riemannian manifold $(\mathcal{M}, g)$ with a locally varying metric $g$. The key insight is that the manifold's geometry can be approximated from the nearest-neighbor graph of the data.

**Step 1: Construct the high-dimensional fuzzy topological representation**

For each point $\mathbf{x}_i$ with $k$-th nearest neighbor at distance $\rho_i$, define the local connectivity-normalized distance:

$$d_i(\mathbf{x}_i, \mathbf{x}_j) = \frac{d(\mathbf{x}_i, \mathbf{x}_j) - \rho_i}{\sigma_i} \tag{19.7}$$

where $\rho_i = \min_{j\in\mathcal{N}_k(i)} d(\mathbf{x}_i, \mathbf{x}_j)$ (distance to nearest neighbor) and $\sigma_i$ is chosen so that $\sum_j \exp(-d_i(\mathbf{x}_i,\mathbf{x}_j)/\sigma_i) = \log_2 k$ (matching target entropy).

This defines a **fuzzy membership strength** (high-dimensional similarity): $$v_{j|i} = \exp!\left(-\frac{d(\mathbf{x}_i, \mathbf{x}_j) - \rho_i}{\sigma_i}\right) \tag{19.8}$$

Symmetrize: $$w_{ij} = v_{j|i} + v_{i|j} - v_{j|i}\cdot v_{i|j} \tag{19.9}$$

This is the probability of the union in fuzzy set theory — it ensures $w_{ij} \in [0,1]$ and $w_{ij} = w_{ji}$. The subtraction of the product prevents over-counting when both directions are strong.

**Step 2: Define low-dimensional fuzzy membership**

$$\hat{w}_{ij} = \left(1 + a|\mathbf{y}_i - \mathbf{y}_j|^{2b}\right)^{-1} \tag{19.10}$$

where $a$ and $b$ are hyperparameters fit from the `min_dist` parameter (controls how tightly packed the embedding is). For `min_dist=0.1`: $a\approx1.929$, $b\approx0.791$.

This is a generalized Student-t kernel that reduces to the t-SNE kernel when $a=1$, $b=1$.

**Step 3: Minimize the cross-entropy**

$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{UMAP}} = \sum_{(i,j)\in E}\left[w_{ij}\log\frac{w_{ij}}{\hat{w}_{ij}} + (1-w_{ij})\log\frac{1-w_{ij}}{1-\hat{w}_{ij}}\right] \tag{19.11}$$

This is the **binary cross-entropy** between the high-dimensional edge weights $w_{ij}$ and low-dimensional weights $\hat{w}_{ij}$ — directly from Module 8. It measures the information needed to recover the high-dimensional graph structure from the low-dimensional embedding.

Compared to t-SNE's KL divergence (Eq. 19.5), UMAP's cross-entropy (Eq. 19.11):

- Includes a **$(1-w_{ij})\log(1-w_{ij})/(1-\hat{w}_{ij})$ term** — penalizes placing two points near each other in the embedding when they are far apart in the original space. This is what t-SNE lacks, and it is why UMAP better preserves global structure.
- Works on the **sparse nearest-neighbor graph** rather than all $O(n^2)$ pairs — dramatically faster.

**Gradient:**

$$\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\mathbf{y}_i} = \sum_j \left[\frac{2ab w_{ij}|\mathbf{y}_i-\mathbf{y}_j|^{2(b-1)}}{1+a|\mathbf{y}_i-\mathbf{y}_j|^{2b}}(\mathbf{y}_i-\mathbf{y}_j) - \frac{2(1-w_{ij})\hat{w}_{ij}}{(0.001+|\mathbf{y}_i-\mathbf{y}_j|^2)(1-\hat{w}_{ij})}(\mathbf{y}_i-\mathbf{y}_j)\right] \tag{19.12}$$

The first term is attractive (for nearby points with high $w_{ij}$); the second is repulsive (for distant points with low $w_{ij}$). UMAP uses **stochastic gradient descent with negative sampling** (sampling random non-edge pairs for the repulsive term) — reducing complexity to $O(n)$ per iteration.

**Complexity:** $O(n^{1.14})$ in practice (dominated by nearest-neighbor computation), effectively $O(n)$ for the optimization. Much faster than t-SNE's $O(n\log n)$.

---

### 19.2.5 UMAP vs t-SNE: The Mathematical Comparison

|Property|t-SNE|UMAP|
|---|---|---|
|Objective|$D_{KL}(P\|Q)$ — KL divergence|Binary cross-entropy $H(w, \hat{w})$|
|High-dim similarity|Gaussian (perplexity-normalized)|Exponential decay with local metric|
|Low-dim similarity|Student-t ($\nu=1$)|Generalized Student-t|
|Global structure|Poor (mode-seeking KL)|Good (BCE penalizes false repulsion)|
|Complexity|$O(n\log n)$ BH-approx|$O(n^{1.14})$ approx|
|Stochastic|Yes|Yes (negative sampling)|
|Theoretical basis|Information theory|Riemannian geometry + fuzzy topology|
|Initialization|Random or PCA|Spectral (Laplacian eigenmaps)|

**Key mathematical insight:** The difference between t-SNE and UMAP objectives is exactly the $(1-w_{ij})\log(1-w_{ij})/(1-\hat{w}_{ij})$ term in UMAP's cross-entropy. This term penalizes UMAP for placing distant points near each other — t-SNE ignores this, which is why its global structure is unreliable.

---

### 19.2.6 PCA as a Special Case — The Linear Limit

Both t-SNE and UMAP reduce to PCA in specific limits:

**t-SNE → PCA** when perplexity → $n/2$ (all points are equally likely neighbors): both the high-dimensional $p_{ij}$ and low-dimensional $q_{ij}$ approach uniform distributions, and the gradient forces reduce to PCA's variance-maximization directions.

**UMAP → PCA** when `n_neighbors` → $n$: the local metric becomes global, the nearest-neighbor graph becomes complete, and the spectral initialization (Laplacian eigenmaps) reduces to PCA.

This confirms PCA occupies the global-structure extreme while t-SNE and UMAP with small neighborhood parameters occupy the local-structure extreme.

---

### 19.2.7 When to Use Each Method

|Task|Method|Reason|
|---|---|---|
|Feature extraction for downstream ML|UMAP|Faster, better global structure preserved|
|Visualization only|t-SNE or UMAP|Both valid; t-SNE more familiar|
|Large datasets ($n > 100K$)|UMAP|t-SNE too slow|
|Global structure important|UMAP|t-SNE loses global distances|
|Cluster separation visualization|t-SNE|Well-separated local clusters|
|Semi-supervised / transfer|UMAP|Supports supervised/metric modes|
|Linear structure sufficient|PCA|Interpretable, deterministic|
|Preprocessing for clustering|UMAP|Preserves density, works with DBSCAN|

---

## 19.3 Numerical Examples

### Example 19.1: Perplexity Calibration

**3 points** in 1D: $x_1=0$, $x_2=1$, $x_3=10$. Target perplexity = 1.5.

**For point $x_1$:** Unnormalized similarities: $e^{-0/(2\sigma^2)}=1$, $e^{-1/(2\sigma^2)}$, $e^{-100/(2\sigma^2)}$.

For $\sigma_1 = 0.7$: $p_{2|1} = e^{-1/0.98}/(e^{-1/0.98}+e^{-100/0.98}) \approx 1.0$, $p_{3|1}\approx 0$.

Entropy: $H = -1\log_2(1) - 0\log_2(0) \approx 0$ bits. Perplexity $= 2^0 = 1$.

For $\sigma_1 = 2.0$: $p_{2|1} = e^{-0.125}/(e^{-0.125}+e^{-12.5}) \approx 0.9999$, perplexity $\approx 1$.

For very large $\sigma_1$: $p_{2|1} \approx p_{3|1} \approx 0.5$. Perplexity $= 2^1 = 2$.

Binary search gives $\sigma_1 \approx 3.16$ for perplexity $= 1.5$: $p_{2|1} \approx 0.75$, $p_{3|1} \approx 0.25$.

This shows that perplexity controls how many effective neighbors each point "sees." Low perplexity → only nearest neighbor matters; high perplexity → many neighbors equally weighted.

---

### Example 19.2: t-SNE Gradient Direction

Two clusters at $\mathbf{y}_1=(0,0)$, $\mathbf{y}_2=(1,0)$ (same cluster, high $p_{12}$) and $\mathbf{y}_3=(5,0)$ (different cluster, low $p_{13}$).

**For pair (1,2):** $p_{12}=0.3$, $q_{12}=(1+1)^{-1}/Z=0.5/Z$. If $q_{12} < p_{12}$: gradient is attractive — pull $\mathbf{y}_1$ toward $\mathbf{y}_2$.

**For pair (1,3):** $p_{13}=0.001$, $q_{13}=(1+25)^{-1}/Z=0.038/Z$. If $q_{13} > p_{13}$: gradient is repulsive — push $\mathbf{y}_1$ away from $\mathbf{y}_3$.

The $(1+|\mathbf{y}_i-\mathbf{y}_j|^2)^{-1}$ factor means the repulsion between distant points decays slowly — ensuring clusters are pushed to well-separated positions.

---

## 19.4 Implementation

```python
import numpy as np
import scipy.spatial.distance as spdist
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.gridspec as gridspec
from typing import Optional, Tuple

# =============================================================================
# MODULE 19: t-SNE & UMAP
# =============================================================================

# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# PART A: t-SNE Implementation
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------

class TSNE:
    """
    t-SNE: t-Distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding.
    van der Maaten & Hinton (2008).
    Implements Eqs. 19.1-19.6.

    This is a pedagogically complete implementation.
    For production use: sklearn.manifold.TSNE or openTSNE.
    """

    def __init__(self, n_components: int = 2,
                  perplexity: float = 30.0,
                  learning_rate: float = 200.0,
                  n_iter: int = 1000,
                  early_exaggeration: float = 12.0,
                  n_iter_early_exag: int = 250,
                  momentum: float = 0.5,
                  final_momentum: float = 0.8,
                  momentum_switch_iter: int = 250,
                  seed: int = 42,
                  verbose: bool = True):
        self.n_components        = n_components
        self.perplexity          = perplexity
        self.lr                  = learning_rate
        self.n_iter              = n_iter
        self.early_exag          = early_exaggeration
        self.n_iter_early_exag   = n_iter_early_exag
        self.momentum            = momentum
        self.final_momentum      = final_momentum
        self.momentum_switch     = momentum_switch_iter
        self.seed                = seed
        self.verbose             = verbose

    def _compute_pairwise_distances(self, X: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
        """Squared Euclidean distances. O(n^2 d)."""
        sq_norms = np.sum(X**2, axis=1)
        D = sq_norms[:, None] + sq_norms[None, :] - 2 * X @ X.T
        np.fill_diagonal(D, 0)
        return np.maximum(D, 0)

    def _perplexity_to_sigma(self, D_row: np.ndarray, i: int,
                              tol: float = 1e-5,
                              max_iter: int = 50) -> Tuple[np.ndarray, float]:
        """
        Binary search for sigma_i such that perplexity matches target.
        Eq. 19.2: Perp(P_i) = 2^{H(P_i)}.
        Returns (p_{j|i}, sigma_i).
        """
        target_H = np.log2(self.perplexity)
        sigma_lo, sigma_hi = 1e-10, 1e10
        sigma = 1.0

        for _ in range(max_iter):
            # Eq. 19.1: compute p_{j|i} with current sigma
            exp_d = np.exp(-D_row / (2 * sigma**2))
            exp_d[i] = 0.0   # exclude self
            sum_exp  = exp_d.sum() + 1e-12
            p_ji     = exp_d / sum_exp

            # Entropy
            H = -np.sum(p_ji[p_ji > 0] * np.log2(p_ji[p_ji > 0] + 1e-12))

            if abs(H - target_H) < tol:
                break
            if H < target_H:
                sigma_lo = sigma
                sigma = (sigma + sigma_hi) / 2 if sigma_hi < 1e9 else sigma * 2
            else:
                sigma_hi = sigma
                sigma = (sigma + sigma_lo) / 2

        return p_ji, sigma

    def _compute_P(self, X: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
        """
        Compute symmetrized joint probability matrix P. Eqs. 19.1-19.3.
        """
        n   = len(X)
        D_sq = self._compute_pairwise_distances(X)
        P   = np.zeros((n, n))

        for i in range(n):
            p_ji, _ = self._perplexity_to_sigma(D_sq[i], i)
            P[i]    = p_ji

        # Symmetrize (Eq. 19.3)
        P = (P + P.T) / (2 * n)
        P = np.maximum(P, 1e-12)   # numerical stability
        return P

    def _compute_Q(self, Y: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
        """
        Student-t similarity in low-dimensional space. Eq. 19.4.
        q_{ij} = (1 + ||y_i - y_j||^2)^{-1} / Z
        """
        n    = len(Y)
        D_sq = self._compute_pairwise_distances(Y)
        inv  = 1.0 / (1.0 + D_sq)
        np.fill_diagonal(inv, 0)
        Q    = inv / inv.sum()
        return np.maximum(Q, 1e-12), inv

    def _gradient(self, P: np.ndarray, Q: np.ndarray,
                   inv: np.ndarray, Y: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
        """
        t-SNE gradient. Eq. 19.6:
        dL/dy_i = 4 * sum_j (p_ij - q_ij)(1+||y_i-y_j||^2)^{-1}(y_i - y_j)
        """
        n    = len(Y)
        PQ   = (P - Q) * inv    # (n, n) — element-wise
        grad = np.zeros_like(Y)

        for i in range(n):
            diff      = Y[i] - Y             # (n, d)
            grad[i]   = 4 * (PQ[i, :, None] * diff).sum(axis=0)

        return grad

    def fit_transform(self, X: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
        """
        Run t-SNE and return 2D embedding.
        """
        rng = np.random.default_rng(self.seed)
        n   = len(X)

        if self.verbose:
            print(f"  t-SNE: n={n}, perplexity={self.perplexity}, "
                  f"n_iter={self.n_iter}")
            print("  Computing high-dimensional similarities P...")

        # Compute P (expensive — O(n^2))
        P = self._compute_P(X)

        # Initialize embedding (PCA or random)
        Y = rng.normal(0, 1e-4, (n, self.n_components))

        # Optimization with momentum
        Y_prev = Y.copy()
        gains  = np.ones_like(Y)   # adaptive gains per dimension
        loss_history = []

        for t in range(1, self.n_iter + 1):
            # Early exaggeration (Eq. 19.5 trick)
            P_eff = P * self.early_exag if t <= self.n_iter_early_exag else P

            # Compute Q
            Q, inv = self._compute_Q(Y)

            # Compute KL divergence (Eq. 19.5)
            kl = np.sum(P_eff * np.log(P_eff / Q))
            loss_history.append(kl)

            # Gradient (Eq. 19.6)
            grad = self._gradient(P_eff, Q, inv, Y)

            # Adaptive learning rate (sign-based gain)
            gains = (gains + 0.2) * ((grad > 0) != (Y - Y_prev > 0)) + \
                    gains * 0.8 * ((grad > 0) == (Y - Y_prev > 0))
            gains = np.maximum(gains, 0.01)

            # Momentum update (Eq. 11.1 from Module 11)
            mom   = self.momentum if t < self.momentum_switch else self.final_momentum
            Y_prev_save = Y.copy()
            Y     = Y - self.lr * gains * grad + mom * (Y - Y_prev)
            Y_prev = Y_prev_save

            # Center embedding
            Y -= Y.mean(axis=0)

            if self.verbose and t % 100 == 0:
                print(f"  Iteration {t:4d}: KL = {kl:.4f}")

        self.embedding_  = Y
        self.loss_history_ = loss_history
        return Y


# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# PART B: UMAP (simplified pedagogical version)
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------

class UMAPSimplified:
    """
    Simplified UMAP implementation for pedagogical clarity.
    Implements core Eqs. 19.7-19.12.

    For production: use the `umap-learn` package (pip install umap-learn).
    This implementation demonstrates the key algorithmic ideas.
    """

    def __init__(self, n_components: int = 2,
                  n_neighbors: int = 15,
                  min_dist: float = 0.1,
                  n_epochs: int = 200,
                  learning_rate: float = 1.0,
                  negative_sample_rate: int = 5,
                  seed: int = 42,
                  verbose: bool = True):
        self.n_components        = n_components
        self.n_neighbors         = n_neighbors
        self.min_dist            = min_dist
        self.n_epochs            = n_epochs
        self.lr                  = learning_rate
        self.negative_sample_rate = negative_sample_rate
        self.seed                = seed
        self.verbose             = verbose

        # Fit a, b to match min_dist (from UMAP paper)
        self.a_, self.b_ = self._find_ab(min_dist)

    def _find_ab(self, min_dist: float) -> Tuple[float, float]:
        """
        Fit a, b parameters for low-dimensional kernel (Eq. 19.10).
        Matches the piecewise function that defines min_dist.
        """
        from scipy.optimize import curve_fit
        def f(x, a, b):
            return 1.0 / (1.0 + a * x**(2*b))

        x = np.linspace(0, 3, 300)
        y = np.where(x < min_dist, 1.0, np.exp(-(x-min_dist)))

        try:
            (a, b), _ = curve_fit(f, x, y, p0=[1.0, 1.0])
            return float(a), float(b)
        except Exception:
            return 1.929, 0.791   # defaults for min_dist=0.1

    def _compute_knn_graph(self, X: np.ndarray) -> Tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]:
        """
        Compute k-nearest neighbor graph. Returns (knn_indices, knn_distances).
        """
        n = len(X)
        k = min(self.n_neighbors, n-1)

        # Brute force for small n (use faiss/annoy for large n)
        D_sq = (np.sum(X**2, axis=1, keepdims=True) +
                np.sum(X**2, axis=1) - 2 * X @ X.T)
        np.fill_diagonal(D_sq, np.inf)
        D_sq = np.maximum(D_sq, 0)

        idx  = np.argsort(D_sq, axis=1)[:, :k]
        dists = np.sqrt(D_sq[np.arange(n)[:, None], idx])
        return idx, dists

    def _compute_high_dim_graph(self, X: np.ndarray,
                                  knn_idx: np.ndarray,
                                  knn_dist: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
        """
        Compute fuzzy membership strengths w_{ij}. Eqs. 19.7-19.9.
        """
        n, k = knn_dist.shape

        # rho_i = distance to nearest neighbor (Eq. 19.7)
        rho = knn_dist[:, 0]

        # sigma_i via binary search to match target entropy = log2(k)
        sigma = np.ones(n)
        target = np.log2(k)

        for i in range(n):
            lo, hi = 0.0, 1e5
            for _ in range(50):
                # Eq. 19.8: v_{j|i} = exp(-(d - rho) / sigma)
                d_shifted = np.maximum(knn_dist[i] - rho[i], 0)
                v         = np.exp(-d_shifted / sigma[i])
                H         = v.sum()

                if abs(H - target) < 1e-5:
                    break
                if H < target:
                    lo = sigma[i]
                    sigma[i] = (sigma[i] + hi) / 2
                else:
                    hi = sigma[i]
                    sigma[i] = (sigma[i] + lo) / 2

        # Build sparse w matrix (n x n)
        W = np.zeros((n, n))
        for i in range(n):
            d_shifted = np.maximum(knn_dist[i] - rho[i], 0)
            v         = np.exp(-d_shifted / sigma[i])
            for j_idx, j in enumerate(knn_idx[i]):
                # Eq. 19.9: w_{ij} = v_{j|i} + v_{i|j} - v_{j|i} * v_{i|j}
                v_ji = v[j_idx]
                # Look up v_{i|j} (approximate here)
                W[i, j] = v_ji

        # Symmetrize: w_{ij} = v_{j|i} + v_{i|j} - v_{j|i} * v_{i|j}
        W_sym = W + W.T - W * W.T
        return np.clip(W_sym, 0, 1)

    def _low_dim_kernel(self, d_sq: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
        """Low-dimensional fuzzy membership. Eq. 19.10."""
        return 1.0 / (1.0 + self.a_ * d_sq**self.b_)

    def fit_transform(self, X: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
        """Run UMAP and return embedding."""
        rng = np.random.default_rng(self.seed)
        n   = len(X)

        if self.verbose:
            print(f"  UMAP: n={n}, n_neighbors={self.n_neighbors}, "
                  f"min_dist={self.min_dist}")
            print("  Computing k-nearest neighbor graph...")

        # Step 1: KNN graph
        knn_idx, knn_dist = self._compute_knn_graph(X)

        if self.verbose:
            print("  Building fuzzy topological representation...")

        # Step 2: High-dim fuzzy graph (Eqs. 19.7-19.9)
        W = self._compute_high_dim_graph(X, knn_idx, knn_dist)

        # Edge list (non-zero entries)
        edges = [(i, j, W[i,j]) for i in range(n)
                  for j in range(i+1, n) if W[i,j] > 1e-4]

        # Step 3: Initialize embedding (spectral approximation or random)
        Y = rng.normal(0, 1e-2, (n, self.n_components))

        # Step 4: Optimize cross-entropy (Eq. 19.11) via SGD with neg. sampling
        if self.verbose:
            print(f"  Optimizing embedding ({self.n_epochs} epochs)...")

        loss_history = []
        edge_arr  = np.array([(i,j,w) for i,j,w in edges])

        for epoch in range(self.n_epochs):
            rng.shuffle(edge_arr)
            epoch_loss = 0.0

            for i, j, w_ij in edge_arr:
                i, j = int(i), int(j)
                diff    = Y[i] - Y[j]
                d_sq    = np.sum(diff**2)
                w_hat   = self._low_dim_kernel(np.array([d_sq]))[0]

                # Attractive gradient (for positive edges)
                # Eq. 19.12, term 1
                grad_pos = (2 * self.a_ * self.b_ * d_sq**(self.b_-1) *
                            w_ij / (1e-6 + (1 + self.a_ * d_sq**self.b_)) * diff)

                Y[i] -= self.lr * grad_pos
                Y[j] += self.lr * grad_pos

                # Repulsive gradient (negative sampling, Eq. 19.12, term 2)
                for _ in range(self.negative_sample_rate):
                    k = rng.integers(n)
                    if k == i:
                        continue
                    diff_neg = Y[i] - Y[k]
                    d_sq_neg = np.sum(diff_neg**2) + 1e-6
                    w_hat_neg = self._low_dim_kernel(np.array([d_sq_neg]))[0]
                    grad_neg  = (2 * (1 - 0) * w_hat_neg /
                                  (d_sq_neg * (1 - w_hat_neg + 1e-6)) * diff_neg)
                    Y[i] += self.lr * grad_neg * min(1.0, 4.0*(1-epoch/self.n_epochs))

                # Binary cross-entropy loss contribution (Eq. 19.11)
                pos_loss = -(w_ij*np.log(w_hat+1e-12) + (1-w_ij)*np.log(1-w_hat+1e-12))
                epoch_loss += pos_loss

            loss_history.append(epoch_loss / len(edge_arr))

            if self.verbose and (epoch+1) % 50 == 0:
                print(f"  Epoch {epoch+1:4d}: loss = {loss_history[-1]:.4f}")

            # Decay learning rate
            self.lr *= 0.99

        self.embedding_  = Y
        self.loss_history_ = loss_history
        return Y


# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# PART C: Complete Visualization Comparison
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def full_visualization(seed: int = 42):
    """
    Compare PCA, t-SNE, and UMAP on multiple datasets.
    Demonstrates the local vs global structure tradeoff.
    """
    from sklearn.datasets import (load_digits, make_swiss_roll,
                                   make_s_curve, make_blobs)
    from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
    from sklearn.manifold import TSNE
    from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    fig = plt.figure(figsize=(18, 14))
    gs  = gridspec.GridSpec(3, 4, wspace=0.32, hspace=0.45)

    # ---- Dataset 1: Swiss Roll (3D manifold in 3D) ----
    X_roll, t_roll = make_swiss_roll(n_samples=1000, noise=0.1, random_state=42)
    sc_roll = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X_roll)

    # PCA
    ax = fig.add_subplot(gs[0, 0])
    Y_pca = PCA(n_components=2).fit_transform(sc_roll)
    sc = ax.scatter(Y_pca[:,0], Y_pca[:,1], c=t_roll, cmap='Spectral', s=6, alpha=0.7)
    ax.set_title("PCA: Swiss Roll\n(Linear — fails to unroll)", fontsize=10, fontweight='bold')
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])

    # t-SNE
    ax = fig.add_subplot(gs[0, 1])
    Y_tsne = TSNE(n_components=2, perplexity=30, random_state=42).fit_transform(sc_roll)
    ax.scatter(Y_tsne[:,0], Y_tsne[:,1], c=t_roll, cmap='Spectral', s=6, alpha=0.7)
    ax.set_title("t-SNE: Swiss Roll\n(Local structure preserved)", fontsize=10, fontweight='bold')
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])

    # ---- Dataset 2: Digits (64D) ----
    digits = load_digits()
    X_dig  = StandardScaler().fit_transform(digits.data)
    y_dig  = digits.target

    # PCA
    ax = fig.add_subplot(gs[0, 2])
    Y_pca2 = PCA(n_components=2).fit_transform(X_dig)
    for k in range(10):
        mask = y_dig == k
        ax.scatter(Y_pca2[mask,0], Y_pca2[mask,1], s=6, alpha=0.6,
                   label=str(k) if k < 5 else None)
    ax.set_title("PCA: Digits\n(Linear separation, overlap)", fontsize=10, fontweight='bold')
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])

    # t-SNE on digits
    ax = fig.add_subplot(gs[0, 3])
    Y_tsne2 = TSNE(n_components=2, perplexity=30, random_state=42).fit_transform(X_dig)
    for k in range(10):
        mask = y_dig == k
        ax.scatter(Y_tsne2[mask,0], Y_tsne2[mask,1], s=6, alpha=0.7, label=str(k))
    ax.set_title("t-SNE: Digits\n(Clear cluster separation)", fontsize=10, fontweight='bold')
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])
    ax.legend(fontsize=7, ncol=2, markerscale=2)

    # ---- Row 2: Perplexity effect ----
    for col_idx, perp in enumerate([5, 30, 100, 500]):
        ax = fig.add_subplot(gs[1, col_idx])
        try:
            Y_p = TSNE(n_components=2, perplexity=min(perp, len(X_dig)-1),
                       random_state=42, n_iter=500).fit_transform(X_dig[:200])
            for k in range(10):
                mask = y_dig[:200] == k
                if mask.sum() > 0:
                    ax.scatter(Y_p[mask,0], Y_p[mask,1], s=8, alpha=0.7)
        except Exception:
            ax.text(0.5, 0.5, f'Perp={perp}\n(n too small)',
                    ha='center', va='center', transform=ax.transAxes)
        ax.set_title(f"t-SNE: perplexity={perp}", fontsize=10, fontweight='bold')
        ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])

    # ---- Row 3: t-SNE vs UMAP objective comparison ----
    # Show the objective function landscapes
    ax = fig.add_subplot(gs[2, :2])
    d_vals = np.linspace(0, 5, 300)

    # High-dim similarities (Gaussian, various sigmas)
    for sigma, col, ls, lbl in [(0.5,'#1a6faf','-','σ=0.5'),
                                  (1.0,'#e84040','--','σ=1.0'),
                                  (2.0,'#2ca02c',':','σ=2.0')]:
        p = np.exp(-d_vals**2 / (2*sigma**2))
        p /= p.sum()
        ax.plot(d_vals, p, color=col, lw=2, linestyle=ls, label=f'Gaussian {lbl} (high-d)')

    # Low-dim similarity: Gaussian vs Student-t
    q_gauss   = np.exp(-d_vals**2) ; q_gauss /= q_gauss.sum()
    q_student = 1/(1+d_vals**2)    ; q_student /= q_student.sum()
    ax.plot(d_vals, q_gauss,   'k--', lw=2, label='Gaussian (low-d, crowding)')
    ax.plot(d_vals, q_student, 'k-',  lw=2.5, label='Student-t (low-d, t-SNE)')
    ax.set_xlabel("Distance", fontsize=11)
    ax.set_ylabel("Similarity / density", fontsize=11)
    ax.set_title("Why Student-t Solves the Crowding Problem\n"
                 "(Heavy tail allows moderate distances to spread out)",
                 fontsize=11, fontweight='bold')
    ax.legend(fontsize=8); ax.grid(alpha=0.3); ax.set_ylim(0, 0.02)

    # ---- KL divergence and CE objectives comparison ----
    ax = fig.add_subplot(gs[2, 2:])
    w_vals  = np.linspace(0.01, 0.99, 300)
    w_hat_vals = np.linspace(0.01, 0.99, 300)
    p_fixed = 0.5   # fixed high-dim similarity

    # t-SNE: KL(P||Q) = p*log(p/q) term for fixed p
    kl_contribution = p_fixed * np.log(p_fixed / w_hat_vals)
    ax.plot(w_hat_vals, kl_contribution, '#1a6faf', lw=2.5, label='t-SNE: p·log(p/q̂) [attracts]')

    # UMAP: BCE includes repulsion term
    bce_pos = -p_fixed * np.log(w_hat_vals)
    bce_neg = -(1-p_fixed) * np.log(1-w_hat_vals)
    ax.plot(w_hat_vals, bce_pos, '#e84040', lw=2.5, linestyle='--',
            label='UMAP: attractive term -p·log(q̂)')
    ax.plot(w_hat_vals, bce_neg, '#2ca02c', lw=2.5, linestyle=':',
            label='UMAP: repulsive term -(1-p)·log(1-q̂)')
    ax.axvline(p_fixed, color='gray', lw=1, linestyle='--', alpha=0.5)
    ax.set_xlabel("$\\hat{w}_{ij}$ (low-dim similarity)", fontsize=11)
    ax.set_ylabel("Loss contribution", fontsize=11)
    ax.set_title("t-SNE vs UMAP Objective Functions\n"
                 "(UMAP's repulsive term preserves global structure)",
                 fontsize=11, fontweight='bold')
    ax.legend(fontsize=9); ax.grid(alpha=0.3); ax.set_ylim(0, 3)

    plt.suptitle("Module 19: t-SNE & UMAP — Nonlinear Dimensionality Reduction",
                 fontsize=14, fontweight='bold', y=1.01)
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.savefig("module19_tsne_umap.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches='tight')
    plt.show()
    print("Saved: module19_tsne_umap.png")

    from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

    ari = adjusted_rand_score(y_blobs, km.labels_)
    print(f"  ARI of K-Means on t-SNE embedding: {ari:.4f} (1.0 = perfect)")

    # --- Full visualization ---
    print("\n" + "=" * 60)
    print("  FULL VISUALIZATION COMPARISON")
    print("=" * 60)
    full_visualization()
```

## 19.5 Interactive t-SNE / UMAP ExplorerAdjust perplexity from 2 to 80 and watch the embedding transform. At very low perplexity each point only considers its immediate neighborhood — producing fragmented, noisy clusters. At high perplexity the algorithm sees more global structure — clusters merge and spread. Switch between t-SNE and UMAP and compare: UMAP preserves the relative cluster positions (inter-class distance metric is more meaningful) while t-SNE pushes all clusters apart equally.

## 19.7 Key Equations Reference Card

$$p_{j|i} = \frac{\exp(-|\mathbf{x}_i-\mathbf{x}_j|^2/2\sigma_i^2)}{\sum_{k\neq i}\exp(-|\mathbf{x}_i-\mathbf{x}_k|^2/2\sigma_i^2)},\quad \text{Perp}(P_i)=2^{H(P_i)} \tag{t-SNE high-d}$$ $$q_{ij} = \frac{(1+|\mathbf{y}_i-\mathbf{y}_j|^2)^{-1}}{\sum_{k\neq l}(1+|\mathbf{y}_k-\mathbf{y}_l|^2)^{-1}} \tag{t-SNE Student-t kernel}$$ $$\mathcal{L}_{\text{t-SNE}} = D_{KL}(P|Q) = \sum_{ij}p_{ij}\log\frac{p_{ij}}{q_{ij}} \tag{t-SNE objective}$$ $$\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\mathbf{y}_i} = 4\sum_j(p_{ij}-q_{ij})(1+|\mathbf{y}_i-\mathbf{y}_j|^2)^{-1}(\mathbf{y}_i-\mathbf{y}_j) \tag{t-SNE gradient}$$ $$w_{ij} = v_{j|i}+v_{i|j}-v_{j|i}\cdot v_{i|j} \tag{UMAP fuzzy membership}$$ $$\hat{w}_{ij} = (1+a|\mathbf{y}_i-\mathbf{y}_j|^{2b})^{-1} \tag{UMAP low-d kernel}$$ $$\mathcal{L}_{\text{UMAP}} = \sum_{ij}\left[w_{ij}\log\frac{w_{ij}}{\hat{w}_{ij}}+(1-w_{ij})\log\frac{1-w_{ij}}{1-\hat{w}_{ij}}\right] \tag{UMAP BCE objective}$$
