Here is **Module 20** of the Mastery Handbook — the module where we build deep learning from its mathematical foundations, proving why depth works and deriving every component of a modern CNN from first principles.

---

# MODULE 20: Deep Learning — MLP & CNN

### _Universal Approximation, Convolutional Feature Extraction & Modern Architectures_

---

## 20.1 Conceptual Overview

### Why Depth — The Exponential Expressivity of Layers

The central question of deep learning theory is: why do deep networks outperform shallow ones? The answer is not empirical accident — it has a precise mathematical foundation rooted in the theory of function approximation.

A single hidden layer network is a **universal approximator** — given enough hidden units, it can approximate any continuous function on a compact domain. But "enough" can mean exponentially many units for functions that deep networks represent efficiently with polynomially many. Depth provides **exponential expressivity** — each additional layer exponentially increases the class of functions representable with fixed parameter count.

**Intuition:** A deep network computes a hierarchy of features. Early layers detect simple patterns (edges, textures); middle layers compose these into parts (eyes, wheels); deep layers combine parts into concepts (faces, cars). This hierarchical composition matches the compositional structure of natural data. A shallow network must represent all of this in a single step — requiring exponentially more neurons.

**Convolutional Neural Networks** add the inductive biases of **translation equivariance** and **weight sharing** — physically motivated assumptions that reduce the parameter count from $O(d^2)$ to $O(k^2)$ (where $k \ll d$ is the kernel size) while improving generalization by encoding domain knowledge about image structure.

---

## 20.2 Mathematical Formalization

### 20.2.1 Multi-Layer Perceptrons — Formal Definition

> **Definition 20.1 (MLP):** A multi-layer perceptron with $L$ layers is a function $f_\theta: \mathbb{R}^{d_0} \to \mathbb{R}^{d_L}$ defined by the composition: $$f_\theta(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{W}^{(L)}\sigma(\mathbf{W}^{(L-1)}\sigma(\cdots\sigma(\mathbf{W}^{(1)}\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{b}^{(1)})\cdots) + \mathbf{b}^{(L-1)}) + \mathbf{b}^{(L)} \tag{20.1}$$
> 
> where $\mathbf{W}^{(l)} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_l \times d_{l-1}}$, $\mathbf{b}^{(l)} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_l}$, and $\sigma$ is an elementwise nonlinear **activation function**.

The parameters are $\theta = {\mathbf{W}^{(l)}, \mathbf{b}^{(l)}}_{l=1}^L$. The total parameter count is $\sum_{l=1}^L (d_l \cdot d_{l-1} + d_l)$.

**Forward pass notation:** $$\mathbf{z}^{(l)} = \mathbf{W}^{(l)}\mathbf{a}^{(l-1)} + \mathbf{b}^{(l)} \quad \text{(pre-activation)} \tag{20.2}$$ $$\mathbf{a}^{(l)} = \sigma(\mathbf{z}^{(l)}) \quad \text{(post-activation)} \tag{20.3}$$ $$\mathbf{a}^{(0)} = \mathbf{x}, \quad f_\theta(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{a}^{(L)} \tag{20.4}$$

---

### 20.2.2 The Universal Approximation Theorem

> **Theorem 20.1 (Universal Approximation — Cybenko, 1989; Hornik, 1991):** Let $\sigma: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be a continuous, bounded, non-constant activation function (e.g., sigmoid). For any continuous function $f: [0,1]^d \to \mathbb{R}$ and any $\varepsilon > 0$, there exists a single hidden layer network: $$F(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{k=1}^N c_k,\sigma(\mathbf{w}_k^\top\mathbf{x} + b_k) \tag{20.5}$$ such that $\sup_{\mathbf{x}\in[0,1]^d}|F(\mathbf{x}) - f(\mathbf{x})| < \varepsilon$.

**Proof sketch (Fourier analysis approach):**

Any $L^2([0,1]^d)$ function has a Fourier series expansion $f(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_\mathbf{k} \hat{f}_\mathbf{k} e^{2\pi i\mathbf{k}^\top\mathbf{x}}$. The sigmoid function, being sigmoidal, can approximate Fourier basis functions $e^{2\pi i\mathbf{k}^\top\mathbf{x}}$ in mean-square sense. Truncating the Fourier series gives a finite approximation, and the approximation error can be made $< \varepsilon$ by taking $N$ large enough. $\blacksquare$

**The depth-width efficiency theorem** (Eldan & Shamir, 2016; Telgarsky, 2016):

> **Theorem 20.2 (Depth Separation):** There exists a function $f$ that can be computed by a depth-$3$ network with $O(n)$ units, but requires $\Omega(2^{\sqrt{n}})$ units to be approximated by a depth-$2$ network to the same accuracy.

The implication: depth provides **exponential** efficiency over width. A function that requires exponentially many neurons in a shallow network may require only polynomially many in a deep one. This is the mathematical justification for deep learning.

---

### 20.2.3 Activation Functions — Theory and Selection

**Sigmoid:** $$\sigma(z) = \frac{1}{1+e^{-z}}, \quad \sigma'(z) = \sigma(z)(1-\sigma(z)) \in (0, 0.25] \tag{20.6}$$

Problem: $\sigma'(z) \to 0$ for $|z| \gg 0$ — **saturating activation** causing vanishing gradients (Module 11, Eq. 11.27). The gradient in layer $l$ involves $\prod_{k=l}^{L-1}\sigma'(z^{(k)}) \leq (0.25)^{L-l} \to 0$ exponentially.

**Hyperbolic tangent:** $$\tanh(z) = \frac{e^z - e^{-z}}{e^z + e^{-z}}, \quad \tanh'(z) = 1 - \tanh^2(z) \in [0,1] \tag{20.7}$$

Zero-centered (unlike sigmoid), but still saturating.

**Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU):** $$\text{ReLU}(z) = \max(0, z), \quad \frac{\partial}{\partial z}\text{ReLU}(z) = \mathbf{1}[z > 0] \tag{20.8}$$

**Why ReLU works:**

- Non-saturating: gradient is 1 for $z > 0$, never decaying with depth
- Sparse activation: only positive units fire — implicit regularization
- Linear for $z > 0$: composing ReLUs gives piecewise linear functions — an MLP with ReLU is a piecewise linear function of the input

**Problem:** Dead neurons — if $z < 0$ always, gradient is 0 forever (dying ReLU).

**Leaky ReLU:** $$\text{LReLU}(z) = \max(\alpha z, z), \quad \alpha \approx 0.01 \tag{20.9}$$

**ELU (Exponential Linear Unit):** $$\text{ELU}(z) = \begin{cases}z & z > 0 \ \alpha(e^z - 1) & z \leq 0\end{cases} \tag{20.10}$$

Smooth at $z=0$, negative saturation means mean activations are closer to zero (natural gradient benefit).

**GELU (Gaussian Error Linear Unit):** $$\text{GELU}(z) = z,\Phi(z) = z\cdot\frac{1}{2}\left[1 + \text{erf}!\left(\frac{z}{\sqrt{2}}\right)\right] \tag{20.11}$$

where $\Phi$ is the standard Gaussian CDF. The standard activation in Transformers (BERT, GPT). It is a smooth, stochastic regularization: $\text{GELU}(z) \approx \mathbb{E}[z \cdot \mathbf{1}[z > N(0,1)]]$ — the expected value of $z$ when randomly zeroed based on its magnitude. Small values are more likely to be dropped; large values are kept.

**SiLU / Swish:** $$\text{SiLU}(z) = z,\sigma(z) \tag{20.12}$$

Self-gated: the output is the input modulated by its own sigmoid. Non-monotone, smooth, unbounded above, bounded below — empirically matches GELU performance.

---

### 20.2.4 Weight Initialization — Breaking the Symmetry Problem

If all weights are initialized identically, all neurons in a layer compute identical functions — they remain identical forever (symmetry problem). We need random initialization, but the scale matters critically.

**The forward pass variance analysis:**

For a layer with $d_{\text{in}}$ inputs, $W_{ij} \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim}(0, \sigma_W^2)$, input $\mathbf{x}$ with $\text{Var}(x_j) = \sigma_x^2$:

$$\text{Var}(z_i) = d_{\text{in}},\sigma_W^2,\sigma_x^2 \tag{20.13}$$

For signal to propagate without exploding or vanishing, we need $\text{Var}(z_i) = \sigma_x^2$, giving: $$\sigma_W^2 = \frac{1}{d_{\text{in}}} \tag{20.14}$$

This is **Xavier/Glorot initialization** (Glorot & Bengio, 2010). For tanh/sigmoid activations.

**For ReLU activations** — the backward pass analysis (He initialization, He et al., 2015):

ReLU zeros half the units, so the effective variance propagated is halved. To maintain variance in both forward and backward passes: $$\sigma_W^2 = \frac{2}{d_{\text{in}}} \tag{20.15}$$

**Variance preservation proof (forward pass with ReLU):**

If $z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_z^2)$, then $a = \text{ReLU}(z)$ has: $$\mathbb{E}[a] = \frac{\sigma_z}{\sqrt{2\pi}}, \quad \mathbb{E}[a^2] = \frac{\sigma_z^2}{2} \tag{20.16}$$

So $\text{Var}(\text{ReLU}(z)) = \sigma_z^2/2$ — half the input variance. To compensate: $\sigma_W^2 = 2/d_{\text{in}}$. $\blacksquare$

---

### 20.2.5 Batch Normalization

Batch Normalization (Ioffe & Szegedy, 2015) addresses **internal covariate shift** — the change in the distribution of layer inputs during training as parameters in previous layers change.

> **Algorithm 20.1 (Batch Normalization):** For a mini-batch ${\mathbf{z}_i}_{i=1}^B$:
> 
> $$\hat{\mu}_B = \frac{1}{B}\sum_{i=1}^B \mathbf{z}_i \tag{20.17}$$ $$\hat{\sigma}^2_B = \frac{1}{B}\sum_{i=1}^B (\mathbf{z}_i - \hat{\mu}_B)^2 \tag{20.18}$$ $$\hat{\mathbf{z}}_i = \frac{\mathbf{z}_i - \hat{\mu}_B}{\sqrt{\hat{\sigma}^2_B + \varepsilon}} \tag{20.19}$$ $$\text{BN}(\mathbf{z}_i) = \boldsymbol\gamma \odot \hat{\mathbf{z}}_i + \boldsymbol\delta \tag{20.20}$$

Parameters $\boldsymbol\gamma$ (scale) and $\boldsymbol\delta$ (shift) are **learned** — allowing the network to undo the normalization if needed.

**Why BN helps — the statistical mechanics view:**

BN constrains the pre-activation distribution to have mean $\approx 0$ and variance $\approx 1$ at each layer. By Theorem 20.1's proof and the GELU motivation: activations with these statistics operate in the most sensitive (non-saturating) regime. BN also adds noise (batch statistics are stochastic) — a regularization effect equivalent to adding noise of variance $\sigma^2/B$ to each activation.

**Gradient through BN** — the chain rule applied to Eqs. 20.17-20.20 gives:

$$\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\mathbf{z}_i} = \frac{\gamma}{\sqrt{\hat\sigma^2_B+\varepsilon}} \cdot \frac{1}{B}\left[B\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\hat{\mathbf{z}}_i} - \sum_j\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\hat{\mathbf{z}}_j} - \hat{\mathbf{z}}_i\sum_j\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\hat{\mathbf{z}}_j}\hat{\mathbf{z}}_j\right] \tag{20.21}$$

The gradient depends on all other samples in the batch — creating an implicit regularization that decorrelates gradient updates.

---

### 20.2.6 The Convolution Operation

**Motivation:** For a $d \times d$ image with a fully connected layer of $d^2$ outputs, we need $d^4$ weights — for $d=256$: over $4$ billion parameters. Two observations about images motivate a better architecture:

1. **Translation equivariance:** The same feature (an edge) can appear anywhere in an image. A detector for that feature should be the same function regardless of location.
2. **Local connectivity:** Features in natural images are local — the top-left and bottom-right pixels of an image are rarely informative about each other.

**The convolution operation:**

For a 1D input $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n$ and kernel $\mathbf{k} \in \mathbb{R}^m$: $$(x * k)[i] = \sum_{j=0}^{m-1} x[i+j], k[j] \tag{20.22}$$

For a 2D image $X \in \mathbb{R}^{H\times W}$ and kernel $K \in \mathbb{R}^{F\times F}$: $$(X * K)[i,j] = \sum_{p=0}^{F-1}\sum_{q=0}^{F-1} X[i+p,, j+q]\cdot K[p,q] \tag{20.23}$$

**In practice (CNNs use cross-correlation, not convolution):** $$(X \star K)[i,j] = \sum_{p=0}^{F-1}\sum_{q=0}^{F-1} X[i+p,, j+q]\cdot K[p,q] \tag{20.24}$$

The difference (flipping the kernel) is absorbed into learned weights. We use cross-correlation throughout.

**Output dimensions:**

With input $H\times W$, kernel $F\times F$, padding $P$, stride $S$: $$H_{\text{out}} = \left\lfloor\frac{H + 2P - F}{S}\right\rfloor + 1 \tag{20.25}$$

**Multi-channel convolution:**

For input with $C_{\text{in}}$ channels and $C_{\text{out}}$ filters, each filter $K_c \in \mathbb{R}^{F\times F\times C_{\text{in}}}$: $$Y_c[i,j] = \sum_{c'=1}^{C_{\text{in}}}\sum_{p,q}X_{c'}[i+p,j+q]\cdot K_c[p,q,c'] + b_c \tag{20.26}$$

Total parameters: $C_{\text{out}} \times (F^2 \times C_{\text{in}} + 1)$ — independent of image size $H\times W$.

**Weight sharing:** The same kernel is applied at every spatial location — this is the mathematical implementation of translation equivariance.

---

### 20.2.7 Backpropagation Through Convolution

The gradient of the loss with respect to the kernel $K$ and input $X$:

**Gradient w.r.t. kernel** (needed for weight update): $$\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial K[p,q]} = \sum_{i,j}\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial Y[i,j]}\cdot X[i+p, j+q] \tag{20.27}$$

This is a convolution of the input $X$ with the upstream gradient $\delta Y = \partial\mathcal{L}/\partial Y$.

**Gradient w.r.t. input** (needed for backprop to earlier layers): $$\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial X[i,j]} = \sum_{p,q}\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial Y[i-p,j-q]}\cdot K[p,q] \tag{20.28}$$

This is a **full convolution** (with zero-padding) of the upstream gradient $\delta Y$ with the flipped kernel $K[-p,-q]$ — a transposed convolution. This is why the backward pass through a convolutional layer is itself a convolutional operation — elegant and computationally efficient.

---

### 20.2.8 Pooling Operations

Pooling reduces spatial dimensions while preserving the most important features.

**Max Pooling:** $$\text{MaxPool}(X)[i,j] = \max_{p\in[0,F), q\in[0,F)} X[i\cdot S+p,, j\cdot S+q] \tag{20.29}$$

Gradient: passes gradient to the position of the maximum (all others receive 0).

**Average Pooling:** $$\text{AvgPool}(X)[i,j] = \frac{1}{F^2}\sum_{p,q} X[i\cdot S+p,, j\cdot S+q] \tag{20.30}$$

**Global Average Pooling (GAP):** $$\text{GAP}(X) = \frac{1}{HW}\sum_{i,j} X[i,j] \tag{20.31}$$

Reduces the entire $H\times W$ feature map to a single number per channel. Used instead of fully-connected layers in modern architectures — dramatically reduces parameter count and prevents overfitting.

---

### 20.2.9 Residual Connections — Solving the Degradation Problem

Deep networks (>20 layers) with standard architectures suffer **degradation** — training error _increases_ with depth despite more capacity. This is not overfitting — it happens on training data.

**He et al. (2015)** identified the cause: optimization becomes harder, not the representational capacity. The solution: **residual (skip) connections**.

> **Definition 20.2 (Residual Block):** $$\mathbf{y} = \mathcal{F}(\mathbf{x}; \theta) + \mathbf{x} \tag{20.32}$$
> 
> where $\mathcal{F}$ is a stack of layers (typically: Conv → BN → ReLU → Conv → BN) and $\mathbf{x}$ is the **skip connection**.

**Why residual connections work — the gradient highway:**

The gradient through a residual block: $$\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\mathbf{x}} = \frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\mathbf{y}}\cdot\left(\frac{\partial\mathcal{F}}{\partial\mathbf{x}} + \mathbf{I}\right) \tag{20.33}$$

The identity term $\mathbf{I}$ creates a **gradient highway** — the gradient flows directly from $\mathbf{y}$ to $\mathbf{x}$ without passing through any transformation. Even if $\partial\mathcal{F}/\partial\mathbf{x} \to 0$ (vanishing gradient in the residual branch), the gradient is still $\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial\mathbf{y}$ — it cannot vanish due to the skip connection.

**What the residual block learns:**

If the identity mapping is optimal (the layers add no useful information), the network can easily set $\mathcal{F} \to 0$ — learning identity is easier than learning a complex function from scratch. The residual block reformulates the learning problem: instead of learning $H(\mathbf{x})$ directly, it learns the **residual** $\mathcal{F}(\mathbf{x}) = H(\mathbf{x}) - \mathbf{x}$.

---

### 20.2.10 The Complete Modern CNN Architecture

**AlexNet architecture evolution → ResNet design principles:**

A typical ResNet block: $$\mathbf{z}^{(1)} = \text{BN}(\text{Conv}_{3\times3}(\mathbf{x})) \to \text{ReLU} \to \mathbf{z}^{(2)} = \text{BN}(\text{Conv}_{3\times3}(\mathbf{z}^{(1)})) \tag{20.34}$$ $$\mathbf{y} = \text{ReLU}(\mathbf{z}^{(2)} + \mathbf{x}) \tag{20.35}$$

**The bottleneck block** (for deeper ResNets — ResNet-50/101/152):

$$1\times1,\text{Conv},(C \to C/4) \to 3\times3,\text{Conv},(C/4 \to C/4) \to 1\times1,\text{Conv},(C/4 \to C) \tag{20.36}$$

The $1\times1$ convolutions project to lower dimensionality (bottleneck) before the expensive $3\times3$ convolution — reducing computation by $\approx 9\times$ vs a single $3\times3$ with full channels.

**Depthwise Separable Convolution** (MobileNet, EfficientNet):

Standard convolution: $F^2 \times C_{\text{in}} \times C_{\text{out}}$ parameters.

Depthwise separable convolution: Apply one $F\times F$ filter per input channel (depthwise), then combine channels with $1\times1$ convolutions (pointwise):

Parameters: $F^2 \times C_{\text{in}} + C_{\text{in}} \times C_{\text{out}}$ — reduced by factor $F^2/(1 + F^2/C_{\text{out}})$. For $F=3$, $C_{\text{out}}=64$: $\approx 9\times$ reduction.

---

## 20.3 Numerical Examples

### Example 20.1: Convolution Output Dimensions

**Input:** $224\times224\times3$ (ImageNet standard). **Kernel:** $7\times7$, $64$ filters. **Stride:** 2. **Padding:** 3.

Output spatial size (Eq. 20.25): $$H_{\text{out}} = \left\lfloor\frac{224 + 2(3) - 7}{2}\right\rfloor + 1 = \lfloor 111.5 \rfloor + 1 = 112$$

Output shape: $112\times112\times64$.

Parameters: $64 \times (7^2 \times 3 + 1) = 64 \times 148 = 9{,}472$ — vs $224^2 \times 3 \times 112^2 \times 64 \approx 269$ billion for a fully connected layer.

---

### Example 20.2: He Initialization Variance Propagation

**Network:** 10 ReLU layers, each with $d=512$ units. With wrong initialization $\sigma_W^2 = 1/d$:

Layer 1: $\text{Var}(z^{(1)}) = d \cdot (1/d) \cdot \text{Var}(x) = 1$. After ReLU: $\text{Var}(a^{(1)}) = 0.5$.

Layer 2: $\text{Var}(z^{(2)}) = d \cdot (1/d) \cdot 0.5 = 0.5$. After ReLU: $0.25$.

After 10 layers: $\text{Var}(a^{(10)}) \approx (0.5)^{10} = 9.77\times10^{-4}$ — signal has collapsed.

With He initialization $\sigma_W^2 = 2/d$:

Layer 1: $\text{Var}(z^{(1)}) = d \cdot (2/d) \cdot 1 = 2$. After ReLU: $\text{Var}(a^{(1)}) = 1$.

Layer 2: $\text{Var}(z^{(2)}) = d \cdot (2/d) \cdot 1 = 2$. After ReLU: $1$.

After 10 layers: $\text{Var}(a^{(10)}) = 1$ — signal preserved exactly.

---

### Example 20.3: Residual Block — Learning Identity

**Scenario:** Optimal mapping is $H(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x}$ (identity).

Standard block: must learn $\mathcal{H}(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x}$ — all weights must conspire to produce the input unchanged. Gradient signals must reach every weight precisely.

Residual block: must learn $\mathcal{F}(\mathbf{x}) = 0$ — weights pushed to zero by L2 regularization naturally. The initialization $\mathbf{W} \approx 0$ already gives $\mathcal{F} \approx 0$. Zero is the natural starting point.

This is why residual networks train more easily at greater depth — the trivial optimal solution (no transformation needed) requires minimal effort to learn.

---

## 20.4 Implementation

```python
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.gridspec as gridspec
from typing import Optional, List, Tuple, Dict, Callable
from dataclasses import dataclass, field

# =============================================================================
# MODULE 20: MLP & CNN — Deep Learning Foundations
# =============================================================================

# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# PART A: Activation Functions Library
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------

class Activations:
    """
    Complete activation function library with forward and backward passes.
    Implements Eqs. 20.6-20.12.
    """

    @staticmethod
    def sigmoid(z: np.ndarray, backward: bool = False) -> np.ndarray:
        """Eq. 20.6. σ(z) = 1/(1+e^{-z}). σ'(z) = σ(z)(1-σ(z))."""
        s = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-np.clip(z, -500, 500)))
        return s * (1 - s) if backward else s

    @staticmethod
    def tanh(z: np.ndarray, backward: bool = False) -> np.ndarray:
        """Eq. 20.7. tanh'(z) = 1 - tanh²(z)."""
        t = np.tanh(z)
        return 1 - t**2 if backward else t

    @staticmethod
    def relu(z: np.ndarray, backward: bool = False) -> np.ndarray:
        """Eq. 20.8. max(0,z). Derivative: 1[z>0]."""
        return (z > 0).astype(float) if backward else np.maximum(0, z)

    @staticmethod
    def leaky_relu(z: np.ndarray, alpha: float = 0.01,
                    backward: bool = False) -> np.ndarray:
        """Eq. 20.9. max(αz, z)."""
        if backward:
            return np.where(z > 0, 1.0, alpha)
        return np.where(z > 0, z, alpha * z)

    @staticmethod
    def elu(z: np.ndarray, alpha: float = 1.0,
             backward: bool = False) -> np.ndarray:
        """Eq. 20.10. ELU activation."""
        if backward:
            return np.where(z > 0, 1.0, alpha * np.exp(np.minimum(z, 0)))
        return np.where(z > 0, z, alpha * (np.exp(np.minimum(z, 0)) - 1))

    @staticmethod
    def gelu(z: np.ndarray, backward: bool = False) -> np.ndarray:
        """
        Eq. 20.11. GELU: z * Φ(z).
        Approximation: z * σ(1.702z) for numerical stability.
        """
        from scipy.special import erf
        phi  = 0.5 * (1 + erf(z / np.sqrt(2)))
        if backward:
            dphi = np.exp(-0.5*z**2) / np.sqrt(2*np.pi)
            return phi + z * dphi
        return z * phi

    @staticmethod
    def silu(z: np.ndarray, backward: bool = False) -> np.ndarray:
        """Eq. 20.12. SiLU/Swish: z * σ(z)."""
        s = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-np.clip(z, -500, 500)))
        if backward:
            return s + z * s * (1 - s)
        return z * s

    @classmethod
    def plot_all(cls):
        """Visualize all activation functions and their derivatives."""
        z    = np.linspace(-4, 4, 300)
        acts = [
            ('Sigmoid',    lambda z: cls.sigmoid(z),    lambda z: cls.sigmoid(z, True),    '#1a6faf'),
            ('Tanh',       lambda z: cls.tanh(z),        lambda z: cls.tanh(z, True),        '#e84040'),
            ('ReLU',       lambda z: cls.relu(z),        lambda z: cls.relu(z, True),        '#2ca02c'),
            ('Leaky ReLU', lambda z: cls.leaky_relu(z),  lambda z: cls.leaky_relu(z, True),  '#9467bd'),
            ('ELU',        lambda z: cls.elu(z),          lambda z: cls.elu(z, True),          '#8c564b'),
            ('GELU',       lambda z: cls.gelu(z),         lambda z: cls.gelu(z, True),         '#e377c2'),
            ('SiLU',       lambda z: cls.silu(z),         lambda z: cls.silu(z, True),         '#ff7f0e'),
        ]

        fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 5))

        for name, fn, dfn, col in acts:
            axes[0].plot(z, fn(z), lw=2, color=col, label=name)
            axes[1].plot(z, dfn(z), lw=2, color=col, label=name)

        for ax, title in zip(axes, ["Activation Functions", "Derivatives"]):
            ax.axhline(0, color='black', lw=0.8, alpha=0.5)
            ax.axvline(0, color='black', lw=0.8, alpha=0.5)
            ax.set_xlabel("z", fontsize=12); ax.set_ylabel("σ(z)", fontsize=12)
            ax.set_title(title, fontsize=12, fontweight='bold')
            ax.legend(fontsize=9, ncol=2); ax.grid(alpha=0.3)
            ax.set_xlim(-4, 4); ax.set_ylim(-1.5, 3)

        plt.suptitle("Activation Functions & Derivatives (Eqs. 20.6-20.12)",
                     fontsize=13, fontweight='bold', y=1.02)
        plt.tight_layout()
        plt.savefig("module20_activations.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches='tight')
        plt.show()


# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# PART B: MLP with Full Backpropagation
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------

class Layer:
    """Single fully connected layer with forward/backward pass."""

    def __init__(self, d_in: int, d_out: int, activation: str = 'relu',
                  init: str = 'he'):
        self.activation = activation

        # Weight initialization (Eqs. 20.14-20.15)
        if init == 'he':
            std = np.sqrt(2.0 / d_in)    # He initialization, Eq. 20.15
        elif init == 'xavier':
            std = np.sqrt(1.0 / d_in)    # Xavier initialization, Eq. 20.14
        else:
            std = 0.01

        self.W = np.random.randn(d_out, d_in) * std
        self.b = np.zeros(d_out)

        # Cache for backprop
        self.cache = {}

    def forward(self, x: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
        """Forward pass: z = Wx + b, a = σ(z). Eqs. 20.2-20.3."""
        z = x @ self.W.T + self.b           # (batch, d_out)
        a = self._activate(z)
        self.cache = {'x': x, 'z': z, 'a': a}
        return a

    def backward(self, da: np.ndarray, lr: float = 0.001) -> np.ndarray:
        """
        Backward pass (chain rule).
        da: gradient of loss w.r.t. output a.
        Returns gradient w.r.t. input x.
        """
        x   = self.cache['x']
        z   = self.cache['z']
        dz  = da * self._activate_grad(z)   # element-wise chain rule
        # Gradients w.r.t. weights and bias (Module 11, Eqs. 11.25-11.26)
        dW  = dz.T @ x / len(x)
        db  = dz.mean(axis=0)
        dx  = dz @ self.W                   # gradient w.r.t. input (Eq. 11.24)
        # Update
        self.W -= lr * dW
        self.b -= lr * db
        return dx

    def _activate(self, z):
        acts = {'relu': Activations.relu, 'sigmoid': Activations.sigmoid,
                'tanh': Activations.tanh, 'gelu': Activations.gelu,
                'silu': Activations.silu, 'linear': lambda z, **kw: z}
        return acts[self.activation](z)

    def _activate_grad(self, z):
        acts = {'relu': lambda z: Activations.relu(z, True),
                'sigmoid': lambda z: Activations.sigmoid(z, True),
                'tanh': lambda z: Activations.tanh(z, True),
                'gelu': lambda z: Activations.gelu(z, True),
                'silu': lambda z: Activations.silu(z, True),
                'linear': lambda z: np.ones_like(z)}
        return acts[self.activation](z)


class BatchNorm:
    """
    Batch Normalization layer. Algorithm 20.1.
    Implements Eqs. 20.17-20.21.
    """

    def __init__(self, d: int, eps: float = 1e-5, momentum: float = 0.9):
        self.gamma   = np.ones(d)    # learnable scale
        self.delta   = np.zeros(d)   # learnable shift
        self.eps     = eps
        self.mom     = momentum
        # Running stats for inference
        self.run_mean = np.zeros(d)
        self.run_var  = np.ones(d)
        self.cache    = {}

    def forward(self, z: np.ndarray, training: bool = True) -> np.ndarray:
        """Forward pass. Eqs. 20.17-20.20."""
        if training:
            mu    = z.mean(axis=0)         # Eq. 20.17
            var   = z.var(axis=0)          # Eq. 20.18
            z_hat = (z - mu) / np.sqrt(var + self.eps)   # Eq. 20.19
            self.run_mean = self.mom*self.run_mean + (1-self.mom)*mu
            self.run_var  = self.mom*self.run_var  + (1-self.mom)*var
            self.cache    = {'z': z, 'z_hat': z_hat, 'mu': mu, 'var': var}
        else:
            z_hat = (z - self.run_mean) / np.sqrt(self.run_var + self.eps)

        return self.gamma * z_hat + self.delta   # Eq. 20.20

    def backward(self, d_out: np.ndarray, lr: float = 0.001) -> np.ndarray:
        """Backward pass. Eq. 20.21."""
        z_hat = self.cache['z_hat']
        var   = self.cache['var']
        B     = d_out.shape[0]

        d_gamma = (d_out * z_hat).sum(axis=0)
        d_delta = d_out.sum(axis=0)

        d_z_hat = d_out * self.gamma
        d_var   = np.sum(d_z_hat * (self.cache['z'] - self.cache['mu']) *
                          -0.5 * (var + self.eps)**(-1.5), axis=0)
        d_mu    = (np.sum(d_z_hat * -(var + self.eps)**(-0.5), axis=0) +
                   d_var * np.mean(-2*(self.cache['z'] - self.cache['mu']), axis=0))

        d_z = (d_z_hat / np.sqrt(var + self.eps) +
               d_var * 2*(self.cache['z']-self.cache['mu'])/B + d_mu/B)

        self.gamma -= lr * d_gamma
        self.delta -= lr * d_delta
        return d_z


class MLP:
    """
    Multi-Layer Perceptron with optional Batch Normalization.
    Implements Eqs. 20.1-20.4 with full backpropagation (Module 11).
    """

    def __init__(self, layer_sizes: List[int],
                  activations: List[str],
                  use_batch_norm: bool = False,
                  init: str = 'he',
                  seed: int = 42):
        np.random.seed(seed)
        assert len(activations) == len(layer_sizes) - 1

        self.layers     = []
        self.bn_layers  = [] if use_batch_norm else None
        self.use_bn     = use_batch_norm

        for l in range(len(layer_sizes)-1):
            self.layers.append(Layer(layer_sizes[l], layer_sizes[l+1],
                                      activations[l], init=init))
            if use_batch_norm and l < len(layer_sizes)-2:
                self.bn_layers.append(BatchNorm(layer_sizes[l+1]))

    def forward(self, x: np.ndarray, training: bool = True) -> np.ndarray:
        """Full forward pass. Eq. 20.1."""
        a = x
        for l, layer in enumerate(self.layers):
            a = layer.forward(a)
            if self.use_bn and self.bn_layers and l < len(self.bn_layers):
                a = self.bn_layers[l].forward(a, training)
        return a

    def backward(self, loss_grad: np.ndarray, lr: float = 0.001):
        """Full backward pass (chain rule through all layers)."""
        grad = loss_grad
        bn_idx = len(self.bn_layers)-1 if self.use_bn and self.bn_layers else -1

        for l in range(len(self.layers)-1, -1, -1):
            if self.use_bn and self.bn_layers and l < len(self.bn_layers):
                grad = self.bn_layers[l].backward(grad, lr)
            grad = self.layers[l].backward(grad, lr)

    def fit(self, X: np.ndarray, y: np.ndarray,
             X_val: np.ndarray, y_val: np.ndarray,
             n_epochs: int = 100, lr: float = 0.001,
             batch_size: int = 32, task: str = 'classification',
             seed: int = 42) -> Dict:
        """Mini-batch training loop with MSE or cross-entropy loss."""
        rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
        n   = len(X)
        train_losses, val_losses, val_accs = [], [], []

        for epoch in range(n_epochs):
            perm = rng.permutation(n)
            epoch_loss = 0.0

            for start in range(0, n, batch_size):
                idx   = perm[start:start+batch_size]
                Xb, yb = X[idx], y[idx]

                # Forward
                logits = self.forward(Xb, training=True)

                # Loss and gradient
                if task == 'regression':
                    loss  = np.mean((logits.ravel() - yb)**2)
                    dL    = 2*(logits.ravel() - yb).reshape(-1,1) / len(yb)
                else:  # classification — cross-entropy
                    # Softmax + cross-entropy combined
                    logits_s = logits - logits.max(axis=1, keepdims=True)
                    exp_l    = np.exp(logits_s)
                    probs    = exp_l / exp_l.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)
                    # One-hot labels
                    K  = logits.shape[1]
                    oh = np.eye(K)[yb.astype(int)]
                    loss = -np.mean(np.sum(oh * np.log(probs+1e-12), axis=1))
                    dL   = (probs - oh) / len(yb)

                epoch_loss += loss

                # Backward
                self.backward(dL, lr)

            train_losses.append(epoch_loss / (n // batch_size))

            # Validation
            val_logits = self.forward(X_val, training=False)
            if task == 'regression':
                val_losses.append(float(np.mean((val_logits.ravel()-y_val)**2)))
                val_accs.append(0.0)
            else:
                val_s = val_logits - val_logits.max(axis=1, keepdims=True)
                val_p = np.exp(val_s) / np.exp(val_s).sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)
                val_losses.append(-np.mean(np.sum(np.eye(val_logits.shape[1])[y_val.astype(int)]*np.log(val_p+1e-12), axis=1)))
                val_accs.append(float(np.mean(np.argmax(val_p, axis=1)==y_val.astype(int))))

        return {'train_loss': train_losses, 'val_loss': val_losses, 'val_acc': val_accs}


# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# PART C: Convolutional Layer (from scratch)
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------

class Conv2D:
    """
    2D Convolutional layer. Implements Eqs. 20.23-20.28.
    Supports forward pass, backward pass (gradient computation),
    and weight updates.
    """

    def __init__(self, C_in: int, C_out: int, kernel_size: int = 3,
                  stride: int = 1, padding: int = 1,
                  init: str = 'he', seed: int = 42):
        np.random.seed(seed)
        self.C_in   = C_in
        self.C_out  = C_out
        self.F      = kernel_size
        self.stride = stride
        self.pad    = padding

        # He initialization for conv filters (Eq. 20.15)
        fan_in = C_in * kernel_size**2
        std    = np.sqrt(2.0 / fan_in) if init == 'he' else np.sqrt(1.0/fan_in)
        self.W = np.random.randn(C_out, C_in, kernel_size, kernel_size) * std
        self.b = np.zeros(C_out)
        self.cache = {}

    def _pad(self, X: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
        """Zero-pad input: (N, C, H, W) → (N, C, H+2P, W+2P)."""
        if self.pad == 0:
            return X
        return np.pad(X, ((0,0),(0,0),(self.pad,self.pad),(self.pad,self.pad)),
                      mode='constant')

    def forward(self, X: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
        """
        Forward pass. Eq. 20.26.
        X: (N, C_in, H, W) → Y: (N, C_out, H_out, W_out)
        """
        N, C, H, W = X.shape
        F, S, P     = self.F, self.stride, self.pad
        H_out = (H + 2*P - F) // S + 1   # Eq. 20.25
        W_out = (W + 2*P - F) // S + 1

        X_pad = self._pad(X)
        Y     = np.zeros((N, self.C_out, H_out, W_out))

        # Cross-correlation (Eq. 20.24)
        for i in range(H_out):
            for j in range(W_out):
                X_slice = X_pad[:, :, i*S:i*S+F, j*S:j*S+F]  # (N, C_in, F, F)
                for c in range(self.C_out):
                    Y[:, c, i, j] = (X_slice * self.W[c]).sum(axis=(1,2,3)) + self.b[c]

        self.cache = {'X': X, 'X_pad': X_pad}
        return Y

    def backward(self, dY: np.ndarray, lr: float = 0.001) -> np.ndarray:
        """
        Backward pass. Eqs. 20.27-20.28.
        dY: (N, C_out, H_out, W_out)
        Returns dX: (N, C_in, H, W)
        """
        X, X_pad = self.cache['X'], self.cache['X_pad']
        N, C, H, W = X.shape
        _, _, H_out, W_out = dY.shape
        F, S = self.F, self.stride

        dX_pad = np.zeros_like(X_pad)
        dW     = np.zeros_like(self.W)
        db     = np.zeros_like(self.b)

        for i in range(H_out):
            for j in range(W_out):
                X_slice = X_pad[:, :, i*S:i*S+F, j*S:j*S+F]   # (N, C_in, F, F)
                for c in range(self.C_out):
                    # Gradient w.r.t. kernel (Eq. 20.27)
                    dW[c] += (X_slice * dY[:, c, i, j][:, None, None, None]).sum(axis=0)
                    # Gradient w.r.t. padded input (Eq. 20.28)
                    dX_pad[:, :, i*S:i*S+F, j*S:j*S+F] += (
                        self.W[c][None] * dY[:, c, i, j][:, None, None, None])
                # Gradient w.r.t. bias
                db += dY[:, :, i, j].sum(axis=0)

        # Update weights
        dW /= N
        db /= N
        self.W -= lr * dW
        self.b -= lr * db

        # Strip padding from input gradient
        if self.pad > 0:
            dX = dX_pad[:, :, self.pad:-self.pad, self.pad:-self.pad]
        else:
            dX = dX_pad
        return dX


class MaxPool2D:
    """Max Pooling. Eq. 20.29."""

    def __init__(self, kernel_size: int = 2, stride: int = 2):
        self.F = kernel_size
        self.S = stride
        self.cache = {}

    def forward(self, X: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
        N, C, H, W = X.shape
        H_out = (H - self.F) // self.S + 1
        W_out = (W - self.F) // self.S + 1
        Y = np.zeros((N, C, H_out, W_out))
        mask = np.zeros_like(X, dtype=bool)

        for i in range(H_out):
            for j in range(W_out):
                patch = X[:, :, i*self.S:i*self.S+self.F, j*self.S:j*self.S+self.F]
                Y[:, :, i, j] = patch.max(axis=(2,3))
                # Track max locations for backward pass
                max_val = Y[:, :, i, j][:, :, None, None]
                m = (patch == max_val)
                mask[:, :, i*self.S:i*self.S+self.F, j*self.S:j*self.S+self.F] |= m

        self.cache = {'X': X, 'mask': mask, 'H_out': H_out, 'W_out': W_out}
        return Y

    def backward(self, dY: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
        """Gradient flows to max position only."""
        X    = self.cache['X']
        mask = self.cache['mask']
        dX   = np.zeros_like(X)

        for i in range(self.cache['H_out']):
            for j in range(self.cache['W_out']):
                dX[:, :, i*self.S:i*self.S+self.F, j*self.S:j*self.S+self.F] += (
                    mask[:, :, i*self.S:i*self.S+self.F, j*self.S:j*self.S+self.F] *
                    dY[:, :, i, j][:, :, None, None])
        return dX

# PART D: Comprehensive Visualization
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------

    ax.legend(fontsize=8); ax.grid(alpha=0.3, which='both')

    # ---- Panel 4: Depth-width comparison ----

    # ---- Row 3: Residual connection benefit ----
    ax = fig.add_subplot(gs[2, :2])

    def make_deep_mlp(use_residual: bool, n_layers: int = 6, seed: int = 42):
        """Simplified deep network with/without residual connections."""
        np.random.seed(seed)
        d     = 32
        layer_losses = []
        x     = rng.normal(0, 1, (64, d))
        y_tgt = rng.normal(0, 1, (64, 1))

        # Track gradient norm per layer
        Ws = [np.random.randn(d, d) * np.sqrt(2/d) for _ in range(n_layers)]
        bs = [np.zeros(d) for _ in range(n_layers)]
        Wo = np.random.randn(1, d) * np.sqrt(2/d)

        grad_norms = []
        for l in range(n_layers):
            z = x @ Ws[l].T + bs[l]
            x_new = np.maximum(0, z)
            if use_residual and x.shape == x_new.shape:
                x_new = x_new + x   # Eq. 20.32
            x = x_new

        out   = x @ Wo.T
        loss  = np.mean((out - y_tgt)**2)

        # Backprop (simplified gradient norm tracking)
        dout  = 2*(out - y_tgt)/len(y_tgt)
        dL_dy = dout @ Wo
        for l in range(n_layers-1, -1, -1):
            grad_norms.append(np.linalg.norm(dL_dy))
            dL_dy = dL_dy * (x > 0)
            if use_residual:
                dL_dy = dL_dy + dL_dy   # skip connection adds gradient

        return list(reversed(grad_norms)), loss

    for use_res, col, label in [(False, '#e84040', 'Plain (no residual)'),
                                  (True,  '#1a6faf', 'ResNet (with residual)')]:
        gnorms, loss = make_deep_mlp(use_res, n_layers=12)
        ax.semilogy(gnorms, 'o-', color=col, lw=2, ms=5, label=f'{label} (loss={loss:.3f})')

    ax.set_xlabel("Layer (from output ← input)")
    ax.set_ylabel("Gradient norm (log scale)")
    ax.set_title("Residual Connections: Gradient Highway (Eq. 20.33)\n"
                 "Skip connections prevent gradient vanishing across layers",
                 fontsize=11, fontweight='bold')
    ax.legend(fontsize=10); ax.grid(alpha=0.3, which='both')

    # ---- ResNet architecture diagram ----
    ax = fig.add_subplot(gs[2, 2:])
    ax.set_xlim(0, 10); ax.set_ylim(0, 6); ax.axis('off')
    ax.set_title("ResNet Block (Eq. 20.34-20.35)\nF(x) + x: learn residual, not identity",
                 fontsize=11, fontweight='bold')

    # Draw residual block
    boxes = [(1,4.5,'Input x'),(3,4.5,'Conv 3×3'),(5,4.5,'BN+ReLU'),
             (7,4.5,'Conv 3×3'),(7,2.5,'BN'),(4,0.8,'Add → ReLU → Output')]
    colors_box = ['#888','#1a6faf','#1a6faf','#1a6faf','#1a6faf','#2ca02c']
    for (x,y,txt), col in zip(boxes, colors_box):

                fontweight='bold', color='white')

    # Arrows (main path)

                                ((6.1,4.5),(5.9,4.5)), ((8.1,4.5),(7.9,4.5)),
                                ((7,4.1),(7,2.9)), ((5.9,2.5),(5.1,2.5))]:
        pass

    # Curved skip connection
    from matplotlib.patches import FancyArrowPatch
    arrow = FancyArrowPatch((1,4.1),(4,1.2), connectionstyle='arc3,rad=-0.4',
                             arrowstyle='->', color='#e84040', lw=2.5,
                             mutation_scale=12)
    ax.add_patch(arrow)
    ax.text(1.5, 2.5, 'Skip\nconnection\nx → F(x)+x', color='#e84040',
            fontsize=8, fontweight='bold', ha='left')

    plt.suptitle("Module 20: MLP & CNN — Deep Learning Foundations",
                 fontsize=14, fontweight='bold', y=1.01)
    plt.savefig("module20_deep_learning.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches='tight')
    plt.show()
```

|Concept|Key Equation|ML Impact|

|Universal approximation|Theorem 20.1: single layer, enough units|Theoretical guarantee for MLPs|
|Depth separation|Theorem 20.2: exponential expressivity gain|Why depth > width|
|ReLU advantage|$\sigma'(z) = \mathbf{1}[z>0]$ — non-saturating|Solves vanishing gradient|
|GELU/SiLU|$z\Phi(z)$, $z\sigma(z)$ — smooth, self-gated|Default in Transformers|
|He initialization|$\sigma_W^2 = 2/d_{\text{in}}$|Preserves variance through ReLU layers|
|Batch normalization|Normalize per batch + learned scale/shift|Stabilizes training, accelerates convergence|
|Convolution|$(X\star K)[i,j] = \sum_{p,q}X[i+p,j+q]K[p,q]$|Translation equivariance, $O(F^2)$ params|
|Conv backward|$\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial K$ = conv of input with upstream gradient|Efficient gradient computation|
|Residual connection|$\mathbf{y} = \mathcal{F}(\mathbf{x}) + \mathbf{x}$|Gradient highway — enables 100+ layer networks|
|Bottleneck block|$1\times1 \to 3\times3 \to 1\times1$|$9\times$ parameter reduction|

$$f_\theta(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{W}^{(L)}\sigma(\cdots\sigma(\mathbf{W}^{(1)}\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{b}^{(1)})\cdots)+\mathbf{b}^{(L)} \tag{MLP}$$ $$\text{ReLU}(z)=\max(0,z),\quad \text{GELU}(z)=z\Phi(z),\quad\text{SiLU}(z)=z\sigma(z) \tag{Activations}$$ $$\sigma_W^2 = 2/d_{\text{in}} \tag{He initialization}$$ $$\hat{\mathbf{z}} = (\mathbf{z}-\hat\mu)/\sqrt{\hat\sigma^2+\varepsilon},\quad \text{BN}(\mathbf{z}) = \gamma\hat{\mathbf{z}}+\delta \tag{Batch Norm}$$ $$(X\star K)[i,j] = \sum_{p,q}X[i+p,j+q]K[p,q] \tag{Convolution}$$ $$H_{\text{out}} = \lfloor(H+2P-F)/S\rfloor + 1 \tag{Output dimensions}$$ $$\mathbf{y} = \mathcal{F}(\mathbf{x};\theta) + \mathbf{x},\quad \partial\mathcal{L}/\partial\mathbf{x} = (\partial\mathcal{F}/\partial\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{I})\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial\mathbf{y} \tag{Residual block}$$
